We present a controlled study on CIFAR-10 using a DDPM U-Net with ranks {2,4,8,16,32}, fixed optimization settings, and a reproducible local-folder pytorch-fid protocol. We report FID, trainable parameters, runtime, and GPU memory, then validate trends with extended-budget DDPM runs (20 epochs; ranks 4/8/16) and a Tiny DiT backbone (10 epochs; ranks 4/8/16). Results show moderate ranks are most efficient: rank 4 achieves the best DDPM FID (124.1380), rank 8 is close (124.2136), and higher ranks provide limited gains despite larger adaptation cost. These findings support small-to-moderate ranks as practical defaults under fixed training budgets.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates optimal LoRA rank selection for diffusion model fine-tuning, finding that small-to-moderate ranks (4-8) offer the best quality-compute trade-off, with rank 4 achieving the best FID score of 124.1380 on CIFAR-10.
AI.motivation: The researchers aimed to address the practical challenge of balancing quality and computational cost when selecting LoRA ranks for diffusion model fine-tuning, as there was no clear guidance on optimal rank selection.
AI.method: The authors conducted a controlled study on CIFAR-10 using a DDPM U-Net with ranks {2,4,8,16,32}, fixed optimization settings, and a reproducible local-folder pytorch-fid protocol. They validated trends with extended-budget DDPM runs (20 epochs; ranks 4/8/16) and a Tiny DiT backbone (10 epochs; ranks 4/8/16).
AI.result: Rank 4 achieved the best DDPM FID (124.1380), rank 8 was close (124.2136), and higher ranks provided limited gains despite larger adaptation cost. Moderate ranks are most efficient under fixed training budgets.
AI.conclusion: Small-to-moderate LoRA ranks (4-8) should be used as practical defaults for diffusion fine-tuning under fixed training budgets, as higher ranks offer diminishing returns relative to their increased computational cost.

title: Generative AI for trustworthy systems - Towards a health check model
summary: The adoption of generative AI in software-intensive systems is proceeding rapidly, but current analytical instruments - principally unidimensional maturity models - compress important configurational variation into a single progressive axis. Drawing on an inductive interview study of eighteen senior practitioners across telecommunications, automotive, defence, aviation, banking, energy, government, and enterprise software services, this paper presents the Trustworthy Autonomy Health Check Model: a structured, multidimensional instrument for characterizing how organizations establish trust in GenAI-assisted software engineering. The model organizes eight empirically grounded dimensions into a system layer (Scope of Agent Authority, Assurance Mechanisms, Data Trustworthiness, Architectural Containment, Traceability & Comprehensibility) and an organizational layer (Governance, Human Oversight Posture, Workforce Capability Sustainability), each on a five-level ordinal scale. A cross-cutting overlay of four trust paradigms - operational, engineering, statistical, and containment-based - captures how trust is established, complementing the dimensions capturing what must be trustworthy. The model is diagnostic rather than prescriptive: it supports cross-organizational comparison, surfaces configurational trade-offs, and locates an organization in a shared space without imposing a single progression path. Higher levels are not inherently better; the goal is alignment across dimensions appropriate to the organization's domain and chosen trust paradigm. This is formalized as the alignment hypothesis: effective trustworthiness is constrained by the fit between the scope of agent authority and the dimensions enabling it, with misalignment producing pathological risk or unnecessary friction. We discuss how practitioners can apply the model and outline directions for empirical validation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the Trustworthy Autonomy Health Check Model, a multidimensional instrument for characterizing how organizations establish trust in GenAI-assisted software engineering. The model comprises eight empirically grounded dimensions organized into system and organizational layers, each on a five-level ordinal scale, with a cross-cutting overlay of four trust paradigms. It is diagnostic rather than prescriptive, supporting cross-organizational comparison without imposing a single progression path.
AI.motivation: Current analytical instruments for evaluating generative AI adoption in software-intensive systems are predominantly unidimensional maturity models, which compress important configurational variation into a single progressive axis. This compression fails to capture the nuanced, multidimensional nature of trust establishment in AI-assisted software engineering.
AI.method: Inductive interview study conducted with eighteen senior practitioners across eight industries: telecommunications, automotive, defence, aviation, banking, energy, government, and enterprise software services.
AI.result: The Trustworthy Autonomy Health Check Model organizes eight empirically grounded dimensions into: (1) System layer - Scope of Agent Authority, Assurance Mechanisms, Data Trustworthiness, Architectural Containment, Traceability & Comprehensibility; (2) Organizational layer - Governance, Human Oversight Posture, Workforce Capability Sustainability. Each dimension uses a five-level ordinal scale. A cross-cutting overlay of four trust paradigms (operational, engineering, statistical, and containment-based) captures how trust is established. The alignment hypothesis is proposed: effective trustworthiness is constrained by the fit between the scope of agent authority and the dimensions enabling it.
AI.conclusion: The model supports cross-organizational comparison, surfaces configurational trade-offs, and locates organizations in a shared space without imposing a single progression path. Higher levels are not inherently better; the goal is alignment across dimensions appropriate to the organization's domain and chosen trust paradigm. Directions for empirical validation are outlined.

title: Meta-Learning for Data-Efficient Plant Growth Estimation via Vision Transformers and Fuzzy Clustering
summary: Accurate plant growth estimation is essential for greenhouse monitoring, yet obtaining labeled data remains costly and time-consuming. To address this, we propose a few-shot regression framework that combines Vision Transformer (ViT) feature embeddings, clustering-based task construction, and gradient-based meta-learning, and show that task construction in embedding space is a primary driver of performance. The approach leverages an unlabeled image pool to organize data into structured tasks using fuzzy c-means clustering, enabling efficient learning from a small number of labeled samples. We systematically evaluate meta-learning methods and show that second-order methods (e.g., Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning variants such as MAML++) outperform classical baselines in the few-shot regime. Furthermore, intra-cluster support selection has a limited and dataset-dependent impact. Experiments on two plant datasets show that structured task design combined with meta-learning enables reliable plant growth estimation under severe label scarcity.

AI.tldr: A few-shot regression framework combining Vision Transformer (ViT) feature embeddings, fuzzy c-means clustering for task construction, and gradient-based meta-learning (MAML++) for plant growth estimation under severe label scarcity.
AI.motivation: Accurate plant growth estimation is essential for greenhouse monitoring, but obtaining labeled data remains costly and time-consuming, necessitating approaches that can learn effectively from very few labeled samples.
AI.method: The framework uses ViT for feature extraction, organizes unlabeled images into structured tasks via fuzzy c-means clustering in embedding space, and applies gradient-based meta-learning (specifically second-order MAML variants) for few-shot regression.
AI.result: Second-order meta-learning methods (MAML++) outperform classical baselines in the few-shot regime. Task construction in embedding space is identified as a primary driver of performance, while intra-cluster support selection shows limited and dataset-dependent impact.
AI.conclusion: Structured task design combined with meta-learning enables reliable plant growth estimation under severe label scarcity, making it practical for greenhouse monitoring applications.

title: Learning Interaction between Image and Layout Priors for Joint Image-Layout Generation in Design Templates
comment: Main paper with supplementary material. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
summary:
In this paper, we address the problem of graphic design template creation, which generates a background image and a layout of foreground elements over the background to form a harmonious composition from an input text.
  Prior work on graphic design generation mostly adopts a sequential paradigm, where design elements are generated sequentially. We argue that such a sequential scheme falls short of faithfully capturing the dependency between the background and layout (and thus the joint image-layout distribution), which limits the quality of generated design templates.
  To overcome this limitation, we propose a model, InterIL, which jointly generates the two modalities, background image and layout, in a single generative process. The novel design of our joint model connects the backbones of pretrained image and layout diffusion models with a learnable communication module to explicitly model bidirectional image-layout interaction. During training, the image and layout backbones are frozen to maintain and leverage the vast pretrained single-modality prior knowledge, while only the communication module is updated, so that the model can focus on learning image-layout interaction and thereby better capture the joint image-layout distribution for improved composition harmony.
  Our model has no design-specific inductive bias, which allows it to better preserve the original characteristics of realistic designs. We further introduce a test-time guidance strategy to enable users to impose their specific preferences on generated results.
  Our experiments show that, compared with prior approaches, our model can generate significantly better results in terms of image, layout and image-layout harmonization, producing outputs closer to real samples. We also demonstrate the flexibility of our model in enforcing user preferences at inference without retraining.

AI.tldr: InterIL is a joint generative model for graphic design template creation that connects pretrained image and layout diffusion models with a learnable communication module to model bidirectional image-layout interaction, producing higher quality and more harmonious compositions than prior sequential approaches.
AI.motivation: Prior sequential approaches for graphic design generation fail to capture the dependency between background and layout, limiting the quality of generated design templates. The sequential paradigm cannot faithfully model the joint image-layout distribution, which is essential for creating harmonious compositions.
AI.method: InterIL uses a joint generation approach that connects pretrained image and layout diffusion models through a learnable communication module. The model explicitly models bidirectional image-layout interaction. During training, both image and layout backbones are frozen to preserve pretrained prior knowledge, while only the communication module is updated to learn image-layout interaction. A test-time guidance strategy is also introduced for user preference enforcement.
AI.result: Experimental results show InterIL generates significantly better results compared to prior approaches in terms of image quality, layout quality, and image-layout harmonization. The outputs are closer to real samples. The model also demonstrates flexibility in enforcing user preferences at inference without requiring retraining.
AI.conclusion: The proposed InterIL model addresses key limitations in graphic design template generation by jointly modeling background images and layouts through a bidirectional interaction mechanism. By connecting pretrained diffusion models with a learnable communication module and freezing backbone models during training, the approach effectively captures the joint image-layout distribution while preserving pretrained knowledge. The method demonstrates superior performance in harmonization quality and offers flexible user control at inference time without retraining.

title: EConv-TasNet: Efficient Conv-TasNet for Effective Speech Separation
summary: Conv-TasNet has served as a strong baseline for time-domain speech separation, and many studies have extended it with advanced architectures such as dual-path networks, U-Nets, and attention mechanisms. However, these methods often introduce high computational cost and complexity, limiting their deployment in resource-constrained scenarios. To address this issue, we propose eConv-TasNet, an efficient variant of Conv-TasNet that improves both effectiveness and efficiency without relying on resource-intensive modules. The proposed model consists of a group-wise early-splitting (GES) module and a multi-group feature aggregation (MGFA) module. GES generates discriminative speaker embeddings at intermediate stages, while MGFA progressively aggregates these group-level representations for refined mask estimation. Experimental results show that eConv-TasNet reduces model size by 22.4%, accelerates inference by 18.9%, and improves SI-SNRi by 14.0%-28.0% across three public benchmarks. Moreover, it achieves competitive performance compared with state-of-the-art methods while requiring significantly fewer parameters and lower inference cost. These results demonstrate a favorable efficiency-effectiveness trade-off for edge deployment.

AI.tldr: eConv-TasNet is an efficient variant of Conv-TasNet for time-domain speech separation that achieves a favorable trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness. It uses a group-wise early-splitting (GES) module and a multi-group feature aggregation (MGFA) module to reduce model size by 22.4%, accelerate inference by 18.9%, and improve SI-SNRi by 14.0%-28.0% across three benchmarks, while maintaining competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Conv-TasNet is a strong baseline for time-domain speech separation, but advanced extensions (dual-path networks, U-Nets, attention mechanisms) introduce high computational cost and complexity, limiting deployment in resource-constrained scenarios. There is a need for an efficient model that maintains strong performance while being suitable for edge deployment.
AI.method: The proposed eConv-TasNet consists of two key modules: (1) Group-wise Early-Splitting (GES) module - generates discriminative speaker embeddings at intermediate stages of the network; (2) Multi-Group Feature Aggregation (MGFA) module - progressively aggregates group-level representations for refined mask estimation. These modules improve effectiveness and efficiency without relying on resource-intensive modules like attention mechanisms.
AI.result: Experimental results on three public benchmarks show: (1) Model size reduction: 22.4%; (2) Inference speedup: 18.9%; (3) SI-SNRi improvement: 14.0%-28.0%. The model achieves competitive performance compared with state-of-the-art methods while requiring significantly fewer parameters and lower inference cost.
AI.conclusion: eConv-TasNet demonstrates a favorable efficiency-effectiveness trade-off for edge deployment. It successfully addresses the trade-off between model efficiency and separation performance, making it suitable for resource-constrained scenarios while maintaining competitive speech separation quality.

title: Artificial Intelligence Algorithms for the Detection of Pathologies Related to Lung Cancer through Image Analysis using Convolutional Neural Networks and Data Augmentation: a systematic mapping of the literature
summary: Lung cancer is one of the leading causes of death worldwide, and its early diagnosis is crucial to improving patients prognosis and quality of life. However, the process of interpreting medical images for the detection of lung cancer is complex and requires trained experts. In this context, artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning (DL) emerge as potential tools to automate and optimize image analysis. The objective of this work is to review the most recent and relevant applications of AI and DL in the field of radiology for the detection of lung cancer. To this end, an exhaustive search was carried out in scientific databases such as PubMed,IEEEXPLORE, Scopus and Web of Science, and 96 articles published from 2015 to the present addressing the use of AI and DL in biomedical engineering were selected. Emphasis is placed on the use of convolutional neural networks (CNN) with transfer learning and Data Augmentation as promising techniques to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the image interpretation process. The results show that the use of AI and DL can offer an effective alternative for the early diagnosis of lung cancer, with high sensitivity and specificity. However, current limitations and challenges that must be addressed to guarantee its responsible and safe application in clinical practice are also identified, such as the lack of standardized data, the ex plainability of the models, patient privacy, and the ethical and social implications. It is concluded that the use of AI and DL can have a positive impact on the care of patients with lung cancer, but further research and regulation are required to ensure its quality and reliability.

AI.tldr: This is a review paper examining 96 articles (2015-present) on AI and deep learning applications in lung cancer detection from medical images. The study focuses on CNNs with transfer learning and data augmentation, finding high sensitivity and specificity but identifying key challenges including data standardization, model explainability, patient privacy, and ethical implications.
AI.motivation: Lung cancer is a leading cause of death globally, and early diagnosis is critical for improving patient outcomes. However, interpreting medical images requires trained experts, making the process complex and time-consuming. Artificial intelligence and deep learning emerge as promising tools to automate and optimize image analysis for lung cancer detection.
AI.method: The authors conducted an exhaustive literature search in four major scientific databases: PubMed, IEEE XPLORE, Scopus, and Web of Science. A total of 96 articles published from 2015 to the present were selected, focusing on AI and DL applications in biomedical engineering for lung cancer detection. The review emphasizes convolutional neural networks (CNN) with transfer learning and data augmentation techniques.
AI.result: The use of AI and deep learning demonstrates an effective alternative for early diagnosis of lung cancer, achieving high sensitivity and specificity. However, several limitations and challenges were identified: lack of standardized data, model explainability issues, patient privacy concerns, and ethical/social implications that must be addressed for responsible clinical application.
AI.conclusion: AI and deep learning can have a positive impact on patient care for lung cancer. However, further research and regulation are required to ensure quality, reliability, and safe clinical implementation. Addressing the identified challenges is essential for responsible and effective AI deployment in medical practice.

title: Quantifying the Memorization-to-Generalization Transition: Scaling Laws and Phase Structure in Grokking
summary: Neural networks trained past memorization frequently undergo a delayed transition to generalization, a phenomenon known as grokking. Despite theoretical progress on \emph{why} this transition occurs, the quantitative structure of \emph{when} it occurs in hyperparameter space remains uncharacterized. We map the memorization-to-generalization boundary across 384 configurations of two-hidden-layer MLPs on modular arithmetic, fitting a power-law scaling relation for generalization onset time: $T_{\mathrm{grok}} \propto H^{-0.27}\, D^{-2.04}\, η^{-0.50}\, λ^{-0.64}$ ($R^2 = 0.732$; $0.821$ with interactions). The exponent hierarchy reveals that data complexity ($D^{-2.04}$) is the dominant driver of regime transition, not model capacity ($H^{-0.27}$): doubling data accelerates generalization by ${\sim}4\times$, while doubling width yields only ${\sim}1.2\times$. A sharp phase boundary at weight decay $λ\gtrsim 1.0$ separates grokking from non-grokking configurations, and weight norm trajectories show monotonic compression during the transition, consistent with implicit regularization selecting low-complexity solutions. These results provide a quantitative foundation for predicting and controlling regime transitions in overparameterized networks.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the quantitative conditions under which neural networks experience grokking—a delayed transition from memorization to generalization. Through experiments across 384 configurations of two-hidden-layer MLPs on modular arithmetic, the authors discover a power-law relationship where data complexity (D) is the dominant factor influencing generalization timing, not model capacity (H). They also identify a sharp phase boundary at weight decay λ≥1.0 that separates grokking from non-grokking regimes.
AI.motivation: While theoretical progress has been made on why grokking occurs, the quantitative structure of when it occurs in hyperparameter space remained uncharacterized. The authors aimed to map the memorization-to-generalization boundary and identify which hyperparameters most strongly influence the timing of regime transitions.
AI.method: The authors trained 384 configurations of two-hidden-layer MLPs on modular arithmetic tasks. They systematically varied hyperparameters including hidden layer width (H), data complexity (D), learning rate (η), and weight decay (λ). They fitted a power-law scaling relation for generalization onset time and analyzed weight norm trajectories to understand implicit regularization effects.
AI.result: The fitted power-law scaling relation is: T_grok ∝ H^-0.27 D^-2.04 η^-0.50 λ^-0.64 (R² = 0.732; 0.821 with interactions). Key findings: (1) Data complexity (D^-2.04) is the dominant driver, not model capacity (H^-0.27); doubling data accelerates generalization by ~4× while doubling width yields only ~1.2×. (2) A sharp phase boundary exists at weight decay λ ≥ 1.0 separating grokking from non-grokking configurations. (3) Weight norm trajectories show monotonic compression during the transition, consistent with implicit regularization selecting low-complexity solutions.
AI.conclusion: Data complexity is the primary driver of grokking timing, not model capacity. A clear phase boundary exists at weight decay λ ≥ 1.0. These results provide a quantitative foundation for predicting and controlling regime transitions in overparameterized networks, with practical implications for training dynamics and generalization.

title: On the Relation between Code Quality and Machine Learning Performance: A Large-scale Empirical Study
summary: Context: Computational notebooks are the standard environment for machine learning (ML) development. Within the ML community, model performance is often the primary considered metric, and code quality is treated as a secondary concern. This prioritization relies on a largely untested assumption that code quality and ML performance are unrelated. Practitioners also reuse existing code that may come from notebooks selected through social signals (popularity, author expertise) whose reliability as quality proxies has never been assessed. Objective: We empirically investigated the relationship between code quality and ML performance in notebooks, and evaluated whether popularity and author expertise give indication on code quality or performance. Method: We conducted a large-scale empirical study of 265,363 Python notebooks submitted to Kaggle competitions. We assessed code quality with two static analysis tools: Pylint, capturing general Python code quality, and SonarQube, configured with a profile of 34 rules targeting data-science and ML-specific practices. Results: The relationship between code quality and performance depends on the notion of quality considered. General Python code quality is decoupled from ML performance, showing negligible or non-significant correlations across all observations. In contrast, ML-specific violations exhibit a consistent, small negative association with performance that persists across all observations. The popularity of a notebook does not give information on the code quality or performance. Code expertise provides no information on quality or performance, but competition expertise correlates with better performance, fewer ML-specific violations, and slightly more Python errors and refactoring violations.

AI.tldr: Study of 265K Kaggle notebooks finds ML-specific code quality negatively correlates with performance, while general Python quality is uncorrelated. Popularity and author expertise are unreliable proxies for code quality or performance.
AI.motivation: Challenge the assumption that code quality and ML performance are unrelated, and evaluate whether social signals (popularity, author expertise) reliably indicate code quality in notebooks
AI.method: Large-scale empirical study of 265,363 Python notebooks from Kaggle competitions, using Pylint for general Python code quality and SonarQube with 34 data-science/ML-specific rules
AI.result: General Python code quality shows negligible/no correlation with ML performance. ML-specific violations show a consistent small negative association with performance. Popularity gives no indication of quality or performance. Competition expertise correlates with better performance but mixed code quality.
AI.conclusion: General Python code quality is decoupled from ML performance, while ML-specific violations show a small negative association with performance. Popularity does not indicate quality or performance. Competition expertise correlates with better performance but mixed code quality metrics.

title: GRADE: Single-Frame Generative Radar Depth Estimation Under Visual Degradation
summary: Dense 3D depth perception fails under smoke, fog, and darkness because optical sensors cannot penetrate airborne particulates. mmWave radar remains usable and measures range accurately under these conditions, but its small aperture limits angular resolution. We present GRADE, which grounds a pretrained generative prior in single-frame radar geometry to estimate high-fidelity metric depth. GRADE first maps raw 4D radar spectra to coarse metric depth. A latent diffusion backbone then recovers structural detail while conditioning every denoising step on this estimate. A pixel-space adapter uses residual camera cues when available and is trained across clear, smoke-degraded, and occluded inputs so the full output approaches the radar-conditioned path as visibility degrades. Trained and evaluated on ~95K frames across 12 buildings with real smoke, GRADE achieves an MAE of 0.303 m in clear scenes and 0.313 m under smoke, outperforming existing baselines. Code and datasets are available at https://phi-lab-rice.github.io/GRADE.

AI.tldr: GRADE is a method that uses mmWave radar combined with latent diffusion models to estimate high-fidelity metric depth in challenging visibility conditions (smoke, fog, darkness) where optical sensors fail.
AI.motivation: Dense 3D depth perception fails under smoke, fog, and darkness because optical sensors cannot penetrate airborne particulates. While mmWave radar remains usable and measures range accurately under these conditions, its small aperture limits angular resolution. This paper aims to overcome this limitation by combining radar with generative priors.
AI.method: GRADE uses a three-stage approach: (1) Maps raw 4D radar spectra to coarse metric depth; (2) Uses a latent diffusion backbone to recover structural detail while conditioning every denoising step on the radar estimate; (3) Employs a pixel-space adapter that uses residual camera cues when available, trained across clear, smoke-degraded, and occluded inputs.
AI.result: GRADE achieves an MAE of 0.303 m in clear scenes and 0.313 m under smoke, outperforming existing baselines. Trained and evaluated on ~95K frames across 12 buildings with real smoke.
AI.conclusion: GRADE successfully combines radar sensing with generative AI to achieve robust metric depth estimation under adverse visibility conditions, with minimal performance degradation (0.010 m difference) between clear and smoke environments.

title: 3D Point Splatting for mmWave Radar Novel View Synthesis
summary: Solving novel view synthesis (NVS) for millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar requires a renderer that is physically faithful, complex-valued, and multi-viewpoint-tractable. No prior method achieves these three properties simultaneously. Differentiable Monte Carlo (MC) ray tracers implement the radar forward model directly with explicit material modeling and complex outputs, but do not scale to the multi-view optimization NVS demands. Optical-NVS ports of NeRF, hash grids, and 3D Gaussians train fast but discard phase and replace explicit material modeling with opaque learned features, restricting them to power-only range-azimuth (RA) magnitudes. We propose 3D Point Splatting (3DPS), the first differentiable point renderer for radar, derived directly from the standard solid-angle form of the radar equation. Each oriented 3D point carries an ITU-R P.2040 material model, evaluated in closed form, with the resulting complex phasor splatted into range bins through a precomputed point spread function (PSF). The complex-valued output makes the renderer product-agnostic. The same optimized scene yields analog-to-digital converter (ADC), complex range profile (CRP), and RA outputs through standard fast Fourier transform (FFT) pipelines without retraining for each format. On six outdoor ColoRadar scenes, 3DPS reaches 0.587 mean Pearson correlation on held-out RA images. This is between 1.7x and 5.2x the three optical-NVS baselines (RadarSplat, Radar Fields, DART). Training takes approximately 3 minutes per scene on a single RTX 4090.

AI.tldr: 3D Point Splatting (3DPS) is the first differentiable point renderer for mmWave radar, derived from the standard solid-angle radar equation. It uses ITU-R P.2040 material modeling with complex-valued outputs, enabling a single optimized scene to produce ADC, CRP, and RA outputs through standard FFT pipelines. The method achieves 0.587 mean Pearson correlation on held-out RA images, outperforming three optical-NVS baselines by 1.7x-5.2x, with training taking ~3 minutes per scene on RTX 4090.
AI.motivation: Solving novel view synthesis (NVS) for millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar requires a renderer that is physically faithful, complex-valued, and multi-viewpoint-tractable simultaneously. Prior methods failed to achieve all three: differentiable MC ray tracers don't scale to multi-view optimization, while optical-NVS methods (NeRF, hash grids, 3D Gaussians) discard phase and replace explicit material modeling with opaque learned features, restricting output to power-only range-azimuth magnitudes.
AI.method: 3DPS derives directly from the standard solid-angle form of the radar equation. Each oriented 3D point carries an ITU-R P.2040 material model evaluated in closed form, with the resulting complex phasor splatted into range bins through a precomputed point spread function (PSF). This enables complex-valued output that is product-agnostic.
AI.result: On six outdoor ColoRadar scenes, 3DPS achieves 0.587 mean Pearson correlation on held-out RA images, which is 1.7x to 5.2x better than three optical-NVS baselines (RadarSplat, Radar Fields, DART). Training takes approximately 3 minutes per scene on a single RTX 4090.
AI.conclusion: 3DPS successfully achieves physically faithful, complex-valued, and multi-viewpoint-tractable radar rendering simultaneously. The same optimized scene yields ADC, complex range profile (CRP), and range-azimuth (RA) outputs through standard FFT pipelines without retraining, demonstrating the method's product-agnostic nature and practical utility for mmWave radar NVS applications.

title: GEOSTEER: Geodesic Optimization for Activation Steering in Large Language Models
summary: Activation steering provides a lightweight way to control large language models (LLMs) by modifying their hidden activations at inference time. Among these approaches, norm-preserving steering aims to change model behavior without altering the activation norm, reducing the risk of representation collapse and degradation. However, existing norm-preserving methods are limited by predefined steering trajectories and by their reliance on one-step updates, which may fail to capture the complex structure of activation distributions. We propose GeoSteer, an optimization-based method for norm-preserving activation steering. GeoSteer formulates steering as a Riemannian optimization problem and updates activations through a sequence of small geodesic steps on the representation manifold. To avoid fixed steering directions, GeoSteer learns a nonlinear activation-space objective that distinguishes desired from undesired activations, and uses this function to adaptively guide each steering step. This multistep formulation yields smoother, more stable, and more consistent steering behavior while preserving the activation norm. Across TruthfulQA, RealToxicityPrompts, and UltraFeedback benchmarks, GeoSteer consistently improves over state-of-the-art activation steering baselines. These results suggest that norm-preserving steering can be made more effective by replacing predefined one-step edits with adaptive, geometry-aware optimization.

AI.tldr: GeoSteer is a novel optimization-based method for norm-preserving activation steering in large language models. It formulates steering as a Riemannian optimization problem, using multi-step geodesic updates on the representation manifold and learning a nonlinear objective to adaptively guide steering, outperforming existing baselines across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Activation steering provides lightweight LLM control by modifying hidden activations at inference time. Existing norm-preserving methods aim to change model behavior without altering activation norm to avoid representation collapse. However, these methods are limited by predefined steering trajectories and one-step updates that fail to capture complex activation distributions.
AI.method: GeoSteer formulates steering as a Riemannian optimization problem and updates activations through a sequence of small geodesic steps on the representation manifold. It learns a nonlinear activation-space objective that distinguishes desired from undesired activations, using this function to adaptively guide each steering step. This multistep approach preserves activation norm while providing smoother, more stable steering behavior.
AI.result: GeoSteer consistently improves over state-of-the-art activation steering baselines across TruthfulQA, RealToxicityPrompts, and UltraFeedback benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Norm-preserving steering can be made more effective by replacing predefined one-step edits with adaptive, geometry-aware optimization. The multi-step Riemannian approach yields smoother, more stable, and more consistent steering behavior.

title: An Open Recipe for IMO Gold: Training Nemotron for Olympiad Mathematics
summary: We study how model post-training and test-time inference design affect natural-language proof generation for hard olympiad mathematics. Starting from Nemotron 3 Ultra, we train two specialist checkpoints using supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, and evaluate checkpoint choice, verification, and refinement. Based on these findings, we present an open-model test-time-compute pipeline. The system operates entirely in natural language, with no formal prover, external tools, or internet access. Three Nemotron 3 Ultra checkpoints - the general-availability model and two post-trained specialists - power an iterative search that generates, verifies, and refines candidate proofs; a separate high-compute stage then selects each final submission. The system scored 30 out of 42 points at IMO 2026, reaching the gold-medal threshold. We release the two post-trained checkpoints as well as the training data, the training and inference code, the submitted solutions, and Nemotron-IMO-Bench, a new benchmark of 200 novel olympiad-level problems.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an open-model test-time-compute pipeline for natural-language proof generation on IMO 2026, achieving gold-medal threshold (30/42 points) using Nemotron 3 Ultra with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning post-training.
AI.motivation: To study how model post-training and test-time inference design affect natural-language proof generation for hard olympiad mathematics, moving beyond formal provers and external tools.
AI.method: Post-train Nemotron 3 Ultra via supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to create two specialist checkpoints. Implement an iterative search pipeline with generate, verify, and refine stages, powered by three model checkpoints, followed by a high-compute selection stage.
AI.result: The system achieved 30 out of 42 points at IMO 2026, reaching the gold-medal threshold. The study also produced Nemotron-IMO-Bench, a benchmark of 200 novel olympiad-level problems.
AI.conclusion: Post-training approach and test-time inference design significantly impact olympiad math performance. The pipeline operates entirely in natural language without formal provers, external tools, or internet access, demonstrating that open models can achieve gold-medal-level performance through careful training and inference strategies.
