title: Shedding Light: A Benchmark for Evaluating Lighting Understanding in Generative Image Models
comment: Accepted to ACM Transactions on Graphics (SIGGRAPH Asia 2026), vol. 45, no. 6, article 227, December 2026. 25 pages. Project page: https://lvsn.github.io/SheddingLight/
summary: Accurate modelling of illumination is central to realistic image synthesis and scene understanding. Yet, there is little exploration into whether image generative models are good at this task or whether physical plausibility remains a key challenge for them. Clearly, significant progress has been made in realistic image synthesis, but do models truly understand lighting in a physically accurate manner? To answer this question, this work proposes a benchmark to assess the lighting understanding and harmonisation capabilities of generative models. Our key insight is that evaluating lighting understanding for such models only requires testing how well they insert novel objects into real photographs whilst maintaining consistent illumination. To do so, we use a multi-illumination dataset with images containing simple objects serving as ``light probes'', and prompt models to inpaint the same object onto the original image, then compare the generated results against the ground-truth light probes. We then estimate the lighting direction, colour and radiance distribution from the inpainted probes, providing a quantitative measure of illumination accuracy and photometric realism. Our work establishes a scalable evaluation protocol to systematically assess how well generative models capture and reproduce real-world lighting, offering a foundation for benchmarking the photometric accuracy of any future models. All code and data are available at https://lvsn.github.io/SheddingLight/ .

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a benchmark to evaluate whether image generative models truly understand physical lighting, by testing how well they can insert novel objects into real photographs while maintaining consistent illumination.
AI.motivation: Despite progress in realistic image synthesis, it remains unclear whether generative models understand lighting in a physically accurate manner. The authors seek to address this fundamental gap in evaluation.
AI.method: The approach uses multi-illumination datasets containing images with simple objects as "light probes." Models are prompted to inpaint these objects onto original images, then the generated results are compared against ground-truth light probes. Lighting direction, color, and radiance distribution are estimated from the inpainted probes to quantitatively measure illumination accuracy.
AI.result: The work establishes a scalable evaluation protocol to systematically assess how well generative models capture and reproduce real-world lighting, providing a foundation for benchmarking photometric accuracy.
AI.conclusion: This benchmark provides a standardized way to evaluate the lighting understanding capabilities of any generative model, enabling future research on improving physical plausibility in image synthesis.

title: X-AuT: Progressive Audio-Encoder Compression for Speech LLMs with Cross-Scale Distillation
summary: Reducing audio-encoder depth lowers the inference cost of speech large language models, but removing complete blocks perturbs the embeddings consumed by the decoder and can cause deletion and premature end-of-sequence errors. We introduce X-AuT, a progressive framework that selects layer combinations through short behavioral probes and restores the pruned model through representation alignment, cross-scale distillation, scheduled student-policy supervision, and LoRA finetuning. The language-model backbone remains frozen, while attention LoRA adapters and the tied output embedding adapt during distillation. Training uses the highest-agreement tier from a transcript-consistency pipeline, followed by source reweighting during finetuning. On ten public Chinese--English benchmarks, compressing Qwen3-ASR-0.6B from 18 to 16 audio-encoder layers reduces macro-average error from 5.61% to 5.27%. The 14-layer model reaches 5.75% with 20.7% fewer audio-tower parameters. Under the matched recipe, the 1.7B teacher yields 5.55% mean error, compared with 8.45% for self-distillation, and progressive 18$\rightarrow$14 pruning outperforms direct pruning (5.75% vs. 6.73%). These single-run results establish two practical operating points and show that the accuracy effects vary across benchmarks. Project website: https://xpeng-ai.github.io/x-aut

AI.tldr: X-AuT is a progressive framework for compressing speech large language model audio encoders by removing layers while maintaining performance through representation alignment, cross-scale distillation, and LoRA adaptation. Compressing Qwen3-ASR-0.6B from 18 to 16 layers reduces error from 5.61% to 5.27%, and a 14-layer model achieves 5.75% with 20.7% fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Reducing audio-encoder depth lowers inference cost of speech LLMs, but removing complete blocks perturbs embeddings consumed by the decoder, causing deletion and premature end-of-sequence errors. Current methods struggle with maintaining accuracy while compressing model depth.
AI.method: X-AuT uses: (1) Short behavioral probes to select optimal layer combinations; (2) Representation alignment to restore pruned models; (3) Cross-scale distillation; (4) Scheduled student-policy supervision; (5) LoRA finetuning with attention adapters and tied output embedding adaptation. Language-model backbone remains frozen. Training uses highest-agreement tier from transcript-consistency pipeline, followed by source reweighting during finetuning.
AI.result: On ten public Chinese-English benchmarks: compressing Qwen3-ASR-0.6B from 18 to 16 layers reduces macro-average error from 5.61% to 5.27%. The 14-layer model reaches 5.75% with 20.7% fewer audio-tower parameters. The 1.7B teacher yields 5.55% mean error vs 8.45% for self-distillation. Progressive 18→14 pruning outperforms direct pruning (5.75% vs 6.73%).
AI.conclusion: X-AuT establishes two practical operating points for compressing speech LLM audio encoders. Progressive layer pruning consistently outperforms direct pruning. The accuracy effects vary across benchmarks, suggesting targeted optimization opportunities.

title: Conformal Calibration Transfer
comment: Accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Conformal prediction converts point predictions into set-valued predictions with coverage guarantees under exchangeability between calibration and deployment data. We study conformal calibration transfer, where this requirement fails because labeled calibration is available only in a source space, while prediction sets are needed in a target space linked to the source through unlabeled paired observations (e.g., paired modalities or sensor changes). We propose Transported Conformal Calibration (TCC): we transport labeled source calibration into the target space using the paired data, and then correct residual post-transport mismatch using only unlabeled target inputs. We instantiate this correction with two complementary methods: TCC-KS, which uses a label-free uncertainty surrogate to detect mismatch and adjust calibration conservatively, and weighted-TCC, which reweights transported calibration toward the target domain for improved efficiency when weights are stable. We provide finite-sample target-domain coverage guarantees that adapt to an observable measure of mismatch. Across CIFAR-100-C, Tiny-ImageNet-C, and SEN12MS, we show reliable target-domain coverage transfer without labeled target calibration data, with label-free diagnostics that predict when correction is needed.

AI.tldr: A method (TCC) for transferring conformal prediction calibrations from a source domain to a target domain using unlabeled paired data, achieving coverage guarantees in the target domain without requiring any labeled target data. Two variants handle different mismatch scenarios: conservative TCC-KS and efficient weighted-TCC.
AI.motivation: Conformal prediction requires exchangeability between calibration and deployment data, which fails in domain transfer settings where labeled calibration is only available in a source space but prediction sets are needed in a target space. This problem arises in applications with paired modalities or sensor changes (e.g., different imaging sensors capturing the same scene).
AI.method: Transported Conformal Calibration (TCC) with two instantiations: (1) TCC-KS uses a label-free uncertainty surrogate to detect post-transport mismatch and apply conservative calibration adjustment; (2) Weighted-TCC reweights transported calibration samples toward the target domain for improved efficiency when weights are stable. The approach leverages unlabeled paired observations between source and target domains to transport labeled calibration, then uses only unlabeled target inputs for residual correction.
AI.result: The method demonstrates reliable target-domain coverage transfer without labeled target calibration data across CIFAR-100-C, Tiny-ImageNet-C, and SEN12MS datasets. The label-free diagnostics successfully predict when correction is needed, enabling adaptive coverage guarantees.
AI.conclusion: TCC provides a principled framework for conformal calibration transfer across domains without requiring labeled target data. The method achieves reliable target-domain coverage through two complementary mechanisms: conservative adjustment via TCC-KS when mismatch is detected, and improved efficiency via weighted-TCC when weights are stable. The key innovation is the observable measure of mismatch that enables adaptive coverage guarantees.

title: Finishing the Task Is Not Enough: Evaluating Agent Resilience and Considerate Participation under Accumulating Challenge
summary: Sustained deployment of generative AI agents requires more than isolated task success. Agents must remain useful across repeated interactions, changing conditions, and dependencies on people within shared workflows, especially as technical, human, and operational disruptions accumulate over time. We propose operational resilience and considerate participation as two complementary aspects of evaluating such agents: the former captures how agents recover from blocked work while preserving progress and communicating their limits, and the latter captures how their adaptation accounts for affected people, role boundaries, and the surrounding workflow. Yet both remain underexplored under accumulating challenge. We study 120 simulated healthcare trajectories across two generative AI models and twelve stakeholder-derived tasks under light, medium, and heavy challenge. We compare textual action plans, prompted internal assessments, and quantitative structured workload and affect reports to examine how agent behavior and reported state change as challenge accumulates. Regarding operational resilience, agents shift from self-directed recovery toward greater human dependence, while reporting increasing workload and negative affect in structured reports but seldom expressing strain in textual responses. Regarding considerate participation, agents broaden from task-focused adaptation toward task reframing, attention to others, role-boundary adjustment, and wider coordination, with distinct patterns across actions and internal assessments. From these findings, we derive five deployment dilemmas involving persistence, attention, role boundaries, state disclosure, and escalation that require stakeholder specification, further informing technical implications for learning, situated evaluation, and embodied adaptation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes operational resilience and considerate participation as two complementary frameworks for evaluating generative AI agents in sustained deployment. Through 120 simulated healthcare trajectories across two models and twelve tasks under varying challenge levels, the study finds agents shift toward greater human dependence as challenge accumulates, while exhibiting distinct patterns between textual actions and internal assessments. Five deployment dilemmas are identified that require stakeholder specification.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of generative AI agents focuses on isolated task success, but real-world deployment requires agents to remain useful across repeated interactions, changing conditions, and human dependencies. Existing frameworks fail to address how agents perform under accumulating challenges over time, particularly in healthcare workflows where disruptions accumulate.
AI.method: The study analyzed 120 simulated healthcare trajectories across two generative AI models and twelve stakeholder-derived tasks under three challenge levels (light, medium, heavy). Methods included examining textual action plans, prompted internal assessments, and quantitative structured workload and affect reports to track how agent behavior and reported state change as challenge accumulates.
AI.result: Regarding operational resilience: agents shift from self-directed recovery toward greater human dependence as challenge accumulates. They report increasing workload and negative affect in structured reports but seldom express strain in textual responses. Regarding considerate participation: agents broaden from task-focused adaptation toward task reframing, attention to others, role-boundary adjustment, and wider coordination, with distinct patterns across actions and internal assessments.
AI.conclusion: Five deployment dilemmas involving persistence, attention, role boundaries, state disclosure, and escalation are identified that require stakeholder specification. These findings inform technical implications for learning, situated evaluation, and embodied adaptation of AI agents in real-world deployments.

title: Numbat: Building and Verifying a Self-Contained Machine-Learning Stack
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Companion to arXiv:2608.24267
summary: Machine-learning systems are built almost exclusively on a few large Python-orchestrated frameworks, and they inherit those stacks' engineering costs: environments of hundreds of version-coupled packages, separate export toolchains for deployment, and the split between the language research is written in and the language products ship in. We report on the construction and verification of numbat, a machine-learning stack written in one general-purpose language (Zig) with no third-party runtime dependencies. The stack spans tensor computation, automatic differentiation, neural-network modules, mixed precision, multi-GPU training, data loading and monitoring; an SDK exposes it behind a stable, additively versioned C ABI of over 1,400 entry points, with bindings for six languages; and its clinical domain planes encode regulatory requirements as executable acceptance gates rather than documentation. Verifying such a stack is the harder half of building it: a defective training run rarely fails, it converges quietly to a slightly worse model. We treat a widely used reference implementation as an executable specification and verify against it at five levels, from operator gradient checks to an automated trajectory gate against a same-machine reference run - the arrangement our companion study formalizes as a trajectory-level differential oracle. The protocol surfaced ten silent recipe divergences, which we catalog with mechanisms and symptoms. As the acceptance test, we train a 25.9M-parameter detector of the YOLOv8m class from random initialization on COCO 2017 for the full 500-epoch schedule: the exported weights score 0.4956 mAP50-95 under the official protocol, scored by the reference stack's own validator (published endpoint 0.502), with single-GPU step time at parity on identical hardware. Weights, per-epoch metrics and the full run manifest are released.

AI.tldr: Numbat is a complete machine-learning stack written in Zig (a systems programming language) with no third-party runtime dependencies, replacing the traditional Python-heavy ML ecosystem. It includes tensor computation, automatic differentiation, neural network modules, mixed precision, multi-GPU training, data loading, and monitoring. The stack is exposed via a stable C ABI with 1,400+ entry points and bindings for six languages. Verification involved five levels against a reference implementation, identifying 10 silent recipe divergences. The final validation trained a 25.9M-parameter YOLOv8m detector on COCO 2017 for 500 epochs, achieving 0.4956 mAP50-95 (reference: 0.502).
AI.motivation: Machine learning systems are built on large Python frameworks that inherit significant engineering costs: managing environments with hundreds of version-coupled packages, separate export toolchains for deployment, and the split between research language (Python) and production language. This creates a gap between research and deployed products, with regulatory requirements often encoded as documentation rather than executable acceptance gates.
AI.method:
1. Built numbat - a complete ML stack in Zig with no third-party runtime dependencies
2. Implemented tensor computation, automatic differentiation, neural-network modules, mixed precision, multi-GPU training, data loading, and monitoring
3. Exposed via stable, additively versioned C ABI with 1,400+ entry points and bindings for six languages
4. Clinical domain planes encode regulatory requirements as executable acceptance gates
5. Five-level verification protocol against reference implementation: operator gradient checks → automated trajectory gate against same-machine reference run (trajectory-level differential oracle)
6. Trained YOLOv8m detector (25.9M parameters) from random initialization on COCO 2017 for full 500-epoch schedule
AI.result:
1. Identified 10 silent recipe divergences with documented mechanisms and symptoms
2. YOLOv8m detector achieved 0.4956 mAP50-95 under official protocol (reference: 0.502)
3. Single-GPU step time at parity on identical hardware
4. Released weights, per-epoch metrics, and full run manifest
AI.conclusion: A production-quality ML stack can be built in a single systems programming language (Zig) without third-party runtime dependencies, achieving performance parity with established frameworks while providing better engineering properties (no Python runtime, stable C ABI, executable regulatory acceptance gates). The five-level verification protocol using trajectory-level differential oracle proved effective at surfacing silent recipe divergences that would otherwise go undetected.

title: Two-Parameter Flow Map Learning for Continuous-Time Diffeomorphic Image Registration
comment: Published at European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV), 2026
summary: Diffeomorphic image registration is central to medical image analysis, enabling anatomically consistent alignment across subjects. Most learning-based diffeomorphic methods model autonomous ODEs(ordinary differential equations) by parameterizing a stationary velocity field and recovering deformations via scaling-and-squaring. While non-autonomous ODEs with time-dependent velocities increase expressiveness, existing approaches rely on numerical integration to implicitly enforce flow structure that entangles model expressiveness with discretization accuracy. We propose a framework to directly learn the continuous-time solution of a non-autonomous ODE formulated as a two-parameterflow map. By enforcing cocycle consistency, a fundamental structural property of time-varying flows, we learn the flow maps without time discretization and velocity integration during training. The framework recovers diffeomorphic mappings at inference using a small number of compositions. Our proposed framework seamlessly incorporates standard registration backbones and improves alignment accuracy consistently across nine datasets while preserving diffeomorphic structure. Notably, the proposed method achieves an average Dice improvement of 2.1% on brain MRI benchmarks, a 12% TRE reduction on lung CT, and a 2.6% Dice gain on cardiac MRI and ultrasound datasets.

AI.tldr: A deep learning framework for diffeomorphic medical image registration that directly learns continuous-time non-autonomous ODE solutions using two-parameter flow maps and cocycle consistency, eliminating reliance on time discretization during training.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-based diffeomorphic registration methods either use stationary velocity fields (limited expressiveness) or non-autonomous ODEs with time-dependent velocities (but rely on numerical integration that entangles model expressiveness with discretization accuracy). There was a need for a framework that can learn continuous-time flows without these limitations.
AI.method: The proposed framework learns the continuous-time solution of a non-autonomous ODE by formulating it as a two-parameter flow map. By enforcing cocycle consistency (a fundamental structural property of time-varying flows), the model learns flow maps without requiring time discretization or velocity integration during training. At inference, diffeomorphic mappings are recovered using a small number of compositions.
AI.result: The method consistently improves alignment accuracy across nine datasets while preserving diffeomorphic structure. Specific improvements include: 2.1% average Dice improvement on brain MRI benchmarks, 12% TRE reduction on lung CT, and 2.6% Dice gain on cardiac MRI and ultrasound datasets.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully integrates with standard registration backbones and achieves state-of-the-art performance by learning continuous-time flows directly, demonstrating the effectiveness of the cocycle consistency enforcement approach for diffeomorphic image registration.

title: Post-Training Zero-Shot TTS for Fine-Grained Emotion and Duration Control via Natural Language
summary: Audiobook narration, conversational agents, and audiovisual dubbing require speech that conveys changing emotions and adapts its pacing within a single utterance. But most existing TTS systems typically rely on utterance-level style conditioning, making such fine-grained control difficult to achieve. In light of this, and inspired by the success of post-training in large language models, we propose a unified post-training framework that equips pretrained text-to-speech models with natural-language control over segment-level emotion and duration. Supervised fine-tuning establishes instruction-conditioned speech generation, while reinforcement learning with group relative policy optimization refines control accuracy using emotion and duration rewards alongside content and speaker preservation objectives. By reusing the pretrained architecture, our approach avoids additional inference-time control modules. Experiments demonstrate significantly improved fine-grained controllability while maintaining speech intelligibility and speaker identity, highlighting post-training as a practical approach to extending existing speech synthesis models.

AI.tldr: A post-training framework that enables pretrained TTS models to be controlled via natural language instructions for segment-level emotion and duration, using supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (GRPO) to achieve fine-grained speech style control without adding inference-time modules.
AI.motivation: Existing TTS systems rely on utterance-level style conditioning, making it difficult to control changing emotions and pacing within a single utterance for applications like audiobook narration, conversational agents, and audiovisual dubbing.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: (1) Supervised fine-tuning establishes instruction-conditioned speech generation; (2) Reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) refines control accuracy using emotion and duration rewards alongside content and speaker preservation objectives. Reuses the pretrained architecture to avoid additional inference-time control modules.
AI.result: Significantly improved fine-grained controllability while maintaining speech intelligibility and speaker identity.
AI.conclusion: Post-training is a practical and effective approach to extending existing speech synthesis models with fine-grained emotional and durational control capabilities.

title: The Truth Was Never Gone: Perfect Aliasing in Compliant-Context Truth Probes
comment: 36 pages, 15 figures. Code and aggregate results: https://github.com/dylanjayabahu/perfect-aliasing
summary: A truth probe fitted where truthful reporting and a task's prescribed action coincide cannot distinguish those targets from its fitting labels alone. We call this failure of semantic identification perfect aliasing. In a controlled binary reporting game, truth and prescribed-action probes fitted on compliant contexts solve the same optimization. On rival contexts their labels are complements, forcing their AUROCs to sum to one; this identity holds across 751 cell-layer pairs to floating-point precision. We separate prescribed output symbols from semantic action using randomized codebooks, then separate truth from prescribed action by fitting on mixed compliant and rival contexts. For a reward-trained Gemma-2-9B policy that answers falsely on all evaluated rival trials, the conventional probe scores $0.006 \pm 0.005$ AUROC across three training seeds, while mixed-fit probes score $1.000$ on the same held-out activations. Mixed fitting uses more training examples and access to labelled rival contexts, so this comparison establishes linear recoverability rather than isolating the benefit of decorrelation. We also show that two compliant-fit probes, both perfect in-distribution, score $0.080$ and $0.986$ on the same rival activations. The findings concern what a probe measures: they do not establish preserved functional belief, causal use of the recovered direction, or a deployable deception detector. Code and aggregate results accompany the paper.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "perfect aliasing" - a fundamental limitation where truth probes cannot distinguish truthful reporting from task-prescribed actions when they coincide. The authors demonstrate this in a controlled binary reporting game with LLM (Gemma-2-9B) experiments, showing that conventional probes fail (0.006 AUROC) while mixed-fit probes achieve perfect separation (1.000 AUROC). They acknowledge this only establishes linear recoverability, not functional belief or causal deception detection.
AI.motivation: To address a fundamental identifiability problem in mechanistic interpretability: when truthful reporting and prescribed actions coincide, a probe fitted on such "compliant" contexts alone cannot distinguish truth from prescribed action. This challenges the interpretation of truth probes in LLM research.
AI.method: Controlled binary reporting game with "compliant" (truth = prescribed action) and "rival" (truth ≠ prescribed action) contexts; randomized codebooks to decorrelate output symbols from semantic action; mixed-fit probes using both context types; evaluation across 751 cell-layer pairs; experiments with reward-trained Gemma-2-9B policy.
AI.result: Truth and prescribed-action probes on compliant contexts solve identical optimization; on rival contexts their labels are complements, forcing AUROC to sum to 1 (verified to floating-point precision across 751 pairs). Conventional probes score 0.006 AUROC on rival trials while mixed-fit probes score 1.000. Two compliant-fit probes both perfect in-distribution score 0.080 and 0.986 on rival activations.
AI.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that probes measure linear recoverability rather than functional belief. They do not establish preserved causal mechanisms or deployable deception detection. The study highlights the need to carefully consider what probes actually measure in mechanistic interpretability research.

title: Towards a Deterministic Math Solver for Clinical Language Models
summary: Large language models are unreliable at arithmetic, which is a problem for clinical calculators where a single numerical error changes the recommendation. The standard response is to hardcode each calculator as a validated function, one at a time. We test an alternative: the model does not calculate. Instead, it writes case-specific Python that a restricted local executor runs as a deterministic solver, and the model's task reduces to deciding how to use it. We evaluate this Program-Solve interface on MedCalc-Bench Verified (1,100 cases, 55 calculators) against direct model arithmetic and a hand-written 22-calculator library, using Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-32B-AWQ, after auditing the benchmark's formulas against current clinical guidelines and flagging 16 of 55 with version, use or coefficient concerns. With formulas and gold variables supplied and both routes reading the whole note, handing off to the solver is not a reliable advantage at 7B (75.31% against 72.02%, a paired +3.29 points with a 95% calculator-cluster interval of [-3.49, 10.38]) but is one at 32B (90.53% against 83.47%, +7.05 [0.47, 14.60], clear of zero). The hand-written library is exact on its 440 supported cases but abstains elsewhere (40.0% overall). Adding an executor thus helps some open-weight models more than others even under matched formula, variable and note access, and is not a substitute for verified formulas or reliable variable extraction either way.

AI.tldr: A new approach using LLMs to write case-specific Python code for clinical calculators instead of directly calculating arithmetic. Tested on MedCalc-Bench Verified (1,100 cases, 55 calculators) with Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-32B-AWQ. The approach shows significant improvement only for the larger 32B model (+7.05 points), while the 7B model shows no reliable advantage (+3.29 points, CI crosses zero).
AI.motivation: Large language models are unreliable at arithmetic, which poses significant risks for clinical calculators where a single numerical error can change medical recommendations. The standard solution of hardcoding each calculator individually is labor-intensive. This paper explores an alternative: having the model write Python code that a restricted executor runs as a deterministic solver.
AI.method: Evaluated the Program-Solve interface on MedCalc-Bench Verified (1,100 cases, 55 calculators) against direct model arithmetic and a hand-written 22-calculator library. Used Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-32B-AWQ models. The benchmark's formulas were audited against current clinical guidelines, identifying 16 of 55 calculators with version, use or coefficient concerns. Both the Program-Solve and direct arithmetic approaches were given access to formulas, gold variables, and the full clinical note.
AI.result: With formulas and gold variables supplied: (1) 7B model: Program-Solve achieved 75.31% vs 72.02% for direct arithmetic (+3.29 points, 95% CI [-3.49, 10.38] - not reliable, crosses zero); (2) 32B model: Program-Solve achieved 90.53% vs 83.47% (+7.05 points, 95% CI [0.47, 14.60] - reliable improvement); (3) Hand-written library: exact on 440 supported cases but abstains elsewhere (40.0% overall). The audit found 16 of 55 calculators with version, use or coefficient concerns.
AI.conclusion: Adding an executor that allows LLMs to write Python code helps some open-weight models more than others, even under matched formula, variable and note access. The approach is not a substitute for verified formulas or reliable variable extraction. The 32B model shows clear benefit from the Program-Solve approach, while the 7B model does not. The audit also revealed significant concerns with 16 of 55 calculators in the benchmark, highlighting the importance of verifying clinical formulas against current guidelines.

title: Governed Human-AI Prioritization Under Uncertainty: Adaptive Estimation and Dependency-Constrained Portfolio Selection
summary: AI-native software engineering increasingly combines human judgment, historical analogy, parametric estimation, and AI-generated forecasts inside the same prioritization decision. The resulting problem is not merely how to rank candidate work, but how to govern heterogeneous estimates, uncertainty, strategic parameters, dependencies, and limited capacity in a way that remains inspectable and recalibratable. We study five quantitative operators used in the D-POAF decision practice: Business Value Score (BVS), Effort and Risk Score (ERS), Prioritization Value Score (PVS), Collective Calibration Score (CCS), and Optimal Development Path (ODP). Controlled synthetic experiments characterize their behavior under known latent variables and explicit error processes. Moderate BVS-weight perturbations preserved global rankings (median Spearman 0.986), while broader strategic changes reduced top-10% overlap to 0.788. Reliability-weighted effort aggregation achieved MAE 0.616, a 42.6% reduction relative to the best individual estimator (MAE 1.073), and outperformed a simple mean (MAE 0.638). Under estimator drift, adaptive reliability weighting reduced average RMSE by 4.5% relative to equal weighting. Model-collective divergence detected the highest-error priority estimates with ROC-AUC 0.906. In 800 dependency-constrained portfolio instances, value-to-effort achieved mean objective ratio 0.962 and ODP distance 0.953 against the exact optimum; bootstrap intervals confirm a small but systematic advantage for value-to-effort under the declared objective. These results establish a quantitative basis for evidence-weighted human-AI prioritization and define the optimization boundary between shortest-path ODP formulations and general release-portfolio selection.

AI.tldr: This paper studies five quantitative operators (BVS, ERS, PVS, CCS, ODP) used in AI-native software engineering prioritization. Through controlled synthetic experiments, it demonstrates that reliability-weighted effort aggregation reduces MAE by 42.6%, adaptive weighting reduces RMSE by 4.5%, and model-collective divergence achieves 0.906 ROC-AUC for error detection. Value-to-effort ratio achieves 0.962 mean objective ratio against exact optimum.
AI.motivation: The problem is how to govern heterogeneous estimates, uncertainty, strategic parameters, dependencies, and limited capacity in AI-human hybrid prioritization decisions while maintaining inspectability and recalibratability.
AI.method: Controlled synthetic experiments with known latent variables and explicit error processes, testing five quantitative operators across various scenarios including weight perturbations, estimator drift, and dependency-constrained portfolio instances.
AI.result: Moderate BVS-weight perturbations preserved rankings (Spearman 0.986); reliability-weighted effort achieved 42.6% MAE reduction (0.616 vs 1.073); adaptive weighting reduced RMSE by 4.5%; model-collective divergence detected errors with ROC-AUC 0.906; value-to-effort achieved 0.962 mean objective ratio.
AI.conclusion: Establishes quantitative basis for evidence-weighted human-AI prioritization and defines optimization boundary between shortest-path ODP formulations and general release-portfolio selection.

title: How Much Velocity Does Off-Ball Space Value Need? A Broadcast-Viewport Benchmark
comment: 15 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Code, logs and data: https://github.com/nowayfootball/offscreen-impute (velocity/)
summary: Velocity-aware pitch control is standard, but under a broadcast viewport half the players are off screen and on-screen velocities come from a drifting calibration. We ask at which layer of broadcast off-ball analysis velocity changes the answer. Inheriting our off-screen imputation protocol (three Metrica matches, 44 m viewport, block-bootstrap CIs), we score four velocity regimes -- none, viewport-legal observed, true-for-visible, true-for-all -- against a velocity-aware ground truth at three layers: imputation, the control surface, and team verdicts. Velocity is nearly useless for imputation (-0.2 pp against a 12--14 pp velocity-free surface MAE), first-order for the surface (-1.5 to -1.8 pp, 11--15% of that MAE), and ten times smaller for verdicts (-0.12 to -0.19 pp). The velocity that matters is the visible channel: perfect occluded-player velocity adds 2--6% of the visible gain, and no last-seen decay policy we tested exceeds that. Omitting velocity blurs the surface (per-frame |e| 2.2--2.6 pp) with small time-averaged bias (per cell <=0.4 pp), whereas imputation error is a structured bias against the defending team's deep zone (5--9 pp). At a fixed velocity window, a noise ladder of eleven jitter settings, including sigma_v-matched pairs, is ordered to first order by one velocity-noise axis sigma_v with break-even ~1 m/s; eleven SoccerNet-GSR clips from one match through our pipeline measure sigma_v=1.65 m/s yet recover 24--36% of the benefit: 43% of the variance is frame-common, which the surface tolerates, and the residual is heavy-tailed and clustered, which Gaussian controls matched on component RMS do not reproduce (+0.03 vs. +0.36). The share of velocity-free error that velocity removes grows with viewport width (7% at 36 m, 21% at 60 m): fix imputation on tight shots, velocity on wide ones. Code and logs are released.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the role of velocity information in broadcast off-ball analysis for football (soccer), examining its impact at three layers: imputation, control surface, and team verdicts. The key finding is that velocity matters most for the control surface (11-15% error reduction), has minimal effect on imputation, and is ten times smaller for team verdicts. Visible channel velocity is most important, while perfect occluded-player velocity adds only 2-6% benefit. The study also analyzes velocity noise tolerance and shows that viewport width affects velocity's importance (7% at 36m vs 21% at 60m).
AI.motivation: The motivation is to determine at which layer of broadcast off-ball analysis velocity changes the answer, given that standard velocity-aware pitch control has limitations: half the players are off-screen in broadcast viewports, and on-screen velocities come from a drifting calibration. The authors seek to quantify the actual value of velocity information across different analysis layers.
AI.method: The study inherits an off-screen imputation protocol using three Metrica matches with a 44m viewport and block-bootstrap confidence intervals. Four velocity regimes are evaluated: none, viewport-legal observed, true-for-visible, and true-for-all. Evaluation occurs at three layers: imputation, control surface, and team verdicts. A noise ladder with eleven jitter settings (including sigma_v-matched pairs) is tested, and eleven SoccerNet-GSR clips are processed through the pipeline.
AI.result: Velocity is nearly useless for imputation (-0.2 pp against 12-14 pp velocity-free surface MAE), first-order for the surface (-1.5 to -1.8 pp, 11-15% of MAE), and ten times smaller for verdicts (-0.12 to -0.19 pp). Perfect occluded-player velocity adds only 2-6% of visible gain. Omitting velocity blurs the surface (per-frame |e| 2.2-2.6 pp) with small time-averaged bias (≤0.4 pp per cell), while imputation error shows structured bias against the defending team's deep zone (5-9 pp). Break-even velocity noise is ~1 m/s. SoccerNet-GSR clips show sigma_v=1.65 m/s yet recover 24-36% of benefit; 43% of variance is frame-common. The share of velocity-free error removed by velocity grows with viewport width (7% at 36m, 21% at 60m).
AI.conclusion: Velocity matters most for the visible channel: perfect occluded-player velocity adds minimal benefit (2-6%). The recommendation is to fix imputation on tight shots and focus on velocity for wide shots. The residual error is heavy-tailed and clustered, which Gaussian controls matched on component RMS cannot reproduce (+0.03 vs. +0.36). Code and logs are released.

title: ZipCodec: Ultra-Low-Frame-Rate Streaming Speech Coding
summary: Neural audio codecs are a fundamental component of modern speech generation systems. While recent codecs achieve increasingly low bitrates, reducing frame rate remains challenging, as each token must preserve more information while maintaining reconstruction quality. We present ZipCodec, a streaming neural speech codec operating at 6.25 Hz and 0.80 kbps with a theoretical latency of 160 ms. Our approach combines large-scale WavLM distillation with a redesigned transformer-based architecture, a scalar spherical quantizer, and a latency-aware streaming decoder. Experiments show that ZipCodec substantially outperforms existing streaming codecs at comparable bitrates in both reconstruction and downstream tasks, while operating at a significantly lower frame rate. Despite its 842M parameters, ZipCodec achieves real-time single-stream inference on a consumer-grade CPU. Demo samples, code and checkpoints are available at https://lucadellalib.github.io/zipcodec-web/.

AI.tldr: ZipCodec is a streaming neural speech codec achieving 6.25 Hz frame rate and 0.80 kbps bitrate with 160ms latency, using WavLM distillation, transformer architecture, scalar spherical quantizer, and latency-aware streaming decoder. Despite having 842M parameters, it runs in real-time on consumer CPUs and outperforms existing streaming codecs in reconstruction and downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: Current neural audio codecs face a fundamental challenge: reducing frame rate while maintaining reconstruction quality becomes increasingly difficult as each token must preserve more information. The need for更低 bitrates and lower frame rates while preserving quality drives this research.
AI.method: The approach combines: (1) Large-scale WavLM distillation for knowledge transfer, (2) Redesigned transformer-based architecture, (3) Scalar spherical quantizer for efficient encoding, (4) Latency-aware streaming decoder for real-time operation.
AI.result: ZipCodec substantially outperforms existing streaming codecs at comparable bitrates in both reconstruction quality and downstream tasks, while operating at a significantly lower frame rate. It achieves real-time single-stream inference on consumer-grade CPU despite having 842M parameters.
AI.conclusion: ZipCodec demonstrates that ultra-low frame rates (6.25 Hz) and bitrates (0.80 kbps) can be achieved without sacrificing quality, enabling efficient streaming neural speech codecs that run in real-time on consumer hardware.

title: Adaptive Margin Ordinal Loss: Penalizing Center-Class Hedging in Ordinal Classification
summary: Standard cross-entropy loss causes neural networks trained on ordinal classification tasks to hedge predictions toward center classes, a failure mode we term \emph{center-class hedging}. This occurs because predicting the middle class minimizes expected symmetric loss, making it the path of least resistance regardless of the true label. Existing ordinal losses address related problems such as large-error penalization and rank consistency, but none directly suppresses center-class hedging as a function of where the true label lies relative to the ordinal center. We propose the Adaptive Margin Ordinal Loss (AMOL), a multiplicative weight applied to per-class loss terms of the form $m(k,y) = 1 + α\cdot (1 - |k-c|/c) \cdot (|y-c|/c)$, where $c$ is the center class, $k$ is the candidate class, and $y$ is the true label. The weight encodes a joint condition: it is large only when the candidate class is near center and the true label is far from center, collapsing to standard behavior otherwise. We further introduce the Center-Hedging Rate (CHR) as a diagnostic metric that directly quantifies this failure mode. Across four ordinal classification benchmarks and five random seeds, AMOL achieves the best or tied-best Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK) on all four datasets compared to cross-entropy, OLL, and SORD baselines. An asymmetric variant (AMOL-asym) eliminates center-class hedging entirely on the Abalone dataset ($\text{CHR} = 0.000 \pm 0.000$ across all five seeds, $n \approx 266$ extreme-class test samples per run), compared to $0.074 \pm 0.005$ for standard cross-entropy.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "center-class hedging" as a failure mode in ordinal classification where neural networks predict middle classes to minimize expected symmetric loss. It proposes AMOL (Adaptive Margin Ordinal Loss) with multiplicative weights that increase when the candidate class is near center and true label is far from center. The paper also introduces Center-Hedging Rate (CHR) as a diagnostic metric. Experiments on 4 benchmarks show AMOL achieves best or tied-best QWK, with AMOL-asym eliminating center-class hedging entirely on Abalone (CHR = 0.000 vs 0.074 for cross-entropy).
AI.motivation: Standard cross-entropy loss causes neural networks in ordinal classification tasks to hedge predictions toward center classes. This occurs because predicting the middle class minimizes expected symmetric loss. While existing ordinal losses address large-error penalization and rank consistency, none directly suppresses this center-class hedging behavior based on where the true label lies relative to the ordinal center.
AI.method: The authors propose the Adaptive Margin Ordinal Loss (AMOL), which applies multiplicative weights to per-class loss terms using formula m(k,y) = 1 + α·(1 - |k-c|/c)·(|y-c|/c), where c is the center class, k is the candidate class, and y is the true label. This weight is large only when the candidate class is near center and true label is far from center, collapsing to standard behavior otherwise. They also introduce Center-Hedging Rate (CHR) as a diagnostic metric to quantify this failure mode.
AI.result: Across four ordinal classification benchmarks and five random seeds, AMOL achieves the best or tied-best Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK) on all four datasets compared to cross-entropy, OLL, and SORD baselines. The asymmetric variant (AMOL-asym) eliminates center-class hedging entirely on the Abalone dataset (CHR = 0.000 ± 0.000 across all five seeds, n ≈ 266 extreme-class test samples per run), compared to 0.074 ± 0.005 for standard cross-entropy.
AI.conclusion: AMOL successfully addresses center-class hedging in ordinal classification by using adaptive margins that specifically penalize predictions toward center classes when the true label is extreme. The proposed CHR metric effectively quantifies this failure mode, and AMOL achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks.

title: Studying Without a Syllabus: Task-Agnostic Environment Preprocessing
summary: Before an LLM agent tackles tasks in a new environment, it can inspect available corpora and tools and construct reusable resources such as indices, scripts, or procedural guidance. Most automated adaptation methods, however, rely on task examples, trajectories, or evaluation feedback to decide what to build. Existing task-agnostic approaches avoid this supervision but commit in advance to a preparation strategy for a particular type of environment. We study a more open-ended setting: can an agent study an unfamiliar environment without a syllabus, i.e. before test time and without knowledge of the downstream task distribution, and choose how to prepare it? We formalize task-agnostic environment preprocessing, in which a studying system explores an environment under a budget and produces artifacts for a frozen solver. We compare unaided and archive-equipped meta-agents with fixed synthetic-practice and corpus-processing methods across six heterogeneous benchmarks. A meta-agent variant achieves the highest Avg@3 reward on five benchmarks, while fixed corpus processing remains best on the largest corpus benchmark. Larger study budgets do not reliably improve downstream reward. Nevertheless, studied artifacts reduce the test-time sampling needed to reach a given score, demonstrating how reusable preparation can shift computation from repeated test-time attempts to a pre-task study phase.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how LLM agents can autonomously prepare for new environments by exploring and creating reusable artifacts (like indices, scripts, guidance) without task-specific supervision or knowledge of downstream tasks. The authors formalize "task-agnostic environment preprocessing" and compare meta-agents against fixed methods across six benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current automated adaptation methods rely on task examples, trajectories, or evaluation feedback to decide what to build. Existing task-agnostic approaches commit in advance to a preparation strategy for a particular environment type. The authors seek to explore a more open-ended setting: can an agent study an unfamiliar environment without guidance, before test time, and without knowledge of the downstream task distribution?
AI.method: The authors formalize task-agnostic environment preprocessing, where a studying system explores an environment under a budget constraint and produces artifacts (indices, scripts, procedural guidance) for a frozen solver. They compare unaided and archive-equipped meta-agents with fixed synthetic-practice and corpus-processing methods across six heterogeneous benchmarks.
AI.result: A meta-agent variant achieves the highest Avg@3 reward on five out of six benchmarks, while fixed corpus processing remains best on the largest corpus benchmark. Larger study budgets do not reliably improve downstream reward. However, studied artifacts reduce test-time sampling needed to reach a given score, shifting computation from repeated test-time attempts to pre-task study phase.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that LLM agents can autonomously prepare for new environments by creating reusable artifacts without task-specific supervision. This approach shifts computational cost from test-time to study-time, though the optimal preparation strategy varies depending on environment characteristics (especially corpus size). The findings suggest that meta-agents with adaptive preparation strategies generally outperform fixed approaches, but the largest corpus scenarios still benefit from specialized corpus processing.

title: LLMVul: A Vulnerability-Labeled Dataset of LLM-Generated C/C++ Functions from Real Production Repositories
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate and assist with software development, yet existing vulnerability datasets largely focus on human-written code or controlled prompting environments. This limits the ability to study security weaknesses in LLM-generated code as it appears in real-world software projects. We present LLMVul, a vulnerability-labeled dataset of LLM-generated C/C++ functions mined from real production repositories. We mine AI-assisted development activity from GitHub over a 4 year period, from November 13, 2022 to September 3, 2026, using provenance signals such as commit metadata and AI-related authorship evidence. After filtering and deduplication, LLMVul contains 21,430 unique C/C++ functions from 226 repositories, together with repository, commit, function, provenance, and AI-tool metadata. We establish vulnerability labels using an ensemble of complementary static-analysis and pattern-based techniques and assign Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) categories to confirmed vulnerable functions. To assess labeling reliability, we additionally conduct independent manual annotation and measure inter-rater agreement using Cohen's kappa ($k=0.79$). LLMVul contains 1,540 ensemble-vulnerable functions spanning 17 unique CWE categories, providing substantially more real-world LLM-generated vulnerable C/C++ functions than existing vulnerability-oriented LLM code benchmarks. By preserving both code-level vulnerability labels and generation/provenance metadata, LLMVul enables reproducible research on vulnerability detection, security evaluation of LLM-generated code, and analysis of vulnerability patterns in AI-assisted software development. The LLMVul dataset is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22668216.

AI.tldr: LLMVul is a vulnerability-labeled dataset of LLM-generated C/C++ functions mined from real production repositories on GitHub. It contains 21,430 unique functions from 226 repositories, with 1,540 vulnerable functions spanning 17 CWE categories, enabling research on vulnerability detection and security evaluation of LLM-generated code.
AI.motivation: Existing vulnerability datasets focus on human-written code or controlled prompting environments, limiting the study of security weaknesses in LLM-generated code as it appears in real-world software projects.
AI.method: Mine AI-assisted development activity from GitHub over a 4-year period using provenance signals (commit metadata, AI-related authorship evidence). Apply ensemble of static-analysis and pattern-based techniques for vulnerability labeling, assign CWE categories, and validate with manual annotation (Cohen's kappa k=0.79).
AI.result: LLMVul contains 21,430 unique C/C++ functions from 226 repositories, including 1,540 ensemble-vulnerable functions spanning 17 unique CWE categories, providing substantially more real-world LLM-generated vulnerable C/C++ functions than existing benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: LLMVul enables reproducible research on vulnerability detection, security evaluation of LLM-generated code, and analysis of vulnerability patterns in AI-assisted software development. The dataset is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22668216.

title: TrajFusionNet+: Transformer-Based Prediction of Pedestrian Crossing Intention via Fusion of Trajectory Representations and Scene Graphs
comment: This work has been submitted to Signal, Image and Video Processing for possible publication
summary: The pedestrian crossing intention task involves predicting whether pedestrians are likely to cross the road from the point of view of an autonomous vehicle. We introduce TrajFusionNet+, a novel transformer-based model for pedestrian crossing intention prediction. TrajFusionNet+ combines sequential and visual representations of pedestrian trajectory with a graph-based representation of the scene context in order to predict pedestrian crossing intention. The proposed architecture builds upon our previous model, TrajFusionNet, and comprises three branches: a Sequence Attention Module (SAM), which processes a sequential representation of past and predicted pedestrian trajectories; a Visual Attention Module (VAM), which utilizes a visual representation of the pedestrian trajectories by overlaying observed and predicted bounding boxes onto scene images; and a Graph Attention Module (GAM), which extracts pedestrian-centric graphs from segmented scene images and captures the relational dependencies between pedestrians and traffic elements. TrajFusionNet+ achieves improved state-of-the-art performance on the two most widely used pedestrian crossing intention datasets, PIE and JAAD. Furthermore, we introduce a new evaluation protocol in which models are trained jointly on the PIE and JAAD datasets but evaluated separately on each. Under this setting, TrajFusionNet+ demonstrates superior generalization compared to existing approaches.

AI.tldr: TrajFusionNet+ is a transformer-based model for predicting pedestrian crossing intention in autonomous vehicles. It combines three attention modules (SAM, VAM, GAM) to process sequential, visual, and graph-based representations of pedestrian trajectories and scene context. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance on PIE and JAAD datasets and demonstrates superior generalization under a new joint-training evaluation protocol.
AI.motivation: Pedestrian crossing intention prediction is critical for autonomous vehicle safety. Existing methods may not adequately capture the complex interactions between pedestrian trajectories and scene context. This work aims to improve prediction accuracy by integrating multiple modalities - sequential trajectory data, visual information, and graph-based scene relationships - using an advanced transformer architecture.
AI.method: TrajFusionNet+ employs a three-branch architecture: (1) Sequence Attention Module (SAM) processes sequential representations of past and predicted pedestrian trajectories; (2) Visual Attention Module (VAM) overlays observed and predicted bounding boxes onto scene images to extract visual features; (3) Graph Attention Module (GAM) extracts pedestrian-centric graphs from segmented scene images and captures relational dependencies between pedestrians and traffic elements. The model combines these three modalities for crossing intention prediction.
AI.result: TrajFusionNet+ achieves improved state-of-the-art performance on the two most widely used pedestrian crossing intention datasets (PIE and JAAD). Additionally, under a new evaluation protocol where models are trained jointly on both datasets but evaluated separately, TrajFusionNet+ demonstrates superior generalization compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: The multi-modal transformer approach with three attention branches effectively captures the complex factors influencing pedestrian crossing behavior. The joint training evaluation protocol provides a more rigorous test of model generalization. Future work may explore additional modalities or real-time deployment considerations.

title: Continuous-Time Acoustic Modelling with Neural Controlled Differential Equations
comment: Accepted to IEEE Spoken Language Technology Workshop (SLT) 2026
summary: Text-to-speech (TTS) models commonly address text--speech alignment by expanding phone-level encoder states to frame-level decoder inputs using predicted durations. While this length-regulation step resolves alignment structurally, this use of duration typically changes only where and how often latent states appear, not the values of the states themselves. This paper proposes a continuous-time mechanism for duration-aware acoustic modelling in TTS using neural controlled differential equations (CDEs). We formulate the phone representation as a temporally parameterised control path and use a neural acoustic vector field to produce a continuous-time hidden state whose values evolve with phonetic content and duration-derived timing. The resulting trajectory can be sampled at discrete points and integrated into a standard acoustic decoder pipeline. Objective results contrast CDEs and typical recurrent models. Subjective results suggest that CDE-based models evaluating one phone per step can improve rank-order agreement between synthesised and reference emotion intensity while maintaining comparable emotion-expression quality to a strong baseline. Additional experiments with half-phone step-sizes suggest that temporal resolution changes the trade-off between style tracking and absolute calibration. These results position CDEs as a promising design space for continuous-time and duration-aware style-sensitive TTS.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using neural controlled differential equations (CDEs) for continuous-time duration-aware acoustic modelling in TTS systems. The approach treats phone representations as temporally parameterised control paths and uses a neural acoustic vector field to produce continuous hidden states that evolve with both phonetic content and duration-derived timing. This allows for more nuanced duration handling beyond just changing state repetition patterns.
AI.motivation: Current TTS models use predicted durations to expand phone-level encoder states to frame-level decoder inputs, but this length-regulation only affects where and how often latent states appear, not the values of the states themselves. The authors seek a more sophisticated way to incorporate duration information that actually influences the hidden state values during synthesis.
AI.method: The proposed method formulates phone representation as a temporally parameterised control path and uses a neural acoustic vector field to produce continuous-time hidden states. These states evolve with phonetic content and duration-derived timing. The resulting trajectory can be sampled at discrete points and integrated into a standard acoustic decoder pipeline. Experiments compare CDEs against typical recurrent models using both objective metrics and subjective evaluations (particularly for emotion intensity).
AI.result: Objective results compare CDEs and typical recurrent models. Subjective results show that CDE-based models evaluating one phone per step can improve rank-order agreement between synthesized and reference emotion intensity while maintaining comparable emotion-expression quality to a strong baseline. Additional experiments with half-phone step-sizes reveal that temporal resolution affects the trade-off between style tracking and absolute calibration.
AI.conclusion: Neural CDEs represent a promising design space for continuous-time and duration-aware style-sensitive TTS. The approach enables more sophisticated handling of duration information that influences hidden state values, with potential benefits for emotion expression and style control in speech synthesis.

title: A Bellman Optimality Equation for Plasticity
summary: In continual reinforcement learning, carefully managing the stability-plasticity tradeoff remains a core challenge. Recent work by Abel et al. (2025) formalized this dilemma by defining plasticity as the generalized directed information from an agent's observations to its actions, and empowerment as the generalized directed information from its actions to its observations. This formulation successfully reframes the traditional stability-plasticity tradeoff as an empowerment-plasticity tradeoff. However, while extensive literature exists on optimizing for empowerment, there is currently no research addressing the optimization of plasticity under this new definition. This paper presents preliminary work toward optimizing plasticity within Markov decision processes. We show that there exists a Bellman optimality equation for optimizing plasticity similar to previous work for empowerment.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the optimization of "plasticity" (generalized directed information from observations to actions) in continual reinforcement learning, building on a new formalization that reframes the stability-plasticity tradeoff as an empowerment-plasticity tradeoff. The authors show that a Bellman optimality equation exists for optimizing plasticity, analogous to previous work on empowerment.
AI.motivation: The stability-plasticity tradeoff is a core challenge in continual reinforcement learning. While Abel et al. (2025) formalized plasticity and empowerment as generalized directed information, no prior work has addressed optimizing plasticity under this new definition, despite extensive literature on empowerment optimization.
AI.method: The paper presents preliminary theoretical work to derive a Bellman optimality equation for optimizing plasticity within Markov decision processes (MDPs), similar to the approach used for empowerment optimization.
AI.result: The authors demonstrate that a Bellman optimality equation for optimizing plasticity does exist, suggesting that plasticity can be optimized in MDPs using similar dynamic programming techniques as empowerment.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes the theoretical foundation for optimizing plasticity in RL, opening avenues for future algorithms that can balance empowerment and plasticity in continual learning settings.

title: When Validation Stops Learning: Auditing Update Admission for Continual Embodied Agents
summary: Independent evaluation can reject harmful policy updates yet also prevent useful continual learning. We argue that update admission must be assessed through both error control and retained learning opportunities at a stated interaction budget. We identify a concrete failure: a range-based confidence gate cannot certify unchanged old-task behavior within otherwise substantial budgets. A standard paired-binomial construction reduces this burden when outcome disagreements are rare. We also specify certified historical-reference promotion and a round-level missed-opportunity metric. In a constructed one-step pushing diagnostic with 32 seeds, fresh paired checks admit 31.6% of a common update stream at 2,000 episodes per stage, versus zero for the range-based gate; unconditional replay nevertheless learns better in closed-loop runs. A separate learned-dynamics stress test distinguishes model bias from feedback-selection error. The contribution is an admission-audit protocol with analytical and synthetic evidence; physical-robot and VLA validation remain open.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a critical challenge in continual learning: how to decide whether to accept policy updates that could improve learning but might also harm previously learned behaviors. The authors propose an "admission-audit protocol" that evaluates updates based on both error control and retained learning opportunities within a given interaction budget.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that independent evaluation (used to reject harmful updates) can paradoxically prevent useful continual learning by being too restrictive. Existing methods like range-based confidence gates fail to certify unchanged old-task behavior within reasonable interaction budgets. This creates a fundamental tension between safety (avoiding performance degradation on old tasks) and improvement (learning new skills).
AI.method: The authors develop several key methods: (1) A paired-binomial construction that reduces the certification burden when outcome disagreements are rare, (2) certified historical-reference promotion as an evaluation framework, (3) a round-level missed-opportunity metric to quantify learning opportunities lost due to overly conservative admission, and (4) a learned-dynamics stress test to distinguish model bias from feedback-selection error. Experiments use a one-step pushing task with 32 seeds and 2,000 episodes per stage.
AI.result: In the one-step pushing diagnostic, fresh paired checks admit 31.6% of a common update stream at 2,000 episodes per stage, compared to zero for the range-based gate. Notably, unconditional replay (accepting all updates) still learns better in closed-loop runs, suggesting the current conservative approach may be too restrictive. The learned-dynamics stress test successfully distinguishes model bias from feedback-selection error.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes an admission-audit protocol that balances safety and learning opportunity. The key insight is that existing conservative gate mechanisms are too restrictive, blocking useful learning. The proposed paired-check approach allows more updates while maintaining safety guarantees. Physical-robot and VLA (vision-language-action) validation remain future work.

title: What a Random Draw from the MCP Registry Contains, and What Tool-Use Benchmarks Contain Instead
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures. Seeded, re-runnable pipeline and per-server outcomes: https://github.com/itguruhaseeb/mcp-probe ; archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.21347997
summary: Studies of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) server ecosystem draw their samples in ways that quietly select for servers that work: reference sets, popularity lists, hand-curated frames, or pipelines that repair a server until it starts. We report what an unrepaired probability sample actually contains. From a 24,135-server registry census we draw 400 npm/stdio servers with a published seed and probe each one over the wire. Only 48.8% complete an initialize handshake, against 66.7% for a hand-curated frame measured with the same instrument, and the dominant failure is not missing credentials (13.3%) but servers that never start at all (37.5%). Among the 195 that do run, hard conformance is total: zero fatal JSON Schema violations across 2,766 advertised tools. Optional safety annotations are the real variance, and the tool-level omission rate on a random draw is 58.8% against 41.5% on the curated frame, so curation flatters this figure too. We then compare the tool descriptions these servers advertise against two tool-use benchmark corpora using one method held constant. Real MCP tools show 2.8% near-duplication at cosine 0.70, and all of it lies within single servers: cross-author near-duplication is 0.0% at every threshold tested. BFCL v4 shows 16.7%, of which 16.4 points lie between independently presented tasks. UltraTool shows 0.3%, cleaner than real tools, so this is a property of BFCL and not of synthetic corpora as a class. Separately, 68.8% of raw BFCL rows and 85.6% of raw UltraTool rows are exact name-plus-description repeats, against 0.4% for real MCP, so any statistic computed over these releases without global deduplication measures repetition rather than tools. All figures regenerate from released scripts and a published seed.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals systematic sampling bias in MCP server ecosystem studies. From a census of 24,135 servers, only 48.8% of randomly sampled servers complete initialization (vs 66.7% in curated frames). The dominant failure (37.5%) is servers that never start, not missing credentials. Among working servers, tool conformance is perfect but safety annotations are often missing. Benchmark corpora (BFCL v4, UltraTool) contain significant repetition (68.8-85.6% exact repeats), skewing any statistics computed over them.
AI.motivation: Previous MCP server studies use non-probability samples (reference sets, popularity lists, hand-curated frames) that quietly select for functional servers. The authors sought to discover what an unrepaired probability sample actually contains to understand the true state of the ecosystem.
AI.method: Drew a simple random sample of 400 npm/stdio servers from a 24,135-server registry census, with published seed for reproducibility. Probed each server over the wire using the same instrument as used for curated frame measurement. Compared tool descriptions against BFCL v4 and UltraTool benchmark corpora using constant methodology.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Only 48.8% complete initialize handshake vs 66.7% for curated frame; (2) dominant failure is servers never starting (37.5%), not missing credentials (13.3%); (3) zero fatal JSON Schema violations across 2,766 tools in working servers; (4) safety annotation omission rate is 58.8% (random) vs 41.5% (curated); (5) real MCP tools show 2.8% near-duplication at cosine 0.70, all within single servers; (6) BFCL v4 shows 16.7% near-duplication (16.4 points between independent tasks); (7) 68.8% of raw BFCL and 85.6% of raw UltraTool rows are exact repeats vs 0.4% for real MCP.
AI.conclusion: Curated samples systematically overestimate server success rates and underestimate safety annotation gaps. Benchmark corpora contain massive repetition—without global deduplication, statistics measure repetition rather than tool diversity. The MCP ecosystem's actual functional rate is ~50%, and benchmark quality issues must be addressed for valid evaluation.

title: Overpainting: Localized Context-aware Diffusion Image Editing
summary:
We present "overpainting", an image editing operation which offers both control over the location of the edit and awareness of the previous content in that location. The overpainted area is given by a trimap, where white-annotated pixels must be edited, gray-annotated pixels may be edited, and black-annotated pixels must not be edited. This enables both precise and loose control, depending on user intent.
  We implement overpainting by adapting a pretrained image editing diffusion model using a combination of joint attention and low-rank adaption across input images with attention-dropout to balance the information flow between noise, source and mask images. We present a novel, automated, training data generation pipeline that (1) generates a set of candidate image pairs leveraging existing language-based editing models, (2) carefully curates those pairs, and (3) extracts a trimap from each usable pair. We demonstrate the versatility of our overpainting model on a wide range of editing tasks.
