title: Counterfactual Marginalisation: Framework for Evaluating Robustness to Nuisance Variables
summary: Machine learning models can achieve strong test performance while relying on demographic or acquisition-related shortcuts. We propose counterfactual (CF) marginalisation as a test-time evaluation procedure for assessing robustness of classification models to such variables. Given a CF image generator, we intervene on nuisance parent variables such as age or sex, generate CF versions of each test image, and average predictions over a target intervention distribution. This produces intervention-aware predictions that marginalise demographic effects while preserving patient-specific latent information. We use these predictions to define metrics for CF risk, calibration, stability and worst-case sensitivity. We demonstrate this framework's utility for quantitative robustness evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes counterfactual marginalization as a test-time evaluation framework to assess ML model robustness to demographic or acquisition-related shortcuts. The method intervenes on nuisance variables (e.g., age, sex), generates counterfactual images, and averages predictions to produce intervention-aware predictions that marginalize demographic effects.
AI.motivation: ML models can achieve high test performance by relying on spurious correlations (demographic or acquisition-related shortcuts) rather than learning true underlying patterns. Current evaluation methods fail to assess robustness to such variables, necessitating a test-time procedure to evaluate model robustness.
AI.method: The proposed counterfactual marginalization approach involves: (1) Using a counterfactual image generator, (2) Intervening on nuisance parent variables (e.g., age, sex), (3) Generating counterfactual versions of each test image, (4) Averaging predictions over a target intervention distribution to produce intervention-aware predictions that preserve patient-specific latent information while marginalizing demographic effects.
AI.result: The framework enables definition of metrics for counterfactual risk, calibration, stability, and worst-case sensitivity, providing quantitative measures for robustness evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Counterfactual marginalization provides a practical test-time evaluation procedure for assessing and quantifying model robustness to demographic shortcuts, with potential applications in clinical ML where demographic bias is a significant concern.

title: Decoupling Readiness from Release for Tail-Aware Scheduling of Agentic LLM Workflows
summary: Agentic LLM workflows consist of sequences of model turns interleaved with tool interactions, so their end-to-end completion time depends not only on inference speed but also on when ready turns are released. Most runtimes release each turn immediately upon readiness. Under contention, this eager release policy can accumulate released but unfinished work; once submitted, those turns can no longer be reordered by the workflow-level policy, increasing tail latency. We present a tail-risk-aware turn release scheduling method that jointly decides which ready turn to release next and how much released but unfinished work to maintain. The method uses a mean--Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) objective to capture the evolving tail risk of unfinished workflows, incorporates online estimates of turn work when prioritizing ready turns, and adapts the released work budget to observed queue pressure. We evaluate the method using real agent execution traces from software engineering tasks across multiple LLMs and workflow arrival rates. The method performs comparably to eager release under light load and substantially reduces the P95 of workflow flow time under contention, achieving up to a \(3.50\times\) speedup.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses tail latency in LLM agentic workflows by proposing a tail-risk-aware turn release scheduling method that intelligently controls when ready turns are released and maintains a budget of released but unfinished work, achieving up to 3.50x speedup in P95 workflow flow time under contention.
AI.motivation: Under contention, eager release policies (releasing turns immediately upon readiness) accumulate released but unfinished work that cannot be reordered, increasing tail latency. Existing runtimes lack mechanisms to control this accumulation.
AI.method: The method uses a mean-Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) objective to capture tail risk of unfinished workflows, incorporates online estimates of turn work when prioritizing ready turns, and adapts the released work budget to observed queue pressure.
AI.result: The method performs comparably to eager release under light load and substantially reduces P95 workflow flow time under contention, achieving up to a 3.50× speedup.
AI.conclusion: Tail-risk-aware turn release scheduling is effective for LLM agentic workflows under contention, balancing throughput and tail latency without requiring changes to the underlying LLM or workflow structure.

title: Engineering Reliable Commit Gates for Agentic AI: Cost-Aware Verification Portfolios under Common-Mode Data Failures
summary: Agentic systems commit state-changing actions, but additional verifiers can inherit the same upstream fault. We present VP-CONTROL, a runtime-assurance design and deterministic benchmark for cost-aware commit gates. Its 48 task templates yield 2,880 scenarios across six fault regimes. A fixed-call 2 x 2 experiment separates verifier-model diversity from evidence-source diversity. On frozen proposals from two local actor families, a cross-model vote over shared evidence approves 62.9% of unsafe proposals, versus 22.9% with an independent source. The source effect is 40.9 percentage points, compared with 11.3 for model diversity. A portfolio controller selects verification plans using only deployment-observable metadata. Approximate cluster-adjusted calibration at a nominal 5% per-task target yields 1.9% unsafe execution and 38.2% automated safe coverage on the locked test. Matched-budget portfolios also improve on fixed verification policies. Transfer remains conditional: unseen fault families yield 16-26% risk, and a FinQA check fails to reproduce the source effect with the tested small verifiers. A preregistered live HTTP/SQLite study tests concurrent writes and lost responses. After-check races defeat verifier-only gates; transactional partial guards prevent only covered failures, while a full atomic guard records no unsafe effects across 216 episodes. Idempotent request identifiers prevent duplicate effects after lost responses. The results motivate explicit evidence lineage, cost-aware selection, and commit-time enforcement, while exposing the limits of approximate calibration and local-tool generalization.

AI.tldr: VP-CONTROL is a runtime-assurance framework for cost-aware commit gates in agentic systems. It addresses the problem where verifiers can inherit the same upstream faults as the agents they check. The system uses evidence-source diversity (40.9 pp effect) more effectively than model diversity (11.3 pp) to reduce unsafe proposal approvals from 62.9% to 22.9%, with calibrated execution achieving 1.9% unsafe rate and 38.2% safe coverage.
AI.motivation: Agentic systems commit state-changing actions, but additional verifiers can inherit the same upstream faults as the agents they're checking. This creates a critical security vulnerability where verification fails to catch errors that originated in the same fault path as the agent's reasoning.
AI.method: VP-CONTROL uses a deterministic benchmark with 48 task templates yielding 2,880 scenarios across six fault regimes. A fixed-call 2x2 experiment separates verifier-model diversity from evidence-source diversity. Cross-model voting over shared evidence is compared against independent evidence sources. A portfolio controller selects verification plans using deployment-observable metadata with approximate cluster-adjusted calibration targeting 5% per-task unsafe rate. A live HTTP/SQLite study tests concurrent writes and lost responses.
AI.result: Cross-model vote over shared evidence approves 62.9% of unsafe proposals, versus 22.9% with an independent source—a 40.9 percentage point source effect vs. 11.3 for model diversity. Calibrated execution yields 1.9% unsafe execution and 38.2% automated safe coverage. Matched-budget portfolios improve on fixed verification policies. Unseen fault families yield 16-26% risk. A FinQA check fails to reproduce the source effect with small verifiers. After-check races defeat verifier-only gates; transactional partial guards prevent only covered failures, while full atomic guard records no unsafe effects across 216 episodes. Idempotent request identifiers prevent duplicate effects after lost responses.
AI.conclusion: The results motivate explicit evidence lineage, cost-aware selection, and commit-time enforcement. Key limitations include: approximate calibration has bounded effectiveness, local-tool generalization is conditional (unseen fault families yield 16-26% risk), and small verifiers fail to reproduce the source effect. Full atomic guards with idempotent request identifiers provide the strongest protection against concurrent writes and lost responses.

title: BodyCam-VQA: Enhanced Body-Worn Camera Video Captioning via Multimodal Reasoning and Probe Question Generation
summary: Police body-worn camera (BWC) footage has emerged as a critical aspect of law enforcement that ensures legal transparency, officer accountability, and the protection of civil rights. However, effectively processing this data remains a significant challenge due to its multimodal video format. BWC videos, in many cases, comprise chaotic scenes with low visual quality, rapid movement/interactions, and high-noise audio that make visual understanding a challenge for even SOTA multimodal models. Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) frequently overlook critical forensic details, such as the presence of valuable evidence or the latent nuances of suspect-officer interactions, which are vital for fair legal outcomes and civilian/officer safety. To address these limitations, we propose an Adaptive Visual Question Answering (VQA) framework engineered for high-stakes law enforcement. Our framework employs a structured reasoning approach to extract fine-grained visual evidence that traditional captioning systems fail to capture. We experiment with multiple question generation models, including foundation models and fine-tuned open-weight models, to observe performance variation among question generation model implementations. Our results demonstrate that this VQA-driven architecture provides a more reliable, objective, and detailed record of enforcement events, ultimately serving as a powerful tool to protect both law enforcement officers and the public through AI-assisted forensic clarity.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an Adaptive Visual Question Answering (VQA) framework for analyzing police body-worn camera (BWC) footage in law enforcement contexts. The framework addresses the challenges of processing multimodal video data with chaotic scenes, low visual quality, and high-noise audio by using a structured reasoning approach to extract fine-grained visual evidence that traditional captioning systems miss.
AI.motivation: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) overlook critical forensic details such as evidence presence and suspect-officer interaction nuances in BWC videos. The high-stakes nature of law enforcement requires more reliable, objective, and detailed records to ensure fair legal outcomes and protect both civilians and officers.
AI.method: The framework employs a structured reasoning approach for extracting fine-grained visual evidence. It experiments with multiple question generation models, including foundation models and fine-tuned open-weight models, to compare performance variations across different implementations.
AI.result: The VQA-driven architecture provides more reliable, objective, and detailed records of enforcement events compared to traditional captioning systems, serving as a tool for AI-assisted forensic clarity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed VQA framework can effectively process challenging BWC footage and extract critical forensic details, making it a valuable tool for protecting both law enforcement officers and the public through AI-assisted analysis.

title: From Connectivity to Rewards: Dense Reward Learning with Directed State Graphs
summary: The integration of graphs with Goal-Conditioned Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (GCHRL) has received increasing attention, as graphs naturally encode task hierarchies for effective subgoal sampling. However, existing methods often overlook intrinsic connectivity information, failing to fully leverage the underlying topology for efficient learning. Most graph-based GCHRL methods use the graph as a stochastic sampling tool rather than as an environmental model that encodes connectivity and state-accessibility information. This limitation is particularly acute in quasimetric environments, where the inherent asymmetry of state transitions poses a fundamental challenge to stable policy learning and robust path planning. In this paper, we address these problems by introducing a state connectivity model designed to predict pairwise state connectivity strength in asymmetric environments. We transform these connectivity strengths into scalar auxiliary dense rewards, providing continuous guidance across multiple hierarchical levels. We demonstrate that our proposed framework, Graph-Guided Quasimetric Dense Reward (G2QDR), can theoretically be integrated into any existing GCHRL architecture, and the state connectivity model is efficiently implemented via a neural network trained on a directed state graph generated during exploration. Empirical results across a wide range of sparse reward environments indicate that, in general, G2QDR can enhance the performance of baseline GCHRL approaches with acceptable computational overhead.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses limitations in Graph-based Goal-Conditioned Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (GCHRL) by introducing a state connectivity model that predicts pairwise state connectivity in asymmetric (quasimetric) environments. The framework, G2QDR, transforms connectivity strengths into scalar auxiliary dense rewards to guide hierarchical learning across multiple levels.
AI.motivation: Existing GCHRL methods use graphs merely as stochastic sampling tools rather than environmental models that encode connectivity and state-accessibility. This is particularly problematic in quasimetric environments where asymmetric state transitions challenge stable policy learning and robust path planning. The paper aims to leverage intrinsic connectivity information that prior methods overlook.
AI.method: The proposed G2QDR framework introduces a state connectivity model implemented as a neural network, trained on a directed state graph generated during exploration. This model predicts pairwise state connectivity strength in asymmetric environments and transforms these strengths into scalar auxiliary dense rewards providing continuous guidance across hierarchical levels.
AI.result: Empirical results across sparse reward environments demonstrate that G2QDR enhances baseline GCHRL approaches with acceptable computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: G2QDR can theoretically be integrated into any existing GCHRL architecture, providing a general framework for leveraging state connectivity information in asymmetric environments. The method shows consistent performance improvements across diverse sparse reward tasks.

title: Demystifying the Privacy-Utility Trade-off in LLM Interactions
summary: The integration of Large Language Models into daily tasks relies on context-rich instructions, inevitably exposing sensitive user information. Current privacy-preserving methods typically employ context-agnostic static rules, causing severe utility degradation. However, the specific mechanisms governing how sanitization impacts downstream performance remain largely underexplored. To address this, we conduct a systematic analysis to deconstruct the privacy-utility trade-off, uncovering three underlying mechanisms: (1) Context-Dependent Utility, which first establishes when to sanitize by revealing that data value shifts from critical constraints to dispensable noise based on user intent; (2) Strategic Adaptation, which subsequently determines how to sanitize by dictating that the choice between removal and replacement depends on the task's reliance on factual integrity versus structural coherence; and (3) Combinatorial Interplay, which finally extends the protection scope by demonstrating that attributes form a semantic web of synergistic dependencies or antagonistic redundancies. Guided by these insights, we introduce an intent-driven local protection framework. By distilling a lightweight model Veilmind-4B to drive a dynamic extraction-sanitization-restoration pipeline, our approach reaches a low-leakage privacy point while preserving substantially higher response utility than existing privacy-oriented baselines, advancing the privacy-utility trade-off toward the Pareto frontier.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses privacy concerns in LLM applications by proposing an intent-driven local protection framework (Veilmind-4B) that uses a dynamic extraction-sanitization-restoration pipeline to balance privacy protection with utility preservation, outperforming existing privacy-oriented baselines.
AI.motivation: Current privacy-preserving methods for LLMs use context-agnostic static rules that cause severe utility degradation. The specific mechanisms governing how sanitization impacts downstream performance remain underexplored, creating a need to understand the privacy-utility trade-off.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic analysis to deconstruct the privacy-utility trade-off, identifying three mechanisms: (1) Context-Dependent Utility - determining when to sanitize based on user intent; (2) Strategic Adaptation - determining how to sanitize (removal vs replacement); and (3) Combinatorial Interplay - understanding attribute dependencies. They then introduce Veilmind-4B, a lightweight model driving a dynamic extraction-sanitization-restoration pipeline.
AI.result: The approach achieves low leakage privacy while preserving substantially higher response utility than existing privacy-oriented baselines, advancing the privacy-utility trade-off toward the Pareto frontier.
AI.conclusion: The three mechanisms (Context-Dependent Utility, Strategic Adaptation, and Combinatorial Interplay) provide a framework for understanding when and how to sanitize sensitive information. The Veilmind-4B model demonstrates that intent-driven dynamic protection can significantly outperform static rule-based approaches in maintaining the privacy-utility balance.

title: RCL: A Retrieval-Confidence Layer for Detecting Insufficient Context in Enterprise Retrieval-Augmented Code Generation
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for code generation has been studied extensively on public repositories, where a model's parametric knowledge often compensates for imperfect retrieval. This breaks down in enterprise codebases, where private APIs, internal frameworks, and undocumented team conventions fall entirely outside any model's pretraining distribution. Recent work on private-library code generation shows that even oracle (perfect) retrieval does not eliminate errors, but locates failures downstream in API usage; separately, confidence-gated retrieval has been studied for open-domain question answering using model-internal confidence. Neither addresses whether retrieval itself was structurally sufficient for a private-code query before generation begins. We introduce RCL (Retrieval-Confidence Layer), a lightweight module inserted between retrieval and generation that combines a call-graph-derived structural coverage score with a novelty score estimating a query's dependence on knowledge outside the model's prior, to detect insufficient retrieval before generation occurs. When confidence falls below a calibrated threshold, RCL triggers a targeted follow-up retrieval or labels the output for human review, rather than generating silently against incomplete context. We describe RCL's architecture, formalize its scoring functions, and propose an evaluation methodology using a private-code benchmark built by injecting synthetic internal APIs into open-source Java repositories, simulating the enterprise condition without proprietary code. We report results (Section 7) comparing RCL against similarity-only retrieval on generation correctness. Our position is that retrieval sufficiency, assessed structurally rather than from model-internal confidence, is a distinct and currently underaddressed signal for building safer code-generation systems in private, enterprise settings.

AI.tldr: RCL (Retrieval-Confidence Layer) is a lightweight module that detects insufficient retrieval in code generation before generation occurs, by combining structural coverage scores (via call graph analysis) with novelty scores (estimating query dependence on out-of-distribution knowledge). When confidence is low, it triggers follow-up retrieval or flags for human review. The approach is evaluated on a synthetic private-code benchmark.
AI.motivation: In enterprise codebases, private APIs and internal frameworks fall outside models' pretraining distribution. Existing work shows that even perfect retrieval doesn't eliminate errors downstream. Neither prior work on private-library code generation nor confidence-gated retrieval addresses whether retrieval itself was structurally sufficient before generation begins.
AI.method: RCL combines two scoring functions: (1) a call-graph-derived structural coverage score, and (2) a novelty score estimating query dependence on knowledge outside the model's prior. A calibrated threshold triggers either targeted follow-up retrieval or labels output for human review when confidence falls below threshold. Evaluation uses a private-code benchmark with synthetic internal APIs injected into open-source Java repositories.
AI.result: Results comparing RCL against similarity-only retrieval on generation correctness are reported in Section 7 (specific metrics not provided in abstract).
AI.conclusion: Retrieval sufficiency, assessed structurally rather than from model-internal confidence, is a distinct and currently underaddressed signal for building safer code-generation systems in private, enterprise settings.

title: Are We Really Doing Few-Shot Learning? A Critical Examination of Pre-Training Assumptions
summary: Few-shot learning is commonly evaluated under protocols that pre-train a model on a large auxiliary set whose classes are disjoint from the target episodes yet drawn from the same visual domain. This paper examines whether such protocols truly reflect low-data learning. We systematically compare no pre-training, class-disjoint in-domain pre-training, supervised out-of-domain pre-training, and label-free out-of-domain pre-training across eight datasets, three few-shot architectures, and multiple way-shot settings. Our results show that class disjointness alone is insufficient to remove the influence of target-domain data. In-domain pre-training improves over no pre-training by 33.41 percentage points on average, whereas supervised out-of-domain pre-training yields 23.75 percentage points, revealing a 9.66-point optimistic bias associated with domain overlap. Although out-of-domain pre-training is more realistic in applications where target-domain data are scarce, its effectiveness depends strongly on the compatibility between source and target domains. We further show that labeled source data are not strictly required, with an augmentation-based label-free strategy reaching an average gain of 27.71 percentage points and closely matching supervised out-of-domain pre-training at 27.97 percentage points. Finally, we introduce a descriptor-based source-selection strategy that estimates source-domain suitability before pre-training, reaching a median gap of only 1.37 percentage points to oracle selection. These findings highlight the need to move beyond in-domain pre-training as the default few-shot evaluation protocol, since it can overestimate performance in realistic scenarios where target-domain data are scarce.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the standard few-shot learning evaluation protocol by showing that in-domain pre-training creates an optimistic bias. The authors systematically compare different pre-training strategies across multiple datasets and architectures, demonstrating that out-of-domain pre-training is more realistic but depends on domain compatibility, and that label-free (augmentation-based) approaches can be nearly as effective as supervised methods.
AI.motivation: The standard few-shot learning evaluation protocol uses class-disjoint in-domain pre-training, but the authors question whether this truly reflects low-data learning in real-world scenarios where target-domain data are scarce. They suspect that in-domain pre-training overestimates performance by inadvertently leaking target-domain information.
AI.method: The authors conducted a systematic comparison across 8 datasets, 3 few-shot architectures, and multiple way-shot settings, evaluating four pre-training strategies: (1) no pre-training, (2) class-disjoint in-domain pre-training, (3) supervised out-of-domain pre-training, and (4) label-free out-of-domain pre-training. They also introduced a descriptor-based source-selection strategy to estimate domain compatibility before pre-training.
AI.result: In-domain pre-training improved over no pre-training by 33.41 percentage points on average. Supervised out-of-domain pre-training yielded 23.75 percentage points improvement, revealing a 9.66-point optimistic bias from domain overlap. The augmentation-based label-free strategy achieved 27.71 percentage points gain, closely matching supervised out-of-domain pre-training at 27.97 percentage points. The descriptor-based source-selection achieved a median gap of only 1.37 percentage points to oracle selection.
AI.conclusion: The standard in-domain pre-training protocol overestimates performance in realistic scenarios. Label-free (augmentation-based) pre-training can nearly match supervised out-of-domain pre-training, and domain compatibility is crucial. The field should move beyond in-domain pre-training as the default evaluation protocol.

title: DR-LabStack: Design and Implementation of a Clinician-Facing Web System for Diabetic Retinopathy Prediction
summary: Pretrained diabetic retinopathy (DR) prediction models differ in their input fields, serialization formats, preprocessing requirements, and output semantics. Making these models accessible through a common clinical interface therefore requires explicit coordination between the user interface and the inference service. We designed and implemented DR-LabStack, a React-Flask web system integrating four externally developed pretrained models: RuleFit, Pruned RuleFit, Elaborative XGBoost, and Two-level Ensemble. A shared form retrieves ordered model features, renders model-specific numerical and categorical controls, and constructs a positional input vector. Backend adapters load heterogeneous artifacts and apply the ensemble's accompanying scaler, while a common JSON response supports binary classification display alongside method and source information. Functional evaluation on September 8, 2026 used copied application files and real model artifacts in a documented isolated environment. All four models loaded and exposed their 14-, 6-, 8-, and 25-field contracts. Sixty-two Flask test-client requests characterized service behavior; 12 limited-vector checks confirmed invocation-path and threshold consistency. Twenty-four browser-component scenarios with mocked transport verified input ordering and result rendering and characterized input-validation behavior. The resulting system demonstrates a reusable interaction and serving workflow for heterogeneous DR models. The contribution is web-system design, integration, and software functionality; clinical effectiveness and clinician usability require separate evaluation.

AI.tldr: DR-LabStack is a React-Flask web system that integrates four heterogeneous pretrained diabetic retinopathy (DR) prediction models (RuleFit, Pruned RuleFit, Elaborative XGBoost, Two-level Ensemble) into a common clinical interface, addressing interoperability challenges through shared forms, backend adapters, and standardized JSON responses.
AI.motivation: Pretrained DR prediction models differ in input fields, serialization formats, preprocessing requirements, and output semantics, making it challenging to expose them through a common clinical interface without explicit coordination between the UI and inference service.
AI.method: Designed a web-system with: (1) shared form retrieving ordered model features and rendering model-specific controls; (2) backend adapters loading heterogeneous artifacts and applying scalers; (3) common JSON response for binary classification. Functional evaluation tested 4 models (14/6/8/25 fields), 62 Flask requests, 12 vector checks, and 24 browser scenarios.
AI.result: All four models loaded successfully with their respective field contracts (14, 6, 8, 25 fields). The system demonstrated consistent invocation-path and threshold behavior, correct input ordering, result rendering, and input-validation behavior.
AI.conclusion: DR-LabStack demonstrates a reusable interaction and serving workflow for heterogeneous DR models. The contribution is the web-system design, integration, and software functionality. However, clinical effectiveness and clinician usability require separate evaluation.

title: Defining AI Agents: A Compendium of Criteria, Metrics, and Benchmarks
summary: The term agent in artificial intelligence lacks a standard definition, complicating the evaluation, comparison, and reproducibility of AI agent research. We address this ambiguity through a survey organized around five dimensions of agenticness: environmental interaction, learning and adaptation, autonomy, goal-directed behavior, and temporal coherence. For each dimension, we examine how the underlying capability has been conceptualized across prior work and synthesize the metrics, benchmarks, and evaluation frameworks used to assess it. This review provides a structured account of the current landscape of agent evaluation, highlighting both established approaches and areas where evaluation remains limited or inconsistent. We additionally introduce the Agent Compendium, a public-facing digital resource that organizes and extends the evaluation methods identified through this review. Together, the survey and compendium provide a common structure for evaluating and comparing agent capabilities across AI systems, supporting more reproducible research, clearer communication, and more systematic study of artificial agents.

AI.tldr: This survey addresses the lack of standard definition for "agent" in AI by organizing the concept around five dimensions of agenticness: environmental interaction, learning and adaptation, autonomy, goal-directed behavior, and temporal coherence. The paper synthesizes evaluation methods across these dimensions and introduces the Agent Compendium as a public resource for organizing evaluation frameworks.
AI.motivation: The term "agent" in artificial intelligence lacks a standard definition, which complicates the evaluation, comparison, and reproducibility of AI agent research. This ambiguity hinders systematic study and clear communication in the field.
AI.method: Survey-based review organized around five dimensions of "agenticness": environmental interaction, learning and adaptation, autonomy, goal-directed behavior, and temporal coherence. For each dimension, the authors examine how the underlying capability has been conceptualized and synthesize the metrics, benchmarks, and evaluation frameworks used to assess it.
AI.result: A structured account of the current landscape of agent evaluation, highlighting both established approaches and areas where evaluation remains limited or inconsistent. The Agent Compendium is introduced as a public-facing digital resource that organizes and extends the evaluation methods identified through the review.
AI.conclusion: The survey and compendium together provide a common structure for evaluating and comparing agent capabilities across AI systems, supporting more reproducible research, clearer communication, and more systematic study of artificial agents.

title: SaltBench: A Referee-Gated Protocol for Measuring Method Effects in Machine-Checked Software Work
summary: SaltBench is a benchmark protocol for one question: How does a machine referee change the way a coding agent works? A machine referee --- a proof kernel, a program verifier, or a withheld test suite --- decides what an agent's work is worth, and the agent cannot argue with it. Here we report a protocol that makes the referee's effect measurable and whose answers cannot be narrated afterwards: every outcome is decided outside the agent's own toolchain; the agent is walled off from the network, the reference solutions and the harness itself, and the wall is tested by probes that try to breach it before any scored run, so the isolation is observed rather than assumed; every run is authorized by a dated freeze with its predictions registered; and a budget stop is a halt, never a failure. In this study, the subject of the benchmark is a ``seat'', meaning an agent session in its standard harness. We tested five systems components, all authored in Rust under a pinned Verus toolchain, with a withheld test suite as the referee for each. Four arms are tested: a plain agent; an agent that is also instructed to create a specification and verify the code against it, in a reduced rendering of the method, as registered; and two arms where the specification is provided a priori, extended under a dated amendment to $k=4$, where the registered sign test reached no verdict (3 of 4, $p = 0.3125$, every premium below the resolvable floor). We found that the arm instructed to specify and verify cost more on all five components, and by a practical margin: across these five components no premium exceeded $2.8879\times$ under either reading of the declared set, and the three cheapest sat below $1.4\times$. That bound is a property of this population and not a promise about larger ones: the premium runs near $1$ on the smallest components and rises with size. We publish the complete record.

AI.tldr: SaltBench is a benchmark protocol designed to measure how machine referees (proof kernels, program verifiers, or withheld test suites) change the behavior of coding agents. The protocol ensures strict isolation through dated freezes, tested wall breaches, and external outcome determination.
AI.motivation: To measure how a machine referee changes the way a coding agent works, with observable rather than assumed isolation. The study aims to quantify the "premium" (cost overhead) when agents must satisfy machine referees rather than human ones.
AI.method: Tested five Rust system components with pinned Verus toolchain across four arms: (1) plain agent, (2) agent instructed to create specification and verify code, (3-4) two arms with a priori specification extended under dated amendment to k=4. Used withheld test suite as referee, with registered sign test reaching no verdict (3 of 4, p=0.3125).
AI.result: The arm instructed to specify and verify cost more on all five components. No premium exceeded 2.8879x under either reading of the declared set; three cheapest components were below 1.4x. Premium runs near 1 on smallest components and rises with size.
AI.conclusion: Specification and verification imposes a practical but bounded cost premium on coding agents. The premium is a property of this specific population (five components) and not a general promise—it correlates with component size, being near 1 for small components and increasing for larger ones.

title: Evaluation of Vision-Language Models Across Diverse Coastal Environments
comment: This work has been accepted for publication with the 2026 IEEE OCEANS conference
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable robotic per- ception by associating visual observations with natural-language concepts. Yet their performance in coastal environments remains largely unexplored. We introduce a densely labeled coastal dataset containing more than 1,000 images collected across seven missions in three regions of Oahu, Hawaii, with 18 semantic classes and over 7,400 annotated instances. We evaluate seven modern VLMs through three complementary experiments mea- suring text-to-mask, mask-to-mask, and mask-to-text alignment. Broad landscape classes are generally recognized more accurately than conventional object and coastal classes, with coastal con- cepts presenting the greatest challenge. However, comparisons of shared conventional classes across coastal and terrestrial datasets reveal no consistent performance difference attributable solely to environmental context. Mask-to-mask matching also remains similar across conventional and coastal classes, while alternative textual labels substantially improve recognition of several coastal concepts. These results suggest that lower performance on coastal classes (at least on the objects/query categories evaluated) is heavily influenced by segmentation and linguistic representation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a new coastal dataset from Hawaii to evaluate vision-language models (VLMs) for robotic perception. Testing seven VLMs across three experiments (text-to-mask, mask-to-mask, mask-to-text), the study finds that landscape classes are recognized better than coastal objects, and performance issues stem more from segmentation and linguistic representation than environmental context.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models are increasingly used for robotic perception, but their performance in coastal environments remains under-explored. The researchers aimed to fill this gap by creating a dedicated coastal dataset and systematically evaluating VLM capabilities in this domain.
AI.method: The researchers created a densely labeled coastal dataset with over 1,000 images from seven missions across three regions in Oahu, Hawaii, containing 18 semantic classes and 7,400+ annotated instances. They evaluated seven modern VLMs through three complementary experiments: (1) text-to-mask alignment, (2) mask-to-mask matching, and (3) mask-to-text alignment.
AI.result: Broad landscape classes were recognized more accurately than conventional object and coastal classes, with coastal concepts presenting the greatest challenge. However, when comparing shared conventional classes across coastal and terrestrial datasets, no consistent performance difference was found due to environmental context alone. Mask-to-mask matching remained similar across conventional and coastal classes, while alternative textual labels substantially improved recognition of several coastal concepts.
AI.conclusion: Lower performance on coastal classes is heavily influenced by segmentation quality and linguistic representation rather than environmental factors alone. The study suggests that VLM performance in coastal domains can be improved through better prompt engineering (alternative textual labels) and addressing segmentation limitations.

title: RiVaT-Fuse: Reliability-Calibrated Variational Tensor Fusion for Multimodal Prediction under Modality Uncertainty
summary: Image-metadata prediction requires fusing heterogeneous evidence whose reliability can vary across samples and latent factors. Existing representation-level fusion methods typically choose an aggregation architecture, such as concatenation, gating, conditional modulation, or attention, without explicitly defining what the fused representation should mean under modality uncertainty. We propose RiVaT-Fuse, a reliability-calibrated variational tensor fusion framework that defines fusion as sample-wise latent-state estimation. Rather than producing a fused vector by direct aggregation, RiVaT-Fuse estimates a consensus latent state through a variational objective that balances image evidence, metadata evidence, structured cross-modal interaction, and stability. The resulting framework replaces scalar modality confidence with matrix-valued trust geometry, decomposes interaction into additive, multiplicative, and relational components, and couples the latent state with conditional robustness and structured multi-task prediction. We provide well-posedness and stability interpretations of the latent solve and instantiate the framework with efficient low-rank-plus-diagonal trust operators. On an image-level image-metadata prediction benchmark, RiVaT-Fuse achieves the strongest overall predictive rank among direct representation-level baselines while improving probability and label stability under perturbation.

AI.tldr: RiVaT-Fuse is a reliability-calibrated variational tensor fusion framework for image-metadata prediction that models fusion as sample-wise latent-state estimation rather than direct aggregation. It replaces scalar modality confidence with matrix-valued trust geometry and decomposes interaction into additive, multiplicative, and relational components.
AI.motivation: Existing representation-level fusion methods (concatenation, gating, conditional modulation, attention) choose an aggregation architecture without explicitly defining what the fused representation should mean under modality uncertainty. The reliability of image and metadata evidence can vary across samples and latent factors, requiring a more principled approach to fusion.
AI.method: RiVaT-Fuse estimates a consensus latent state through a variational objective that balances: (1) image evidence, (2) metadata evidence, (3) structured cross-modal interaction, and (4) stability. Key innovations include: matrix-valued trust geometry (replacing scalar modality confidence), decomposition of interaction into additive, multiplicative, and relational components, coupling with conditional robustness and structured multi-task prediction. Implementation uses efficient low-rank-plus-diagonal trust operators.
AI.result: On an image-level image-metadata prediction benchmark, RiVaT-Fuse achieves the strongest overall predictive rank among direct representation-level baselines while improving probability and label stability under perturbation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed variational framework provides a well-posed and stable approach to fusion by explicitly modeling reliability through trust geometry rather than relying on ad-hoc aggregation architectures. The method demonstrates superior predictive performance with improved robustness to perturbations.

title: The Agent Incident Registry: Toward Preventing Repeated AI Agent Failures
summary: AI agents increasingly act through tools and delegated authority, but general incident repositories rarely capture the mechanisms needed to compare public failures with agent-security evaluations. We present the Agent Incident Registry (AIR), a source-linked catalog containing \N{} records of agent-related events disclosed from \Yfirst{} through \Ylast{}. Each record includes supporting evidence, a stable identifier, and missingness-aware labels for causal role, disclosure class, mechanism, and outcome. Among the \Nprimary{} generative-system records in which the agent acted, \Rprimary{} involved realized harm (\Pprimary\%). Realized outcomes concentrate in in-the-wild and safety-failure records, while responsible disclosures and research demonstrations are overwhelmingly demonstrated; the aggregate share therefore characterizes collection composition rather than deployment risk. After initial curation, a second human reviewer checked all \N{} records and their existing labels for completeness and correctness. In a deployment-analogue audit, InjecAgent's \NInjecAgentCases{} cases occupy three of AIR's twelve surfaces and are all attacker-triggered, whereas AIR contains \Nsafety{} no-adversary safety failures. AIR supports source-grounded case retrieval and evaluation-scope auditing, not failure-rate or control-efficacy estimation.

title: A Model-Centric DevOps Architecture for DEVS-Based Digital Twin Simulation Services
comment: Submitted to Software and Systems Modeling (Springer). Under review
summary: Digital twin simulation models are evolved and redeployed like software, yet DEVS-based engines offer a sound formal basis with little support for versioning, automated validation, or continuous delivery in cloud-native environments, leaving model lifecycle management ad hoc in most deployments. This paper proposes a model-centric DevOps architecture for deploying DEVS-based digital twin simulations as managed services. Simulation models are treated as first-class DevOps artefacts defined in a declarative YAML language with a formal mapping to multiPDEVS, supporting structural and semantic validation in a CI/CD pipeline that produces immutable versioned artefacts, so that reverting to an earlier validated version reduces to pinning its identifier. The platform is decomposed into containerised microservices on Kubernetes, with engine adaptations for state externalisation and lifecycle control. An initial case study on the Riga Route 22 public-transit corridor, the first instantiation of a planned city-wide multi-modal transport digital twin for Riga, Latvia, exercises the full lifecycle and reports single-container engine throughput for a scenario with roughly 47,870 DEVS atomic components; pipeline-level catch statistics and cluster-level concurrent multi-scenario execution are the subject of companion empirical studies.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a model-centric DevOps architecture for deploying DEVS-based digital twin simulations as managed services in cloud-native environments, addressing gaps in versioning, automated validation, and continuous delivery. The approach uses a declarative YAML language with formal mapping to multiPDEVS, CI/CD pipelines for validation, and Kubernetes-based microservices. A case study on Riga's Route 22 transit corridor demonstrates the system with ~47,870 DEVS atomic components.
AI.motivation: Digital twin simulation models are evolved and redeployed like software, yet existing DEVS-based engines lack support for versioning, automated validation, or continuous delivery in cloud-native environments. This leaves model lifecycle management ad hoc in most deployments, creating a need for systematic DevOps practices tailored to simulation models.
AI.method: The paper proposes: (1) A declarative YAML language for defining simulation models as first-class DevOps artifacts with formal mapping to multiPDEVS; (2) Structural and semantic validation in a CI/CD pipeline producing immutable versioned artifacts; (3) Platform decomposition into containerized microservices on Kubernetes with engine adaptations for state externalization and lifecycle control.
AI.result: The case study on Riga Route 22 public-transit corridor (first instantiation of Riga's planned city-wide multi-modal transport digital twin) exercises the full lifecycle. Results include single-container engine throughput for ~47,870 DEVS atomic components, with pipeline-level catch statistics and cluster-level concurrent multi-scenario execution studied empirically.
AI.conclusion: The proposed model-centric DevOps architecture enables systematic lifecycle management of DEVS-based digital twin simulations as managed services in cloud-native environments, with benefits including versioned immutable artifacts, automated validation, and the ability to revert to earlier validated versions by pinning identifiers.

title: Symmetry-aware super-resolution of crystal orientation maps via invariant latent-space learning
summary: Crystal-orientation maps are physical fields defined only up to crystal symmetry; electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) resolves them experimentally, but acquisition-time constraints limit spatial resolution. Unlike conventional images, EBSD data lie on the quotient space $\mathrm{SO}(3)/G$, where $G$ is the crystal-symmetry group. Standard Euclidean interpolation can therefore mix symmetry-equivalent representations and blur grain boundaries. We introduce the Symmetry-Group-Aware Super-Resolution Attention Network (SG-SRAN), which incorporates crystal symmetry and boundary preservation by design. A frozen, locally isometric encoder maps equivalent orientations to a common latent representation in which Euclidean distance approximates misorientation. Super-resolution is performed in this space, with each high-resolution token restricted to a feature-consistent local support to prevent cross-boundary mixing. A dictionary-based decoder then recovers valid orientations. Across FCC and HCP benchmarks, SG-SRAN matches 15-16 million parameter backbones using only 27-49k trainable parameters, while achieving the lowest p68 errors, highest inverse-pole-figure fidelity, and zero-shot transfer to unseen alloys.

AI.tldr: SG-SRAN is a highly efficient super-resolution network for crystal-orientation maps from EBSD data. It leverages crystal symmetry by mapping equivalent orientations to a common latent space where Euclidean distance approximates misorientation, achieving comparable performance to models with 300x more parameters while preserving grain boundaries and enabling zero-shot transfer to unseen alloys.
AI.motivation: EBSD crystal-orientation maps are defined on the quotient space SO(3)/G, where G is the crystal symmetry group. Conventional Euclidean interpolation incorrectly mixes symmetry-equivalent representations and blurs grain boundaries, while acquisition-time constraints limit spatial resolution. A method that respects crystal symmetry while enabling efficient super-resolution was needed.
AI.method: The method introduces a frozen, locally isometric encoder that maps symmetry-equivalent orientations to a common latent representation where Euclidean distance approximates misorientation. Super-resolution is performed in this latent space with each high-resolution token restricted to a feature-consistent local support to prevent cross-boundary mixing. A dictionary-based decoder then recovers valid orientations from the super-resolved features.
AI.result: SG-SRAN achieves performance comparable to 15-16 million parameter backbone models using only 27-49k trainable parameters (approximately 300x reduction). It achieves the lowest p68 errors, highest inverse-pole-figure fidelity, and demonstrates zero-shot transfer to unseen alloys across FCC and HCP benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The symmetry-group-aware approach successfully enables efficient super-resolution of EBSD orientation maps while preserving grain boundaries. The extreme parameter efficiency suggests the frozen encoder provides strong prior knowledge, and the method's zero-shot transfer capability indicates good generalization to unseen alloys.

title: Processing and classifying bird songs using wavelet techniques and supervised learning
summary: This study proposes an integrated framework for the processing and classification of invasive bird species vocalizations within natural soundscapes, characterized by high levels of environmental noise. We address the challenge of signal degradation by employing a Bayesian wavelet shrinkage methodology based on the Epanechnikov kernel prior, which offers a closed form decision rule and high computational efficiency for processing large bioacoustic datasets. The methodology was applied to recordings of three species obtained from the iNaturalist platform: \textit{Euphonia violacea}, \textit{Leiothrix lutea}, and \textit{Passer domesticus}. After signal denoising, we extracted a comprehensive set of features, including Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs) and spectral indices such as entropy and zero-crossing rate. Several supervised learning models: Random Forest, Multinomial Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machine (SVM) were evaluated across different feature dimensionalities. Our results demonstrate that the proposed wavelet based preprocessing significantly enhances classification performance, with the SVM model achieving the highest accuracy (up to 0.9398) under a 10-dimensional MFCC configuration. This research provides a robust statistical tool for automated ecological monitoring and the management of biological invasions.

title: Grounding Agent Memory: Environment-Probing Curation for Enterprise Agents
summary: Persistent memory is entering production-oriented agent platforms to help long-horizon agents accumulate experience across sessions. Yet a post-task curator agent restricted to completed trajectories can preserve errors, overgeneralize partial evidence, or retain stale knowledge. We introduce environment-probing curation, a deployment-compatible extension that gives an existing asynchronous curator agent least-privilege, read-only world tools to check, scope, and refresh candidate memories. It requires no model retraining and leaves the task agent, retriever, memory representation, and production write authority unchanged. In a production-like GitHub Copilot (GHCP) harness built on its SDK, we compare stateless execution, full in-context learning, GHCP + Mem, and GHCP + Mem (w/ Env Probing) on CLBench database exploration and 90 adapted APEX management-consulting tasks. On CLBench, probing raises pass rate from 39% to 73% and pass-discounted reward from 8.60 to 22.60 while reducing queries from 8.8 to 4.7 per question and task-agent cost from \$3.38 to \$1.68. Across six APEX worlds, all 18 memory-versus-baseline mean reward comparisons are positive and task-agent tool calls fall by 16--75%; probing gives the best task-agent reward gain per dollar in five worlds. Probing also attains higher mean reward than GHCP + Mem on both Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7 without schema drift. Environment probing therefore turns existing agent-memory curation into an environment-informed, auditable process while preserving a compact task-time interface.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "environment-probing curation" to improve memory management in production AI agents. The approach gives a curator agent read-only tools to verify and refresh memories against the current environment, without requiring model retraining or changing the existing system architecture. Experiments on GitHub Copilot show significant improvements in task success rates while reducing costs.
AI.motivation: Current post-task curator agents in production agent platforms are limited to completed trajectories, which causes them to preserve errors, overgeneralize from partial evidence, or retain stale knowledge. This leads to degraded performance in long-horizon tasks where accumulated memories become outdated or incorrect.
AI.method: The authors propose environment-probing curation - a deployment-compatible extension that provides an existing asynchronous curator agent with least-privilege, read-only world tools to check, scope, and refresh candidate memories. The approach requires no model retraining and leaves the task agent, retriever, memory representation, and production write authority unchanged.
AI.result: On CLBench database exploration tasks, probing raised pass rate from 39% to 73% and pass-discounted reward from 8.60 to 22.60 while reducing queries from 8.8 to 4.7 per question and task-agent cost from $3.38 to $1.68. Across six APEX management-consulting worlds, all 18 memory-versus-baseline mean reward comparisons were positive and task-agent tool calls fell by 16-75%. Probing achieved the best task-agent reward gain per dollar in five worlds and attained higher mean reward than GHCP + Mem on both Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7 without schema drift.
AI.conclusion: Environment probing transforms existing agent-memory curation into an environment-informed, auditable process while preserving a compact task-time interface. It effectively addresses memory staleness and error propagation issues in production agent systems without requiring architectural changes or model retraining.

title: FST Pay: Deterministic Safety-Gated Architecture for Youth Digital Payments
summary: Digital payment infrastructures increasingly provide adolescent users with direct access to real-time financial services. While early access promotes financial literacy and digital inclusion, it exposes young users to severe risks of impulsive spending, social engineering frauds, unauthorized transactions, and merchant exploitation. Conventional countermeasures rely on probabilistic machine learning or rigid static controls. However, allowing probabilistic or generative artificial intelligence (AI) models to directly influence real-time payment authorization introduces non-determinism, unpredictable edge-case behavior, and critical audit vulnerabilities. This paper introduces Financial Safety for Teens Pay (FST Pay) as an architectural and formal specification. FST Pay is founded on an immutable operational boundary: strict deterministic safety gating on the real-time authorization path coupled with decoupled downstream AI explanation. Transactions initiated via rails like UPI are subjected to six deterministic invariant checks covering spending limits, guardian co-sign policies, transaction amount thresholds, merchant category codes, temporal access intervals, and hardware integrity constraints. Transactions are classified strictly into ALLOW, REVIEW, or BLOCK outcomes through an ordered, mutually exclusive decision function. High-risk transactions trigger an asynchronous guardian co-sign workflow. Generative AI is relegated entirely downstream of settlement, consuming published post-decision events solely to generate natural-language financial insights without holding mutation privileges over the ledger.

AI.tldr: FST Pay is a deterministic architectural framework for securing adolescent digital payment transactions. It enforces six invariant checks (spending limits, guardian co-sign policies, amount thresholds, merchant category codes, temporal access, hardware integrity) on the real-time authorization path, classifying transactions as ALLOW, REVIEW, or BLOCK. Generative AI is confined downstream for post-decision insights only, avoiding non-determinism in the payment ledger.
AI.motivation: Adolescent users of digital payment systems face severe risks including impulsive spending, social engineering fraud, unauthorized transactions, and merchant exploitation. Conventional ML-based or static control approaches are inadequate: probabilistic models introduce unpredictability, while rigid static controls lack flexibility. There is a need for a solution that ensures financial safety without compromising auditability or introducing non-determinism into real-time payment authorization.
AI.method: The paper proposes FST Pay as an architectural and formal specification combining deterministic safety gating with decoupled downstream AI. Six deterministic invariant checks are applied in an ordered, mutually exclusive decision function: spending limits, guardian co-sign policies, transaction amount thresholds, merchant category codes, temporal access intervals, and hardware integrity constraints. Transactions are classified into ALLOW, REVIEW, or BLOCK outcomes. High-risk transactions trigger asynchronous guardian co-sign workflows. Generative AI operates entirely downstream of settlement, consuming post-decision events solely for natural-language financial insights without mutation privileges.
AI.result: The framework introduces an immutable operational boundary that separates real-time deterministic authorization from asynchronous AI-driven insights. Transactions via UPI rails are subjected to strict deterministic checks, ensuring predictable behavior and auditability. Generative AI is relegated to downstream post-settlement analysis, eliminating non-determinism and edge-case unpredictability in the payment authorization path.
AI.conclusion: FST Pay provides a novel architectural approach that balances financial inclusion and digital literacy promotion for adolescents with robust safety guarantees. By enforcing deterministic safety gating on the real-time authorization path while leveraging generative AI only for downstream insights, the framework achieves both security and explainability without compromising system determinism or audit capabilities.

title: HiPerViT: A Hierarchical Perceiver-Vision Transformer Architecture for Multi-Scale Texture Recognition
summary: Texture recognition remains challenging for modern vision models because discriminative evidence is often carried by higher-order spatial statistics rather than by object shape alone. While Vision Transformers provide strong long-range modeling capacity, their standard object-centric representations do not explicitly expose such statistical structure, which limits texture sensitivity in fine-grained recognition settings. We present HiPerViT, a compact vision-only architecture that injects an explicit second-order statistical prior into a transformer-based recognition pipeline. The method combines global and local image views with a compact bilinear descriptor encoded as a statistical token, and integrates this token with first-order spatial representations through Perceiver-style latent distillation. This design enables direct interaction between spatial tokens and second-order feature co-occurrence statistics, providing the model with explicit access to texture-relevant information without requiring multimodal pretraining or ensemble construction. Across six texture recognition benchmarks, HiPerViT achieves consistent improvements over strong vision-only baselines under the reported evaluation protocols, including gains of +3.05 percentage points on DTD, +10.48 on GTOS-Mobile, and +10.10 on 1200Tex. Beyond benchmark performance, our analyses show that these gains are largely invariant to the backbone depth used to extract second-order statistics and to the ordering of interaction and distillation stages. This pattern suggests that the primary source of improvement is not a specific fusion topology, but the explicit availability of second-order statistical information as a first-class representational signal. These results support explicit statistical tokenization as an effective and robust design principle for texture-centric visual recognition.

AI.tldr: HiPerViT is a compact vision-only architecture that injects second-order statistical priors into a transformer-based pipeline for texture recognition. It combines global and local image views with a bilinear descriptor encoded as a statistical token, integrated through Perceiver-style latent distillation.
AI.motivation: Texture recognition is challenging because discriminative evidence lies in higher-order spatial statistics rather than object shape alone. Vision Transformers have strong long-range modeling but their standard object-centric representations don't expose statistical structure, limiting texture sensitivity in fine-grained recognition.
AI.method: HiPerViT combines global and local image views with a compact bilinear descriptor encoded as a statistical token. This token integrates with first-order spatial representations through Perceiver-style latent distillation, enabling direct interaction between spatial tokens and second-order feature co-occurrence statistics without multimodal pretraining or ensemble construction.
AI.result: Across six texture recognition benchmarks, HiPerViT achieves consistent improvements over strong vision-only baselines: +3.05 percentage points on DTD, +10.48 on GTOS-Mobile, and +10.10 on 1200Tex. Gains are invariant to backbone depth and ordering of interaction/distillation stages.
AI.conclusion: The primary improvement source is the explicit availability of second-order statistical information as a first-class representational signal, not a specific fusion topology. Explicit statistical tokenization is an effective and robust design principle for texture-centric visual recognition.

title: Flow Duality and Source Geometry for Categorical Generation
summary: Continuous and discrete flow matching are usually treated as separate constructions. This paper identifies a duality between them: projecting continuous convex-interpolant paths with one-hot targets through a position-wise argmax yields discrete convex-interpolant paths. The result requires source laws with appropriate coordinate symmetry and boundary regularity, and it makes the continuous source distribution an explicit design choice for categorical generation. We derive the induced discrete interpolation behavior for Gaussian, bounded-uniform, and centered negative-exponential sources, showing that different source geometries lead to qualitatively different transition timing and vocabulary-size dependence. Small visual diagnostics and a short language-modeling pilot suggest that these source-design effects can also appear in learned transports and early generative quality.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals a theoretical duality between continuous and discrete flow matching, showing that discrete convex-interpolant paths can be obtained by projecting continuous ones through argmax. The choice of continuous source distribution (Gaussian, bounded-uniform, or centered negative-exponential) significantly affects discrete interpolation behavior, including transition timing and vocabulary-size dependence, with implications for practical generative modeling.
AI.motivation: Continuous and discrete flow matching have been treated as separate constructions. This paper aims to unify them by identifying a theoretical duality, making the continuous source distribution an explicit design choice for categorical generation.
AI.method: The paper identifies a duality between continuous and discrete flow matching by projecting continuous convex-interpolant paths with one-hot targets through position-wise argmax. The analysis requires source laws with coordinate symmetry and boundary regularity. Three source distributions are analyzed: Gaussian, bounded-uniform, and centered negative-exponential, examining their induced discrete interpolation behavior.
AI.result: Different source geometries lead to qualitatively different transition timing and vocabulary-size dependence. Empirical diagnostics in visual and language modeling suggest these source-design effects can appear in learned transports and early generative quality.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a theoretical duality between continuous and discrete flow matching, showing that discrete versions can be derived from continuous projections with appropriate source distributions. This framework makes the continuous source distribution an explicit design choice, with Gaussian, bounded-uniform, and centered negative-exponential sources exhibiting different interpolation behaviors. The findings suggest that source geometry significantly impacts transition timing and vocabulary-size dependence, with implications for practical generative modeling in visual and language domains.

title: Fork Where the Model Changes Its Mind: Belief-Shift Branching for Tree-Structured Reinforcement Learning
summary: Tree-structured rollouts give critic-free reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) step-level credit: fork a chain at an intermediate point, and sibling outcome differences estimate step value. Each fork adds sampling cost, so realistic budgets typically allow only a few forks per chain. A fork placed where the outcome is already largely settled yields siblings that mostly agree and provide almost no credit signal; hence, for a given tree size, where forks are placed largely determines how much step-level RL can gain. Most existing mainstream methods place forks by structure, such as fixed lengths, midpoints, and delimiters, or by next-token entropy. We formalize fork placement as locating the \emph{pivots} of the chain's value curve, where the expected outcome turns. We propose \emph{belief-shift branching}: read the model's answer belief at candidate boundaries and fork just before the step where consecutive beliefs diverge most. Three instantiations, none needing step-level supervision, span access levels: a black-box probe, a logit-lens depth profile, and a learned activation direction, which is fit offline and therefore used only in the validation before RL training. The signal only \emph{places} forks, and the probe costs about $1\%$ of step compute on mathematics and under $5\%$ on code when it runs inside the rollout engine. In that validation, against Monte-Carlo value curves, a belief-shift signal ranks first in each of the eight model$\times$benchmark panels, ahead of entropy, structural, and LLM-judge baselines. In RL across three model families and two domains, belief-shift forking leads every mathematics aggregate, on OLMo-3-7B by $+2.6$ aggregate and $+2.9$ on AIME 2026 over the strongest baseline, and sweeps every OLMo code column, by $+6.5$ on LiveCodeBench-medium.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses optimal fork placement in tree-structured rollouts for critic-free RL by proposing "belief-shift branching" - forking just before the step where the model's answer belief diverges most. Three implementations are provided across different access levels, achieving state-of-the-art results on math and code benchmarks with minimal computational overhead.
AI.motivation: In critic-free reinforcement learning with tree-structured rollouts (RLVR), step-level credit assignment is achieved by forking chains at intermediate points and comparing sibling outcomes. However, fork placement is critical: forks placed where outcomes are already settled yield siblings that mostly agree, providing almost no credit signal. With realistic sampling budgets allowing only a few forks per chain, optimal fork placement largely determines the effectiveness of step-level RL. Existing methods (fixed lengths, midpoints, entropy-based) are suboptimal.
AI.method: The paper proposes "belief-shift branching" to locate pivots where the model's answer belief changes most. Three instantiations are presented: (1) black-box probe that reads answer belief at candidate boundaries, (2) logit-lens depth profile examining internal representations, and (3) learned activation direction fitted offline. The core insight is to fork just before the step where consecutive beliefs diverge most, as this indicates where the expected outcome turns. The signal only determines fork placement, not the credit assignment itself.
AI.result: In validation against Monte-Carlo value curves, belief-shift ranking achieves first place in all eight model×benchmark panels, outperforming entropy, structural, and LLM-judge baselines. In RL training across three model families and two domains: (1) OLMo-3-7B mathematics: +2.6 aggregate improvement, +2.9 on AIME 2026 over strongest baseline; (2) OLMo code: sweeps every column, +6.5 on LiveCodeBench-medium. The probe incurs minimal computational cost (~1% step compute on mathematics, under 5% on code).
AI.conclusion: Belief-shift branching consistently outperforms all baselines across diverse models and domains. The method achieves +2.6 aggregate improvement on OLMo-3-7B mathematics, +2.9 on AIME 2026, and +6.5 on LiveCodeBench-medium. The probe operates with minimal computational overhead (~1% on math, <5% on code), making it practical for real RL training. The approach requires no step-level supervision and works across different access levels (black-box, logit-lens, learned).

title: TripleBound: Triplet-Guided Heterogeneous Graph Learning for Microservice Decomposition
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures. Replication package available on GitHub
summary: Cloud computing and DevOps have made microservices a common architecture for scalable, maintainable software systems. However, migrating monoliths to microservices remains challenging due to tight coupling and unclear service boundaries. Existing decomposition approaches typically rely on either structural dependencies or semantic similarity signals, but rarely integrate both within a unified representation learning objective. This paper proposes TripleBound, a hybrid framework for automated monolith-to-microservices decomposition that augments a heterogeneous graph neural network with weakly supervised triplet constraints derived from parser-inferred service groups based on package structure, naming conventions, and code location. TripleBound injects triplet-based constraints directly into the shared structural latent space, enabling both signals to be jointly optimized during representation learning. Structural dependencies are captured using CHGNN, which models the monolith as a heterogeneous graph with program nodes, resource nodes, CALL edges, and CRUD edges. Semantic relationships are incorporated through triplet constraints generated from parser-inferred service groups. Evaluation on AcmeAir, DayTrader, PlantsByWebSphere, and JPetStore shows that TripleBound achieves the highest composite decomposition score under the selected weighting on AcmeAir, DayTrader, and JPetStore compared to CHGNN and MonoEmbed, while CHGNN remains stronger on PlantsByWebSphere. Per-metric analysis reveals trade-offs: gains in structural modularity and inter-partition coupling are accompanied by higher entity distribution imbalance on some datasets. Alternative composite weightings preserve TripleBound's first-place ranking on AcmeAir and DayTrader but not on JPetStore, showing that the aggregate ranking is metric-dependent.

AI.tldr: TripleBound is a hybrid framework that combines graph neural networks with weakly supervised triplet constraints to automatically decompose monolithic applications into microservices. It augments CHGNN with parser-inferred service groups to jointly optimize structural dependencies and semantic relationships.
AI.motivation: Migration from monoliths to microservices remains challenging due to tight coupling and unclear service boundaries. Existing approaches rely on either structural dependencies or semantic similarity, but rarely integrate both within a unified representation learning objective.
AI.method: TripleBound uses CHGNN to model the monolith as a heterogeneous graph with program nodes, resource nodes, CALL edges, and CRUD edges. It injects triplet-based constraints derived from parser-inferred service groups (based on package structure, naming conventions, and code location) directly into the shared structural latent space for joint optimization.
AI.result: TripleBound achieves the highest composite decomposition score on AcmeAir, DayTrader, and JPetStore compared to CHGNN and MonoEmbed, while CHGNN remains stronger on PlantsByWebSphere. Trade-offs include gains in structural modularity and inter-partition coupling but higher entity distribution imbalance on some datasets. Performance is metric-dependent.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid approach combining structural dependencies and semantic relationships through triplet constraints is effective for microservices decomposition, though performance varies across datasets and metrics. The method shows promise but has trade-offs in distribution balance.

title: CamPilot: A Multi-Agent Cinematic Assistant for Camera-Controlled Movie Generation
summary: The integration of large language models (LLMs) into video generation has enabled rapid text-to-video creation and improved visual quality. However, it still falls short of professional filmmaking, where cinematographic language is less refined than human-crafted camera work and multi-shot continuity remains challenging. To address these limitations, we introduce CamPilot, a multi-agent framework that integrates cinematographic planning and camera-work control to produce more coherent, logically structured, and human-aesthetic movies. CamPilot adopts a GRPO-based learning paradigm to learn camera work planning from 14K real-world professional movies, internalizing motion patterns and composition principles that support reasoning over shooting techniques (e.g., camera angle, motion, and focal behavior) and cross-shot relationships for controllable camera-viewpoint generation. Multiple agents further collaborate and evolve to improve overall output quality. To support this work and further studies in this domain, we establish CamEval, a benchmark for evaluating camera work quality and cinematic engagement. Empirical results show that CamPilot outperforms state-of-the-art text-to-movie generation methods on cinematographic control and quality, highlighting the impact of professional camera design on movie generation.

title: Certifying Lower Bounds for Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning under Adversarial State Perturbations
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) agents deployed in real-world environments are often vulnerable to adversarial perturbations in state observations, creating risks in safety-critical applications. Certification methods can improve robustness against adversarial perturbations by providing lower bounds on expected cumulative rewards. Existing certification methods, however, mainly focus on risk-neutral objectives. In this paper, we extend certification methods to risk-sensitive objectives by establishing lower bounds on the exponential utility of cumulative rewards under $l_{p}$-norm-bounded state adversarial perturbations ($1\leq p <\infty$). By introducing a $φ$-divergence relaxation of the perturbation set, we formulate the risk-sensitive certification problem as a convex optimization and derive its dual to obtain a tractable approximation of the certified lower bound. We further propose an empirical method that improves certified lower bounds by selecting the training risk-aversion parameter $β$ independently of the risk level used during evaluation. Experiments on both OpenAI Gym environments and a machine replacement problem show that, compared to risk-neutral training, risk-averse training generally yields policies with higher certified lower bounds, particularly under larger perturbation budgets. Moreover, under both risk-neutral and risk-averse evaluation settings, increasing risk aversion during training leads to non-monotonic certification performance, where certified lower bounds initially improve but eventually decrease due to overly conservative policies.

AI.tldr: This paper extends adversarial certification methods in reinforcement learning from risk-neutral to risk-sensitive objectives, using exponential utility and φ-divergence relaxation to derive tractable lower bounds on cumulative rewards under adversarial state perturbations.
AI.motivation: Existing RL certification methods only address risk-neutral objectives, but real-world safety-critical applications require risk-sensitive guarantees. This work aims to provide certified lower bounds on expected rewards under adversarial perturbations for risk-averse decision-making.
AI.method: The paper introduces a φ-divergence relaxation of the perturbation set to formulate the risk-sensitive certification problem as convex optimization, then derives its dual for tractable computation. An empirical method selects training risk-aversion parameter β independently of evaluation risk level.
AI.result: Risk-averse training yields higher certified lower bounds than risk-neutral training, especially under larger perturbation budgets.
