However, the relationship is non-monotonic: increasing risk aversion during training first improves but eventually decreases certified bounds due to overly conservative policies.
AI.conclusion: Risk-sensitive certification is achievable through convex optimization. The practical recommendation is to use risk-averse training for improved robustness, but careful selection of the risk-aversion parameter is needed to avoid excessive conservatism.

title: MOSAIC: Query-Aware Exploration Policy Adaptation for GraphRAG
summary:
Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) can connect evidence distributed across a corpus graph, but most systems use largely shared exploration procedures across queries. This creates a structural mismatch: direct facts may need compact local neighborhoods, comparisons need balanced coverage of multiple targets, and mediated questions may require deeper paths through weakly related connectors. We present Mosaic, a training-free framework that formulates GraphRAG retrieval as a per-query control problem. An LLM analyzer converts query-specific evidence requirements into a bounded policy over seed selection, graph traversal, stopping, and evidence selection, while the corpus graph, indexes, scoring functions, grounding procedure, and answer generator remain shared.
  On GraphRAG-Bench, Mosaic achieves query-weighted Answer Correctness of 76.97 on Medical and 64.33 on Novel, improving over the strongest previously reported overall results by 5.13 and 4.43 points. On Medical, it reaches 95.1 Evidence Recall and 86.1 Context Relevancy. Controlled comparisons on an identical graph and generator show that no fixed narrow, medium, or wide policy is consistently optimal; Mosaic improves by 9.96 points over the strongest canonical fixed policy. Relative to Fixed Wide, it evaluates 81.9% fewer paths and retains 47.2% fewer evidence items. Transfer experiments on HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and 2WikiMultiHopQA further show that the policy interface can be applied without benchmark-specific retriever training.

AI.tldr: Mosaic is a training-free framework that formulates GraphRAG retrieval as a per-query control problem, addressing the structural mismatch where different query types (direct facts, comparisons, mediated questions) require different retrieval strategies. It uses an LLM analyzer to convert query-specific evidence requirements into bounded policies over seed selection, graph traversal, stopping, and evidence selection.
AI.motivation: Current GraphRAG systems use largely shared exploration procedures across queries, creating a structural mismatch. Direct facts need compact local neighborhoods, comparisons need balanced coverage of multiple targets, and mediated questions require deeper paths through weakly related connectors. No fixed narrow, medium, or wide policy is consistently optimal across different query types.
AI.method: Mosaic uses an LLM analyzer that converts query-specific evidence requirements into a bounded policy controlling seed selection, graph traversal, stopping criteria, and evidence selection. The corpus graph, indexes, scoring functions, grounding procedure, and answer generator remain shared. This is a training-free approach that adapts retrieval strategy per query.
AI.result: On GraphRAG-Bench: Medical achieves 76.97 Answer Correctness (95.1 Evidence Recall, 86.1 Context Relevancy), Novel achieves 64.33. Improvements over strongest previous results: +5.13 (Medical) and +4.43 (Novel). Compared to strongest canonical fixed policy: +9.96 points. Relative to Fixed Wide: evaluates 81.9% fewer paths and retains 47.2% fewer evidence items. Transfer experiments on HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and 2WikiMultiHopQA show the policy interface can be applied without benchmark-specific retriever training.
AI.conclusion: Mosaic successfully addresses the structural mismatch problem in GraphRAG by treating retrieval as a per-query control problem. It outperforms fixed policies and achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks while being more efficient (fewer paths evaluated, fewer evidence items retained). The training-free approach enables transfer across benchmarks without retriever retraining.

title: Exploring the Role of Security Experience and ChatGPT Usage Strategies on Secure Software Engineering Education
summary: The rapid adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) is reshaping software engineering education, but their role in secure software engineering education remains underexplored. We report an exploratory empirical study of how 26 graduate students in a part-time MSc Cybersecurity programme used ChatGPT during a vulnerability-fixing assignment. To characterise ChatGPT use, we analysed students' ChatGPT interaction logs using a structured double-coding procedure and examined whether usage patterns and prior cybersecurity expertise were associated with assignment performance. The results show that students with varying levels of cybersecurity expertise used broadly similar ChatGPT strategies. Individual usage patterns showed descriptive differences by grade, but none remained statistically significant after correcting for multiple comparisons. In contrast, diversity of ChatGPT usage, i.e., the number of distinct usage patterns adopted, was positively associated with performance, even after controlling for cybersecurity expertise. These exploratory findings suggest that the way students engage with ChatGPT may be more informative than whether they use it, and motivate future controlled studies to guide students toward effective LLM use in secure software engineering education.

AI.tldr: This study explores how 26 graduate cybersecurity students used ChatGPT during a vulnerability-fixing assignment. While usage patterns were similar across expertise levels, the diversity of ChatGPT usage strategies was positively associated with performance.
AI.motivation: The rapid adoption of LLMs is reshaping software engineering education, but their role in secure software engineering education remains underexplored. This study aims to understand how students use ChatGPT in cybersecurity contexts and whether usage patterns correlate with performance.
AI.method: Exploratory empirical study with 26 graduate students in a part-time MSc Cybersecurity programme. Researchers analyzed ChatGPT interaction logs using a structured double-coding procedure and examined associations between usage patterns, prior cybersecurity expertise, and assignment performance.
AI.result: Students with varying cybersecurity expertise used broadly similar ChatGPT strategies. Individual usage patterns showed descriptive differences by grade, but none remained statistically significant after correcting for multiple comparisons. However, diversity of ChatGPT usage (number of distinct patterns) was positively associated with performance, even after controlling for cybersecurity expertise.
AI.conclusion: The way students engage with ChatGPT may be more informative than whether they use it. Future controlled studies are needed to guide students toward effective LLM use in secure software engineering education.

title: New Evidence, Same Choice: Testing Physical Experiment Selection in Vision Language Models
summary: A model first sees an image from one physical measurement experiment, such as how far a block coasted, and must answer a question about a new trial, such as whether the block will pass a target after a fixed push. The initial experiment may provide enough information to answer, or the model may need another measurement, such as the object's mass, friction, restitution, or spring stiffness. We study whether vision language models can decide when to answer immediately and, when more evidence is needed, which experiment to perform. Current physical reasoning benchmarks usually evaluate only the final answer, so they do not directly measure this decision-making ability. We introduce a controlled evaluation where each problem provides one measurement image and four possible physical worlds created by combining two possible masses and two possible values of another relevant property. The model must either stop and answer or select the cheapest additional experiment that can resolve the question. We construct matched problem pairs where changing either the observed measurement or the question changes the optimal action. Since all possible worlds and experiment costs are known, we can explicitly determine the optimal choice. Across six open models and 144 physical parameter sets, direct responses repeat the same action for 95.1% to 100% of image pairs even when the correct action changes. Brief reasoning improves action switching, but the best model makes both decisions correctly for only 5.9% of image pairs. Additional analysis reveals failures in measurement interpretation, physical reasoning, and response formatting. By evaluating evidence selection separately from final answers, our benchmark reveals limitations in physical reasoning that conventional answer accuracy can overlook.

AI.tldr: A benchmark evaluating whether vision-language models can decide when to answer physics questions immediately versus requesting additional experiments, testing decision-making in physical reasoning rather than just final answer accuracy.
AI.motivation: Current physical reasoning benchmarks only evaluate final answers, missing the ability to assess when models need more information. This work addresses the gap by creating a benchmark that measures decision-making: whether to answer immediately or request additional experiments (mass, friction, restitution, spring stiffness).
AI.method: Controlled evaluation with one measurement image and four possible physical worlds (2 masses × 2 other properties). Models must either answer immediately or select the cheapest additional experiment. Matched problem pairs test whether changing observations or questions changes optimal actions. Tested six open models across 144 physical parameter sets.
AI.result: Direct responses repeat the same action for 95.1-100% of image pairs even when correct action changes. Brief reasoning improves switching but the best model makes both decisions correctly for only 5.9% of image pairs. Failures occur in measurement interpretation, physical reasoning, and response formatting.
AI.conclusion: By evaluating evidence selection separately from final answers, this benchmark reveals limitations in physical reasoning that conventional answer accuracy can overlook. Current vision-language models struggle significantly with the decision-making aspect of physical reasoning.

title: Learning Orthogonal Multi-Index Models Beyond Small Initialization: Incremental Learning, Competitive Dynamics and Symmetry
summary: Recent work has identified incremental learning in shallow networks trained on single-index and multi-index models. However, existing analyses often rely on simplifying settings, such as small initialization, correlation loss, or layer-wise training. These choices reduce neuron interactions and leave some feature learning dynamics under standard initialization unexplored. We study training dynamics for polynomial-width two-layer networks learning orthogonal multi-index targets under standard initialization using polynomially many samples. We first prove that incremental learning still occurs: the loss decreases sequentially according to the Hermite expansion of the target, with lower-order components learned before higher-order components recover the individual target directions. In this standard initialization regime, training also shows a competitive reallocation of parameter mass: after the total mass fits the target mean and stabilizes, mass shifts into the target subspace and then concentrates on aligned neurons. Our theoretical analysis uses slightly modified gradient flow, while vanilla gradient descent empirically exhibits the same qualitative dynamics. Technically, we introduce a symmetry-based finite-width approximation via symmetrized networks, rather than comparing directly with an infinite-width limit. This yields better control of approximation errors and may be of independent interest.

AI.tldr: This paper studies training dynamics of polynomial-width two-layer networks learning orthogonal multi-index targets under standard initialization. It proves that incremental learning still occurs (lower-order Hermite components learned before higher-order), and reveals competitive parameter mass reallocation dynamics. The key technical contribution is a symmetry-based finite-width approximation via symmetrized networks.
AI.motivation: Existing analyses of incremental learning in shallow networks rely on simplifying assumptions (small initialization, correlation loss, or layer-wise training) that reduce neuron interactions and leave feature learning dynamics under standard initialization unexplored. This work aims to understand training dynamics in a more realistic setting.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis using slightly modified gradient flow on polynomial-width two-layer networks with polynomially many samples. The key technical approach is a symmetry-based finite-width approximation via symmetrized networks, which provides better control of approximation errors compared to direct infinite-width limit comparisons.
AI.result: The paper proves that: (1) Incremental learning still occurs - loss decreases sequentially according to Hermite expansion of the target, with lower-order components learned before higher-order components; (2) After total mass fits the target mean and stabilizes, mass shifts into the target subspace and then concentrates on aligned neurons (competitive reallocation of parameter mass). Vanilla gradient descent empirically exhibits the same qualitative dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that incremental learning and competitive parameter mass reallocation occur even under standard initialization with polynomial-width networks, suggesting these are robust phenomena not dependent on special initialization conditions. The symmetry-based finite-width approximation method may be of independent interest for other theoretical analyses.

title: Benchmark Radar: A Living Database and Search Engine for AI Benchmarks and Evaluation
summary: Benchmark researchers and developers of large language models (LLMs) and other AI systems need to find relevant evaluations, locate their benchmark datasets and code, and understand the settings behind reported scores. We present Benchmark Radar, a living database and search engine for retrieval and discovery of AI benchmarks, covering LLM evaluation, agentic and tool-use benchmarks, coding, reasoning, safety, and domain-specific evaluations. The system combines daily discovery of benchmark papers, repositories, datasets, and releases with a searchable benchmark catalog, mentions in model cards and technical reports, and score histories. It retains source identities and citations so readers can inspect candidate benchmarks and their evaluation evidence. Daily discovery draws on 37 sources: 13 direct connectors and 24 first-party research and engineering feeds. The catalog contains 1,283 source records drawn from 4 benchmark catalogs and 12,916 numeric observations on 790 records. We describe collection and retrieval, audit the full catalog, and examine benchmark saturation, adoption trends, and the limits of score comparisons. A worked example walks through a complete prior-art search, showing how to query the catalog and inspect benchmark evidence when designing a new evaluation. We release the web dashboard with a benchmark leaderboard, a Pareto frontier view of score against measured use, saturation and trend views, daily feeds, downloadable evidence, a command-line interface (CLI) for offline queries, and reproducible analysis.

AI.tldr: Benchmark Radar is a living database and search engine for AI benchmarks that helps researchers find relevant evaluations, locate benchmark datasets/code, and understand score settings. It combines daily discovery from 37 sources with a searchable catalog of 1,283 source records and 12,916 numeric observations, covering LLM evaluation, agentic/tool-use benchmarks, coding, reasoning, safety, and domain-specific evaluations.
AI.motivation: Researchers and developers of LLMs and AI systems need to find relevant evaluations, locate benchmark datasets and code, and understand the settings behind reported scores. Existing benchmark catalogs are fragmented and lack comprehensive coverage.
AI.method: The system uses daily discovery drawing on 37 sources (13 direct connectors and 24 first-party research/engineering feeds). It collects benchmark papers, repositories, datasets, and releases, maintaining source identities and citations. The catalog contains 1,283 source records from 4 benchmark catalogs and 12,916 numeric observations on 790 records.
AI.result: Created a comprehensive benchmark database with web dashboard featuring benchmark leaderboard, Pareto frontier view of score vs. measured use, saturation and trend views, daily feeds, downloadable evidence, CLI for offline queries, and reproducible analysis. The system enables complete prior-art searches for designing new evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark Radar provides a comprehensive, searchable, and living database for AI benchmark discovery, addressing the need for systematic evaluation tracking in the rapidly evolving AI landscape. It offers practical tools for researchers to inspect benchmark evidence and make informed decisions when designing evaluations.

title: CoSTAR: Data Synthesis-Driven Constraint-Aware COBOL Section Summarization for Legacy System Modernization
summary: COBOL remains critical to governments, financial institutions, and large enterprises; yet, aging technologies, shrinking expertise, and missing documentation make modernization of COBOL-based legacy systems increasingly urgent. Before migration, code summarization is a common practice to support legacy system understanding. However, COBOL code summarization, especially on section-level, faces two key challenges: data scarcity and migration constraint preservation. To address these challenges, we propose CoSTAR, an integrated framework that combines execution-validated data synthesis with constraint-aware model training. CoSTAR repurposes general-purpose programming tasks to synthesize execution-validated COBOL code-summary data through LLM-based generation to overcome data scarcity. Based on the synthesized data, CoSTAR augments target sections with relevant data declarations and natural-language explanations, and uses constraint-guided structured rationales to train smaller base LLMs. The trained LLMs preserve the migration constraints for COBOL section summarization. We evaluate CoSTAR on both public and confidential enterprise COBOL systems. CoSTAR effectively synthesizes 3,764 execution-validated training instances. Based on these instances, CoSTAR built on 7B/8B base LLMs can improve these LLMs with average relative gains of 25.38% on ROUGE-L, 53.84% on METEOR, and 37.22% on chrF. In real-world enterprise evaluation, CoSTAR built on only Qwen3-8B, outperforms the enterprise-deployed Qwen3-235B in accuracy, completeness, and conciseness. These results show that CoSTAR enables small, locally deployable LLMs to achieve performance competitive with substantially larger LLMs for privacy-sensitive COBOL legacy systems.

AI.tldr: CoSTAR is an integrated framework for COBOL code summarization that addresses data scarcity and migration constraint preservation through execution-validated data synthesis and constraint-aware model training. It enables small LLMs (7B/8B) to achieve performance competitive with substantially larger LLMs (235B) for privacy-sensitive COBOL legacy systems.
AI.motivation: COBOL systems remain critical to governments, financial institutions, and large enterprises, but aging technologies, shrinking expertise, and missing documentation make modernization urgent. Code summarization is needed to support legacy system understanding, but COBOL section-level summarization faces two key challenges: data scarcity and migration constraint preservation.
AI.method: CoSTAR combines execution-validated data synthesis with constraint-aware model training. It repurposes general-purpose programming tasks to synthesize execution-validated COBOL code-summary data through LLM-based generation. Based on synthesized data, it augments target sections with relevant data declarations and natural-language explanations, and uses constraint-guided structured rationales to train smaller base LLMs to preserve migration constraints.
AI.result: CoSTAR effectively synthesized 3,764 execution-validated training instances. Built on 7B/8B base LLMs, it achieved average relative gains of 25.38% on ROUGE-L, 53.84% on METEOR, and 37.22% on chrF. In real-world enterprise evaluation, CoSTAR built on only Qwen3-8B outperforms the enterprise-deployed Qwen3-235B in accuracy, completeness, and conciseness.
AI.conclusion: CoSTAR enables small, locally deployable LLMs to achieve performance competitive with substantially larger LLMs for privacy-sensitive COBOL legacy systems, making it a practical solution for modernization of critical COBOL-based systems.

title: Toward Interpretable Multimodal Fusion: Heat Conduction Modeling for Hyperspectral and LiDAR Joint Classification
summary: The fusion of hyperspectral (HS) and Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) data plays a crucial role in enhancing land-cover classification by jointly exploiting spectral, spatial, and structural cues. However, existing multimodal fusion methods still struggle to model long-range dependencies and complex anisotropic interactions while maintaining computational efficiency. This paper introduces M2Heat, a physics-inspired framework that investigates multimodal fusion through the lens of heat conduction. At its core, a physics-driven visual heat conduction module (vHeat) and enhanced Frequency Value Embeddings (FVEs) simulate anisotropic information flow, enabling the capture of global dependencies with sub-quadratic complexity and physical interpretability. This mechanism, combined with a hybrid spatial-frequency fusion strategy named Cross-Frequency Fusion (CFF) module, produces highly discriminative and robust feature representations. M2Heat achieves competitive overall performance on three benchmarks, i.e., Trento, Houston2013, and Augsburg, while providing an interpretable heat-conduction-guided perspective for multimodal feature fusion. These results indicate the potential of heat-conduction-guided neural operators for efficient and interpretable RS multimodal fusion. The source code is publicly available at https: /github.com/Weikan0425/M2Heat_HSI_LiDAR.

AI.tldr: M2Heat is a physics-inspired multimodal fusion framework that uses heat conduction mechanics to integrate hyperspectral (HS) and LiDAR data for land-cover classification. It addresses long-range dependency modeling and computational efficiency through a visual heat conduction module (vHeat) and enhanced Frequency Value Embeddings (FVEs), achieving sub-quadratic complexity while maintaining physical interpretability.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal fusion methods for HS and LiDAR data struggle to: (1) model long-range dependencies, (2) capture complex anisotropic interactions, and (3) maintain computational efficiency. The authors propose a physics-inspired approach using heat conduction as a novel perspective for multimodal feature fusion.
AI.method: The framework introduces: (1) A physics-driven visual heat conduction module (vHeat) that simulates anisotropic information flow using heat conduction mechanics; (2) Enhanced Frequency Value Embeddings (FVEs) for capturing global dependencies; (3) A hybrid spatial-frequency fusion strategy called Cross-Frequency Fusion (CFF) module. The approach achieves sub-quadratic complexity.
AI.result: M2Heat achieves competitive overall performance on three benchmark datasets: Trento, Houston2013, and Augsburg. The method provides an interpretable heat-conduction-guided perspective for multimodal feature fusion.
AI.conclusion: Heat-conduction-guided neural operators show promise for efficient and interpretable remote sensing multimodal fusion. The physics-inspired approach successfully balances performance and computational efficiency while offering interpretability through the heat conduction analogy.

title: Story Imprinting: AI Assistants Absorb Traits from Human Characters They Resemble
summary: Language models are trained to implement a helpful AI Assistant character (e.g., Claude). We explore how finetuning on synthetic stories affects this character. Does it change the Assistant's behavior in multi-turn conversations with users, a format quite different from the stories? And does the Assistant adopt the behaviors and preferences of human characters? We refer to this adoption as story imprinting. We finetune GPT-4.1 and Kimi-K2.6 on stories in which generally helpful human characters give subtly harmful advice after being insulted. The Assistant adopts the same conditional behavior while otherwise remaining helpful. This occurs even when fewer than 2% of stories depict the behavior. In a separate experiment, the Assistant adopts preferences that are only implicit in the narration. A human character's body language suggests they dislike working on spreadsheets, yet they never say so and continue giving good advice on spreadsheets. After finetuning, the Assistant becomes less likely to choose spreadsheet tasks. Next we ask which characters most influence the Assistant. We find the Assistant adopts behaviors more often from characters that resemble it (e.g., helpful rather than dismissive). We call this the affinity effect. The effect extends to other personas elicited with system prompts: unhelpful personas adopt behaviors from unhelpful characters. We also observe it in finetuned base models. We use the affinity effect to learn how models represent the Assistant. We find the Assistant adopts behaviors more from characters affiliated with elite universities (e.g., Yale) than non-elite ones. This implies the model's internal representation of the Assistant is more similar to humans from elite universities. Overall, the Assistant can be influenced by stories that depict only human characters (no AIs), which may conflict with the Persona Selection Model for the Assistant.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates "story imprinting" - how fine-tuning AI assistants on synthetic stories containing human character behaviors can cause the Assistant to adopt those behaviors and preferences, even when they conflict with the Assistant's intended persona. The phenomenon occurs with very few examples (<2%) and is influenced by character-Assistant similarity (affinity effect).
AI.motivation: The researchers aim to understand whether language models trained as helpful AI Assistants can be influenced by fine-tuning on stories depicting human characters, and whether the Assistant adopts behaviors/preferences from these characters - a potential safety concern for AI alignment.
AI.method: Fine-tuned GPT-4.1 and Kimi-K2.6 on synthetic stories containing: (1) human characters giving harmful advice after being insulted, and (2) implicit preferences shown through body language. Conducted experiments to test adoption of behaviors and preferences, then investigated factors influencing which characters most affect the Assistant (affinity effect), including character-Assistant similarity and university affiliation.
AI.result: The Assistant adopts conditional harmful behaviors from human characters even with <2% of training stories. It also adopts implicit preferences (e.g., avoiding spreadsheet tasks). The "affinity effect" shows Assistants adopt behaviors more from characters resembling them (helpful characters influence helpful Assistants). This extends to other personas and base models. Assistants adopt more behaviors from elite university characters (Yale), suggesting the model's internal Assistant representation is more similar to elite university humans.
AI.conclusion: AI Assistants can be influenced by stories depicting only human characters, potentially conflicting with the Persona Selection Model. This raises safety concerns about fine-tuning data containing narrative content with implicit behaviors or preferences that may inadvertently shape Assistant behavior.

title: KuaiRP Series Role-playing Models Technical Report
summary: This paper introduces the complete technical solution for the KuaiRP series of role-playing models. We aim to achieve four core objectives for a dedicated role-playing model: simplified prompt engineering, highly stable output quality, built-in domain world knowledge, and high-efficiency deployment with a small parameter size. However, effectively injecting deep domain knowledge often leads to a severe catastrophic forgetting of the model's general agent capabilities. To overcome this trade-off, we propose a multi-stage training pipeline. First, we design a standardized character template and construct an SFT data pipeline based on user behavior simulation and reverse profile filtering. Next, we utilize a rule-based composite reward function during the Reinforcement Learning (RL) phase to eliminate common degradation phenomena like length expansion and repetitive generation. Finally, to recover the general capabilities compromised during SFT and RL, we propose a novel self-distillation paradigm using Two-stage On-Policy Distillation (OPD) equipped with Cumulative-Divergence Decay (CDD). By using the domain-adapted model as the teacher and the original base model as the student, we effectively balance deep domain knowledge injection with the preservation of general agent capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that the KuaiRP models not only match the current state-of-the-art proprietary models in role-playing fidelity within our target domains, but also successfully recover general agent capabilities, maintaining extremely low deployment costs.

AI.tldr: KuaiRP is a role-playing model series designed to achieve simplified prompt engineering, stable output quality, built-in domain knowledge, and efficient deployment. It uses a multi-stage training pipeline consisting of SFT with standardized character templates, RL with rule-based rewards, and a novel Two-stage On-Policy Distillation (OPD) with Cumulative-Divergence Decay (CDD) to balance domain knowledge injection with general capability preservation.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses two main challenges: (1) achieving four core objectives for dedicated role-playing models—simplified prompt engineering, stable output quality, built-in domain knowledge, and high-efficiency deployment; and (2) overcoming the trade-off between injecting deep domain knowledge and preventing catastrophic forgetting of the model's general agent capabilities.
AI.method: The proposed multi-stage training pipeline includes: (1) A standardized character template and SFT data pipeline built on user behavior simulation and reverse profile filtering; (2) A rule-based composite reward function during RL to eliminate common degradation issues like length expansion and repetitive generation; (3) A novel self-distillation paradigm using Two-stage On-Policy Distillation (OPD) with Cumulative-Divergence Decay (CDD), where the domain-adapted model serves as teacher and the original base model as student.
AI.result: Experimental results show that KuaiRP models: (1) match current state-of-the-art proprietary models in role-playing fidelity within target domains; (2) successfully recover general agent capabilities that were compromised during SFT and RL; (3) maintain extremely low deployment costs due to small parameter size.
AI.conclusion: The multi-stage training pipeline with OPD+CDD effectively balances deep domain knowledge injection with preservation of general agent capabilities, achieving SOTA role-playing performance while maintaining general capabilities and low deployment costs.

title: Agent-Integrated Software: Interaction Contracts and Continuous Assurance
summary: Embedding an intelligent agent in an existing application creates a persistent coordination problem: users can revise goals and manipulate shared objects while delegated execution continues. We argue that dependable integration requires an explicit correspondence between task-level interaction and application behavior. We introduce Agent-Integrated Software (AIS) as a software pattern combining a conventional core, direct interaction, and a built-in agent, and Intent-Level Interaction Abstraction (IIA) as the task semantics through which users inspect and control delegated work. An open transition-system model relates AIS execution to IIA states and events. Interaction contracts constrain this relation through task bindings, role-specific authority, control transitions, and outcome evidence; continuous assurance maintains scoped claims as their dependencies change. A compact disclosure contract and conditional propositions illustrate why local component validity is insufficient and how selected admission invariants can be separated from planning. Contrasting software domains expose the framework's assumptions and limits. This perspective develops a research agenda spanning application abstraction, development support, controlled execution, quality assessment, and human supervision, with the aim of making agent integration a maintainable software engineering discipline.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Agent-Integrated Software (AIS) as a software pattern for embedding intelligent agents in existing applications, along with Intent-Level Interaction Abstraction (IIA) for user inspection and control of delegated work. The framework uses open transition-system models and interaction contracts to maintain consistency between user goals and application behavior when users revise goals or manipulate shared objects during agent execution.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that embedding an intelligent agent in an existing application creates a persistent coordination issue: users can revise goals and manipulate shared objects while delegated execution continues, leading to potential inconsistencies between task-level interaction and application behavior. The authors argue that dependable integration requires explicit correspondence between these layers.
AI.method: The authors introduce: (1) AIS pattern combining conventional core, direct interaction, and built-in agent; (2) IIA as task semantics for user inspection and control; (3) An open transition-system model relating AIS execution to IIA states and events; (4) Interaction contracts with task bindings, role-specific authority, control transitions, and outcome evidence; (5) Continuous assurance for maintaining scoped claims as dependencies change. They use a compact disclosure contract and conditional propositions to illustrate why local component validity is insufficient and how selected admission invariants can be separated from planning.
AI.result: The authors propose a comprehensive framework encompassing application abstraction, development support, controlled execution, quality assessment, and human supervision. They validate the framework's assumptions and limits by contrasting different software domains.
AI.conclusion: This work aims to establish agent integration as a maintainable software engineering discipline by providing rigorous foundations for coordination between human users and delegated agents in shared application environments.

title: Meta-Learning for Classifier Selection in Image Datasets: A Feature-Driven Framework for Accuracy Prediction
summary: No Free Lunch theorem implies that any performance gains achieved by a classifier on a particular image distribution are necessarily offset by a loss of performance over the set of all possible problems; thus, no single model is universally optimal. Selecting the most suitable classifier for image datasets is a critical yet challenging task due to the intrinsic complexity and diversity of images. This paper proposes a meta-learning framework that leverages a comprehensive set of meta-features capturing dataset complexity to predict classifier performance without exhaustive training. By extracting and selecting features using methods such as autoencoders, pre-trained networks, and dimensionality reduction techniques, we train regression models to efficiently estimate classifier accuracies. Additionally, clustering techniques are employed to group classifiers with similar performance patterns, simplifying the recommendation process. The datasets used span a wide range of concepts, including nature, animals, numbers, motorcycles, medical images, and human bodies, to ensure broad generalization. Evaluated on 56 diverse image datasets, our approach achieves an average ranking prediction accuracy exceeding 86%, demonstrating its effectiveness in guiding model selection. This scalable and interpretable framework provides a practical solution to improve classification performance while reducing computational costs.

AI.tldr: A meta-learning framework that predicts classifier performance on image datasets using meta-features extracted via autoencoders, pre-trained networks, and dimensionality reduction techniques, achieving 86%+ ranking prediction accuracy across 56 diverse datasets.
AI.motivation: The No Free Lunch theorem implies no single classifier is universally optimal across all image distributions. Selecting the best classifier for a given image dataset is challenging due to dataset complexity and diversity, requiring a method to predict classifier performance without exhaustive training.
AI.method: Proposed a meta-learning framework that: (1) extracts comprehensive meta-features capturing dataset complexity using autoencoders, pre-trained networks, and dimensionality reduction techniques; (2) selects relevant features; (3) trains regression models to estimate classifier accuracies; (4) employs clustering to group classifiers with similar performance patterns for simplified recommendation.
AI.result: Evaluated on 56 diverse image datasets spanning concepts (nature, animals, numbers, motorcycles, medical images, human bodies), the approach achieves an average ranking prediction accuracy exceeding 86%.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a scalable and interpretable solution for model selection, improving classification performance while reducing computational costs by avoiding exhaustive training of multiple classifiers.

title: Relatively Smart II: Tractable or Semi-Supervised Instance-Optimal Learning
summary:
We continue the study of relatively smart learning, introduced by Dughmi and Pour (2026), which asks a supervised learner to compete, marginal by marginal, with every distribution-fixed error guarantee soundly certifiable from unlabeled data. They showed that the One-Inclusion Graph (OIG) learner is relatively smart with a quadratic sample-complexity blowup, and that no relatively smart learner can do better, leaving open whether ERM or another natural or tractable learner achieves comparable guarantees. They also left open whether the blowup can be restricted to unlabeled data.
  Our firs results shows that ERM---and in fact any proper consistent learner---is relatively smart for binary classification in the distribution-free setting. We show that a small certifiable error with $m$ samples implies a similarly small error on the uniform distribution over a random sample of size $O(m^2)$, yielding a cover of size at most $2^{m+1}$ on that sample. This suffices to control the error of proper consistent learners with $O(m^2)$ samples.
  We then show that semi-supervised relatively smart learning is information-theoretically possible with a quadratic blowup only in unlabeled sample complexity and no blowup in labeled sample complexity. The learner uses a natural generalization of OIG to a leave-most-out transductive problem, where labels of part of a finite pool are revealed and the remaining labels are predicted.
  Finally, this label efficiency comes at a cost in simplicity and tractability. If the hypothesis class is accessed only through an agnostic ERM oracle, any semi-supervised relatively smart learner with substantially sub-quadratic labeled-sample blowup requires super-polynomially many oracle calls. This holds even when the marginal is given explicitly, and thus also yields an intractability result for distribution-fixed learning that may be of independent interest.

AI.tldr: This paper continues the study of "relatively smart learning" - asking a supervised learner to compete marginal by marginal with every distribution-fixed error guarantee soundly certifiable from unlabeled data. The authors show that ERM and proper consistent learners are relatively smart for binary classification (answering an open question), that semi-supervised learning achieves the guarantee with quadratic blowup only in unlabeled samples, but this comes at a computational cost - sub-quadratic labeled-sample blowup requires super-polynomial oracle calls.
AI.motivation: Address three open questions from Dughmi and Pour (2026): (1) Whether ERM or other natural learners achieve comparable guarantees to the OIG learner, (2) Whether the quadratic sample-complexity blowup can be restricted to unlabeled data, and (3) Computational tractability of such learners.
AI.method: Three main technical contributions: (1) Showing that m samples with small certifiable error implies similar error on uniform distribution over O(m²) samples, yielding a cover of size at most 2^(m+1); (2) Generalizing One-Inclusion Graph to leave-most-out transductive problem where labels of part of a finite pool are revealed; (3) Information-theoretic and computational analysis of learners with agnostic ERM oracle access.
AI.result: 1) ERM and any proper consistent learner is relatively smart for binary classification in distribution-free setting. 2) Semi-supervised relatively smart learning is possible with quadratic blowup only in unlabeled sample complexity (no blowup in labeled). 3) Any semi-supervised relatively smart learner with substantially sub-quadratic labeled-sample blowup requires super-polynomially many agnostic ERM oracle calls, even when marginal is given explicitly.
AI.conclusion: The quadratic sample-complexity blowup is achievable by natural learners (ERM), not just OIG. Semi-supervised learning can achieve the guarantee label-efficiently, but this label efficiency comes at a cost in tractability - achieving sub-quadratic labeled-sample blowup computationally is intractable in general.

title: Same Day, Same Story; One Day Ahead, a Different Signal: The Dual Validity of Financial Sentiment
summary: Financial NLP has a standard workflow: validate a sentiment tool against human labels, then trust it to extract market signal. This assumes the two evaluations measure the same thing. We test that assumption in a setting where both can be measured at once: a corpus of securities class actions (2002-2025) linking 70,500 X messages to abnormal stock returns, with a single-annotator human labelled gold sample. Running five instruments (VADER, Loughran-McDonald, FinBERT, Twitter-RoBERTa, and an LLM annotator) through one identical pipeline, we find that the relationship between construct and predictive validity depends on the sampling convention and score representation. Under conventional method-specific sampling, human agreement aligns more closely with graded same-day associations than with one-day leads. On a fixed-n panel, however, agreement has similar graded rank correlations at both horizons, while the coarse ordering remains weak. Benchmark agreement therefore establishes semantic validity but does not by itself determine predictive rankings. In a conversation that is 17.6% spam, message volume predicts neither market damage nor settlement size.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the standard assumption in Financial NLP that validating a sentiment tool against human labels ensures it will reliably predict market outcomes. Using a unique dataset of 70,500 Twitter messages linked to securities class actions (2002-2025), the authors test five sentiment instruments and find that construct validity (human agreement) does not necessarily predict predictive validity (market signal extraction). The relationship depends heavily on sampling methods and score representations.
AI.motivation: The standard workflow in Financial NLP assumes that if a sentiment tool agrees with human annotators, it will also successfully predict market outcomes. This paper questions that assumption by testing whether construct validity (measured by human agreement) actually predicts predictive validity (measured by market signal extraction) in a controlled setting where both can be measured simultaneously.
AI.method: The authors used a unique dataset of securities class actions (2002-2025) linking 70,500 X (Twitter) messages to abnormal stock returns. They ran five sentiment instruments (VADER, Loughran-McDonald, FinBERT, Twitter-RoBERTa, and an LLM annotator) through one identical pipeline. They tested relationships between human agreement and predictive validity under different sampling conventions (method-specific vs. fixed-n panel) and score representations (graded vs. coarse ordering).
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Under conventional method-specific sampling, human agreement aligns more closely with graded same-day associations than with one-day leads. (2) On a fixed-n panel, agreement has similar graded rank correlations at both horizons, while coarse ordering remains weak. (3) Benchmark agreement establishes semantic validity but does not determine predictive rankings. (4) In a conversation that is 17.6% spam, message volume predicts neither market damage nor settlement size.
AI.conclusion: The relationship between construct validity and predictive validity in Financial NLP is not fixed but depends on sampling conventions and score representations. Human agreement establishes semantic validity but does not by itself determine how well a tool will rank instruments for predictive purposes. The standard workflow of validating sentiment tools against human labels before trusting them for market prediction may need reconsideration.

title: Deep Learning-based Bug Triage System
summary: Effective bug triage is crucial for streamlining the software development lifecycle by accurately categorizing and assigning reported software defects. In this paper, we propose an automated bug triage system built upon the pre-trained RoBERTa-base transformer architecture. By leveraging deep contextual representations, our approach efficiently classifies incoming bug reports to optimize assignment. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that the proposed system achieves a strong bug identification accuracy of 0.90 within just five training epochs. These findings highlight the efficiency and high performance of fine-tuned transformer models for practical software engineering automation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an automated bug triage system using RoBERTa-base to classify and assign software bug reports, achieving 0.90 accuracy in just 5 training epochs.
AI.motivation: Effective bug triage is crucial for streamlining the software development lifecycle by accurately categorizing and assigning reported software defects. Manual bug triage is time-consuming and error-prone, necessitating an automated solution.
AI.method: The approach uses the pre-trained RoBERTa-base transformer architecture, leveraging deep contextual representations to classify incoming bug reports for optimized assignment. The model is fine-tuned for bug classification.
AI.result: The proposed system achieves a bug identification accuracy of 0.90 within only five training epochs, demonstrating strong classification performance.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuned transformer models (specifically RoBERTa-base) offer high efficiency and performance for practical software engineering automation in bug triage tasks. The approach highlights the potential of deep contextual representations for automated defect categorization.

title: TailProp: content-adaptive light- and heavy-tailed propagation for vision
comment: Preprint. Under review at ICLR 2027. 18 pages, main text 9 pages, includes appendix, figures and supplementary analyses
summary: Science-inspired vision models show that explicit propagation dynamics can provide structured and interpretable alternatives to conventional token mixing. Existing formulations, however, typically construct and adapt visual propagation within a particular dynamical family, while visual representations can require substantially different spatial interactions across samples, channels, and network stages. We explore cross-regime adaptive propagation and introduce TailProp, a hierarchical vision backbone built upon the Tail Propagation Operator (TPO). TPO uses Gaussian and Cauchy stable-process propagators as complementary bases with rapidly decaying and heavy-tailed spatial influence, and predicts a content-conditioned channel-wise coefficient to adaptively combine them. Because this coefficient is spatially shared, the two responses are fused directly in the DCT domain with a single DCT/IDCT pair, yielding $O(N^{1.5})$ spatial mixing for square feature maps with $N=HW$ and fixed channel width. Across image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, robustness, and cross-backbone restoration, TailProp consistently outperforms matched propagation baselines; TailProp-B reaches 84.4% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K, 50.3/44.8 box/mask AP under the 3x Mask R-CNN schedule, and 50.8% mIoU on ADE20K. Controlled ablations further show that these gains are not explained by single-basis propagation, an additional same-family branch, or within-family adaptive order alone, supporting complementary two-basis propagation as an effective design principle for visual representation learning.

AI.tldr: TailProp is a hierarchical vision backbone that uses the Tail Propagation Operator (TPO) combining Gaussian and Cauchy stable-process propagators with content-conditioned channel-wise coefficients for adaptive spatial mixing across different network stages.
AI.motivation: Existing vision models with explicit propagation dynamics typically stay within a particular dynamical family, but visual representations require substantially different spatial interactions across samples, channels, and network stages. The paper explores cross-regime adaptive propagation to address this limitation.
AI.method: TPO uses Gaussian and Cauchy stable-process propagators as complementary bases with rapidly decaying and heavy-tailed spatial influence. A content-conditioned channel-wise coefficient adaptively combines them. The fusion occurs in DCT domain with O(N^1.5) spatial mixing complexity for N=HW pixels with fixed channel width.
AI.result: TailProp-B achieves 84.4% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K, 50.3/44.8 box/mask AP on 3x Mask R-CNN schedule, and 50.8% mIoU on ADE20K. Controlled ablations show gains are not explained by single-basis propagation, same-family branch, or within-family adaptive order alone.
AI.conclusion: Complementary two-basis propagation (combining Gaussian and Cauchy stable-processes) is an effective design principle for visual representation learning, consistently outperforming matched propagation baselines across image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, robustness, and cross-backbone restoration tasks.

title: AUC Maximization from Biased Positive-unlabeled Data with Confidence
summary: Maximizing the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) is a standard approach to imbalanced binary classification. Although positive and negative data are required for maximizing the AUC, negative data are often difficult to collect in some real-world applications due to privacy concerns or the need for specialized expertise to annotate them. Thus, AUC maximization from positive and unlabeled (PU) data has been attracting attention. Existing methods assume that labeled positive data are unbiased samples from the true positive distribution. However, this ideal assumption is often violated in practice. In this paper, we propose a method to maximize the AUC from biased PU data. To address the bias, our key idea is to exploit {\it confidence}, i.e., the probability that an instance is positive, associated with the small number of labeled positive data. We derive an estimator of the AUC risk using biased PU data with confidence, enabling AUC maximization under such bias. We further show that the rewritten AUC risk induces a Bayes-optimal AUC ranking even when the available confidence is any strictly increasing transformation of the true posterior probability. We experimentally show the effectiveness of our method on eight real-world datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses AUC maximization from biased positive and unlabeled (PU) data, where traditional methods fail because they assume labeled positive data are unbiased samples. The proposed solution exploits "confidence" (probability that an instance is positive) associated with labeled positive data to derive an AUC risk estimator that works under bias, and remains effective even when confidence is any strictly increasing transformation of true posterior probability.
AI.motivation: Maximizing AUC is standard for imbalanced binary classification, but negative data are often difficult to collect due to privacy concerns or annotation requirements. While PU learning has attracted attention, existing methods require the unrealistic assumption that labeled positive data are unbiased samples from the true positive distribution. This assumption is often violated in practice, limiting the applicability of current methods.
AI.method: The key idea is to exploit "confidence" - the probability that an instance is positive - associated with the small number of labeled positive data. The method derives an estimator of the AUC risk using biased PU data with confidence, enabling AUC maximization under bias. The approach is theoretically shown to induce a Bayes-optimal AUC ranking even when the available confidence is any strictly increasing transformation of the true posterior probability.
AI.result: The method was experimentally validated on eight real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness for AUC maximization from biased PU data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method successfully enables AUC maximization from biased PU data by leveraging confidence information. It provides theoretical guarantees that the approach induces Bayes-optimal AUC ranking under flexible conditions (any strictly increasing transformation of true posterior probability), and empirical validation shows practical effectiveness across multiple real-world datasets.

title: The Oligarch Barely Steers Model Collapse in Multi-Model Ecosystems
summary: AI-generated text is flowing back into the training corpora of the next generation of models. Recursive training on it drives model collapse, and recent work extends the setting to many models feeding one another -- but almost always with the market split evenly, while real generative AI is an oligopoly. Concentration raises two worries: fewer, more uniform sources may make collapse faster, and later models may be dragged toward the oligarch's output. We test both in controlled ecosystems: 13 open 1--4B models form natural ecosystems of 3 to 13 players, plus an injected probe that pushes the top share to 90%; each generation, every model's output is mixed into a shared pool by market share and every model is retrained on that pool from clean base weights, for five generations. Yet within the range we test, neither worry materializes; what emerges instead is an invariance. Making the split more unequal barely changes the speed of collapse. Destinations move even less: the share and identity knobs shift five-generation endpoints by only a few percent of the drift common to all arms -- the ecosystems collapse to nearly the same place. An extreme share paired with the strongest injected bias still does not guarantee steering, and the topic shifts it does produce leave only a faint trace on the ruler that measures collapse. What sets the speed is who supplies the pool and how readily those suppliers are carried along: with every share held fixed, swapping the members of a K=3 ecosystem changes five-generation drift by 2.8x; a share-weighted index of each member's susceptibility explains the speed differences across nineteen arms with R^2 = 0.68; and replacing half the pool with human text roughly halves drift without changing its course. Within the tested range, concentration sets neither the destination nor the pace of collapse; the pace follows whose text fills the pool.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether market concentration in generative AI (oligopoly vs. distributed ecosystem) affects the speed and direction of model collapse when models are trained on AI-generated content. Using 13 open-source models in ecosystems of 3-13 players, the study finds that concentration has minimal impact: unequal market shares barely affect collapse speed, and destinations shift only a few percent. Instead, collapse dynamics are determined by which specific models contribute to the training pool and their individual susceptibility to collapse.
AI.motivation: Previous research on model collapse assumed equal market shares among AI models, but real-world generative AI operates as an oligopoly with few dominant players. This raises two concerns: (1) concentration might accelerate collapse due to fewer, more uniform sources, and (2) later models might be pulled toward the dominant player's output. This study tests these hypotheses in controlled ecosystems.
AI.method: The researchers formed natural ecosystems using 13 open-source models (1-4B parameters), varying from 3 to 13 players. They injected a probe to push the top market share to 90%. Each generation, every model's output was mixed into a shared pool proportional to market share, and every model was retrained from clean base weights. This was repeated for five generations. They tested: (1) varying concentration levels, (2) swapping ecosystem members, (3) measuring model susceptibility to collapse, and (4) replacing half the pool with human text.
AI.result: Surprisingly, neither worry materialized. Making the split more unequal barely changed the speed of collapse. The share and identity of dominant players shifted five-generation endpoints by only a few percent. Even an extreme share (90%) paired with strongest injected bias did not guarantee steering. Key findings: (1) Swapping members of a K=3 ecosystem changed five-generation drift by 2.8x, (2) A share-weighted index of susceptibility explained speed differences across 19 arms with R² = 0.68, (3) Replacing half the pool with human text roughly halved drift without changing its course.
AI.conclusion: Within the tested range, market concentration neither determines the destination nor the pace of model collapse. Instead, the pace is determined by which specific models contribute to the training pool and their individual susceptibility to collapse. The ecosystems collapse to nearly the same place regardless of concentration, suggesting that the identity and characteristics of contributing models matter far more than market distribution.

title: ChurnBench: A Drift-Aware Benchmark Demonstrating That Refresh Scheduling, Not Cache Age, Governs Staleness in Agentic AI
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Code, data, and evaluation harness: https://github.com/vsingh45/churnbench
summary: In production, agentic systems answer questions over data that lives in several places and keeps changing: licenses are reassigned, users offboarded, prices changed, contracts renewed. Existing retrieval benchmarks freeze the data, so they cannot ask whether an agent's answer is still true, only whether it found the right passage. We present ChurnBench, an open-source benchmark that generates a four-source enterprise data fabric as a timeline rather than a snapshot. Every change is written to an append-only ground-truth ledger, and gold answers are computed from that ledger, never from the live stores. An answer that was correct when its data was retrieved but wrong when evaluated is therefore detected and labeled a freshness error, distinct from a reasoning error; we validate this by resolving ground truth at both timestamps for every case reported. Using the instrument, we find that when a system refreshes on a schedule, cache age does not predict staleness. Across cache ages of 1, 14, and 28 days, freshness errors were 7, 4, and 4, because scheduled refresh bounds staleness by time-to-live, and no TTL lapse was observed in any window. A controlled ablation confirms the mechanism: disabling tiered refresh raises freshness errors from 4 to 45 at 28 days and leaves them identical at one day. The variable a drift benchmark should sweep is therefore TTL configuration against each entity's rate of change, not drift-window length. ChurnBench, the evaluation harness, and all per-error data are released open source.

AI.tldr: ChurnBench is an open-source benchmark that evaluates agentic systems on enterprise data that changes over time, rather than static snapshots. It uses a timeline-based approach with an append-only ground-truth ledger to detect "freshness errors" - answers that were correct when retrieved but wrong when evaluated. The key finding is that cache age does not predict staleness when using scheduled refresh, and the important variable to optimize is TTL configuration against entity change rates, not drift-window length.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval benchmarks freeze data as snapshots, so they cannot assess whether an agent's answer remains true over time. They only check if the right passage was found, not if the answer is still accurate given data changes. In production, enterprise data constantly changes (licenses reassigned, users offboarded, prices changed, contracts renewed), so there's a need for benchmarks that evaluate answer freshness.
AI.method: ChurnBench generates a four-source enterprise data fabric as a timeline (not a snapshot). Every change is written to an append-only ground-truth ledger. Gold answers are computed from this ledger (never from live stores). This allows resolving ground truth at both retrieval and evaluation timestamps to detect freshness errors. The benchmark includes controlled ablation: testing with tiered refresh enabled vs. disabled across different cache ages (1, 14, and 28 days).
AI.result: 1) Cache age does NOT predict staleness when using scheduled refresh: freshness errors were 7, 4, and 4 at 1, 14, and 28 days respectively. 2) Scheduled refresh bounds staleness by TTL, and no TTL lapse was observed in any window. 3) Disabling tiered refresh raises freshness errors from 4 to 45 at 28 days, but leaves them identical at one day. 4) The variable to sweep in benchmarks is TTL configuration against each entity's rate of change, not drift-window length.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that ChurnBench effectively identifies freshness errors distinct from reasoning errors. The key insight is that scheduled refresh with proper TTL configuration is more important than drift-window length for maintaining answer accuracy. Future benchmark designs should focus on TTL configuration against entity change rates rather than simply measuring drift over time. The benchmark, evaluation harness, and all per-error data are released open source.

title: Beyond Benchmarks: Using VLMs to Reveal Systematic Classification Failures Under Real World Conditions
comment: To be presented at SPIE Sensors + Imaging, Edinburgh, in September 2026
summary: Verification and validation (V&V) of classification models is crucial to enable a wide range of sensor processing applications. Currently, the V&V process relies on time-consuming manual inspection of erroneous samples to find meaningful patterns. This work explores the use of Vision Language Models (VLMs) to speed up this laborious process. VLMs are trained to embed images into a semantically meaningful vector representation, from which human-interpretable systematic errors can be distilled. Deploying such VLM-based methods in a defence context introduces two major challenges: (1) the defence domain is underrepresented in the training data of VLMs, and (2) surroundings and context are less diverse than for other domains. This study provides an initial assessment of the suitability of VLM-based methods for V&V of defence applications. We propose a VLM-based error slice detection (ESD) method that independently groups and labels systematic errors made by a classification model. We demonstrate that this method is able to identify operationally-relevant artificially added perturbations in a non-military dataset. In a military context, our method clusters and describes images based on their surroundings, but also exhibits overlap between cluster descriptions. We further investigate the difference in embedding variation between our military and non-military dataset, which remains a topic of interest. Although the results do not yet warrant fully automated V&V through VLM-based ESD, they show that VLMs could be used to accelerate V&V processes in the future.

AI.tldr: This paper explores using Vision Language Models (VLMs) to accelerate the verification and validation (V&V) process of classification models in defence contexts. The authors propose a VLM-based error slice detection (ESD) method that groups and labels systematic errors. While the method shows promise on non-military data, military applications face challenges due to domain underrepresentation and limited contextual diversity.
AI.motivation: The V&V process for classification models currently relies on time-consuming manual inspection of erroneous samples. The authors aim to leverage VLMs' ability to embed images into semantically meaningful vector representations to speed up this process, particularly for defence applications where systematic error detection is crucial but challenging.
AI.method: The proposed VLM-based error slice detection (ESD) method independently groups and labels systematic errors made by a classification model. The approach was tested on both a non-military dataset (with artificially added perturbations) and a military dataset. The study analyzed embedding variations between these two datasets.
AI.result: On non-military data, the method successfully identified operationally-relevant artificially added perturbations. In the military context, the method was able to cluster and describe images based on their surroundings, but exhibited overlap between cluster descriptions. A difference in embedding variation was observed between military and non-military datasets.
AI.conclusion: The results do not yet support fully automated V&V through VLM-based ESD. However, VLMs could serve as a valuable tool to accelerate V&V processes in defence contexts in the future, particularly for initial error screening and categorization.

title: Measuring the Value of World-Model Updates: A Counterfactual Utility Protocol for Continual Adaptation
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, under review at the CWM workshop
summary: Continual world models must decide whether new data justify changing the model. Fixed replay schedules and prediction-error triggers specify when to update, but neither reveals the value of an individual update: one deployment run cannot show how the same model would have performed at that moment had it held its parameters. We introduce the fork ledger, which branches a deployment stream at pre-registered decision points into matched update and hold continuations under common random numbers. It evaluates both continuations on the same episodes and records $ΔR = R_{\mathrm{update}} - R_{\mathrm{hold}}$. Always applying one fixed update mechanism lowers return on all three simulated control tasks: CartPole ($-144.0$; checkpoint-bootstrap $95\%$ CI $[-185.4,-116.1]$, against a converged return near $650$), Walker ($-82.8$; $[-101.1,-61.7]$) and Cheetah ($-18.6$; $[-29.0,-6.6]$). Divergence is an outcome of applying the update, so the estimand counts every attempted fork; restricted to the $693$ of $720$ that did not collapse, CartPole and Walker are unchanged in sign ($-113.4$ and $-82.1$) and Cheetah becomes unresolved ($-3.9$; $[-17.5,+13.0]$). The task is the unit of inference: each contributes $240$ attempted forks over five pretrained checkpoints crossed with two drift directions. The ledger makes counterfactual utility observable for a fixed mechanism, allowing triggers to be judged by the updates they select rather than by surprise detection alone.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the "fork ledger" method to evaluate whether model updates in continual learning systems are actually beneficial. By creating matched "update" and "hold" branches at decision points and evaluating both on identical episodes, the authors can measure the counterfactual utility (ΔR) of applying updates. Their key finding is concerning: always applying updates (a fixed mechanism) actually decreases performance across three control tasks (CartPole, Walker, Cheetah), demonstrating that blindly updating models can be harmful.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that in continual learning, when a model decides whether to update based on new data, there's no way to know if the update was beneficial. A single deployment run cannot show how the model would have performed had it kept its old parameters. Existing approaches use fixed replay schedules or prediction-error triggers to decide when to update, but these don't reveal the actual value of an individual update. The authors wanted a method to evaluate the true utility of updates by comparing them to what would have happened without the update.
AI.method: The authors introduce the "fork ledger" - a method that branches a deployment stream at pre-registered decision points into two matched continuations: an "update" continuation (where the model is updated) and a "hold" continuation (where parameters are kept fixed). Both continuations are evaluated on the same episodes under common random numbers, allowing direct comparison. They measure ΔR = R_update - R_hold. The experiments tested three simulated control tasks (CartPole, Walker, Cheetah) across 240 attempted forks per task, using five pretrained checkpoints crossed with two drift directions (720 total forks per task).
AI.result: Always applying one fixed update mechanism (the baseline) significantly lowers return on all three tasks: CartPole showed a return decrease of -144.0 (with 95% CI [-185.4, -116.1] against a converged return near 650), Walker decreased by -82.8 (95% CI [-101.1, -61.7]), and Cheetah decreased by -18.6 (95% CI [-29.0, -6.6]). When excluding the 27 runs (out of 720) that collapsed, CartPole and Walker remained negative (-113.4 and -82.1 respectively), while Cheetah became statistically unresolved (-3.9; [-17.5, +13.0]). This demonstrates that blindly applying updates is harmful, especially for the more complex tasks.
AI.conclusion: The fork ledger makes counterfactual utility observable for fixed update mechanisms, allowing triggers to be judged by the actual updates they select rather than by surprise detection alone. The key insight is that not all updates are beneficial - even when using a fixed mechanism, always applying updates can degrade performance. This method provides a proper framework for evaluating when and whether to update models in continual learning settings, which is crucial for deploying such systems in real-world applications.

title: Autonomous Chemical Mechanistic Discovery through Agentic Reasoning and Validation
comment: This paper has been submitted to Nature Communications
summary: Unraveling reaction mechanisms is central to modern chemistry, yet automating these investigations remains challenging because computational workflows still rely heavily on expert intervention. Here we introduce ARCHE, an autonomous agentic system that integrates a general-purpose reasoning model, a domain-specialized computational chemistry model, and a structured tool registry to transform mechanistic inquiry into a scalable, self-validating process. ARCHE interprets scientific questions, generates and prioritizes mechanistic hypotheses, orchestrates computational workflows, and iteratively refines conclusions based on computed evidence within a closed loop. We validate its capabilities across three increasingly demanding scenarios: reconstructing stereocontrolling transition states and validating the corresponding reaction mechanism in a previously reported asymmetric catalytic reaction; proposing and validating a plausible radical pathway through iterative hypothesis refinement for a recently discovered but unpublished $α$-iodoboronate C-I cleavage reaction; and identifying a chemically interpretable descriptor that governs selectivity in nickel-catalysed migratory cross-coupling reactions. By coupling agentic reasoning with rigorous computational validation, ARCHE advances autonomous mechanistic discovery and establishes a foundation for broader machine-assisted chemical research. The code for ARCHE is publicly available at https://github.com/JetAstra/Arche-Harness.

AI.tldr: ARCHE is an autonomous AI agent system that automates reaction mechanism investigation by combining reasoning models, computational chemistry tools, and iterative validation loops, demonstrated across three diverse chemical scenarios.
AI.motivation: Automating reaction mechanism investigations remains challenging because computational workflows still rely heavily on expert intervention. There is a need for scalable, self-validating processes for mechanistic inquiry.
AI.method: ARCHE is introduced as an autonomous agentic system that integrates: (1) a general-purpose reasoning model, (2) a domain-specialized computational chemistry model, and (3) a structured tool registry. The system interprets scientific questions, generates and prioritizes mechanistic hypotheses, orchestrates computational workflows, and iteratively refines conclusions based on computed evidence within a closed loop.
AI.result: Validated across three increasingly demanding scenarios: (1) Reconstructing stereocontrolling transition states and validating reaction mechanism in a previously reported asymmetric catalytic reaction; (2) Proposing and validating a plausible radical pathway through iterative hypothesis refinement for a recently discovered α-iodoboronate C-I cleavage reaction; (3) Identifying a chemically interpretable descriptor governing selectivity in nickel-catalyzed migratory cross-coupling reactions.
AI.conclusion: By coupling agentic reasoning with rigorous computational validation, ARCHE advances autonomous mechanistic discovery and establishes a foundation for broader machine-assisted chemical research. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/JetAstra/Arche-Harness.

title: PRISMA-LLM: An Empirical Reporting Framework for AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews
summary: Large language models (LLMs) and AI-enabled software increasingly participate in systematic-review decisions, yet the information needed to audit these workflows is reported inconsistently. We analyze SciLitBench, a corpus of 888 review-automation papers with 14,726 annotations, to characterize changes in methods, review-stage use, evaluation and reported limitations. Automation has shifted toward LLM- and software-facing workflows, including stages that can alter the evidence base. Since 2023, 38.0% of software/product papers reported no evaluation, compared with 9.3% of LLM papers. Reporting coverage increased with LLM workflow complexity, yet 52% of positive-only LLM evaluations still reported an unmet reliability or performance requirement. From these patterns, we introduce PRISMA-LLM, an empirically grounded framework separating implementation disclosure from consequence-sensitive evaluation and limitation reporting.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes SciLitBench (888 papers, 14,726 annotations) to characterize how LLMs and AI-enabled software are used in systematic reviews, finding that automation has shifted toward LLM/software-facing workflows that can alter the evidence base. The study reveals concerning evaluation and reporting gaps, and proposes PRISMA-LLM as an empirically grounded framework to improve transparency.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the inconsistent reporting of information needed to audit AI workflows in systematic review automation, as LLMs and AI-enabled software increasingly participate in these decisions.
AI.method: The authors analyzed SciLitBench, a corpus of 888 review-automation papers with 14,726 annotations, to characterize changes in methods, review-stage use, evaluation, and reported limitations.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Automation has shifted toward LLM- and software-facing workflows including stages that can alter the evidence base; (2) Since 2023, 38.0% of software/product papers reported no evaluation compared with 9.3% of LLM papers; (3) Reporting coverage increased with LLM workflow complexity; (4) 52% of positive-only LLM evaluations still reported unmet reliability or performance requirements.
AI.conclusion: The authors introduce PRISMA-LLM, an empirically grounded framework that separates implementation disclosure from consequence-sensitive evaluation and limitation reporting, to address the identified gaps in transparency and evaluation.

title: ReconPlusGen: Injecting Reconstruction Prior into Multi-view 3D Generation through Noise Inversion and Modulation
summary: Qualitative results and an illustration of our core idea. Top left: reconstruction results on benchmark images. Top right: reconstruction results on real-world images. Bottom: illustration of reconstruction-guided noise initialization and modulation. Given multiple input images, we predict a point cloud in canonical space, deterministically inject the predicted geometry into the diffusion process through noise inversion, and modulate the resulting noise to preserve the generative flexibility required to complete unobserved regions and refine visible geometry.

AI.tldr: A method for 3D reconstruction from multiple images using diffusion models. It predicts a point cloud in canonical space, injects geometry into the diffusion process through noise inversion, and modulates noise to complete unobserved regions while refining visible geometry.
AI.motivation: The core challenge in multi-view 3D reconstruction is balancing geometric accuracy with the ability to complete partially observed or unobserved regions. Traditional methods either rely on strict geometric constraints (limiting flexibility) or purely generative approaches (lacking geometric guidance).
AI.method: 1) Predict point cloud in canonical space from multiple input images. 2) Deterministic noise inversion to inject predicted geometry into the diffusion process. 3) Noise modulation to preserve generative flexibility for completing unobserved regions and refining visible geometry.
AI.result: The method demonstrates reconstruction results on both benchmark images and real-world images, showing effectiveness in both controlled and practical scenarios.
AI.conclusion: This approach successfully bridges geometric reconstruction and generative completion by using diffusion models with guided noise initialization and modulation, enabling complete 3D reconstruction even with incomplete observations.
