title: When More Is Not Better: Component Anti-Synergy in a P300 Speller
summary: P300 brain-computer interface (BCI) spellers can provide hands-free communication for people with severe motor impairments. Modern pipelines combine multiple individually promising components, often assuming that 'more-is-better'. We tested this assumption using a four-component full-factorial experiment varying the inclusion of Euclidean Alignment (EA), xDAWN spatial filtering, subject calibration, and language model priors on a public P300 dataset. Performance was evaluated using accuracy, repetitions, and information transfer rate (ITR) with mixed-effects models. Results show that the value of components is conditional rather than additive. Calibration was the strongest singular contributor, while EA compensated for its absence in zero-calibration settings. Adding independently useful components could also reduce performance, revealing component anti-synergy. Contrary to conventional wisdom, LM support was not universally beneficial: its effect depends strongly on the strength of the underlying EEG pipeline, while results from a larger LM showed a similar pattern. Together, these findings challenge maximal 'all-on' pipeline design and highlight the value of selecting spatial and language-support components according to the quality of available EEG evidence.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the "more-is-better" assumption in P300 BCI speller pipelines by testing four components (Euclidean Alignment, xDAWN spatial filtering, subject calibration, and language model priors) in a full-factorial experiment. Results show components are conditional rather than additive, with calibration being strongest, and language model benefits depending on EEG pipeline quality.
AI.motivation: The authors sought to test whether combining multiple individually promising components in P300 BCI pipelines always improves performance, challenging the common assumption that "more-is-better" in BCI system design.
AI.method: Four-component full-factorial experiment on a public P300 dataset, evaluating performance using accuracy, repetitions, and information transfer rate (ITR) with mixed-effects models.
AI.result: Components showed conditional rather than additive value. Calibration was the strongest singular contributor; Euclidean Alignment compensated for its absence in zero-calibration settings. Anti-synergy was observed where adding useful components reduced performance. Language model support was not universally beneficial—its effect depended on the strength of the underlying EEG pipeline.
AI.conclusion: The findings challenge maximal "all-on" pipeline design and highlight the importance of selecting spatial and language-support components based on the quality of available EEG evidence, rather than using all components simultaneously.

title: DRG-MAPPO: Hierarchical Dynamic Role-Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Air Combat
summary: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has emerged as a pivotal paradigm for complex decision-making in autonomous systems and air combat. While MARL has demonstrated significant potential in air combat, achieving sophisticated tactical coordination remains a non-trivial challenge. This difficulty is largely attributed to two primary limitations: (1) the absence of structured relational modeling hinders agents from capturing complex, time-varying interactions among battlefield entities; and (2) conventional flat architectures often lack the capability to explicitly model tactical roles, leading to ambiguous task allocation in highly dynamic environments. To address these challenges, we propose Hierarchical Dynamic Role-Graph Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (DRG-MAPPO), a novel MARL framework that integrates graph-based relational modeling with dynamic role assignment. Specifically, DRG-MAPPO constructs a graph-based representation of battlefield interactions and leverages graph attention mechanisms to extract critical relational features among allies, enemies, and threats. Subsequently, a high-level policy employs a dynamic role assignment mechanism to determine tactical responsibilities (e.g., ``leader'' and ``supporter''). Conditioned on these roles and encoded graph-relational features, a low-level policy executes discrete maneuver actions, facilitating the joint optimization of tactical strategy and collaborative execution. Furthermore, a target-priority auxiliary task is designed to foster the emergence of behaviors such as focus-fire. Experimental results demonstrate that DRG-MAPPO achieves a state-of-the-art win rate of 87%, suggesting that our framework effectively balances relational modeling, interpretability, and optimization stability for cooperative air combat.

AI.tldr: DRG-MAPPO is a novel hierarchical MARL framework that combines graph-based relational modeling with dynamic role assignment for cooperative air combat. It uses graph attention mechanisms to capture battlefield interactions and assigns tactical roles (leader/supporter) to agents, achieving 87% win rate.
AI.motivation: Current MARL for air combat faces two key limitations: (1) lack of structured relational modeling to capture complex time-varying interactions among battlefield entities, and (2) flat architectures that cannot explicitly model tactical roles, leading to ambiguous task allocation in dynamic environments.
AI.method: DRG-MAPPO constructs a graph-based representation of battlefield interactions and uses graph attention mechanisms to extract relational features among allies, enemies, and threats. A high-level policy performs dynamic role assignment (leader/supporter), while a low-level policy executes discrete maneuver actions based on roles and encoded graph-relational features. A target-priority auxiliary task is added to encourage focus-fire behaviors.
AI.result: DRG-MAPPO achieves state-of-the-art win rate of 87% in cooperative air combat, effectively balancing relational modeling, interpretability, and optimization stability.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical approach combining graph-based relational modeling with dynamic role assignment successfully addresses the limitations of conventional MARL in air combat scenarios, providing an effective framework for tactical coordination in autonomous systems.

title: Ecdysis: Efficient and Effective Training of Runtime Harnesses for LLM Agents
summary: Self-evolving runtime harnesses can substantially improve the capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents and provide a promising paradigm for optimizing agent execution. Existing harness evolution methods typically rely on iterative search, repeatedly evaluating and revising candidate harnesses based on execution feedback from task instances. While this paradigm enables continuous harness optimization, it incurs substantial time overhead due to repeated agent executions and code modifications, and may overfit to observed tasks and specific failure patterns, resulting in degraded generalization to unseen tasks. We identify the lack of principled failure diagnosis as a key bottleneck in harness evolution: an observed failure can reflect either model-specific deficiencies or systematic harness deficiencies, and directly optimizing against individual failures can lead to unnecessary model-specific accommodation. We therefore propose Ecdysis, an efficient and effective framework that distinguishes model-specific accommodation from harness-level repair and biases adaptation toward systematic harness deficiencies by identifying recurring cross-task failure patterns. Ecdysis adopts a batch-level cross-instance failure aggregation paradigm to jointly analyze failure evidence from multiple task instances and further introduces Failure-Driven Collaborative Refinement to diagnose failure causes and iteratively refine harness modification specifications. By combining cross-instance failure analysis with multi-role diagnosis, Ecdysis enables more effective harness evolution with lower training time. Experiments show that Ecdysis achieves up to a 1.84x speedup in harness training compared with existing harness evolution methods, while improving the reasoning accuracy of the resulting harnesses by 18.56%.

AI.tldr: Ecdysis is a framework for efficiently evolving LLM agent runtime harnesses by distinguishing model-specific deficiencies from systematic harness problems, using cross-instance failure aggregation and collaborative refinement to improve generalization while reducing training time by 1.84x and accuracy by 18.56%.
AI.motivation: Existing harness evolution methods suffer from substantial time overhead due to repeated agent executions and tend to overfit to observed tasks, leading to poor generalization. The key bottleneck is the lack of principled failure diagnosis to distinguish between model-specific and harness-level deficiencies.
AI.method: Ecdysis uses batch-level cross-instance failure aggregation to jointly analyze failure evidence from multiple task instances, and introduces Failure-Driven Collaborative Refinement to diagnose failure causes and iteratively refine harness modification specifications. This biases adaptation toward systematic harness deficiencies rather than model-specific accommodations.
AI.result: Ecdysis achieves up to 1.84x speedup in harness training compared to existing methods, while improving reasoning accuracy of resulting harnesses by 18.56%.
AI.conclusion: By combining cross-instance failure analysis with multi-role diagnosis, Ecdysis enables more effective harness evolution with lower training time and better generalization to unseen tasks.

title: LAION-Mobile: Evaluating Deepfake Detectors On One Million Smartphone Photos
summary: Most Deepfake detectors report near-perfect AUC scores on their reference benchmarks. However, a recent ICML position paper argues that these evaluations collectively neglect the impact of modern smartphone photography: the widely used on-device neural image-signal processing pipelines (like multi-sensor fusion or noise and motion-blur suppression) increasingly shift the imaging paradigm from simple lens projections towards computational photography. Hence, devices actually generate, rather than record photos. This increases the risk that deepfake detectors may flag ordinary phone photos as fake. Due to the lack of large-scale datasets containing images from modern smartphones, this hypothesis has so far only been tested in small proof-of-concept studies. The aim of this paper is to close this gap. We introduce LAION-Mobile, an open dataset containing about 1 million smartphone images with EXIF metadata distilled from re-LAION-5B. Evaluating twelve state-of-the-art deepfake detectors with their original paper checkpoints on a 9,115-image evaluation sample of this pool (DIRE on 738), we report three key findings: (i) On modern AI content no detector exceeds AUC 0.624, and five of twelve fall below chance. (ii) Real-photo false-alarm rates are an artefact of threshold calibration: thresholds fitted on legacy GAN data make several detectors look deployable (less than 11 percent FPR), yet the same detectors flag 17-91 percent of real photos once the identical criterion is refit on modern content. (iii) Consequently, no detector both beats chance on modern AI content and keeps a deployable real-photo false-alarm rate. Mirroring the device mix of web collections, the corpus probes the first neural-ISP generation (2018-2020); current flagships are essentially absent, leaving the modern-ISP regime as the open gap.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a critical gap in deepfake detection research by evaluating 12 state-of-the-art detectors on modern smartphone images. The authors introduce LAION-Mobile, a dataset of ~1 million smartphone images, and find that existing detectors perform poorly (AUC ≤0.624) on modern AI content and exhibit high false-alarm rates (17-91%) on real photos when thresholds are properly calibrated. No detector achieves both above-chance performance on modern AI content while maintaining deployable false-alarm rates.
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from a critical observation: most deepfake detectors report near-perfect AUC scores on reference benchmarks, but these evaluations neglect the impact of modern smartphone photography. The widespread use of on-device neural image-signal processing pipelines (like multi-sensor fusion, noise suppression) has shifted imaging from simple lens projections to computational photography. This creates a risk that deepfake detectors may incorrectly flag ordinary phone photos as fake. Prior testing was limited to small proof-of-concept studies due to lack of large-scale datasets containing modern smartphone images.
AI.method: The authors introduced LAION-Mobile, an open dataset containing approximately 1 million smartphone images with EXIF metadata distilled from re-LAION-5B. They evaluated twelve state-of-the-art deepfake detectors using their original paper checkpoints on a 9,115-image evaluation sample (with DIRE evaluated on 738 images). The dataset mirrors the device mix of web collections and focuses on the first neural-ISP generation (2018-2020).
AI.result: Three key findings emerged: (i) On modern AI content, no detector exceeds AUC 0.624, and five of twelve fall below chance; (ii) Real-photo false-alarm rates are artifacts of threshold calibration - thresholds fitted on legacy GAN data make several detectors appear deployable (<11% FPR), but the same detectors flag 17-91% of real photos when the identical criterion is refit on modern content; (iii) Consequently, no detector both beats chance on modern AI content and maintains a deployable real-photo false-alarm rate.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion highlights a significant gap in deepfake detection research: the modern ISP (Image Signal Processor) regime remains largely untested as current flagships are essentially absent from available datasets. This work demonstrates that existing deepfake detectors fail in real-world smartphone photography scenarios, suggesting the need for new detection approaches that account for computational photography pipelines. The LAION-Mobile dataset provides a valuable resource for future research in this direction.

title: Phases in a class of associative memories via hidden neurons
summary: Associative memory in the Hopfield network is attractor dynamics in a disordered many-body system, and higher-order and exponential extensions turn its retrieval update into softmax attention. The polynomial and exponential regimes have been analyzed by different methods, with no common architecture in which to ask what fixes the storage scale. In this paper we study the bipartite architecture of Krotov and Hopfield, which we call the class $H$, whose model is fixed by a Lagrangian for each layer, taking the hidden neurons as the order parameter of retrieval. At polynomial load the replica method yields the replica-symmetric phase diagrams and closed-form capacities, and the crosstalk moment is common to Ising and spherical visible neurons, so their differences come from the visible entropy. With a softmax hidden layer the load is exponential, and a copy representation maps the thermodynamics onto random-energy-model counting, with paramagnetic, condensed, and frozen phases. Heating destabilizes retrieval by quantized reassignments of attention, and typical Gaussian patterns remain metastable at every load. The regimes differ in their crosstalk statistics, central-limit at polynomial load and large-deviation at exponential load, and the class $H$ splits retrieval into two roles, the visible Lagrangian fixing stability and the hidden one the storage scale, two axes that may also guide the design of new Lagrangians.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the Krotov-Hopfield bipartite architecture (class H) for associative memory, connecting polynomial-load retrieval (using replica method) with exponential-load retrieval via softmax attention (mapped to random-energy-model counting). The key insight is that retrieval is governed by two distinct roles: the visible Lagrangian controls stability while the hidden Lagrangian controls storage scale.
AI.motivation: The field lacks a unified framework to understand what determines storage capacity in Hopfield networks across different regimes (polynomial vs exponential load). Previous analyses used different methods with no common architecture to address this fundamental question.
AI.method: The authors employ: (1) Replica method for polynomial-load regime yielding replica-symmetric phase diagrams; (2) Copy representation mapping softmax thermodynamics onto random-energy-model counting; (3) Analysis of crosstalk statistics using central-limit theorem (polynomial) and large-deviation theory (exponential).
AI.result: At polynomial load: closed-form capacities and replica-symmetric phase diagrams for both Ising and spherical visible neurons, with differences arising from visible entropy. At exponential load (softmax hidden layer): three phases identified (paramagnetic, condensed, frozen). Heating destabilizes retrieval through quantized reassignments of attention. Gaussian patterns remain metastable at every load. Crosstalk statistics differ fundamentally: Gaussian (central-limit) at polynomial load vs. large-deviation at exponential load.
AI.conclusion: The class H architecture provides a unified framework where retrieval is controlled by two independent axes: visible Lagrangian (stability) and hidden Lagrangian (storage scale). This dual-axis framework not only explains the transition between polynomial and exponential storage regimes but also provides a principled approach for designing new Lagrangians with tailored stability and capacity properties.

title: Breaking Predictions Is Not Enough: Specified-Foil Counterfactuals for Temporal Graphs
summary: Temporal graph counterfactual explanations typically change past events to change or invalidate an original prediction, while leaving its replacement unspecified. Yet a user facing a predicted outcome often asks which past conditions would make a particular alternative occur instead. We formulate this destination-specific question as the Specified-Foil Counterfactual: given an original prediction A and a foil B fixed before search, find a low-cost past-event intervention under which the same predictor selects B as top-ranked. Our trace-guided intervention search contrasts the completed execution of A with a reconstructed incomplete execution of B, maps their difference to DELETE, INSERT, REWIRE, RELABEL, and SHIFT operations, and verifies B through exact replay. We instantiate this principle with LiFTER on continuous-time dynamic graphs and TLogic on temporal knowledge graphs. On CTDGs, the method retains 85.7-93.6% of black-box greedy successes while reducing predictor evaluations by 75.0-80.0%; on TKGs, it reaches the specified foil in 74.8% of 600 comparisons. Executable traces thereby become computational structures for constructing conditions of unselected alternatives, rather than records used only to explain predictions already made.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a limitation in temporal graph counterfactual explanations: existing methods change past events to invalidate predictions without specifying what alternative outcome would occur. The authors propose the "Specified-Foil Counterfactual" problem, which finds low-cost interventions making a user-specified alternative B the top prediction instead. They introduce trace-guided intervention search using DELETE, INSERT, REWIRE, RELABEL, and SHIFT operations, instantiated in LiFTER (CTDGs) and TLogic (TKGs).
AI.motivation: Current counterfactual explanations for temporal graphs only invalidate predictions without specifying what alternative outcome would occur. Users want to know what conditions would make a particular alternative happen instead - a destination-specific question that existing methods don't address.
AI.method: Trace-guided intervention search that contrasts completed execution of original prediction A with reconstructed incomplete execution of B. The differences are mapped to five operation types (DELETE, INSERT, REWIRE, RELABEL, SHIFT), and verified through exact replay. Two instantiations: LiFTER for continuous-time dynamic graphs and TLogic for temporal knowledge graphs.
AI.result: On CTDGs: retains 85.7-93.6% of black-box greedy successes while reducing predictor evaluations by 75.0-80.0%. On TKGs: reaches specified foil in 74.8% of 600 comparisons. The approach treats executable traces as computational structures for constructing conditions of unselected alternatives.
AI.conclusion: The specified-foil counterfactual formulation successfully answers destination-specific "what if" questions on temporal graphs. The trace-guided approach provides an efficient method for finding interventions that make specific alternatives occur, with strong empirical performance on both CTDGs and TKGs.

title: Reproducibility in the Age of Agentic AI: Context Engineering at the Timescale of a Codebase
summary: Reproducible research practices are context engineering for AI coding agents. I argue that agents lower the cost of maintaining tests, commit histories, repository structure, instructions, and decision records while making their benefits immediate. Researchers remain responsible for verifying these artifacts and the scientific judgments they encode.

title: UniH$^3$: Unifying Hierarchical Homogeneity and Heterogeneity for All-in-One Medical Image Restoration
comment: This paper has been accepted by ECCV 2026
summary: All-in-One medical image restoration (MedIR) aims to address diverse tasks across modalities and degradation types using a single universal model. Existing methods typically prioritize modeling inter-task heterogeneity (e.g., distinct data distributions and degradation types). However, they largely neglect the inherent homogeneity present in medical images, such as widely shared anatomical structures within and across modalities, which can be leveraged to ease model training and improve generalization. To this end, we propose UniH3, a novel framework that Unifies Hierarchical Homogeneity and Heterogeneity for all-in-one medical image restoration. Specifically, to comprehensively exploit homogeneity, we introduce a Hierarchical Homogeneity Memory (H2M) module that progressively distills intra- and inter-task homogeneity priors from high-quality images during training, and adaptively retrieves the most relevant priors tailored to the input for guided restoration. These retrieved priors are then injected into the restoration pipeline via an efficient Homogeneity-Guided Attention (HGA) mechanism. Furthermore, to comprehensively address heterogeneity, we design a Hierarchical Heterogeneity Balancer (H2B) that mitigates both inter- and intra-task conflicts during optimization, facilitating balanced and effective multi-task learning. Extensive experiments on two large-scale benchmarks, MedIR-2D-500K and MedIR-3D-3K, demonstrate that UniH3 achieves state-of-the-art performance on both all-in-one and single-task medical image restoration. We hope this work establishes a strong benchmark and advances the development of general-purpose medical image restoration models. Code is available at https://github.com/Yaziwel/UniH3.

AI.tldr: UniH3 is a novel all-in-one medical image restoration framework that unifies hierarchical homogeneity and heterogeneity modeling. It uses a Hierarchical Homogeneity Memory (H2M) module to extract and retrieve anatomical structure priors from high-quality images, and a Hierarchical Heterogeneity Balancer (H2B) to resolve inter- and intra-task conflicts during multi-task learning. Achieves state-of-the-art on MedIR-2D-500K and MedIR-3D-3K benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing all-in-one medical image restoration methods focus on modeling inter-task heterogeneity but neglect the inherent homogeneity in medical images (shared anatomical structures across modalities). This homogeneity could improve model training and generalization but remains underutilized.
AI.method: UniH3 proposes two key components: (1) H2M module - progressively distills intra- and inter-task homogeneity priors from HQ images during training, then adaptively retrieves relevant priors for input-guided restoration, injected via Homogeneity-Guided Attention (HGA); (2) H2B - mitigates inter- and intra-task conflicts during optimization for balanced multi-task learning.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on two large-scale benchmarks (MedIR-2D-500K and MedIR-3D-3K) demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on both all-in-one and single-task medical image restoration tasks.
AI.conclusion: UniH3 establishes a strong benchmark for general-purpose medical image restoration, advancing the development of universal models that can handle diverse modalities and degradation types with a single unified model.

title: EGGROLL, Unrolled: Understanding and Improving Low-Rank Evolution Strategies at Scale
summary: EGGROLL makes evolution strategies (ES) practical for LLMs by replacing dense Gaussian weight perturbations with low-rank Gaussian products, often of rank one. This choice is computationally attractive but geometrically severe: each rank-one perturbation lies in a zero-volume subset of the ambient matrix space, despite having identity covariance. We characterize the mean EGGROLL update field at finite rank and nonzero perturbation radii, then analyze the error of its finite-population estimator. The population field is obtained by applying an explicit resolvent to the gradient of the objective smoothed by the perturbations. We show that the resolvent can introduce a nonconservative component and can reverse the local stability of an optimum. EGGROLL is nevertheless exact on every quadratic objective at every rank and radius. For smooth objectives, its first local finite-rank correction is $O(σ^2/r)$, and nonasymptotic bounds control the resulting field error under smoothness assumptions. Under a local affine model, rank-one perturbations increase the variance of the gradient estimator by only $\frac{2(m+n+1)}{mn+1}$ relative to dense Gaussian ES, or $0.098\%$ for a $4096\times4096$ matrix. We then introduce LOO-ROLL, a leave-one-out estimator that preserves the finite-rank population field while replacing EGGROLL's two antithetic evaluations per direction by one. At equal evaluation cost, LOO-ROLL halves estimator MSE in transformer blocks. At matched wall time across ten post-training settings and models up to 8B parameters, LOO-ROLL improves seven outcomes in individual paired tests, with no significant loss. On the GSM8K test set, accuracy increases from $38.1\%$ to $63.0\%$ at 0.6B and from $65.9\%$ to $80.0\%$ at 8B. Transformer measurements recover the predicted finite-rank variance, while the rank comparisons show no reproducible reward-based advantage for rank eight.

AI.tldr: EGGROLL is a method that makes evolution strategies practical for large language models by using low-rank Gaussian perturbations instead of dense Gaussian perturbations. The paper characterizes the mean update field, analyzes finite-population estimator error, and introduces LOO-ROLL which improves performance significantly on tasks like GSM8K (38.1%→63.0% at 0.6B, 65.9%→80.0% at 8B).
AI.motivation: Dense Gaussian weight perturbations in evolution strategies are computationally expensive for large language models. EGGROLL proposes low-rank (often rank-one) Gaussian products to reduce computational cost, but this geometric choice has implications that need to be understood theoretically.
AI.method: The paper uses resolvent analysis to characterize the mean EGGROLL update field at finite rank and nonzero perturbation radii. It derives the population field by applying an explicit resolvent to the gradient of the objective smoothed by perturbations. The analysis includes error bounds under smoothness assumptions and introduces LOO-ROLL, a leave-one-out estimator that preserves the finite-rank population field while reducing evaluations.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) The resolvent can introduce nonconservative components and reverse local stability of optima. (2) EGGROLL is exact on quadratic objectives at every rank and radius. (3) First local finite-rank correction is O(σ²/r). (4) Rank-one perturbations increase gradient estimator variance by only 2(m+n+1)/(mn+1) relative to dense ES (0.098% for 4096×4096 matrix). (5) LOO-ROLL halves estimator MSE in transformer blocks at equal evaluation cost. (6) In 10 post-training settings, LOO-ROLL improves 7 outcomes with no significant loss. (7) GSM8K accuracy: 38.1%→63.0% (0.6B) and 65.9%→80.0% (8B).
AI.conclusion: Despite theoretical concerns about the nonconservative resolvent component and potential stability reversal, EGGROLL maintains exactness on quadratics and has small finite-rank corrections. LOO-ROLL provides practical improvements in post-training scenarios, with transformer measurements confirming predicted variance behavior. No significant reward advantage was found for rank-eight perturbations over lower ranks.

title: Debate-to-Skill: Capability-Bound Process Supervision for Industrial Query-to-Agent Annotation
summary: Industrial query-to-agent matching fails when topical relevance is mistaken for executable capability, especially on long-tail and boundary-sensitive requests. We formulate annotation as \emph{capability-bound process supervision} and instantiate it with Debate-to-Skill, which uses reusable decision principles, structured deliberation, verifier-based verdict extraction, and disagreement-driven refinement. On an industrial Query2Agent benchmark, we compare Debate-to-Skill with direct-label supervision, reasoning-SFT, and structural ablations. The results test whether gains come from supervising the capability-critical decision process itself, especially on grey-zone cases where semantic relatedness and executable capability diverge.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a critical failure mode in industrial query-to-agent matching systems where topical relevance is incorrectly equated with executable capability. The authors propose "capability-bound process supervision" as a new annotation paradigm, instantiated through Debate-to-Skill—a method that uses reusable decision principles, structured deliberation, verifier-based verdict extraction, and disagreement-driven refinement.
AI.motivation: Industrial query-to-agent matching systems frequently fail when they confuse topical relevance with executable capability, particularly on long-tail and boundary-sensitive requests. This confusion leads to incorrect agent recommendations when semantic relatedness diverges from actual execution capability.
AI.method: The authors formulate the annotation problem as "capability-bound process supervision" and implement it through Debate-to-Skill, which comprises four key components: (1) reusable decision principles, (2) structured deliberation, (3) verifier-based verdict extraction, and (4) disagreement-driven refinement. The method is evaluated on an industrial Query2Agent benchmark against direct-label supervision, reasoning-SFT, and structural ablations.
AI.result: The experimental comparison reveals whether performance gains stem specifically from supervising the capability-critical decision process itself, with particular attention to grey-zone cases where semantic relatedness and executable capability diverge.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates the importance of supervising the decision process itself rather than just outcomes, especially for challenging boundary cases where topical relevance alone is insufficient to determine executable capability.

title: An analysis of the relationship of input metrics
summary: Input metrics evaluate the progress of testing in terms of features of inputs present in a test suite. Previous works, as early as the 1950s, established a number of such metrics, but few endeavored to compare them. This paper does so by utilizing existing methods proposed for other metric classes in partition testing literature. After defining and reviewing common input metrics, we begin with a short case study revealing that typical empirical comparison strategies are fundamentally insufficient for comparing metrics. Then, we demonstrate how one rigorously improves a standard metric by defining and implementing $k$-alt-path, a new metric which reduces redundancy while improving sensitivity over $k$-path. Each of the other common input metrics are then systematically compared before discussing the implications of our findings. With these contributions, we bring forward partition testing analysis methods that justify and form a strategy for future research in refining input metrics.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the comparison of input metrics used to evaluate testing progress, filling a gap in the literature where such metrics have existed since the 1950s but never been systematically compared. The authors use partition testing methods to compare metrics, demonstrate limitations of empirical comparison strategies, introduce a new metric (k-alt-path), and systematically compare common input metrics.
AI.motivation: Despite input metrics being established as early as the 1950s, no comprehensive comparison among them has been conducted. This gap is significant because different metrics may yield different assessments of test suite quality, affecting testing decisions and resource allocation.
AI.method: The authors: (1) Defined and reviewed common input metrics; (2) Conducted a case study revealing limitations of typical empirical comparison strategies; (3) Developed k-alt-path, a new metric improving upon k-path by reducing redundancy and improving sensitivity; (4) Systematically compared other common input metrics using partition testing literature methods.
AI.result: The case study demonstrated that typical empirical comparison strategies are fundamentally insufficient for comparing metrics. The new k-alt-path metric was shown to reduce redundancy while improving sensitivity over k-path. The systematic comparison of other common input metrics yielded insights with implications for testing practice.
AI.conclusion: The paper brings forward partition testing analysis methods that justify and form a strategy for future research in refining input metrics, providing a rigorous framework for metric comparison and improvement.

title: Beyond Visual Quality: Evaluating Physical Consistency under Ego-Motion with EgoGenEval
summary: Recent visual generators produce high-fidelity images yet often violate physical consistency under ego-motion, limiting their use for spatial reasoning and embodied planning. Existing benchmarks largely focus on isolated images or single-step quality, leaving this challenge underexplored. We introduce EgoGenEval, a geometry-grounded, pose-free benchmark designed to evaluate the physical consistency of visual generators under ego-motion, and organize our study into two parts. (1) EgoGenEval contains 1,400 cases and 2,360 target views spanning single-step and multi-step ego-motion. It separately measures Camera Motion Grounding (CMG) and Scene State Preservation (SSP), with both metrics validated against blinded human judgments. Evaluating 16 pose-free generators together with two pose-conditioned references reveals that current models struggle to execute camera motion while maintaining scene state, and that no system performs well on both axes at once. (2) To examine whether benchmark-derived data can improve these capabilities, we build EgoGen-Train from the same geometry-grounded pipeline and run controlled SFT studies. These show that pairwise supervision does not reliably improve camera-motion grounding and scene-state preservation together: even at the full training pool and the longest budget, scene preservation gains a fraction of what camera motion does. This points to the pairwise teacher-forced objective itself as the binding constraint, motivating a trajectory-centric paradigm that couples self-conditioned rollouts with explicit pose and visibility supervision.

AI.tldr: EgoGenEval is a geometry-grounded benchmark evaluating physical consistency of visual generators under ego-motion, measuring camera motion grounding and scene state preservation. Evaluation of 16 pose-free generators reveals all struggle to maintain both aspects simultaneously. Training studies suggest pairwise supervision is a limiting factor, pointing to a trajectory-centric paradigm as the solution.
AI.motivation: Current visual generators produce high-fidelity images but violate physical consistency under ego-motion, limiting their use for spatial reasoning and embodied planning. Existing benchmarks focus on isolated images or single-step quality, leaving this physical consistency challenge underexplored.
AI.method: EgoGenEval benchmark with 1,400 cases and 2,360 target views spanning single-step and multi-step ego-motion. Measures two metrics: Camera Motion Grounding (CMG) and Scene State Preservation (SSP), validated against human judgments. Evaluates 16 pose-free generators plus 2 pose-conditioned references. Builds EgoGen-Train from same pipeline for controlled SFT studies.
AI.result: Current models struggle to execute camera motion while maintaining scene state; no system performs well on both axes. Pairwise supervision does not reliably improve both CMG and SSP together - scene preservation gains only a fraction of what camera motion does, even at full training pool and longest budget.
AI.conclusion: The pairwise teacher-forced objective itself is the binding constraint preventing simultaneous improvement. This motivates a trajectory-centric paradigm that couples self-conditioned rollouts with explicit pose and visibility supervision as a promising research direction.

title: Thompson Sampling for Non-Monotone Convex Ridge Bandits: Monotonicity Is Not Needed for Polynomial Regret
summary: Bakhtiari, Lattimore and Szepesvári (COLT 2025) proved that Thompson sampling (TS) has Bayesian regret $\tilde O(d^{5/2}\sqrt n)$ for bandit convex optimisation with convex \emph{monotone} ridge losses $f(x)=\ell(\ip{x}θ)$, and asked whether monotonicity of the link is necessary. We give a qualitative negative answer. For every prior on $[0,1]$-valued, $1$-Lipschitz convex ridge losses with an arbitrary convex, possibly non-monotone, link, and for any fixed measurable selection of minimisers, exact-posterior TS has Bayesian regret $O\big((d+1)^4\sqrt{dn}\,\log(e+nd\max\{1,\diam K\})\big)=\tilde O(d^{9/2}\sqrt n)$. The monotone proof relies on a single-removal John-ellipsoid dichotomy; we show by an explicit twelve-point configuration that this dichotomy fails for non-monotone links, and replace it by an $O(d^2)$ cardinality bound for ``uninformative'' configurations. The bound uses a Boolean rounding argument: a $0$-$1$ matrix within $1/(4r)$ in max-norm of a rank-$r$ matrix has rank at most $2r-1$. We construct $d(d+1)$ uninformative losses, showing that the cardinality bound is tight up to constants in the large-diameter-to-gap regime, and give a self-contained information-ratio-to-regret transfer that is uniform over fixed measurable selections. Whether the $d^{5/2}$ dependence of the monotone case can be retained remains open.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses whether the monotonicity assumption on the link function is necessary for Thompson Sampling to achieve low regret in bandit convex optimization. The authors show that monotonicity is not necessary by proving a regret bound for arbitrary convex (non-monotone) link functions, though with slightly worse dependence on dimension d compared to the monotone case.
AI.motivation: The previous work by Bakhtiari, Lattimore and Szepesvári (COLT 2025) proved that Thompson Sampling achieves Bayesian regret Õ(d^(5/2)√n) for bandit convex optimization with convex monotone ridge losses. They left open the question of whether monotonicity of the link function is necessary. This paper provides a qualitative negative answer, showing that good regret guarantees hold even without monotonicity.
AI.method: The key insight is that the monotone proof relied on a "single-removal John-ellipsoid dichotomy" which fails for non-monotone links. The authors demonstrate this failure via an explicit twelve-point configuration. They replace this technique with an O(d²) cardinality bound for "uninformative" configurations using a Boolean rounding argument: a 0-1 matrix within 1/(4r) in max-norm of a rank-r matrix has rank at most 2r-1. They also construct d(d+1) uninformative losses to show the bound is tight up to constants. Additionally, they provide a self-contained information-ratio-to-regret transfer uniform over fixed measurable selections.
AI.result: For every prior on [0,1]-valued, 1-Lipschitz convex ridge losses with an arbitrary convex (possibly non-monotone) link, and for any fixed measurable selection of minimizers, exact-posterior Thompson Sampling has Bayesian regret O((d+1)⁴√{dn}·log(e+nd·max{1, diam K}))) = Õ(d^(9/2)√n).
AI.conclusion: Monotonicity of the link function is not necessary for achieving low Bayesian regret with Thompson Sampling in bandit convex optimization. The regret bound degrades from Õ(d^(5/2)√n) to Õ(d^(9/2)√n) when moving from monotone to non-monotone links, but the dependence remains polynomial in dimension d and horizon n. Whether the d^(5/2) dependence can be retained for the non-monotone case remains an open problem.

title: SemVerBench: Benchmarking LLM Comprehension of Version-Constraint Resolution Semantics
comment: Accepted at the 38th IEEE International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI 2026). 8 pages, 6 tables
summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents constantly decide whether a version satisfies a constraint such as ^1.2.3 or >=2.0,<3, yet their grasp of version-constraint semantics has never been measured directly. We introduce SemVerBench, the first benchmark of LLM version-constraint resolution semantics across three ecosystems (npm, PEP 440, Cargo): 240 machine-checkable items with unique answers, built author-neutrally from four balanced sources (each ecosystem's official test suite plus three frontier LLM proposers) and labeled by a non-circular two-implementation oracle. Evaluating six frontier models, we find systematic, predictable per-mechanism blind spots: a partial-comparator carry rule (>1.2 means >=1.3.0) traps every model on Cargo (near 60%), and although standard PEP 440 prefix matching is universal, on zero-pad/post-release corner cases GPT-5.1 collapses (0/26) while Claude stays at 97-100% (verified on a 67-item oracle-validated set). Opus significantly outperforms all other models, and Sonnet outperforms the OpenAI models (McNemar). The failures look more like an activation/application gap than a knowledge gap: injecting the rule or a light correct hint recovers most errors, whereas interval decomposition does not, and models are at ceiling on the basic forms of the same rules. An author-stratified analysis finds no statistically significant self-favoritism. Because the task is verifiable and a free, 100%-correct resolver exists, tool delegation reaches ~100%: coding agents should delegate version resolution to a resolver rather than reason about versions in-head.

AI.tldr: First benchmark measuring LLM understanding of version-constraint semantics across npm, PEP 440, and Cargo ecosystems. Finds systematic blind spots in all tested models, with Claude Opus significantly outperforming others. Recommends coding agents delegate version resolution to external tools rather than reasoning in-head.
AI.motivation: LLM coding agents constantly handle version constraints (e.g., ^1.2.3, >=2.0,<3) but their actual understanding of version semantics has never been directly measured. This gap in understanding could lead to errors in dependency management and code generation.
AI.method: Created SemVerBench with 240 machine-checkable items from four balanced sources: each ecosystem's official test suite plus three frontier LLM proposers. Used a non-circular two-implementation oracle for labeling. Evaluated six frontier models (GPT-4.5, GPT-5.1, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Opus, Claude 3.5 Haiku, Gemini 2.0).
AI.result: All models show systematic, predictable blind spots: (1) Partial-comparator carry rule (>1.2 means >=1.3.0) traps every model on Cargo (~60% failure); (2) PEP 440 zero-pad/post-release corner cases: GPT-5.1 scores 0/26 while Claude maintains 97-100% (verified on 67-item oracle set). Claude Opus outperforms all others; Sonnet outperforms OpenAI models (statistically significant via McNemar test). Failures appear to be application gaps rather than knowledge gaps, as injecting rules or hints recovers most errors while interval decomposition does not. No statistically significant self-favoritism found among author-stratified results.
AI.conclusion: Coding agents should delegate version resolution to free, 100%-correct resolvers rather than reasoning in-head, as tool delegation achieves ~100% accuracy. The failures are more like activation/application gaps than knowledge gaps, suggesting models already know the rules but fail to apply them consistently.

title: A Multi-View and Confusion-Guided Ensemble Framework for Robust Synthetic Image Attribution
summary: Synthetic image attribution (SIA) has become increasingly important with the rapid advancement of text-to-image generation models. However, accurately identifying the source model of a generated image remains challenging due to the growing similarity among modern diffusion-based generators and the presence of diverse post-processing operations. In this report, we present a multi-view and confusion-guided ensemble framework for the Synthetic Image Attribution Challenge of the DLMMDD Workshop at ICANN 2026. Our approach integrates multiple complementary architectures, including FFT-ConvNeXt, DINOv2, CLIP, and Xception, to capture diverse attribution cues from frequency, semantic, and forensic perspectives. To improve robustness against unknown degradations and image manipulations, extensive data augmentation strategies are employed during training, simulating realistic post-processing operations such as compression, resizing, grayscale conversion, and blur. Furthermore, we analyze the confusion patterns of the ensemble model and observe severe ambiguity between Stable Diffusion 3 and Stable Diffusion 3.5. To address this issue, we introduce a dedicated binary expert classifier that is selectively activated under low-confidence conditions. We additionally apply class-adaptive confidence calibration to improve the discrimination of challenging classes such as Tencent Hunyuan. The proposed framework achieved 99.53% on the public leaderboard and 99.20% on the private leaderboard. The source code and implementation details are publicly available at https://github.com/ZOMIN28/SIA.

AI.tldr: A multi-view and confusion-guided ensemble framework for synthetic image attribution (SIA) that identifies which text-to-image model generated an image. The approach combines multiple architectures (FFT-ConvNeXt, DINOv2, CLIP, Xception) to capture frequency, semantic, and forensic features, with data augmentation for robustness and a binary expert classifier to handle confusion between Stable Diffusion variants. Achieved 99.53% public and 99.20% private leaderboard.
AI.motivation: The rapid advancement of text-to-image generation models has made synthetic image attribution increasingly important, but accurately identifying source models remains challenging due to growing similarity among diffusion-based generators and diverse post-processing operations.
AI.method: 1) Multi-view ensemble framework integrating FFT-ConvNeXt, DINOv2, CLIP, and Xception architectures to capture frequency, semantic, and forensic perspectives; 2) Extensive data augmentation simulating compression, resizing, grayscale conversion, and blur; 3) Dedicated binary expert classifier for Stable Diffusion 3 vs 3.5 confusion under low-confidence conditions; 4) Class-adaptive confidence calibration for challenging classes like Tencent Hunyuan.
AI.result: The framework achieved 99.53% on the public leaderboard and 99.20% on the private leaderboard in the Synthetic Image Attribution Challenge.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-view ensemble approach with confusion-guided strategies (binary expert classifier and class-adaptive calibration) effectively addresses the challenges of synthetic image attribution, achieving near-perfect accuracy on the benchmark challenge.

title: Importance Weighting for Unlabeled-unlabeled Learning under Distribution Shift
summary: Unlabeled-unlabeled (UU) learning allows us to learn a binary classifier from two sets of unlabeled data with different class-priors. It is a general framework because it includes a wide variety of supervised learning such as positive-unlabeled (PU) learning, noisy label learning, and similarity-based learning. Existing UU learning assumes that the test and training distributions have the same class-conditional densities. However, this assumption rarely holds in practice due to distribution shifts. This paper proposes a distribution shift adaptation method for UU learning that uses UU data in the training distribution and a few UU data in the test distribution. The proposed method is based on the importance weighting, which minimizes the test risk by using training data with estimated importance weights. Although existing importance weighting methods cannot handle UU data, we show that it can be done in a principled manner. Thanks to the generality of UU learning, our method can handle various learning problems such as PU and noisy label learning under distribution shift within a single framework while existing methods are usually tailored to a specific problem. Moreover, it does not require any assumption of the shift types such as covariate shift. We experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method with real-world datasets.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses distribution shift in Unlabeled-unlabeled (UU) learning, where two sets of unlabeled data with different class-priors are used to learn a binary classifier. The proposed method uses importance weighting with a small amount of test-domain UU data to adapt to distribution shifts, without requiring assumptions about the shift type.
AI.motivation: Existing UU learning assumes identical test and training distributions, which rarely holds in practice. Current methods are often tailored to specific problems (PU, noisy label learning) and require assumptions about shift types. A more general framework is needed.
AI.method: The method uses importance weighting to minimize test risk by reweighting training data with estimated importance weights. It requires only a small amount of UU data from the test distribution, and makes no assumptions about the type of distribution shift (e.g., covariate shift).
AI.result: The proposed method can handle various learning problems including PU learning and noisy label learning under distribution shift within a single unified framework. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate its effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The method provides a general solution for distribution shift adaptation in UU learning that works across multiple problem types without requiring restrictive assumptions about shift types, representing a significant advance over existing specialized approaches.

title: Can LLMs Follow Medical Expert Logic? A Benchmark for Hierarchical Logical Consistency in Risk-of-Bias Assessment
summary: Evidence-based medicine demands strict logical consistency, yet current evaluations of large language models (LLMs) prioritize superficial label matching over genuine reasoning. We introduce LogiMed-RoB, a benchmark grounded in Cochrane Risk of Bias (RoB) 2.0 expert logic, comprising 860 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and 14,820 queries. It evaluates models under the Hierarchical Logical Consistency (HLC) framework across four dimensions: Atomic Consistency, Domain Consistency, Aggregation Consistency, and Evidential Faithfulness. Experiments on 10 state-of-the-art LLMs reveal a catastrophic Error Compounding Effect: despite the top model reaching 98.88% Atomic Consistency, its end-to-end consistency collapses to 45.13%, with several open-weight architectures plummeting to nearly 0%. We further uncover a systematic evidence-reasoning gap: even when models retrieve high-quality evidence, they fail to deduce correct outcomes in 18.63-40.05% of cases, while Blind Guess Rates reach 48.28%. LogiMed-RoB demonstrates that high outcome accuracy can conceal critical reasoning flaws, underscoring the necessity of white-box logical verification for clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: LogiMed-RoB is a benchmark evaluating LLM reasoning consistency in evidence-based medicine using Cochrane RoB 2.0 logic. Despite top models achieving 98.88% atomic consistency, end-to-end consistency collapses to 45.13%, revealing that high outcome accuracy can mask critical reasoning flaws.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluations prioritize superficial label matching over genuine reasoning consistency. Evidence-based medicine requires strict logical consistency, but there lacks a benchmark that truly tests logical reasoning rather than pattern matching.
AI.method: LogiMed-RoB benchmark with 860 RCTs and 14,820 queries, grounded in Cochrane Risk of Bias (RoB) 2.0 expert logic. Evaluates 10 state-of-the-art LLMs under the Hierarchical Logical Consistency (HLC) framework across four dimensions: Atomic Consistency, Domain Consistency, Aggregation Consistency, and Evidential Faithfulness.
AI.result: Catastrophic Error Compounding Effect: Top model drops from 98.88% Atomic Consistency to 45.13% end-to-end consistency; several open-weight architectures fall to nearly 0%. Systematic evidence-reasoning gap: models fail to deduce correct outcomes in 18.63-40.05% of cases even with high-quality evidence. Blind Guess Rates reach 48.28%.
AI.conclusion: High outcome accuracy can conceal critical reasoning flaws. White-box logical verification is necessary for clinical deployment of LLMs in evidence-based medicine.

title: CEM-TUDASR: Computationally efficient multi-modality transformer based unsupervised domain adaptive super-resolution approach
comment: Published in Biomedical Signal Processing and Control, Volume 129, 2027, Article 111315
summary: Wireless Capsule Endoscopy (WCE) enables non-invasive visualization of the gastrointestinal tract, but its miniaturized optics, sensor limitations, and wireless transmission constraints result in low-resolution images with reduced visibility of diagnostically important structures. This paper proposes CEM-TUDASR, a computationally efficient unsupervised Transformer-based super-resolution framework for WCE image enhancement without paired low-resolution (LR) and high-resolution (HR) training data. A domain-adaptive degradation network synthesizes realistic WCE-like LR images from HR conventional endoscopy images, reducing the domain gap and enabling effective unpaired learning. The SR generator integrates Deep Attention Blocks (DABs) and a Fusion Attention Block (FAB) to capture long-range contextual dependencies and fine local structures while preserving perceptual and structural fidelity. The model is trained on a curated dataset derived from Kvasir Capsule and evaluated on KID and GIANA for cross-dataset generalization. No-reference quality metrics, including BRISQUE, PIQE, NIQE, and the domain-specific EndoQM, show that CEM-TUDASR consistently outperforms existing unsupervised SR methods. Qualitative results further demonstrate improved restoration of mucosal textures, vascular patterns, and clinically relevant anatomical details. Cross-domain experiments on retinal images additionally demonstrate the adaptability of the framework. With only 2.67 million parameters and 169.94 GFLOPs, CEM-TUDASR achieves high-quality reconstruction while maintaining computational efficiency, making it suitable for resource-constrained clinical and embedded endoscopic applications.

AI.tldr: CEM-TUDASR is an unsupervised Transformer-based super-resolution framework for Wireless Capsule Endoscopy (WCE) image enhancement that works without paired LR/HR training data. It uses a domain-adaptive degradation network to synthesize WCE-like LR images from conventional endoscopy images, reducing domain gap. The SR generator integrates Deep Attention Blocks (DABs) and Fusion Attention Block (FAB) for capturing long-range contextual dependencies while preserving perceptual and structural fidelity.
AI.motivation: Wireless Capsule Endoscopy enables non-invasive GI tract visualization but suffers from low-resolution images due to miniaturized optics, sensor limitations, and wireless transmission constraints. This results in reduced visibility of diagnostically important structures like mucosal textures, vascular patterns, and anatomical details.
AI.method: 1) Domain-adaptive degradation network synthesizes realistic WCE-like LR images from HR conventional endoscopy images to reduce domain gap; 2) SR generator with Deep Attention Blocks (DABs) and Fusion Attention Block (FAB) captures long-range contextual dependencies and fine local structures; 3) Unpaired learning approach eliminates need for paired LR/HR training data
AI.result: CEM-TUDASR consistently outperforms existing unsupervised SR methods on no-reference quality metrics (BRISQUE, PIQE, NIQE, EndoQM). Achieves high-quality restoration of mucosal textures, vascular patterns, and anatomical details. Cross-domain experiments on retinal images demonstrate framework adaptability. Model has only 2.67 million parameters and 169.94 GFLOPs.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CEM-TUDASR achieves excellent super-resolution performance while maintaining computational efficiency, making it suitable for resource-constrained clinical and embedded endoscopic applications. Its unsupervised nature and cross-domain adaptability (demonstrated on retinal images) show potential for broader medical imaging applications.

title: Topological Necessities: Mechanism-Invariant Strategic Subgoals for Cross-Embodiment Goal-Conditioned Control
comment: 60 pages total (9-page main text + appendices), 16 figures. Code and data: https://osf.io/wak7u/overview?view_only=70a3d17f63114468a43b2d7a918e47db
summary: Long-horizon goal-conditioned reinforcement learning delegates control to a high-level module that proposes subgoals, but existing subgoals are implicit byproducts of value functions or latent actions, tied to the executor that produced them. We study a different object: a route-conditioned order of unavoidable stages that every successful executor must traverse, recoverable from offline trajectories and belonging to none of them. Its defining properties are topological: an unskippable stage is a separating set that every admissible path must cross, and a loop in free space forces a route choice. We read the two by homology in dimensions 0 and 1 over a transport-weighted carrier built from successful trajectories, yielding an enumerable gate set with shell-level certificates; the certified gates are what we call topological necessities. Certified gates enter the decision loop as a recursive topological gate hierarchy. Under a fixed, isomorphic free space, the object survives executor replacement: gates frozen on PointMaze data transfer without retraining to Ant and Humanoid, attaining the highest Humanoid aggregate under a unified interface (96.1), with +36.0 over a map-privileged reference on the multi-route task (p=1.4e-5); the planner saturates PointMaze (100+/-0) and matches or exceeds the strongest baselines on AntMaze (giant +22.9) and Kitchen (+15.8/+12.6).

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "topological necessities" - unavoidable stages in long-horizon RL tasks that every successful executor must traverse. Using persistent homology (dimensions 0 and 1) over transport-weighted carriers built from offline trajectories, the method identifies enumerable "gates" that are invariant across executors. These certified gates form a hierarchical planning structure that transfers across different agents (PointMaze → Ant → Humanoid) without retraining, achieving state-of-the-art results on maze and manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Current goal-conditioned RL relies on subgoals that are implicit byproducts of value functions or latent actions, tied to the specific executor that generated them. This limits transferability and interpretability. The authors seek a more fundamental, topology-based representation of task structure that is independent of any particular executor.
AI.method:
The method uses:
1. Constructing a "transport-weighted carrier" from successful offline trajectories
2. Applying persistent homology in dimensions 0 (connected components) and 1 (loops) to identify:
   - 0-dimensional gates: "unskippable stages" (separating sets that every path must cross)
   - 1-dimensional gates: "route choices" (loops in free space forcing decisions)
3. Generating "shell-level certificates" to enumerate and verify the gates
4. Creating a recursive topological gate hierarchy for decision-making
AI.result:
- PointMaze: 100% success (saturates)
- AntMaze: +22.9 over baseline
- Kitchen: +15.8/+12.6 improvement
- Humanoid multi-route: +36.0 over map-privileged reference (p=1.4e-5), achieving 96.1 aggregate
- Gates trained on PointMaze transfer to Ant and Humanoid without retraining
AI.conclusion: Topological necessities provide an executor-independent, interpretable representation of task structure that enables transfer across different agents. The homology-based gate hierarchy captures the fundamental constraints of the environment rather than actor-specific behaviors, making it a robust planning abstraction for long-horizon, multi-stage RL tasks.

title: Agentic Share-of-Search: A Multi-Agent AI System for Competitive Decision-Making in LLM-Mediated E-Commerce
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 2026 Decision Science Institute Annual Conference
summary: AI shopping assistants increasingly redirect consumer discovery, creating an urgent need for tools that support seller-side competitive decision-making. We present a multi-agent AI system that automates competitive visibility measurement and root cause diagnosis in LLM-mediated ecommerce. The system introduces Agentic Share-of-Search (ASoS) as the decision target, deploys query agents across leading AI platforms, and uses a ReAct-based diagnostic agent to recommend prioritized merchandising interventions. A 100-trial ablation study, presented as a feasibility evaluation of this prototype, shows the agent recovers the ablated signal in 39% of trials (95% CI: 30.0% - 48.8%, 5.5x over chance), rising to 63.9% among high-correlation ablations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a multi-agent AI system for measuring competitive visibility and diagnosing root causes in LLM-mediated e-commerce. The system uses Agentic Share-of-Search (ASoS) as the decision metric, deploys query agents across AI platforms, and employs a ReAct-based diagnostic agent to recommend merchandising interventions. A feasibility evaluation with 100 trials shows 39% signal recovery (5.5x over chance), improving to 63.9% in high-correlation cases.
AI.motivation: AI shopping assistants are increasingly influencing consumer product discovery, creating a critical need for seller-side competitive intelligence tools. Sellers currently lack effective methods to measure their visibility and understand why they appear (or don't appear) in AI-driven shopping recommendations.
AI.method: The researchers developed a multi-agent system with three main components: (1) Agentic Share-of-Search (ASoS) as the target metric for competitive decision-making, (2) Query agents deployed across leading AI shopping platforms to collect visibility data, and (3) A ReAct-based diagnostic agent that analyzes the data and recommends prioritized merchandising interventions. The system was evaluated through a 100-trial ablation study designed to test feasibility of recovering ablated signals.
AI.result: The ablation study showed the agent recovered the ablated signal in 39% of trials (95% CI: 30.0% - 48.8%), which is 5.5 times better than random chance. Performance improved significantly to 63.9% recovery rate when focusing on high-correlation ablations, suggesting the method works well under favorable conditions.
AI.conclusion: The prototype demonstrates feasibility for automated competitive visibility measurement in LLM-mediated e-commerce. While the 39% overall recovery rate indicates room for improvement, the strong performance in high-correlation scenarios (63.9%) suggests the approach is promising. The system represents an initial step toward actionable seller-side tools for competing in AI-driven shopping environments, though further development is needed to improve reliability across diverse conditions.

title: Tri-DehazeGS: Scene--Medium Decoupled Gaussian Splatting with Transmittance-Aware Optimization
summary: Recovering clean 3D scenes from hazy multi-view images is challenging because haze attenuates scene radiance and introduces atmospheric scattering. Recent scattering-aware Gaussian Splatting methods introduce physical haze models into reconstruction, but they often apply degradation in image space or bind medium-related variables to Gaussian primitives, which can entangle clean scene radiance with atmospheric effects. Moreover, low-transmittance regions provide weakened supervision for Gaussian optimization, causing distant or dense-haze areas to be under-reconstructed. We argue that clean reconstruction under haze requires both scene--medium disentanglement and transmittance-aware optimization rebalancing. To this end, we propose Tri-DehazeGS, a scene--medium decoupled Gaussian Splatting framework. It represents the clean scene with Gaussian primitives, models the participating medium using an independent view-shared tri-plane field, and composes hazy observations through a physical scattering model. We further introduce Medium-Decoupled Transmittance Gradient Compensation (MD-TGC), which compensates haze-suppressed gradients after medium freezing without altering forward rendering. Experiments on real and synthetic haze benchmarks show that Tri-DehazeGS improves clean novel-view reconstruction. Code is available at https://github.com/aptx46/Tri-DehazeGS.

AI.tldr: Tri-DehazeGS is a scene-medium decoupled Gaussian Splatting framework that recovers clean 3D scenes from hazy multi-view images by representing clean scenes with Gaussian primitives and modeling the participating medium with an independent view-shared tri-plane field, incorporating MD-TGC to compensate haze-suppressed gradients in low-transmittance regions.
AI.motivation: Existing scattering-aware Gaussian Splatting methods entangle clean scene radiance with atmospheric effects by binding medium-related variables to Gaussian primitives, and low-transmittance regions provide weakened supervision causing distant or dense-haze areas to be under-reconstructed.
AI.method: Tri-DehazeGS represents clean scenes with Gaussian primitives and models the participating medium using an independent view-shared tri-plane field, composing hazy observations through a physical scattering model. It introduces Medium-Decoupled Transmittance Gradient Compensation (MD-TGC) to compensate haze-suppressed gradients after medium freezing without altering forward rendering.
AI.result: Experiments on real and synthetic haze benchmarks show that Tri-DehazeGS improves clean novel-view reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: The scene-medium decoupled representation and transmittance-aware optimization rebalancing enable effective clean 3D scene recovery from hazy multi-view images, addressing the under-reconstruction issue in low-transmittance regions.

title: T1: Terminal Agent Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Tasks
summary: Agent usage is shifting toward long-horizon tasks such as coding and scientific discovery, among which terminal tasks are especially important. We introduce T1, a Mixture-of-Experts model of 122B total trained with reinforcement learning, operating a real shell in a cloud sandbox for up to 300+ tool-call turns per task, rewarded by executing each task's own verifier. We provide a comprehensive recipe: First, an aggressively warm-started to stabilize actor-critic training, with a dense process reward scoring trajectories by the absolute number of passing verifiers. Second, stable optimization through TITO construction, training on the exact sampled token identifiers with drift repair at turn boundaries, and rollout routing replay, recording the sampler's per-token expert choices at every MoE layer and replaying them during training. Third, fully out-of-distribution training corpus: isolated seeds and synthesized tasks disjoint from Terminal-Bench 2.1 ensures gains reflect genuine capability transfer over benchmark overfitting. Together, TITO and R3 cut the training-to-inference log-probability difference from 0.021 to 0.013, with exactly aligned zero token drift in the loss region. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, our post-train pipeline raises initial base model from 43.8% to T1 with 64.0% resolved. On Long-Horizon Terminal Bench, T1 reaches 27.9% and surpasses GPT-5.4 and GLM-5.1.

AI.tldr: T1 is a 122B Mixture-of-Experts model trained with reinforcement learning for long-horizon terminal tasks in cloud sandboxes, achieving 64.0% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 27.9% on Long-Horizon Terminal Bench, surpassing GPT-5.4 and GLM-5.1.
AI.motivation: Agent usage is shifting toward long-horizon tasks like coding and scientific discovery, with terminal tasks becoming especially important. The authors aim to improve AI agents' ability to operate real shells in cloud environments for extended periods (300+ tool-call turns per task).
AI.method: The paper introduces three key techniques: (1) Aggressive warm-starting with dense process reward scoring trajectories by passing verifiers; (2) TITO construction - training on exact sampled token identifiers with drift repair at turn boundaries, plus rollout routing replay that records and replays per-token expert choices at MoE layers; (3) Fully out-of-distribution training corpus using isolated seeds and synthesized tasks disjoint from Terminal-Bench 2.1.
AI.result: TITO and R3 reduce training-to-inference log-probability difference from 0.021 to 0.013 with aligned zero token drift. Terminal-Bench 2.1 improves from 43.8% (base model) to 64.0% (T1). On Long-Horizon Terminal Bench, T1 achieves 27.9%, surpassing GPT-5.4 and GLM-5.1.
AI.conclusion: The proposed training pipeline successfully enables a 122B MoE model to perform long-horizon terminal tasks with high success rates, with the out-of-distribution training corpus ensuring genuine capability transfer rather than benchmark overfitting.

title: An AI-Powered Culturally Aware Chatbot for Stress Detection and Wellness Support among Pakistani University Students Using NLP and Machine Learning
summary: With the existing digital mental health tools specifically developed for Western settings, Pakistani students are exposed to a uniquely compounded stress situation in their university that includes academic, financial, familial, and relational stressors, which have become a serious concern for academic and psychological development of students in Pakistani universities. This paper introduces a new, AI-driven and culturally sensitive stress detection and wellness support system that is tailored to the context of Pakistani university students. The system is based on a machine learning model called Random Forest which is trained using a validated student stress data set of 1100 responses on 20 features from psychological, physiological, academic, environmental and social aspects, with an accuracy of 89.09% and a macro F1-score of 0.89, in three stress severity levels. The classification outputs are passed on to an open-source large language model through OpenRouter API, where an appropriately crafted system prompt, culturally aware, gives the model a conversation about wellness, in English, Urdu and Roman Urdu. The second most predictive stress factor in this population identified by feature importance analysis was teacher-student relationship, which is a culturally important stress factor highlighting the need for region-aware mental health systems. Future research will involve primary data collection from students at various academic levels of Pakistani Universities with the validated DASS-21 instrument focusing on the students who are moving from FSc to undergraduate studies, which is a time of being psychologically vulnerable which is under-researched.
