LILA (\emph{Latent-Informed Layer Analysis}) scores neuron importance via the Kolmogorov--Smirnov (KS) distance between empirical singular value distributions of the full and neuron-ablated feed-forward network (FFN) weight matrix, providing a closed-form spectral rule requiring no training, calibration data, or auxiliary network. Without any fine-tuning, LILA surpasses PruneNet (45M-parameter RL policy) by 1.57~pp in zero-shot accuracy on LLaMA-2-7B at 25\% sparsity, and outperforms WikiText-2-calibrated SliceGPT by up to 6.0~pp across all sparsity levels, while preserving the original architecture. After one epoch of LoRA recovery fine-tuning, LILA achieves highly competitive performance, matching the heavily calibrated SliceGPT baseline to within a 0.48~pp margin across LLaMA-2-7B and Phi-2, despite using zero calibration data. A Neural Tangent Kernel analysis confirms a 22$\times$ reduction in functional distortion versus random pruning, providing theoretical grounding for the spectral importance criterion. Finally, extending LILA to dynamically allocate sparsity budgets via KS-scores yields state-of-the-art generative preservation at moderate compression, while uncovering fundamental single-layer architectural bottlenecks at higher compression regimes.

AI.tldr: LILA is a calibration-free structured pruning method for LLMs that uses KS distance between singular value distributions to score neuron importance, achieving state-of-the-art results without any fine-tuning and matching calibrated methods within 0.48pp after minimal LoRA recovery.
AI.motivation: Existing structured pruning methods for LLMs require calibration data, gradient computation, or large auxiliary policy networks at pruning time, which are computationally expensive and impractical.
AI.method: LILA scores neuron importance via the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) distance between empirical singular value distributions of the full and neuron-ablated feed-forward network (FFN) weight matrix. This provides a closed-form spectral rule requiring no training, calibration data, or auxiliary network.
AI.result: Without fine-tuning, LILA surpasses PruneNet by 1.57pp in zero-shot accuracy on LLaMA-2-7B at 25% sparsity, and outperforms WikiText-2-calibrated SliceGPT by up to 6.0pp across all sparsity levels. After one epoch of LoRA recovery fine-tuning, LILA matches the heavily calibrated SliceGPT baseline to within 0.48pp across LLaMA-2-7B and Phi-2. NTK analysis confirms a 22x reduction in functional distortion versus random pruning.
AI.conclusion: LILA introduces a calibration-free, gradient-free structured pruning method that achieves state-of-the-art results. It outperforms PruneNet by 1.57pp and SliceGPT by up to 6.0pp without fine-tuning. After one epoch of LoRA recovery, it matches SliceGPT within 0.48pp. The NTK analysis provides theoretical validation showing 22x reduction in functional distortion. The method also identifies architectural bottlenecks at high compression and enables dynamic sparsity allocation.

title: When Does Text Inform? Benchmarking Information-Theoretic Metrics for Multimodal Time-Series Forecasting
summary: Multimodal forecasting models that combine time series with text annotations promise richer prediction through textual context, but how do we know whether a text annotation meaningfully contributes to the forecasters prediction? This is an information-theoretic question, but to evaluate whether information-theoretic metrics can reliably measure the predictive value an annotation provides, a ground truth benchmark is needed, and none currently exist. We create a synthetic time series signal with annotations in three categories: semantically correct, incorrect, and irrelevant. Because the data generation process is fully controlled, ground-truth information content is known exactly, enabling principled evaluation of six complementary mutual information estimators (KSG, MINE, InfoNCE, CCA, PID and V-information). We show that all six estimators identify correct annotations as most informative, and are able to audit the quality of mixed text corpora, choosing the annotations that result in the best downstream forecasting results without the need for model training. Our benchmark identifies limitations of each estimator, and these are validated on seven real-world datasets, which show how estimator performance differs on weak signals. Finally, we establish practical rules for implementing these metrics for annotation auditing and fusion selection.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of evaluating whether text annotations meaningfully contribute to multimodal forecasting models. The authors create a synthetic benchmark with known ground truth to evaluate six information-theoretic mutual information estimators (KSG, MINE, InfoNCE, CCA, PID, V-information), finding all can identify informative annotations, and establish practical rules for annotation auditing.
AI.motivation: Multimodal forecasting models combining time series with text annotations promise richer predictions, but there is no reliable way to measure whether a text annotation actually contributes predictive information. Existing information-theoretic metrics need evaluation against ground truth, which currently does not exist.
AI.method: Created a synthetic time series benchmark with annotations in three categories (semantically correct, incorrect, and irrelevant) with fully controlled data generation allowing exact ground-truth information content. Evaluated six complementary mutual information estimators: KSG, MINE, InfoNCE, CCA, PID, and V-information. Validated findings on seven real-world datasets.
AI.result: All six estimators successfully identify correct annotations as most informative and can audit annotation quality without model training. The benchmark identified limitations of each estimator, with performance differences observed on weak signals in real-world validation.
AI.conclusion: Information-theoretic metrics can reliably measure the predictive value of text annotations in multimodal forecasting. Practical rules were established for implementing these metrics for annotation auditing and fusion selection. The benchmark provides a principled evaluation framework for comparing different mutual information estimators.

title: SAMV-DUSt3R: Instance-Centric 3D Scene Decoupling from Sparse Multi-Views
summary: With the rising demand to decouple objects from 3D scenes, we propose SAMV-DUSt3R, an end-to-end model that injects SAM2 2D masks into MV-DUSt3R reconstruction. A Cross Flow Mask Block uses these masks to steer the network toward the target instance, jointly improving shape accuracy and achieving object-level disentanglement without multi-stage pipelines. To ensure reconstruction stability, a lightweight Spatial RankGNN selects the optimal reference view with a selection accuracy of 73.5\%. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method boosts average reconstruction precision by 11\% across various metrics compared to state-of-the-art baselines. These results reveal a strong instance-disentanglement capability and clear benefits for driving, robotics, AR/VR, and heritage digitisation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SAMV-DUSt3R, an end-to-end 3D reconstruction method that decouples objects from 3D scenes by injecting SAM2 2D masks into MV-DUSt3R. It uses a Cross Flow Mask Block for instance-aware reconstruction and a Spatial RankGNN for optimal reference view selection.
AI.motivation: The rising demand to decouple/separate individual objects from 3D scenes, enabling object-level disentanglement without requiring multi-stage pipelines.
AI.method: SAMV-DUSt3R integrates SAM2 2D masks into MV-DUSt3R reconstruction via a Cross Flow Mask Block that steers the network toward target instances. A lightweight Spatial RankGNN selects optimal reference views to ensure reconstruction stability.
AI.result: Achieves 73.5% view selection accuracy and boosts average reconstruction precision by 11% across various metrics compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Demonstrates strong instance-disentanglement capability.
AI.conclusion: The method provides clear benefits for driving, robotics, AR/VR, and heritage digitisation applications by enabling accurate object-level 3D reconstruction from scenes.

title: When does a spectral prior help graph learning? Connectivity-loss estimation under road-network disruptions
comment: 24 pages, 7 figures, 7 tables. Code and data: doi:10.5281/zenodo.22307723
summary: Rapid evaluation of many simultaneous road-link disruptions requires a practical compromise between exact spectral recomputation and local approximation. We estimate relative algebraic-connectivity loss after multi-edge deletion using graph neural networks (GNNs) that learn a bounded correction to a first-order Fiedler sensitivity. The study considers independent, spatially clustered, and edge-betweenness-targeted failures, with graph-disjoint synthetic splits and zero-shot transfer to 13 OpenStreetMap (OSM) areas in six countries. GCN, GraphSAGE, and edge-aware MPNN backbones are compared with analytical baselines. In expanded OSM tests, residual GCN improves spatial-failure MAE by 0.0391 (95% hierarchical interval 0.0151-0.0662), while residual GraphSAGE improves targeted-failure MAE by 0.0257 (0.0095-0.0446). Second-order perturbation improves first-order MAE by only 0.0028-0.0053. Correction slopes decrease under targeted transfer, indicating residual shrinkage around systematic prior error. Leave-one-country-out OSM-to-OSM transfer is mixed: residual GCN improves targeted-failure MAE by 0.0622 (0.0169-0.1153) but worsens the spatial point estimate. Sparse scaling extends to 20,000 nodes and separates one-time spectral setup from amortized screening cost. These results characterize the spectral residual as a useful but domain-sensitive inductive bias for structural connectivity screening. Code, cached networks, and reproducibility artifacts are archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22307723.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using GNNs to estimate algebraic connectivity loss in road networks after multiple edge deletions, improving upon first-order Fiedler sensitivity approximations.
AI.motivation: Rapid evaluation of simultaneous road-link disruptions requires a practical compromise between exact spectral recomputation (computationally expensive) and local approximation (potentially inaccurate). The goal is to develop a fast yet accurate method for assessing structural connectivity loss.
AI.method: The study trains Graph Neural Networks (GCN, GraphSAGE, edge-aware MPNN) to learn a bounded correction to first-order Fiedler sensitivity. They test on three failure types: independent, spatially clustered, and edge-betweenness-targeted failures. Evaluation uses synthetic graph splits and zero-shot transfer to 13 OpenStreetMap areas across six countries, with sparse scaling tested up to 20,000 nodes.
AI.result: Residual GCN improves spatial-failure MAE by 0.0391 (CI: 0.0151-0.0662), while residual GraphSAGE improves targeted-failure MAE by 0.0257 (CI: 0.0095-0.0446). Second-order perturbation only marginally improves over first-order (0.0028-0.0053). Leave-one-country-out transfer shows mixed results: residual GCN improves targeted-failure MAE by 0.0622 but worsens spatial point estimates. The method scales to 20,000 nodes.
AI.conclusion: The spectral residual (GNN-learned correction to first-order sensitivity) serves as a useful but domain-sensitive inductive bias for structural connectivity screening. Performance varies across failure types and geographic domains, suggesting the need for domain adaptation when transferring to new regions.

title: Generating a Consistent Enterprise: Synthesis and Reference-Free Evaluation of Multi-System Business Data
summary: Synthetic relational data is normally produced by a model trained on a real dataset, and its quality is measured as the distance to that dataset. This paper describes a generator that has no real dataset at either end. Given an industry, a company size, a business model, a set of business applications, and a random seed, it produces a complete fictional enterprise: a workforce, a customer base, sales deals, support tickets, recorded calls, chat messages, and documents, all consistent with one another. One entity graph is projected into the native formats of 66 business products, so the same customer appears in the CRM, the support desk, and the call system under one identity. Because no real counterpart exists, realism is built in from cited reference statistics and verified by reference-free measurement: a five-axis scorecard of 28 statistical checks, an adversarial detector that hunts for the marks of synthetic generation, and a set of soundness checks that include a classifier test against an independently shuffled copy of the data. Because these instruments existed before the generator was tuned, progress is measured under a fixed yardstick: over 23 generated companies, mean realism climbed from 60.3 to 99.1, the weakest company from 41.1 to 94.9, and the detector, which initially flagged 55.2% of all records, now flags none. The scores hold on a seed never used during development. A second generator builds relational databases from a list of business questions. It forces qualifying rows for each answerable question, adds controlled near misses, and computes exact labels from the finished tables. The generator runs as a hosted service at https://console.era.eon.io. A company built there to a specification is served through its simulators over MCP and REST, and the simulators are also published as container images for offline use

AI.tldr: This paper presents two synthetic data generators that create realistic fictional enterprise data (workforce, customers, sales, support tickets, calls, chat, documents) without any real dataset. The first generator projects consistent entity graphs into 66 business product formats, while the second generates relational databases from business questions. Using a five-axis verification framework, they achieved 99.1% mean realism with 0% detection rate by adversarial classifiers.
AI.motivation: The problem is that synthetic relational data is typically generated by training on real datasets, creating a dependency on sensitive data. This paper addresses the challenge of generating realistic, consistent enterprise data without any real dataset at either training or reference stage.
AI.method: Two generators: (1) A generator producing complete fictional enterprises from industry/company size/business model parameters, projecting entity graphs into 66 business product formats with consistent identity across systems; (2) A generator building relational databases from business questions by forcing qualifying rows and computing exact labels. Verification uses a five-axis scorecard with 28 statistical checks, an adversarial detector for synthetic marks, and classifier tests against independently shuffled data.
AI.result: Over 23 generated companies, mean realism increased from 60.3 to 99.1, weakest company improved from 41.1 to 94.9, and the adversarial detector's flagging rate dropped from 55.2% to 0%. Results held on a seed never used during development.
AI.conclusion: The system successfully generates highly realistic synthetic enterprise data across 66 business products without any real training data. The five-axis verification framework (statistical checks, adversarial detector, classifier tests) achieved 99.1% mean realism and 0% detection rate. A second generator creates relational databases from business questions, and the entire system is deployed as a hosted service with containerized simulators.

title: Your Model Already Knows Don't Teach It, Learn to Ask It: Soft Prompting for Few-Shot Adaptation of Vision-Language Models
summary:
We address few-shot object detection with vision-language models (VLMs) in out-of-domain settings such as aerial, industrial, and medical imagery, using only ten annotated images for supervision. Existing adaptation methods are discrete prompt optimization and LoRA fine-tuning. We revisit a third option: soft prompting, where a small number of continuous prompt tokens are optimized while the pretrained backbone remains frozen.
  We identify two key design choices. First, placing prompt tokens at the cross-modal boundary between visual and text tokens outperforms other placements (10.0 vs. 8.4 mAP). Second, initializing prompts from the empty space token outperforms semantic and random initialization.
  With these choices, one to three learned tokens (7,168 parameters on average) match the best LoRA configuration on Roboflow20-VL (14.2 mAP, 10-shot) while training over 20,000x fewer parameters. Soft prompting remains harder to optimize, exhibiting higher variance across random seeds. Unlike LoRA, however, it causes no forgetting: the LoRA rank matching our accuracy reduces NaturalBench VQA accuracy by 35% relative, rising to 56% at the largest rank, whereas soft prompting leaves pretrained performance unchanged.
  The learned tokens behave like prompts rather than weights. They transfer to a newer model without retraining (+0.8 mAP on Qwen3.5-9B) and can be verbalized into readable prompts competitive with prompt-search methods (matching DetPO and outperforming GEPA).
  The approach also extends beyond detection. On RoboCasa manipulation tasks, the frozen $π_{0.5}$ vision-language-action policy benefits from soft prompting, matching the LoRA baseline on two of three tasks when tokens are placed at the gradient bottleneck. These results suggest modern VLMs already encode much of what is needed for specialized domains; the challenge is learning how to ask.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using soft prompting (continuous prompt tokens) for few-shot object detection with VLMs in out-of-domain settings (aerial, industrial, medical imagery). By placing prompt tokens at the cross-modal boundary and initializing from empty space tokens, 1-3 learned tokens (~7,168 parameters) can match LoRA performance while training 20,000x fewer parameters, without causing catastrophic forgetting.
AI.motivation: Few-shot object detection in out-of-domain settings (aerial, industrial, medical imagery) using only 10 annotated images remains challenging. Existing adaptation methods (discrete prompt optimization and LoRA fine-tuning) have trade-offs: LoRA causes catastrophic forgetting while soft prompting is harder to optimize. The authors revisit soft prompting as a third option to address these limitations.
AI.method: The authors investigate two key design choices for soft prompting: (1) prompt token placement at the cross-modal boundary between visual and text tokens, and (2) initialization from empty space token instead of semantic or random initialization. They use 1-3 learned tokens (~7,168 parameters) and evaluate on Roboflow20-VL (10-shot), NaturalBench VQA, and RoboCasa manipulation tasks.
AI.result: Cross-modal boundary placement outperforms other placements (10.0 vs 8.4 mAP). Empty space token initialization outperforms semantic and random initialization. One to three learned tokens match the best LoRA configuration on Roboflow20-VL (14.2 mAP, 10-shot) while training 20,000x fewer parameters. Unlike LoRA, soft prompting causes no forgetting (LoRA reduces VQA accuracy by 35-56% while soft prompting leaves pretrained performance unchanged). Learned tokens transfer to newer models without retraining (+0.8 mAP on Qwen3.5-9B) and can be verbalized into readable prompts competitive with prompt-search methods.
AI.conclusion: Modern VLMs already encode much of what is needed for specialized domains; the challenge is learning how to ask. Soft prompting offers a parameter-efficient, forgetting-free alternative to LoRA for adapting VLMs to novel domains, with better transferability to newer models. The approach also extends beyond detection to manipulation tasks, matching LoRA on two of three RoboCasa tasks.

title: Semi-Tensor Product-Based Multi-Term Randomized T-SVD and Its Visual Applications
summary: Tensor singular value decomposition (T-SVD), which is built upon the tensor-tensor product (t-product), has emerged as a powerful tool for processing high-dimensional visual data such as color images and videos. However, the standard t-product imposes strict dimensional compatibility constraints. Although extensions based on the semi-tensor product (STP) relax this restriction, their single-term formulations still suffer from limited approximation accuracy. Moreover, these deterministic methods incur high computational costs when processing large-scale tensor data. To address these issues, this paper introduces a novel semi-tensor product for third-order tensors under the t-product framework induced by arbitrary invertible linear transforms. The resulting tensor semi-tensor product breaks the rigid dimension matching requirement of the standard t-product, while retaining the closed-form property of T-SVD. Based on this construction, we develop a multi-term semi-tensor product singular value decomposition (MSTP-SVD), which integrates multiple orthogonal decomposition terms to significantly improve low-rank approximation accuracy compared with single-term schemes. To reduce the computational cost of multi-term modeling, we incorporate randomized projection and power iteration techniques into the MSTP-SVD framework, yielding an accelerated multi-term randomized semi-tensor product SVD (MRSTP-SVD) algorithm that achieves a balance between reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency. Experiments on image and video compression and completion tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel semi-tensor product for third-order tensors under t-product framework with arbitrary invertible linear transforms, and develops MSTP-SVD (and its randomized variant MRSTP-SVD) to improve low-rank approximation accuracy while reducing computational costs for image and video processing tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard t-product in T-SVD imposes strict dimensional compatibility constraints. While semi-tensor product (STP) extensions relax this restriction, single-term formulations still suffer from limited approximation accuracy. Additionally, deterministic methods incur high computational costs when processing large-scale tensor data.
AI.method: 1) Introduces a novel semi-tensor product for third-order tensors under the t-product framework induced by arbitrary invertible linear transforms. 2) Develops multi-term semi-tensor product SVD (MSTP-SVD) integrating multiple orthogonal decomposition terms. 3) Incorporates randomized projection and power iteration to create accelerated MRSTP-SVD algorithm.
AI.result: The proposed semi-tensor product breaks rigid dimension matching requirements while retaining the closed-form property of T-SVD. MSTP-SVD significantly improves low-rank approximation accuracy compared with single-term schemes. MRSTP-SVD achieves a balance between reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Experiments on image and video compression and completion tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, showing improved performance over existing single-term t-product approaches.

title: Off-Target Effects of Response-Style Alignment in a Korean 27B Language Model
comment: 19 pages. Korean-language evaluation (KoBBQ); all uncertainty estimates over KoBBQ items are clustered on the benchmark template
summary:
We post-train Qwen3.8-27B for Korean response style -- verbosity, list and markdown usage, discourse structure and register -- and measure two behaviours the objective never targets: abstention on ambiguous social questions in KoBBQ, where the benchmark-correct answer is UNKNOWN, and unprompted disclosure in securities guidance. Both move, and the changes are expressed primarily through the model's emission policy: how often it answers and how much it says.
  Matched target-form controls show that answer propensity depends on the training target, not the prompt set or recipe alone. Holding prompts, recipe, data volume and serving fixed and changing only the target text, three style seeds give positive answer-rate point estimates (mean +0.82 pp) and three neutral seeds negative ones (mean -1.53 pp); the observed seed ranges do not overlap and the means differ by 2.34 pp. A length-matched arm lies between them, and a fourth arm that stays short while preserving hedging is unstable across seeds, so which feature of the form is responsible is unresolved.
  For absolute stereotyped exposure the decomposition into an answer-propensity term and a conditional-composition term is an algebraic identity, not a finding; its empirical content is where the movement went. Across the trained checkpoints the changes are dominated by answer propensity while the composition term stays small, and because that term is evaluated on treatment-dependent answered subsets we do not read it as evidence about latent preference.
  Two measurement results follow. A between-arm contrast in conditional stereotyped share does not identify a change in conditional content preference when answer status is treatment-dependent. And agreement between two rule detectors for the same construct runs from 0.44 to 0.99 depending on which checkpoint produced the text -- observable without any reference labels.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how post-training on Korean response style affects a language model's behavior in two unintended ways: abstention on ambiguous social questions (KoBBQ benchmark) and unprompted disclosure in securities guidance. The key finding is that changes in stereotyped exposure are primarily driven by answer propensity (how often the model answers), not by changes in conditional content preference. The study uses matched target-form controls to show that answer propensity depends on the training target rather than prompts or recipe alone.
AI.motivation: The researchers aim to understand what happens when training a model for specific response styles (verbosity, list usage, markdown, discourse structure, register) - specifically, whether the training affects behaviors that were never explicitly targeted. They want to measure two things: (1) whether the model abstains on ambiguous social questions where the correct answer is "UNKNOWN", and (2) whether the model makes unprompted disclosures in securities guidance contexts.
AI.method: The study uses Qwen3.8-27B post-trained for Korean response style. They employ matched target-form controls, varying only the target text while keeping prompts, recipe, data volume, and serving fixed. They test three positive style seeds (mean +0.82 pp answer rate), three neutral style seeds (mean -1.53 pp), and a length-matched arm. They decompose stereotyped exposure into an answer-propensity term and a conditional-composition term, and compare two rule detectors for agreement measurement.
AI.result: Answer propensity depends on training target, not prompt set or recipe alone. Positive style seeds increase answer rate by +0.82 pp on average, while neutral seeds decrease it by -1.53 pp, with non-overlapping ranges and a 2.34 pp difference between means. The length-matched arm falls between them. Changes in stereotyped exposure are dominated by answer propensity, while the composition term remains small. A between-arm contrast in conditional stereotyped share does not identify changes in latent preference. Agreement between two rule detectors ranges from 0.44 to 0.99 depending on the checkpoint.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that post-training for response style primarily affects the model's emission policy (how often it answers and how much it says) rather than its underlying content preferences. The decomposition into answer propensity and composition terms is an algebraic identity, but the empirical finding shows that answer propensity is the main driver of behavioral changes. The conditional composition term cannot be interpreted as evidence about latent preference because it's evaluated on treatment-dependent subsets. Additionally, rule detector agreement varies dramatically (0.44-0.99) across checkpoints, highlighting the challenge of measuring training effects without reference labels.

title: GRIPNet: Gaussian Radial Intensity Prior Guided Architecture for Pulmonary Nodule Detection in CT
summary: Lung cancer causes more deaths than any other malignancy, and low-dose CT screening is the main pathway to early diagnosis. That pathway hinges on the smallest lesions, yet nodules below six millimeters remain hard to detect, because most methods treat a nodule as a generic object and ignore the imaging physics behind its appearance. We show that this appearance is highly regular. Intensity peaks at the geometric center of a nodule and decays radially in a Gaussian pattern, and a fit to 18,218 annotated lesions from three public benchmarks yields a mean radial coefficient of determination above 0.86 in every dataset and size stratum. A square convolution samples both axes uniformly and is mismatched to this radial signal, most severely for small nodules. Guided by this evidence, we propose GRIPNet (Gaussian Radial Intensity Prior Network), a detector in which every module maps to a measurable property of the intensity distribution. Pinwheel convolutions decompose radial gradients, a dual-frequency module separates boundary detail from structural context, dilated masked attention matches the decay extent, and an adaptive loss reweights samples by conspicuity. GRIPNet raises mAP@0.5 to 95.3, 91.6 and 97.9 percent on KanserSet, LUNA16 and Lung-PET-CT-Dx while sharpening high-IoU localization at real-time speed.

AI.tldr: GRIPNet is a deep learning detector for small lung nodules in CT scans that leverages the Gaussian radial intensity pattern inherent in nodule appearance. It addresses the challenge of detecting nodules below 6mm by incorporating imaging physics into the network architecture, achieving state-of-the-art mAP@0.5 of 95.3%, 91.6%, and 97.9% on three public benchmarks while maintaining real-time speed.
AI.motivation: Lung cancer causes the most cancer deaths, and early detection via low-dose CT screening is critical. However, nodules below 6mm remain difficult to detect because existing methods treat nodules as generic objects and ignore the imaging physics behind their appearance. The authors discovered that nodule intensity follows a highly regular Gaussian radial pattern from the geometric center.
AI.method: The authors first analyzed 18,218 annotated lesions from three public benchmarks and found that intensity peaks at the geometric center and decays radially in a Gaussian pattern (R² > 0.86). Based on this finding, they designed GRIPNet with four key modules: (1) Pinwheel convolutions to decompose radial gradients, (2) Dual-frequency module to separate boundary detail from structural context, (3) Dilated masked attention to match the decay extent, and (4) Adaptive loss that reweights samples by conspicuity.
AI.result: GRIPNet achieves mAP@0.5 of 95.3% on KanserSet, 91.6% on LUNA16, and 97.9% on Lung-PET-CT-Dx. It also improves high-IoU localization while operating at real-time speed. The analysis of 18,218 lesions showed mean radial coefficient of determination above 0.86 across all datasets and size strata.
AI.conclusion: The Gaussian radial intensity pattern is a generalizable property of lung nodules that can be exploited for detection. GRIPNet's architecture, where each module maps to a measurable property of the intensity distribution, successfully addresses the challenge of detecting small nodules and achieves superior performance compared to existing methods.

title: Hierarchical Clustering Can Jointly Satisfy Richness, Consistency, and Scale Invariance
summary: Despite its ubiquity, clustering lacks a universally accepted definition of what is a cluster. Kleinberg's Impossibility Theorem formalizes this difficulty by showing that no flat clustering method can simultaneously satisfy three natural axioms: scale invariance, richness, and consistency. In this paper, we ask whether this impossibility persists when the output is a hierarchy rather than a single partition. We show that, in contrast to the flat clustering setting, the hierarchical analog of these axioms are jointly satisfiable. In fact, there exist uncountably many hierarchical clustering methods satisfying these axioms, which we call admissible. We explicitly construct several admissible methods, including methods based on well-separated clusters and a non-binary version of single linkage. For certain pairs of admissible methods, the hierarchy produced by one always refines that produced by the other. This refinement relation defines a partial order on the class of admissible methods. This partially ordered set has no greatest element and contains uncountably many pairwise incompatible maximal elements, revealing substantial diversity among admissible methods. Nevertheless, this diversity is constrained: every admissible method contains a hierarchy of sufficiently well-separated clusters, and every finite collection of admissible methods shares such a nontrivial common backbone.

AI.tldr: Kleinberg's Impossibility Theorem states no flat clustering method can satisfy scale invariance, richness, and consistency simultaneously. This paper shows this impossibility does NOT persist in hierarchical clustering - the hierarchical analogs of these axioms ARE jointly satisfiable, with uncountably many admissible methods existing. The paper explores the partial order structure of these methods and shows that while diversity is substantial, all admissible methods share a common backbone.
AI.motivation: Kleinberg's Impossibility Theorem formalizes the lack of a universal cluster definition by proving that no flat clustering method can simultaneously satisfy three natural axioms: scale invariance, richness, and consistency. The authors investigate whether this fundamental limitation persists when output is a hierarchy rather than a single partition.
AI.method: The paper formulates hierarchical analogs of Kleinberg's three axioms and proves they are jointly satisfiable. The authors explicitly construct several admissible hierarchical clustering methods, including those based on well-separated clusters and non-binary single linkage. They analyze the refinement relations between methods and study the partial order structure of admissible methods.
AI.result: 1) Uncountably many hierarchical clustering methods satisfy the hierarchical analogs of Kleinberg's axioms (admissible methods). 2) Some pairs of admissible methods have a refinement relationship (one always produces hierarchies that refine the other). 3) This refinement defines a partial order with no greatest element and uncountably many pairwise incompatible maximal elements. 4) Every admissible method contains a hierarchy of sufficiently well-separated clusters. 5) Every finite collection of admissible methods shares a nontrivial common backbone.
AI.conclusion: The diversity among admissible hierarchical clustering methods is substantial but constrained. While there is no single "best" hierarchical clustering method and uncountably many incompatible maximal methods exist, all admissible methods share a common structural backbone - they all contain hierarchies of well-separated clusters and any finite collection has a common refinement.

title: Memory Compression for High-Fanout Agent Sandboxes
summary:
High-fanout agent workloads create a growing memory bottleneck because a single task may spawn many concurrent sandbox sessions. Yet these sandboxes are far from independent: they originate from a shared template and execute related trajectories, exposing substantial template-relative and cross-sandbox memory redundancy. Conventional memory compression is poorly matched to this setting in three fundamental dimensions: how to compress, because they fail to exploit similarity across non-identical sandbox pages; what to compress, because they control page-fault overhead through conservative page selection; and when to compress, because compression is either triggered by memory pressure or performed without awareness of agent execution phases.
  We present AgentZip, the first memory compression system designed specifically for AI-agent sandboxes. AgentZip introduces compression mechanisms that exploit both the template-relative and cross-sandbox redundancy. It broadens the compression scope to any page with a profitable representation and shifts overhead control from compression-time page selection to restore-time prefetching. It further aligns expensive compression with LLM waiting periods to avoid interfering with foreground tool execution. Across LLM training and inference workloads, AgentZip reduces sandbox-owned memory by up to 8.7x, compared with 2.1x for the Linux configuration. Restore prefetching and agent-execution-aware scheduling reduce the slowdown of aggressive compression from as high as 3.1x to 1.40x while retaining nearly all of its memory-saving benefit.

AI.tldr: AgentZip is the first memory compression system specifically designed for AI-agent sandboxes. It addresses the memory bottleneck in high-fanout agent workloads by exploiting template-relative and cross-sandbox redundancy, achieving up to 8.7x memory reduction while minimizing performance overhead through intelligent prefetching and execution-aware scheduling.
AI.motivation: The rapid growth of AI agent workloads creates a critical memory bottleneck as single tasks spawn many concurrent sandbox sessions. These sandboxes share templates and execute related trajectories, exposing substantial memory redundancy that conventional compression systems fail to exploit effectively.
AI.method: AgentZip introduces three key innovations: (1) Compression mechanisms that exploit both template-relative and cross-sandbox redundancy across non-identical sandbox pages; (2) Broadened compression scope to any page with profitable representation, shifting overhead control from compression-time page selection to restore-time prefetching; (3) Alignment of expensive compression with LLM waiting periods to avoid interfering with foreground tool execution.
AI.result: AgentZip reduces sandbox-owned memory by up to 8.7x, compared with 2.1x for standard Linux configuration. Restore prefetching and agent-execution-aware scheduling reduce the slowdown of aggressive compression from as high as 3.1x to 1.40x while retaining nearly all of its memory-saving benefit.
AI.conclusion: AgentZip successfully addresses the memory compression challenge for AI-agent sandboxes by exploiting cross-sandbox redundancy and aligning compression with LLM idle periods, achieving significant memory savings (8.7x) with minimal performance overhead (1.40x slowdown).

title: Mi-Ripple: Restoring Images Degraded by Iterative AI Editing
summary: Iterative reference-conditioned image editing can introduce grid-like and granular textures, commonly described as digital ripple. We present Mi-Ripple, a diagnosis-guided restoration workflow that suppresses this digital ripple while protecting image structure. Mi-Ripple separates periodic lattice artifacts from content-entangled granular texture, then combines selective spectral notching, structure-aware smoothing, and cleaned-reference regeneration. This separation enables low-distortion filtering when artifacts are spectrally isolated and visual reconstruction when filtering would erase legitimate detail. Across fourteen notch-only executions, whole-image residual standard deviation is 0.08--0.44 in CIELAB lightness units. In a paired regeneration example, reference cleaning reduces output debris density by 45\%. Mi-Ripple links measurable artifact reduction to visibly cleaner generated images, rather than optimizing a spectral score alone.

AI.tldr: Mi-Ripple is a diagnosis-guided restoration workflow that suppresses digital ripple artifacts (grid-like and granular textures) in iterative reference-conditioned image editing while preserving image structure. It separates periodic lattice artifacts from content-entangled granular texture and combines selective spectral notching, structure-aware smoothing, and cleaned-reference regeneration.
AI.motivation: Iterative reference-conditioned image editing introduces grid-like and granular textures commonly described as "digital ripple," which degrades image quality. Existing methods fail to address this artifact without losing legitimate image details.
AI.method: Mi-Ripple employs three key techniques: (1) Separation of periodic lattice artifacts from content-entangled granular texture; (2) Selective spectral notching for low-distortion filtering when artifacts are spectrally isolated; (3) Structure-aware smoothing and cleaned-reference regeneration for visual reconstruction when filtering would erase legitimate detail.
AI.result: Across fourteen notch-only executions, whole-image residual standard deviation is 0.08-0.44 in CIELAB lightness units. In a paired regeneration example, reference cleaning reduces output debris density by 45%.
AI.conclusion: Mi-Ripple successfully links measurable artifact reduction to visibly cleaner generated images by combining spectral filtering and regeneration approaches, rather than optimizing a spectral score alone. The method achieves low distortion (0.08-0.44 CIELAB lightness units) and significant debris reduction (45%).

title: Convex Optimization with Nested Evolving Feasible Sets (CONES) under Time-Varying Loss Functions
summary: Convex Optimization with Nested Evolving Feasible Sets (CONES)} was introduced in \cite{CONESVaze} where the objective function \(f\) remains fixed but the feasible region evolves over time as a nested sequence \(S_1 \supseteq S_2 \supseteq \cdots \supseteq S_T\). The goal of an online algorithm is to simultaneously minimize the regret with respect to hindsight static optimal benchmark and the total movement cost $M_\cA(T)$ while ensuring feasibility at all times. CONES is an optimization-oriented generalization of the well-known \emph{nested convex body chasing} (NCBC). In this paper, we extend CONES to allow for loss functions $f_t'$s to also change over time. When all loss functions are convex, we show that the projected proximal algorithm achieves $O(T^{1-β}), O(T^β)$ simultaneous regret and movement cost, respectively, for any $β\in [0,1)$, over a time horizon of $T$. We also show that any {\it weakly adaptive} online algorithm with $O(T^β)$ regret has a movement cost of $Ω\left(T^{\frac{1-β}{2}}\right)$ for any $β\in [0,1)$. When all loss functions are strongly convex, we show that the projected proximal algorithm simultaneously achieves $O(1)$ regret and a movement cost of $O(\log T)$. To complement this, we show that any online algorithm with sublinear {\it anytime} regret has a movement cost of $Ω\left(\log T\right)$.

AI.tldr: This paper extends CONES (Convex Optimization with Nested Evolving Feasible Sets) to handle time-varying loss functions in addition to nested feasible sets. For convex loss functions, the projected proximal algorithm achieves O(T^(1-β)) regret and O(T^β) movement cost simultaneously. For strongly convex functions, it achieves O(1) regret and O(log T) movement cost. Lower bounds are also established.
AI.motivation: Extend CONES (a generalization of nested convex body chasing) to handle time-varying loss functions, while balancing regret minimization and movement cost constraints in online optimization.
AI.method: Projected proximal algorithm for online convex optimization; analysis of weakly adaptive algorithms; lower bound proofs using information-theoretic arguments.
AI.result: For convex loss functions: O(T^(1-β)) regret and O(T^β) movement cost for any β∈[0,1). For strongly convex functions: O(1) regret and O(log T) movement cost. Lower bounds: Ω(T^((1-β)/2)) movement cost for any weakly adaptive algorithm with O(T^β) regret; Ω(log T) for sublinear anytime regret.
AI.conclusion: The projected proximal algorithm achieves near-optimal tradeoffs between regret and movement cost. The lower bounds show fundamental tradeoffs: any algorithm with sublinear regret must incur polynomial or logarithmic movement costs depending on convexity assumptions.

title: Routing by Reasoning Need: Trajectory-Aware Decoding Control for Diffusion Vision-Language Models
comment: 17 pages, 9 figures. Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: Diffusion vision-language models generate answers through iterative refinement, exposing intermediate answer trajectories that can be inspected and controlled at inference time. However, this controllability creates a reasoning-need mismatch, where a universal generation length is applied to questions with different reasoning demands. Visually closed questions may be harmed by continued refinement after a stable answer has formed, whereas reasoning-sensitive questions may be harmed by premature commitment. We formulate this problem as reasoning-budget mismatch and study it in LLaDA-V. Rather than choosing a universal generation length, our training-free controller routes each example to early commitment, baseline preservation, or reasoning-supportive decoding using trajectory signals from answer closure, commitment evidence, and representation revision pressure, without using ground-truth answers. Across answer-focused, mixed-reasoning, and CoT-sensitive benchmarks, routed control improves robustness over fixed long decoding, pure short decoding, and single-rule interventions. The gains are not explained by shorter outputs alone. Answer-closed examples often benefit from commitment, whereas CoT-sensitive examples require preserving or supporting intermediate reasoning. Taken together, these results suggest diffusion VLM decoding should route inference-time control by the state suggested by the observed trajectory instead of relying on a universal decoding length.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses a "reasoning-budget mismatch" problem in diffusion vision-language models (specifically LLaDA-V), where a universal generation length is applied to questions with varying reasoning demands. The authors propose a training-free controller that routes each input to one of three decoding strategies (early commitment, baseline preservation, or reasoning-supportive decoding) using trajectory signals, without requiring ground-truth answers.
AI.motivation: Diffusion VLMs generate answers through iterative refinement, exposing intermediate trajectories that can be inspected at inference time. However, this creates a mismatch: visually closed questions may be harmed by continued refinement after a stable answer forms, while reasoning-sensitive questions may be harmed by premature commitment. The core motivation is to dynamically adjust the generation length based on each question's reasoning needs rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach.
AI.method:
The proposed method is a training-free controller that routes each example to one of three decoding strategies:
1. Early commitment
2. Baseline preservation
3. Reasoning-supportive decoding

The routing decisions are based on three trajectory signals:
- Answer closure (when stable answer forms)
- Commitment evidence
- Representation revision pressure

No ground-truth answers are used in this process.
AI.result: Routed control improves robustness across answer-focused, mixed-reasoning, and CoT-sensitive benchmarks, outperforming fixed long decoding, pure short decoding, and single-rule interventions. The gains are not explained by shorter outputs alone. Key finding: answer-closed examples benefit from commitment, while CoT-sensitive examples require preserving or supporting intermediate reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion VLM decoding should route inference-time control based on the state suggested by the observed trajectory rather than relying on a universal decoding length. This adaptive approach addresses the reasoning-need mismatch by matching generation strategy to each question's specific requirements.

title: Predictive Multi-Landmark OCT Tracking for Increased Motion Robustness
summary: Optical coherence tomography is a promising modality for markerless motion tracking due to its high spatial resolution and inherent depth perception. However, existing OCT-based tracking approaches are limited in terms of trackable velocity, particularly when multiple landmarks are tracked sequentially for 6D pose estimation. In this work, we present a predictive tracking approach that propagates positional updates between multiple tracked landmarks to obtain a global pose prediction. This enables more robust tracking under high velocities. Our results demonstrate RMSEs below 1 mm for velocities up to 100 mm/s and up to nine consecutively tracked landmarks, highlighting the potential of global motion propagation and prediction for improving the robustness of OCT-based tracking.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a predictive tracking approach for optical coherence tomography (OCT) that propagates positional updates between multiple tracked landmarks to enable robust 6D pose estimation under high velocities. The method achieves RMSEs below 1 mm for velocities up to 100 mm/s with up to nine consecutively tracked landmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing OCT-based tracking approaches are limited in trackable velocity, particularly when multiple landmarks are tracked sequentially for 6D pose estimation. There is a need for more robust tracking under high velocities.
AI.method: The authors present a predictive tracking approach that propagates positional updates between multiple tracked landmarks to obtain a global pose prediction, enabling more robust tracking under high velocities.
AI.result: The method demonstrates RMSEs below 1 mm for velocities up to 100 mm/s and up to nine consecutively tracked landmarks, highlighting the potential of global motion propagation and prediction for improving OCT-based tracking robustness.
AI.conclusion: Global motion propagation and prediction significantly improves the robustness of OCT-based tracking, enabling accurate markerless motion tracking at high velocities with multiple landmarks.

title: REVA: Reusable Evidence View Aggregation for Context-Efficient RAG Serving
comment: Author's accepted manuscript. Accepted for publication in the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Data Mining (ICDM)
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves knowledge-intensive large language model (LLM) applications by conditioning generation on retrieved documents, but longer contexts increase latency, key-value (KV) cache memory, and token cost. Post-retrieval compression can reduce this cost, yet existing compressors often operate independently for each query, rely on auxiliary models or rewriting, and introduce online overhead that can offset the benefit of shorter prompts. We revisit RAG compression from a data-mining perspective by aggregating historical query--document--model interactions into reusable evidence views. We first show that modern compressors have unstable gains over simple truncation and can add substantial inference-time latency. We then propose Reusable Evidence View Aggregation (REVA), a framework that mines the target generator's historical attention traces into a document-keyed, budget-agnostic score store. REVA maps token-level attention to readable word units, aggregates importance across repeated document accesses, and renders budget-specific plain-text views that preserve document order and the standard RAG interface. Across four representative benchmarks and modern LLMs, REVA improves generation quality by 1.0--5.8 points over existing advances, while reducing compression overhead by a factor of 5.3 to 15.6, adding less than 40 ms of latency.

AI.tldr: REVA is a novel RAG compression framework that aggregates historical query-document-model interactions into reusable evidence views, improving generation quality by 1.0-5.8 points while reducing compression overhead by 5.3-15.6x with less than 40ms latency.
AI.motivation: RAG improves knowledge-intensive LLM applications but increases latency, KV cache memory, and token cost with longer contexts. Existing post-retrieval compressors operate independently per query, rely on auxiliary models, and introduce online overhead that can offset benefits of shorter prompts.
AI.method: REVA mines the target generator's historical attention traces into a document-keyed, budget-agnostic score store. It maps token-level attention to readable word units, aggregates importance across repeated document accesses, and renders budget-specific plain-text views that preserve document order and standard RAG interface.
AI.result: Across four representative benchmarks and modern LLMs, REVA improves generation quality by 1.0-5.8 points over existing advances, while reducing compression overhead by a factor of 5.3 to 15.6, adding less than 40 ms of latency.
AI.conclusion: REVA successfully addresses RAG compression limitations by leveraging historical attention data to create reusable evidence views, achieving better quality and significantly lower overhead than existing compression methods.

title: Mr.LHDR: A Benchmark for Multimodal Real-World Long-Horizon Deep Research Agents
comment: Code and data are available at https://github.com/minghaoguo20/Mr-LHDR-eval
summary: Deep research agents are increasingly capable of web search, tool use, multimodal evidence analysis, and information synthesis. However, existing benchmarks mainly evaluate medium-horizon exploration and rarely test whether agents can sustain long, dependency-heavy research processes. We introduce Mr.LHDR (Multimodal real-world Long-Horizon Deep Research), a benchmark for evaluating real-world deep research over long, irreducible chains of interdependent evidence across eight categories. Each question is constructed from a hidden Node-Relation graph and requires an average of 12.1 necessary intermediate conclusions with a mean dependency depth of 10.4 before reaching a short, unique, and verifiable answer. Questions incorporate multimodal evidence, including images, maps, PDFs, logos, charts, tables, and video frames, with at least one non-text element that changes the reasoning state. Mr.LHDR evaluates both final answers and the correctness of intermediate conclusions under annotated dependencies. We evaluate general models, deep research systems, and agent frameworks using Overall Accuracy (OA), Strict Accuracy (SA), Checklist Score (CS), and Dependency-Aware Checklist Score (DACS). Results show that even the strongest system achieves only 43.1% OA and 34.3% SA, indicating that final-answer accuracy substantially overestimates complete research success. Removing images reduces DACS by 12.6 points, demonstrating the importance of multimodal evidence, while SA consistently declines as reasoning chains become longer. These findings reveal sustained, dependency-consistent evidence integration, rather than isolated fact retrieval, as a key bottleneck for current deep research agents.

AI.tldr: Mr.LHDR is a new benchmark for evaluating real-world deep research agents on long, dependency-heavy reasoning chains across 8 categories. It requires an average of 12.1 intermediate conclusions with mean dependency depth of 10.4, incorporating multimodal evidence (images, maps, PDFs, etc.). Even the strongest systems achieve only 43.1% Overall Accuracy and 34.3% Strict Accuracy, revealing that sustained evidence integration is the key bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate medium-horizon exploration and rarely test whether agents can sustain long, dependency-heavy research processes. Current benchmarks fail to assess the ability of deep research agents to handle complex, interconnected evidence chains required for real-world research tasks.
AI.method: The benchmark constructs questions from a hidden Node-Relation graph requiring an average of 12.1 necessary intermediate conclusions with mean dependency depth of 10.4 before reaching a short, unique, and verifiable answer. Questions incorporate multimodal evidence (images, maps, PDFs, logos, charts, tables, video frames), with at least one non-text element that changes reasoning state. Evaluation uses Overall Accuracy (OA), Strict Accuracy (SA), Checklist Score (CS), and Dependency-Aware Checklist Score (DACS).
AI.result: Even the strongest system achieves only 43.1% OA and 34.3% SA, indicating final-answer accuracy substantially overestimates complete research success. Removing images reduces DACS by 12.6 points, demonstrating the importance of multimodal evidence. SA consistently declines as reasoning chains become longer.
AI.conclusion: Sustained, dependency-consistent evidence integration, rather than isolated fact retrieval, is the key bottleneck for current deep research agents. The benchmark reveals that current systems struggle with long-horizon, dependency-heavy research processes involving multimodal evidence.

title: R4Tun: LLM-guided adaptive segmental tunnel lining segmentation in point clouds
summary: Automated inspection of segmental tunnel linings requires adaptive segmentation from 3D point clouds, yet expert-tuned pipelines often degrade when tunnel conditions vary. This paper presents R4Tun, a large language model (LLM)-driven adaptation framework that extends an expert-designed pipeline (SAM4Tun) with bounded parameter tuning informed by structured context: memory ($m$), state ($s$), and knowledge ($k$). Evaluated on 30 selected Seg2Tunnel subsets (13 regular, 17 complex) across three LLMs, the full $m+s+k$ design raised mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU) from 0.18 to 0.43--0.48 and overall accuracy (OA) from 0.42 to 0.59--0.65 relative to the static SAM4Tun baseline, with the near-reference regular (staggered) subsets reaching mIoU 0.784--0.796 across LLMs. Across 270 (30 tunnels $\times$ 3 different LLMs $\times$ 3 context settings) runs, the LLMs showed similar parameter-adjustment trends (with overlapping 95\% CIs on mean gains) and consistently adjusted a shared set of critical parameters. These results support R4Tun as a controlled, label-free, cross-LLM adaptation mechanism in the tested SAM4Tun--Seg2Tunnel setting, demonstrating consistent accuracy gains; we position R4Tun as a mechanism contribution rather than a deployable final-inspection system, in which each bounded parameter change is auditable via logged rationales.

AI.tldr: R4Tun is an LLM-driven adaptation framework that enhances segmental tunnel lining segmentation from 3D point clouds by dynamically tuning parameters using structured context (memory, state, knowledge). It improves mIoU from 0.18 to 0.43-0.48 and OA from 0.42 to 0.59-0.65 across 30 tunnel subsets tested with 3 different LLMs.
AI.motivation: Expert-tuned segmentation pipelines (like SAM4Tun) for automated tunnel lining inspection degrade when tunnel conditions vary, as static parameters cannot adapt to different tunnel geometries and conditions. There is a need for adaptive, label-free parameter tuning that can generalize across varying tunnel environments.
AI.method: R4Tun extends SAM4Tun pipeline with bounded parameter tuning using three context dimensions: memory (m), state (s), and knowledge (k). Evaluated on 30 Seg2Tunnel subsets (13 regular, 17 complex) using 3 LLMs across 3 context settings (270 total runs). Parameter adjustments and their rationales are logged for auditability.
AI.result: The full m+s+k design raised mean IoU from 0.18 to 0.43-0.48 and overall accuracy from 0.42 to 0.59-0.65 relative to static SAM4Tun. Regular (staggered) subsets achieved mIoU 0.784-0.796. LLMs showed similar parameter-adjustment trends with overlapping 95% CIs, consistently adjusting a shared set of critical parameters.
AI.conclusion: R4Tun demonstrates consistent, controlled, and label-free cross-LLM adaptation in the SAM4Tun-Seg2Tunnel setting. It is positioned as a mechanism contribution rather than a deployable inspection system, with each parameter change being auditable via logged rationales. The approach shows promise as a general adaptation mechanism for vision pipelines in similar inspection domains.

title: Legible Failures: Detecting and Repairing In-Context Binding Errors
summary: A wrong answer does not show whether the model lacked the needed information or held it and failed to use it. On an entity-obligation binding task, a language model can emit an incorrect prompt-supplied binding while a linear probe can recover the correct one from its frozen hidden state. We measure how often this occurs across 16 public checkpoints, each evaluated with three seeds. We fit a probe on a training fold, select its layer on a validation fold, and report results on a disjoint test fold. On the trials each model gets wrong, probe accuracy exceeds the strict present-obligation baseline, 1/K = 0.125, by +0.196 (95% CI [+0.101, +0.296], bootstrapped over models). A query-entity counterfactual rules out token presence and recency. A score built from the sign of probe-output disagreement improves failure detection over the model's own confidence by +0.079 AUROC (95% CI [+0.036, +0.126]). Raw probe confidence gives no measurable improvement over model confidence. Steering the residual stream toward the probe-decoded binding, with no gold label, raises accuracy on all eight models tested by a mean of +0.168 (95% CI [+0.066, +0.280]). Where recent studies report that probe-detected errors are resistant to interventions, we find that in-context binding is a setting in which probes are actionable.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether language models possess correct information but fail to use it when answering incorrectly. Using linear probes on entity-obligation binding tasks across 16 checkpoints, the authors find that probes can recover correct bindings even when models give wrong answers. They demonstrate that probe information can be used to both detect failures and actively improve model performance through residual stream steering.
AI.motivation: The core problem is distinguishing whether a wrong model answer is due to missing knowledge or failed utilization of stored information. This distinction is crucial for understanding model capabilities and developing interventions.
AI.method: Linear probes trained on frozen hidden states across 16 public checkpoints with 3 seeds each. Uses train/validation/test fold methodology. Query-entity counterfactual to rule out token presence/recency. Probe-output disagreement for failure detection. Residual stream steering without gold labels.
AI.result: On wrong trials, probe accuracy exceeds baseline (0.125) by +0.196. Counterfactual rules out token presence/recency. Disagreement-based scoring improves failure detection by +0.079 AUROC over model confidence. Raw probe confidence shows no improvement. Steering raises accuracy by +0.168 mean across 8 models.
AI.conclusion: In-context binding is a setting where probes are actionable - they can detect failures and enable intervention through steering. This contrasts with prior studies reporting probe-detected errors as resistant to intervention, suggesting the approach may generalize to similar tasks.

title: Magenta: Closing the Loop Between Mathematical Reasoning and Lean Verification
summary: Most of mathematical knowledge has been communicated through so-called informal use of mathematics and natural language. With large language models (LLMs) being highly adept in using natural language, they achieve strong performance, yet not perfect, in informal mathematical reasoning. Restraining LLMs to informal reasoning misses out on the opportunity to use the discrete verification abilities that machines offer through machine-checkable proofs. In this paper, we bridge the gap between informal and formal reasoning by integrating Lean signals into the informal reasoning process. We introduce Magenta, a training-free agentic pipeline that, given only a natural-language problem, produces an answer, expresses it as a Lean 4 statement, and constructs a machine-checked proof. A statement judge verifies whether the formalisation preserves the original problem, while an error-attribution judge routes failed attempts either to mathematical re-derivation or local Lean repair. Magenta achieves 100% accuracy across all evaluated olympiad benchmarks, including AIME 2025, AIME 2026, and HMMT February 2026. When paired with the open-weight K2-Horizon-7B reasoner, it solves all six IMO 2026 problems. Our analysis shows that statement adjudication is essential for preventing false certificates and that feedback-guided correction outperforms independent resampling on difficult problems.

AI.tldr: Magenta is a training-free agentic pipeline that combines natural language reasoning with formal Lean 4 verification, achieving 100% accuracy on olympiad benchmarks (AIME 2025/2026, HMMT Feb 2026) and solving all 6 IMO 2026 problems with K2-Horizon-7B. Key innovations include statement adjudication and error-attribution judges for routing corrections.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between informal mathematical reasoning (what LLMs excel at) and formal reasoning (machine-checkable proofs using proof assistants like Lean). While LLMs perform well on informal math, they miss the opportunity to use discrete verification abilities that machines offer through machine-checkable proofs. The goal is to combine natural language reasoning with formal verification.
AI.method: Introduce Magenta, a training-free agentic pipeline that: (1) Takes a natural-language math problem; (2) Produces an answer; (3) Expresses it as a Lean 4 statement; (4) Constructs a machine-checked proof. Uses two key judges: a statement judge to verify formalization preserves the original problem, and an error-attribution judge to route failed attempts to mathematical re-derivation or local Lean repair.
AI.result: Achieves 100% accuracy across all evaluated olympiad benchmarks (AIME 2025, AIME 2026, HMMT February 2026). When paired with open-weight K2-Horizon-7B reasoner, it solves all six IMO 2026 problems. Statement adjudication is essential for preventing false certificates. Feedback-guided correction outperforms independent resampling on difficult problems.
AI.conclusion: The integration of formal verification (Lean 4) into informal reasoning pipelines is both feasible and highly effective. The combination of statement adjudication and feedback-guided correction enables near-perfect performance on challenging mathematical competition problems, demonstrating the potential of hybrid informal-formal reasoning systems.

title: Vision Transformer-Based Multi-Level Feature Fusion for Multi-Label Sewer Defect Classification
summary: Automated classification of sewer defects is essential for infrastructure condition assessment and maintenance decision-making, but existing deep learning methods struggle to balance classification accuracy and computational complexity in large-scale multi-label scenarios. This study develops Sewer-Transformer-ML, a hierarchical vision Transformer with multi-level feature fusion, together with two lightweight architectures, Sewer-MobileNet-ML and Sewer-Mobile-TransNet, for resource-constrained inspection scenarios. On the Sewer-ML test set, Sewer-Transformer-ML-Base achieved an $F2_{\text{CIW}}$ of 65.68% and an $F1_{\text{Normal}}$ of 92.68%, ranking first on the public leaderboard and exceeding the second-ranked method by 7.6 percentage points in $F2_{\text{CIW}}$. Sewer-MobileNet-ML achieved an $F2_{\text{CIW}}$ of 65.73% with only 17 M parameters, representing an approximately 95% parameter reduction relative to the base model. Under the standard Sewer-Capsule data split, Sewer-Mobile-TransNet achieved 96.43% classification accuracy. When the training set was reduced to 1,177 images, pretraining on Sewer-ML consistently improved model performance. Ablation experiments further showed that direct concatenation was more effective for Transformer features, whereas attention-based fusion better supported multiscale CNN features. These findings provide a computational basis for automated sewer inspection, lightweight model design, and adaptation across civil infrastructure inspection platforms.

AI.tldr: This paper develops deep learning models for automated multi-label sewer defect classification, proposing a hierarchical vision Transformer (Sewer-Transformer-ML) and two lightweight architectures (Sewer-MobileNet-ML and Sewer-Mobile-TransNet) to balance classification accuracy and computational complexity for large-scale infrastructure inspection.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning methods struggle to balance classification accuracy and computational complexity in large-scale multi-label sewer defect classification scenarios, creating a need for more efficient yet accurate solutions.
AI.method: Developed three models: (1) Sewer-Transformer-ML - hierarchical vision Transformer with multi-level feature fusion; (2) Sewer-MobileNet-ML - lightweight architecture for resource-constrained scenarios; (3) Sewer-Mobile-TransNet - hybrid architecture. Ablation experiments compared direct concatenation vs. attention-based fusion for Transformer and CNN features.
AI.result: Sewer-Transformer-ML-Base achieved F2_CIW of 65.68% and F1_Normal of 92.68%, ranking first on public leaderboard and exceeding second-ranked method by 7.6 percentage points. Sewer-MobileNet-ML achieved 65.73% F2_CIW with only 17M parameters (95% parameter reduction). Sewer-Mobile-TransNet achieved 96.43% accuracy. Pretraining on Sewer-ML improved performance even with only 1,177 training images. Direct concatenation was more effective for Transformer features; attention-based fusion better supported multiscale CNN features.
AI.conclusion: The proposed models provide an effective computational basis for automated sewer inspection, with the lightweight models enabling deployment in resource-constrained scenarios. The findings offer valuable insights for lightweight model design and adaptation across civil infrastructure inspection platforms.

title: Polyhedral Geometry of Time-to-First-Spike Neural Networks
summary: We study the expressivity of spiking neural networks, which provide a natural framework for asynchronous, event-driven computation complementary to conventional feedforward neural networks. We consider the time-to-first-spike model in a setting for which the input-output map is continuous and piecewise linear, with affine pieces governed by causal feasibility constraints that determine which presynaptic spikes occur before a neuron fires. We first show that each neuron's firing time admits a maxout-like representation with exponentially many, highly constrained affine pieces. We then formalize causal regions as polyhedral regions with fixed causal sets and derive upper and lower bounds on the maximal number of causal regions in both shallow and multilayer feedforward spiking networks. Our theoretical and experimental results show that spiking networks can generate richer partitions of the input space than conventional feedforward ReLU networks.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the expressive power of spiking neural networks (SNNs) using the time-to-first-spike model. The authors show that SNNs can create richer input space partitions than conventional ReLU networks by deriving bounds on the number of causal regions (polyhedral regions with fixed causal sets) in both shallow and multilayer architectures.
AI.motivation: Spiking neural networks provide an asynchronous, event-driven computational framework that complements conventional feedforward neural networks. However, their expressive power relative to traditional networks like ReLU networks has not been well understood. This work aims to theoretically characterize the computational capacity of SNNs.
AI.method: The authors analyze the time-to-first-spike model where the input-output map is continuous and piecewise linear with affine pieces governed by causal feasibility constraints. They use a maxout-like representation to characterize each neuron's firing time and formalize causal regions as polyhedral regions with fixed causal sets.
AI.result: The authors prove that each neuron's firing time admits a maxout-like representation with exponentially many, highly constrained affine pieces. They derive upper and lower bounds on the maximal number of causal regions in both shallow and multilayer feedforward spiking networks. Their theoretical and experimental results demonstrate that spiking networks can generate richer partitions of the input space compared to conventional feedforward ReLU networks.
AI.conclusion: Spiking neural networks have greater expressive power than conventional feedforward ReLU networks in terms of input space partitioning. This work provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the computational advantages of event-driven, asynchronous neural computation models.

title: AI Exposure and AI Resilience: A Two-Dimensional Assessment Framework for Software and Software-Based Business Model
summary: Artificial intelligence is changing both software production and the economics of software-based business models. Classical technology due diligence mainly examines technical properties such as architecture, scalability, and technical debt. These criteria do not fully capture how AI can affect a company's value proposition, competitive position, margins, or access to customers. This paper develops Artificial Intelligence Exposure and Resilience (AI-ER) as a two-dimensional assessment framework. AI exposure describes the pressure for change that AI creates for a business model. AI resilience describes the company's ability to absorb that pressure, adapt to changed conditions, and use AI in an economically viable way. Metrics for both dimensions are derived from current AI capabilities, their deployment conditions, and relevant research on business models and organizational adaptability. The model keeps exposure and resilience separate and adds an explicit assessment of evidence quality and confidence. It can be applied first with public information and later refined with internal evidence. The result is a traceable company profile that supports comparison without concealing uncertainty in the underlying evidence. The paper also specifies an initial score logic and a procedure for empirical validation.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an Artificial Intelligence Exposure and Resilience (AI-ER) framework for assessing how AI affects company value in technology due diligence. It addresses the gap where traditional technical assessments fail to capture AI's impact on business models, competitive positioning, and economics.
AI.motivation: Classical technology due diligence focuses on technical properties (architecture, scalability, technical debt) but misses how AI impacts value propositions, competitive positions, margins, and customer access. A new assessment approach is needed to capture AI's business model implications.
AI.method: Develops a two-dimensional framework: (1) AI Exposure - measures pressure for change AI creates on business models; (2) AI Resilience - measures company's ability to absorb pressure, adapt, and use AI economically. Metrics derived from current AI capabilities, deployment conditions, business model research, and organizational adaptability. Includes explicit assessment of evidence quality and confidence. Can be applied first with public information, then refined internally.
AI.result: Produces a traceable company profile supporting comparison while explicitly handling uncertainty in evidence. Includes initial score logic and procedure for empirical validation.
AI.conclusion: The AI-ER framework provides a comprehensive tool for assessing AI's business impact beyond technical metrics, enabling more accurate technology due diligence and company valuation in the AI era.

authors: for the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative
title: Brain-PACE: A Deep Siamese MRI Framework for Modelling Longitudinal Brain Acceleration
summary: Brain age estimation has become a popular research proxy for assessing brain health and disease, yet longitudinal trajectories of brain ageing are still poorly defined, and clinical use is limited. Building on existing Siamese longitudinal frameworks, we develop Brain-Predicted Age Acceleration (Brain-PACE) to directly estimate the pace of structural brain ageing from paired T1-weighted MRI. Brain-PACE identified accelerated ageing in $42.6$% of participants with mild cognitive impairment. Faster Brain-PACE was associated with greater functional and cognitive impairment (FAQ; $r=0.35$, ADAS13; $r=0.30$, CDR-SB; $r=0.32$) and greater regional tau burden in the posterior cingulate ($r=0.59$), precuneus ($r=0.47$), and entorhinal cortex ($r=0.37$). These associations were stronger than those observed when pace was calculated indirectly from repeated cross-sectional brain age estimates, suggesting that direct longitudinal modelling captures complementary information relevant to ongoing pathological change. Methodologically, Brain-PACE extends the LILAC framework by combining spatial attention with soft label distribution learning and a Cramér distance objective, improving probabilistic performance and reducing prediction bias while providing measures of predictive uncertainty. Together, these findings support Brain-PACE as a complementary longitudinal imaging phenotype with sensitivity to relevant clinical and biological changes in early neurodegeneration.

AI.tldr: Brain-PACE is a novel method for directly estimating the pace of structural brain ageing from paired T1-weighted MRI, extending the LILAC framework with spatial attention, soft label distribution learning, and Cramér distance objective. It identified accelerated ageing in 42.6% of MCI participants and showed stronger associations with clinical and biological markers than indirect methods.
AI.motivation: Brain age estimation is a popular research proxy for assessing brain health and disease, but longitudinal trajectories of brain ageing are poorly defined and clinical use is limited. Existing methods using repeated cross-sectional brain age estimates provide indirect pace measurements that may miss complementary information relevant to ongoing pathological change.
AI.method: Brain-PACE extends the LILAC (Longitudinal Interpolation of Longitudinal Analysis of Changes) framework by combining: (1) spatial attention mechanism, (2) soft label distribution learning, and (3) a Cramér distance objective. This allows direct estimation of the pace of structural brain ageing from paired T1-weighted MRI scans, providing probabilistic performance improvement, reduced prediction bias, and measures of predictive uncertainty.
AI.result: Brain-PACE identified accelerated ageing in 42.6% of participants with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Faster Brain-PACE was significantly associated with greater functional impairment (FAQ; r=0.35), greater cognitive impairment (ADAS13; r=0.30, CDR-SB; r=0.32), and greater regional tau burden in the posterior cingulate (r=0.59), precuneus (r=0.47), and entorhinal cortex (r=0.37). These associations were stronger than those observed when pace was calculated indirectly from repeated cross-sectional brain age estimates.
AI.conclusion: Brain-PACE serves as a complementary longitudinal imaging phenotype with sensitivity to relevant clinical and biological changes in early neurodegeneration.
