The direct longitudinal modelling captures complementary information relevant to ongoing pathological change that indirect methods miss, supporting its potential as a valuable tool for assessing brain health and disease progression.

title: Solving Few-Shot Multiobjective Multitask Optimization via Iterative Sequential Transfer
summary: Applying knowledge transfer across multiple optimization tasks, multitask optimization (MTO) emerges as a promising approach to solving synergistic optimization tasks simultaneously. However, the development of effective knowledge transfer mechanisms in MTO fundamentally relies on aligning elite solution distributions across tasks. This dependency creates a critical bottleneck in few-shot optimization regimes, as restricted evaluation budgets impede the identification of elite solution distributions required for beneficial transfer. This challenge is exacerbated in multiobjective multitask problems, where each optimizer must approximate a continuous Pareto manifold rather than a single optimal point. This paper introduces Iterative Sequential Transfer (IST) to circumvent this bottleneck. We model MTO as a sequence of sequential transfer optimization problems, concentrating evaluations on a single target per iteration. We propose a likelihood-informed task prioritization mechanism to maximize transfer utility by identifying the task most likely ready for knowledge integration. Empirical results on benchmark and real-world problems verify the effectiveness of the proposed method under tight budgets.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses few-shot multiobjective multitask optimization (MTO) by proposing Iterative Sequential Transfer (IST), which converts simultaneous optimization into sequential transfer problems focusing on one target per iteration. A likelihood-informed task prioritization mechanism identifies the most suitable task for knowledge transfer at each step.
AI.motivation: The research addresses a critical bottleneck in MTO: effective knowledge transfer requires alignment of elite solution distributions across tasks, but few-shot optimization regimes (with tight evaluation budgets) make it difficult to identify these elite distributions. This problem is especially severe in multiobjective multitask problems where optimizers must approximate continuous Pareto manifolds rather than single optimal points.
AI.method: The paper proposes Iterative Sequential Transfer (IST) which models MTO as a sequence of sequential transfer optimization problems. Instead of optimizing all tasks simultaneously, it concentrates evaluations on a single target per iteration. A likelihood-informed task prioritization mechanism is introduced to maximize transfer utility by identifying the task most likely ready for knowledge integration.
AI.result: Empirical results on benchmark and real-world problems verify the effectiveness of the proposed method under tight budgets.
AI.conclusion: IST successfully circumvents the bottleneck of needing elite solution distributions for beneficial transfer in few-shot MTO scenarios. The likelihood-informed task prioritization effectively identifies when tasks are ready for knowledge integration, enabling effective multitask optimization even with very limited evaluation budgets.

title: Exploring Diffusion Transformers for Cross-Modal Augmentation in Multimodal Brain State Decoding
comment: CoMA-DiT, a cross-modal augmentation framework built on Diffusion Transformer, extends multimodal learning beyond fusion by leveraging paired modalities as mutual generative supervision to enrich training data and improve brain state decoding
summary: Multimodal brain state decoding has largely focused on fusing paired modalities for prediction, but has rarely explored how their correspondence can be further exploited to enrich training data and improve multimodal representation learning. To address this gap, we propose CoMA-DiT, a bidirectional cross-modal Diffusion Transformer for latent augmentation that treats paired modalities as sources of mutual generative supervision rather than merely as inputs to be fused. CoMA-DiT conditions velocity prediction on the paired modality through cross-modal attention and adaptively injects the resulting variation via a reliability-gated residual mechanism. Experiments on multimodal auditory attention decoding and emotion recognition showed that CoMA-DiT consistently outperformed 20 representative baselines, achieving absolute gains of 4.28% and 6.70% in accuracy and macro-F1 over the no-augmentation baseline, respectively. Extensive ablation, sensitivity, visualization, and interpretability analyses further demonstrated its robustness, generalizability, and ability to capture functionally relevant cross-modal interactions. These findings support a broader view of multimodal learning: Paired modalities can serve not only as inputs for fusion but also as supervision sources that augment one another.

AI.tldr: CoMA-DiT is a bidirectional cross-modal Diffusion Transformer that treats paired modalities as mutual generative supervision rather than mere fusion inputs. It uses cross-modal attention for velocity prediction and a reliability-gated residual mechanism for adaptive variation injection. The method achieved 4.28% accuracy and 6.70% macro-F1 improvements over no-augmentation baselines on multimodal auditory attention decoding and emotion recognition tasks.
AI.motivation: Multimodal brain state decoding has largely focused on fusing paired modalities for prediction, but has rarely explored how their correspondence can be exploited to enrich training data and improve multimodal representation learning. The authors identified this gap and proposed treating paired modalities as sources of mutual generative supervision rather than merely as inputs to be fused.
AI.method: CoMA-DiT uses a bidirectional cross-modal Diffusion Transformer architecture for latent augmentation. It conditions velocity prediction on the paired modality through cross-modal attention and adaptively injects the resulting variation via a reliability-gated residual mechanism. The approach was evaluated on multimodal auditory attention decoding and emotion recognition tasks.
AI.result: CoMA-DiT consistently outperformed 20 representative baselines, achieving absolute gains of 4.28% in accuracy and 6.70% in macro-F1 over the no-augmentation baseline. Extensive ablation, sensitivity, visualization, and interpretability analyses demonstrated its robustness, generalizability, and ability to capture functionally relevant cross-modal interactions.
AI.conclusion: Paired modalities can serve not only as inputs for fusion but also as supervision sources that augment one another. This work supports a broader view of multimodal learning where modalities provide mutual generative supervision rather than simple fusion inputs.

title: DINO-Med: A Unified Patch-Based Adaptation Framework for Multi-Modal Medical Image Analysis Applied to Liver Fibrosis Staging
summary: Adapting natural-image foundation models like DINOv3 to multi-modal medical imaging is challenging due to the significant domain gap between natural color images and multi-channel medical scans. We present a unified, patch-based framework that processes raw multimodal imaging through training-free registration, automated localization, and mask-filtered patch extraction. This architecture culminates in a hierarchical strategy that aggregates patch-level insights into subject-level diagnostics. Using liver fibrosis staging as a case study, we evaluate four patch-level feature representations: handcrafted Radiomics features, learned ResNet features, pre-trained foundation model SAM-Med2D features, and frozen DINOv3 features. To ensure a controlled comparison, all models utilize the same lightweight MLP head and are evaluated across both rigid and deformable registration settings. Our training protocol focuses on mild fibrosis (S1) and cirrhosis (S4) classes only, enabling a single classifier to address both substantial fibrosis detection and cirrhosis staging. Evaluated via 10 random train (90%)/ test (10%) splits on 360 subjects from the CARE 2025 Liver Track 4 cohort, our DINOv3-based framework significantly outperforms all baselines, achieving the best classification accuracy of 78.4% for S1 and 75.8% for S4.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a unified patch-based framework for adapting natural-image foundation models (like DINOv3) to multi-modal medical imaging, specifically for liver fibrosis staging. The method uses training-free registration, automated localization, and mask-filtered patch extraction with hierarchical aggregation to achieve subject-level diagnostics.
AI.motivation: The significant domain gap between natural color images and multi-channel medical scans makes it challenging to adapt foundation models like DINOv3 to multi-modal medical imaging. There is a need for methods to effectively transfer natural-image representations to medical imaging tasks.
AI.method: The framework processes raw multimodal imaging through training-free registration, automated localization, and mask-filtered patch extraction. It uses a hierarchical strategy aggregating patch-level insights into subject-level diagnostics. Four patch-level feature representations were compared: handcrafted Radiomics, learned ResNet, pre-trained SAM-Med2D, and frozen DINOv3 features. All models used the same lightweight MLP head and were evaluated across both rigid and deformable registration settings. The study focused on S1 (mild fibrosis) and S4 (cirrhosis) classes, evaluated via 10 random 90%/10% train/test splits on 360 subjects from the CARE 2025 Liver Track 4 cohort.
AI.result: The DINOv3-based framework significantly outperformed all baselines, achieving the best classification accuracy of 78.4% for S1 and 75.8% for S4.
AI.conclusion: The DINOv3-based framework effectively adapts natural-image foundation models to multi-modal medical imaging, demonstrating that frozen DINOv3 features can be successfully transferred to medical imaging tasks with appropriate patch-based processing and hierarchical aggregation strategies.

title: MUtE: A Dual Framework for Concept Erasure and Counterfactual Interventions
summary: Erasing concept-specific information from representations has been proven useful for mitigating bias or interpreting model decisions. The joint objective is to transform the original representations such that the target concept becomes unpredictable, while maximally preserving concept-unrelated information. In this work, we revisit the optimal bounds of concept erasure to derive a novel class of erasure functions that naturally induce a deterministic, dual counterfactual mapping. Bridging the gap between theoretical optimality and practical representation learning, we design an implementation that imposes a translational bias on counterfactual trajectories - a constraint that aligns with how many concepts geometrically manifest in modern language models. Our framework enables seamless navigation between concept erasure and counterfactual generation. We empirically demonstrate its efficacy in improving downstream algorithmic fairness and generating counterfactual texts.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a novel framework for erasing concept-specific information from neural network representations while preserving unrelated information. The method derives optimal erasure functions that create deterministic dual counterfactual mappings, with a translational bias implementation aligned with how concepts appear in language models.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to improve model fairness and interpretability by removing bias from representations. The key challenge is erasing concept information without destroying useful, unrelated information in the representations.
AI.method: The paper derives a novel class of erasure functions based on optimal bounds of concept erasure. This induces a deterministic, dual counterfactual mapping. The implementation imposes a translational bias on counterfactual trajectories, which aligns with geometric manifestations of concepts in modern language models.
AI.result: The framework enables seamless navigation between concept erasure and counterfactual generation. It demonstrates efficacy in improving downstream algorithmic fairness and generating counterfactual texts.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach successfully bridges theoretical optimality with practical representation learning, providing a unified framework for both erasing unwanted concepts and generating counterfactuals.

title: Portable Semantics, Private Dialects: Reuse and Negative Transfer in Latent Communication Between Language-Model Cells
comment: 17 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Companion to arXiv:2608.20054. Code and evaluation records: https://github.com/tokenosopher/populus-evidence-partitioning ; checkpoints and fitted alignment maps: https://huggingface.co/tokenosopher/populus-evidence-partitioning-checkpoints
summary: In shared-genome language-model societies, restricted evidence visibility favors reusable, value-indexed latent packet interfaces, whereas the sole high-performing globally visible model in the parent study learned an episode-entangled code. This companion study asks whether independently trained societies share one packet language, where strict zero-shot transfer fails, and whether inherited interface state helps or harms later learning. First, a leakage-controlled causal interoperability audit over all 30 ordered pairs of six independently trained restricted societies -- under sealed held-out structure and a preregistered raw/orthogonal/linear/nonlinear alignment ladder -- shows the six semantically similar interfaces do not form one raw language: one same-initialization pair is exactly interoperable in both directions, a second shows asymmetric partial compatibility, and all 26 cross-initialization directions fail every frozen alignment rung. Second, within the tested decomposition and a single sealed source formulation, a source-span control localizes strict zero-shot failure to interpretation and execution of the new operator instructions. Third, in a matched adaptation factorial, the globally trained communication interface acts as a severe negative-transfer prior: reinitializing only the packet reader, writer, and mouth raises final depth-three accuracy from 0.169 to 0.857. Fourth, across two restricted checkpoints and two independently frozen target streams each, inherited interfaces never exceeded fresh-interface controls by the preregistered 0.10 margin. All primary conclusions are bounded to a near-transfer 17-state setting; the negative-transfer factorial concerns one globally visible parent-cohort checkpoint, while an appendix adds a post hoc tagged-global twin case study.

AI.tldr: This companion study investigates whether independently trained language model societies can share a common communication interface ("packet language") and whether inherited interface states help or harm subsequent learning. The study finds that six semantically similar interfaces do not form one universal language - only same-initialization pairs show interoperability. Globally trained interfaces serve as negative transfer priors, harming later learning (accuracy drops from 0.857 to 0.169 when using inherited global interfaces). Inherited interfaces in restricted settings never significantly outperform fresh interfaces.
AI.motivation: The parent study showed that restricted evidence visibility favors reusable, value-indexed latent packet interfaces, while globally visible models learn episode-entangled codes. This study asks: (1) Do independently trained societies share one packet language? (2) Does inherited interface state help or harm later learning? The key hypothesis is that independently trained models might develop incompatible communication protocols, and that inherited interfaces from different training regimes may negatively impact new learning.
AI.method: Four primary experiments were conducted: (1) A leakage-controlled causal interoperability audit over all 30 ordered pairs of six independently trained restricted societies, using a sealed held-out structure with a preregistered alignment ladder (raw/orthogonal/linear/nonlinear); (2) A decomposition test with sealed source formulation to localize zero-shot failure; (3) A matched adaptation factorial testing negative transfer from globally trained interfaces; (4) A factorial test across two restricted checkpoints and two independently frozen target streams testing inherited interfaces. All experiments use a near-transfer 17-state setting.
AI.result: Four main findings: (1) The six semantically similar interfaces do not form one raw language - one same-initialization pair is exactly interoperable in both directions, a second shows asymmetric partial compatibility, and all 26 cross-initialization directions fail every frozen alignment rung; (2) Strict zero-shot failure localizes to interpretation and execution of new operator instructions; (3) The globally trained communication interface acts as a severe negative-transfer prior - reinitializing only the packet reader, writer, and mouth raises final depth-three accuracy from 0.169 to 0.857 (a 5x improvement); (4) Inherited interfaces never exceeded fresh-interface controls by the preregistered 0.10 margin across all tested conditions.
AI.conclusion: Independently trained language model societies do not share a universal packet language - only models with identical initializations can communicate effectively. Inherited interfaces from global training serve as severe negative transfer priors, significantly harming learning performance. In restricted settings, fresh interfaces outperform inherited ones. These findings are bounded to a near-transfer 17-state setting, with the negative-transfer finding concerning one globally visible parent-cohort checkpoint. The study suggests that interface compatibility requires identical initialization, and that training regime strongly influences interface utility for transfer learning.

title: Multi-Modal Controlled Coherent Motion Generation
summary: It is natural for humans to walk and talk simultaneously. This paper tackles the challenge of replicating such natural behaviors in 3D avatar motion generation driven by concurrent multimodal inputs, such as a text description of a man walking alongside speech audio. Existing methods, constrained by the scarcity of aligned multimodal data, typically combine motions from individual modalities sequentially or through weighted sums. However, they often result in mismatched or unrealistic movements. To overcome these limitations, we propose MOCO, a novel diffusion-based framework capable of processing multiple simultaneous inputs, including speech audio, text descriptions, and trajectory data, to generate coherent and lifelike motions without requiring aligned multimodal data. Our key innovation lies in decoupling the motion generation process. During each denoising step, the diffusion model independently generates motions for each modality from the input noise and assembles the body parts according to predefined spatial rules. The resulting combined motion is then diffused and serves as the input noise for the subsequent denoising step. This iterative approach enables each modality to refine its contribution within the context of the overall motion, progressively harmonizing movements across modalities. Consequently, the generated motions become increasingly natural and fluid with each iteration, achieving coherent and synchronized behaviors. We evaluate our approach using a purpose-built multimodal benchmark. Experimental results demonstrate that MOCO outperforms existing baselines, advancing the field of multimodal motion generation for 3D avatars.

AI.tldr: MOCO is a diffusion-based framework for generating coherent 3D avatar motions from concurrent multimodal inputs (speech audio, text, trajectory) without requiring aligned training data. It uses an iterative decoupled generation process where each modality refines its motion contribution progressively.
AI.motivation: Humans naturally walk and talk simultaneously, but existing methods struggle to replicate this in 3D avatars. Current approaches are limited by scarcity of aligned multimodal data and typically use sequential processing or weighted sums, resulting in mismatched or unrealistic movements.
AI.method: MOCO introduces a decoupled motion generation process within a diffusion model. During each denoising step, the model independently generates motions for each modality from input noise, assembles body parts according to predefined spatial rules, and then diffuses the combined motion to serve as input noise for the next step. This iterative refinement harmonizes movements across modalities.
AI.result: MOCO outperforms existing baselines on a purpose-built multimodal benchmark, achieving more natural and fluid motions with coherent and synchronized behaviors across modalities.
AI.conclusion: The proposed iterative decoupled generation approach successfully enables multimodal motion generation without aligned training data, advancing the field of 3D avatar motion synthesis.

title: A Dynamic Fusion Large Language Model for Traffic Flow Prediction
summary: Traffic flow prediction is a core supporting technology for intelligent transportation systems. It uses historical data to infer future traffic dynamics in specific areas, thereby helping to alleviate congestion and improve resource allocation efficiency. Traditional neural networks struggle to break through accuracy limits due to their reliance on singular feature modeling, while large language models (LLMs) suffer from insufficient capture of spatial topological information and mining spatiotemporal correlation. This study proposes a Dynamic Fusion Large Language Model (DF-LLM) for traffic flow prediction. The model incorporates three core components: spatiotemporal embedding module, spatiotemporal fusion module, and LLM backbone. The spatiotemporal embedding module enables synergistic representation of multi-scale spatiotemporal features. The spatiotemporal fusion module integrates spatial topology and dynamic dependencies via graph convolution. The LLM backbone adopts a differentiated parameter adaptation strategy to balance training efficiency and traffic data adaptability. Additionally, it introduces a context aggregation attention module to strengthens global dependencies. More importantly, the LLM backbone takes the residual connections to mitigate the gradient vanishing in deep networks. Experiments show that DF-LLM has achieved better performance by comparing the metrics on all the four datasets.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes DF-LLM, a novel dynamic fusion large language model for traffic flow prediction that addresses limitations of traditional neural networks and LLMs in capturing spatiotemporal correlations and spatial topological information. The model integrates spatiotemporal embedding, spatiotemporal fusion modules, and an LLM backbone with differentiated parameter adaptation and context aggregation attention.
AI.motivation: Traditional neural networks are limited by singular feature modeling, while LLMs insufficiently capture spatial topological information and spatiotemporal correlations. Traffic flow prediction is crucial for intelligent transportation systems to alleviate congestion and improve resource allocation efficiency.
AI.method: The DF-LLM incorporates three core components: (1) Spatiotemporal embedding module for multi-scale spatiotemporal feature representation; (2) Spatiotemporal fusion module integrating spatial topology and dynamic dependencies via graph convolution; (3) LLM backbone with differentiated parameter adaptation strategy, context aggregation attention module for global dependencies, and residual connections to mitigate gradient vanishing in deep networks.
AI.result: DF-LLM achieved better performance compared to baselines on all four datasets in terms of evaluation metrics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DF-LLM successfully integrates large language models with spatiotemporal modeling for traffic flow prediction, achieving superior performance through its dynamic fusion architecture and specialized attention mechanisms.

title: RAMamba-Net: A Reliability-Aware and Mamba-Based Multimodal Fusion Network for Auditory Attention Detection
comment: RAMamba-Net, a reliability-aware Mamba-based multimodal fusion network for auditory attention decoding
summary: Auditory attention decoding (AAD) identifies the attended speaker from physiological signals, supporting neuro-steered hearing devices and natural human-machine interaction. Electroencephalography (EEG) is the dominant modality for AAD but provides incomplete evidence in naturalistic audio-visual scenes, motivating EEG and electrooculography (EOG) fusion. Existing approaches remain limited by weak cross-modal interaction, inefficient temporal modeling, and low robustness to sample variations. To address the limitations, we propose RAMamba-Net, a reliability-aware Mamba-based multimodal fusion network for AAD. RAMamba-Net employs a Mamba-enhanced band-aware convolutional Transformer to capture band-specific EEG patterns and long-range temporal dynamics. A dual-branch temporal-spatial encoder models EOG temporal and inter-channel dependencies. Cross-modal attention enables explicit modality interaction. Then, a reliability-aware module is introduced to estimate sample-wise modality weights for feature and prediction consistency, thereby enhancing multimodal fusion. Experiments on two AAD benchmarks demonstrate that RAMamba-Net effectively exploits complementary EEG-EOG information, yielding accuracy gains of 5.76% over unimodal baselines, together with more robust decoding and discriminative representations. Further analyses show that explicit cross-modal interaction improves multimodal alignment, while the reliability-aware module suppresses unreliable modality evidence and is robust to signal perturbation and parameter variation.

AI.tldr: RAMamba-Net is a novel multimodal fusion network that combines EEG and EOG signals for auditory attention decoding (AAD). It uses Mamba-enhanced band-aware convolutional Transformers for EEG, dual-branch temporal-spatial encoders for EOG, cross-modal attention, and a reliability-aware module to dynamically weight modalities. The method achieves 5.76% accuracy improvement over unimodal baselines on two benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: Current EEG-based AAD provides incomplete evidence in naturalistic audio-visual scenes. Existing EEG-EOG fusion approaches suffer from weak cross-modal interaction, inefficient temporal modeling, and low robustness to sample variations. There is a need for a more effective multimodal fusion method that can better exploit complementary EEG-EOG information.
AI.method: RAMamba-Net employs: (1) Mamba-enhanced band-aware convolutional Transformer to capture band-specific EEG patterns and long-range temporal dynamics; (2) Dual-branch temporal-spatial encoder for EOG to model temporal and inter-channel dependencies; (3) Cross-modal attention for explicit modality interaction; (4) Reliability-aware module to estimate sample-wise modality weights for feature and prediction consistency.
AI.result: Experiments on two AAD benchmarks show RAMamba-Net achieves 5.76% accuracy gain over unimodal baselines. Further analysis demonstrates: explicit cross-modal interaction improves multimodal alignment; the reliability-aware module suppresses unreliable modality evidence and is robust to signal perturbation and parameter variation.
AI.conclusion: RAMamba-Net effectively exploits complementary EEG-EOG information for AAD, yielding improved accuracy, more robust decoding, and discriminative representations. The reliability-aware mechanism enhances robustness to signal variations.

title: BruNet: A Cross-Domain Transfer Framework for Bruise Segmentation
summary: Segmenting bruises is a challenging task in medical imaging due to limited data and annotations, diffuse boundaries, and highly variable appearance. In this work, we propose BruNet, a segmentation framework that combines a ViT-based visual encoder (a self-supervised DINOv3 or a pretrained LingBot-Vision backbone) with a SAM-based mask decoder. BruNet is trained on the HAM10000 skin lesion dataset and evaluated on a separate bruise dataset without additional fine-tuning. Although a small number of prior studies have explored machine learning and computer vision for bruise analysis, existing work has primarily focused on detection, classification, or colour analysis rather than pixel-level localisation. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to address automatic bruise segmentation. Our results show that BruNet outperforms CNN-based models, state-of-the-art segmentation models, ChatGPT-4o/5-assisted SAM2 zero-shot baselines, and the medical-oriented MedSAM model, demonstrating strong cross-domain generalisation to bruise segmentation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces BruNet, the first automatic bruise segmentation framework combining a ViT-based visual encoder (DINOv3 or LingBot-Vision) with a SAM-based mask decoder. Trained on HAM10000 and evaluated on a separate bruise dataset without fine-tuning, BruNet outperforms CNN-based models, state-of-the-art segmentation models, and various SAM-based baselines including MedSAM.
AI.motivation: Bruise segmentation in medical imaging is challenging due to limited data, diffuse boundaries, and highly variable appearance. Prior work focused on detection, classification, or color analysis rather than pixel-level localization. This is the first study addressing automatic bruise segmentation.
AI.method: BruNet combines a ViT-based visual encoder (self-supervised DINOv3 or pretrained LingBot-Vision) with a SAM-based mask decoder. The model is trained on HAM10000 skin lesion dataset and evaluated on a separate bruise dataset without additional fine-tuning to test cross-domain generalization.
AI.result: BruNet outperforms CNN-based models, state-of-the-art segmentation models, ChatGPT-4o/5-assisted SAM2 zero-shot baselines, and the medical-oriented MedSAM model, demonstrating strong cross-domain generalization to bruise segmentation.
AI.conclusion: BruNet represents the first automatic bruise segmentation solution, achieving superior performance over existing approaches including medical-specific models, and showing promising cross-domain generalization capabilities.

title: Beyond Confidence: Stability-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for LLM Reasoning
summary: Test-time adaptation has emerged as a lightweight alternative to costly post-training for improving the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) on downstream tasks. Predictive entropy provides a model-derived signal for such adaptation, guiding models toward higher-confidence reasoning states without external verifiers or reward models. However, higher confidence does not necessarily imply correctness, as LLMs may remain highly confident along incorrect reasoning trajectories. We observe that high-confidence reasoning is more likely to be correct when confidence remains stable under local perturbations. Based on this observation, we propose Test-Time Adaptation via Stability-Aware Confidence Optimization (TASCO), a framework that incorporates local stability into confidence-based test-time adaptation while keeping the LLM frozen. TASCO operationalizes local stability by optimizing a lightweight task-level prefix under two alternative perturbation strategies: Random Perturbation promotes distributional stability across trajectories induced by nearby perturbed prefixes, whereas Sharpness-Aware Perturbation targets worst-case local sensitivity. Experiments demonstrate that TASCO improves reasoning accuracy and token efficiency across diverse LLMs and reasoning benchmarks, while behavioral analyses show that it maintains stable confidence under local perturbations without prematurely concentrating the model's predictive distribution.

AI.tldr: TASCO is a test-time adaptation framework that improves LLM reasoning by incorporating local stability into confidence-based adaptation, using two perturbation strategies (Random and Sharpness-Aware) to optimize a lightweight task-level prefix while keeping the LLM frozen.
AI.motivation: Test-time adaptation offers a lightweight alternative to post-training for improving LLM reasoning. However, predictive entropy-based confidence signals have a critical flaw: higher confidence doesn't guarantee correctness, as LLMs can be highly confident in incorrect reasoning. The key insight is that high-confidence reasoning is more likely correct when confidence remains stable under local perturbations.
AI.method: TASCO incorporates local stability into confidence-based test-time adaptation while keeping the LLM frozen. It operationalizes local stability by optimizing a lightweight task-level prefix under two perturbation strategies: (1) Random Perturbation - promotes distributional stability across trajectories induced by nearby perturbed prefixes; (2) Sharpness-Aware Perturbation - targets worst-case local sensitivity.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that TASCO improves reasoning accuracy and token efficiency across diverse LLMs and reasoning benchmarks. Behavioral analyses show it maintains stable confidence under local perturbations without prematurely concentrating the model's predictive distribution.
AI.conclusion: TASCO provides an effective test-time adaptation approach that leverages stability-aware confidence optimization, achieving improved reasoning performance and efficiency while maintaining stable confidence behavior across various benchmarks and model architectures.

title: BridgeMatch: Conditional Transport Bridges in Matching Matrix Space for 3D Deformable Registration
summary: Reliable non-rigid point cloud correspondences are important for deformable anatomical registration, embodied perception and manipulation, and dynamic 3D reconstruction. Coarse-to-fine methods reduce computational cost by selecting the top-\(K\) coarse regions. However, this pruning may remove weak but correct hypotheses and restrict fine matching to an incomplete search space. We present \paper, a two-stage generative solver that maintains the complete soft matching matrix at both coarse and high resolutions. Stage~I uses denoising diffusion to estimate a global matching matrix in the compact coarse-resolution space. We then lift this matrix to high resolution while preserving its hierarchy. The lifted matrix is rank-bounded and block-constant. Stage~II refines it through a conditional transport bridge. We implement the bridge with two types of dynamics: a deterministic endpoint-parameterized conditional Flow Matching (CFM) ODE and a stochastic Brownian-bridge SDE inspired by Schrödinger bridges. Both variants share the lifted source, a time-conditioned transformer, and a matching-matrix endpoint predictor. Experiments on 4DMatch and 4DLoMatch show that both variants produce more accurate correspondences than the compared methods and improve downstream registration, with larger gains in low-overlap cases. They also improve cross-dataset generalization on CAPE and DeepDeform without target-domain adaptation while using the same deformation solver.

AI.tldr: A two-stage generative solver for non-rigid point cloud correspondence that maintains complete soft matching at both coarse and high resolutions, using denoising diffusion for global matching estimation followed by conditional transport bridge refinement.
AI.motivation: Coarse-to-fine methods prune weak but correct hypotheses by selecting top-K regions, restricting fine matching to incomplete search space. This work aims to maintain the complete search space while managing computational cost.
AI.method: Stage I: Denoising diffusion to estimate global matching matrix in compact coarse-resolution space, then lift to high resolution while preserving hierarchy (rank-bounded and block-constant). Stage II: Conditional transport bridge with two variants - deterministic CFM ODE and stochastic Brownian-bridge SDE, both using lifted source, time-conditioned transformer, and matching-matrix endpoint predictor.
AI.result: Both variants produce more accurate correspondences than compared methods on 4DMatch and 4DLoMatch, improve downstream registration (especially in low-overlap cases), and show cross-dataset generalization on CAPE and DeepDeform without target-domain adaptation.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage generative approach effectively addresses the limitation of coarse-to-fine pruning by maintaining complete soft matching matrices, achieving superior accuracy and generalization for non-rigid point cloud correspondence tasks.

title: Reification as a Transferable Vocabulary: Zero-Shot Link Prediction with Vanilla GNNs
summary: Knowledge graph foundation models such as ULTRA achieve zero-shot link prediction on unseen graphs through dedicated architectures that hard-code a transfer mechanism. In this work we move that mechanism out of the architecture and into the representation, by \emph{reifying} the input graph: every fact becomes a node, connected to its subject, object, and relation type through a fixed vocabulary of six meta-relations, with relation types as anonymous shared nodes rather than model parameters. On this representation, five textbook GNNs (GAT, GINE with sum and with mean+max aggregation, GraphSAGE, R-GCN), each trained on a single knowledge graph of 4,245 triples for 30 minutes on one NVIDIA A100, transfer zero-shot to 40 inductive link-prediction benchmarks. The best of them, an off-the-shelf GAT, matches ULTRA, a dedicated foundation model pretrained on three graphs, across ULTRA's own evaluation suite. The same fixed vocabulary extends to relational databases, a row becoming an entity and a foreign-key column a relation type; a preliminary probe on two unseen databases, with no cell values, schema text or in-context labels, shows a model of this family pretrained on three knowledge graphs ranking foreign-key targets far above random-initialization and degree controls. We release the code, the checkpoints, and the evaluation pipeline for all 40 benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel approach to zero-shot transfer for knowledge graph link prediction by reifying the input graph—representing every fact as a node connected to subject, object, and relation via six meta-relations. This allows standard GNNs to achieve transfer performance comparable to ULTRA, a dedicated foundation model, using only a single training graph.
AI.motivation: Current knowledge graph foundation models like ULTRA hard-code the transfer mechanism into their architecture. This work aims to move that mechanism into the representation itself, enabling any standard GNN to achieve zero-shot transfer to unseen graphs without specialized architecture.
AI.method: The approach reifies the input knowledge graph: every fact becomes a node connected to its subject, object, and relation type through a fixed vocabulary of six meta-relations. Relation types are treated as anonymous shared nodes rather than model parameters. Five standard GNNs (GAT, GINE with sum and mean+max aggregation, GraphSAGE, R-GCN) were trained on a single knowledge graph (4,245 triples) for 30 minutes on one NVIDIA A100.
AI.result: The best model (GAT) matches ULTRA's performance across ULTRA's own evaluation suite of 40 inductive link-prediction benchmarks, despite ULTRA being pretrained on three graphs. The approach also extends to relational databases, where a preliminary experiment on two unseen databases showed pretrained models ranking foreign-key targets far above random initialization and degree controls.
AI.conclusion: Moving the transfer mechanism from architecture to representation enables standard GNNs to achieve foundation model-level zero-shot transfer performance on knowledge graphs and relational databases. This reification approach provides a simple yet effective way to generalize across unseen graphs without specialized architectures.

title: From Queries to Narratives: Cultural Heritage Data Stories for Knowledge Graph Exploration and Quality Assessment
summary: Cultural-heritage KGs such as the NFDI4Culture-KG contain millions of triples about artworks, music, inscriptions, historical events, and the people and places connected to them. For many users, however, discovering this knowledge can be difficult. While SPARQL can be learned, writing meaningful queries first requires an in-depth understanding of the graph's data model, an investment many domain researchers and practitioners are unwilling to make. Even with existing user interfaces, a starting point and some guidance are usually needed, because the data contained in the graph is highly specialized, heterogeneous, and constantly growing, making it challenging to know what it contains or which questions it can answer. In this paper, we present data stories as a way not only to lower this barrier, but also to turn exploration into data-quality assessment, and thus combine accessible querying with the discovery of issues that remain hidden in aggregate statistics. In this contribution, a data story is understood as a narrative document that integrates explanatory text and images with executable SPARQL queries and their visualized results. It is described how they are authored against the graph and how they serve several purposes: guiding users through an unfamiliar graph, creating reproducible narratives, and surfacing data-quality issues previously hidden in aggregate statistics. The authoring platform LODEON including its Sparnatural and AI-supported authoring assistants is introduced as a proof-of-concept. Within the authoring environment, every claim made about the data can be backed by an explicit query, making these narratives transparent and reproducible. This paper also reflects on lessons learned from hands-on seminars and workshops. Early experience suggests that such data stories make cultural-heritage knowledge graphs more accessible for both exploration and quality assessment.

AI.tldr: This paper presents "data stories" as a solution to make cultural-heritage knowledge graphs (like NFDI4Culture-KG) more accessible. Data stories are narrative documents that combine explanatory text and images with executable SPARQL queries and their visualized results. The authors introduce LODEON, a proof-of-concept authoring platform with Sparnatural and AI-supported authoring assistants that enables creating reproducible narratives backed by explicit queries.
AI.motivation: Cultural-heritage KGs contain millions of triples but remain difficult for most users to explore. Writing SPARQL queries requires in-depth understanding of the graph's data model, which many domain researchers are unwilling to invest. Even with existing UIs, users need guidance because the data is specialized, heterogeneous, and constantly growing—making it challenging to know what the graph contains or which questions it can answer.
AI.method: The authors propose data stories as narrative documents that integrate explanatory text, images, executable SPARQL queries, and visualized results. They developed LODEON, a proof-of-concept authoring platform including Sparnatural (a visual SPARQL query builder) and AI-supported authoring assistants. Every claim in these narratives is backed by an explicit query, making them transparent and reproducible. The approach was evaluated through hands-on seminars and workshops.
AI.result: Early experience suggests that data stories make cultural-heritage knowledge graphs more accessible for both exploration and quality assessment. The approach serves three purposes: (1) guiding users through unfamiliar graphs, (2) creating reproducible narratives, and (3) surfacing data-quality issues that remain hidden in aggregate statistics.
AI.conclusion: Data stories effectively lower the barrier to entry for exploring cultural-heritage knowledge graphs while combining accessibility with data-quality assessment. The LODEON platform demonstrates a viable approach to authoring these interactive narratives. Future work may focus on scaling the approach and enhancing AI-assisted authoring capabilities.

title: Pre- and Post-Treatment Brain Metastases Segmentation Using nnU-Net with Post-Processing for BraTS 2026
summary: Brain metastases exhibit high inter-lesion variability in size, enhancement pattern, and post-treatment appearance, making volumetric segmentation of both pre- and post-treatment cases the central challenge of the BraTS 2026 Task 1 (Brain Metastases). We build a pragmatic pipeline on a 5-fold nnU-Net ResEnc-L ensemble, in which each fold is trained independently for 1,000 epochs with the standard Dice + cross-entropy loss on 1,296 four-modality training cases. This ensemble is followed by a rule-based post-processing cascade tuned for the lesion-wise Dice similarity coefficient (LW-DSC), a detection-oriented metric that behaves very differently from the traditional global Dice. The final pipeline reaches an LW-DSC of 0.733 / 0.751 / 0.713 / 0.549 on the enhancing tumour (ET), tumour core (TC), whole tumour (WT), and resection cavity (RC) sub-regions on the official validation leaderboard. Rather than trusting these leaderboard gains, we audit every post-processing stage with a five-fold out-of-fold (OOF) analysis with no model-training leakage over all 1,296 training cases, scored with the official BraTS evaluation code (BraTS_evaluation): it confirms two stages as robust, per-fold-consistent improvements while the third improves only the leaderboard and does not reproduce out-of-fold. We further provide a mechanistic analysis of the LW-DSC metric that explains why recall-recovering post-processing carries low risk whereas component deletion does not, and we report thirteen negative results spanning loss engineering, alternative backbones, and inference-time settings, several of which run counter to widely held intuitions. Source code is released under Apache-2.0 at https://github.com/hornbeamliu/brats2026-met.

AI.tldr: A pragmatic pipeline for brain metastases segmentation using 5-fold nnU-Net ResEnc-L ensemble with rule-based post-processing, evaluated using lesion-wise Dice similarity coefficient (LW-DSC). The paper emphasizes rigorous validation through out-of-fold analysis and reports 13 negative results.
AI.motivation: Brain metastases exhibit high inter-lesion variability in size, enhancement pattern, and post-treatment appearance, making volumetric segmentation challenging. The task focuses on the BraTS 2026 Challenge, requiring robust segmentation across pre- and post-treatment cases.
AI.method: 5-fold nnU-Net ResEnc-L ensemble, each trained independently for 1,000 epochs with standard Dice + cross-entropy loss on 1,296 four-modality training cases, followed by rule-based post-processing cascade tuned for lesion-wise Dice (LW-DSC).
AI.result: Achieves LW-DSC of 0.733/0.751/0.713/0.549 for enhancing tumour (ET), tumour core (TC), whole tumour (WT), and resection cavity (RC) on validation leaderboard. OOF analysis confirms two post-processing stages as robust improvements while one stage only improves leaderboard without OOF reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the importance of rigorous out-of-fold validation for post-processing stages. It provides mechanistic analysis of LW-DSC explaining why recall-recovering post-processing carries low risk while component deletion does not. Additionally, it reports 13 negative results spanning loss engineering, alternative backbones, and inference-time settings, challenging widely held intuitions.

title: Local Robustness Quantification for Naive Bayes Classifiers and Generative Forests: a General Approach
summary: We provide methods for calculating the robustness of the predictions of two types of generative classifiers whose underlying distribution is a Probabilistic Graphical Model (PGM): naive Bayes classifiers and generative forests (a probabilistic extension of random forests). Following the paradigm of robustness quantification, we define the robustness of a prediction as the extent to which the distribution of the classifier can be perturbed without changing this prediction. We consider perturbations obtained by varying the local models of the PGMs within general neighborhoods and focus in particular on epsilon-contamination, total variation distance and chi-squared divergence balls. We test our methods on benchmark datasets, demonstrate that the robustness value of a prediction serves as an indicator for its trustworthiness and compare our approach with other such indicators.

AI.tldr: The paper presents methods for calculating the robustness of predictions made by two types of generative classifiers (naive Bayes and generative forests) whose underlying distribution is a Probabilistic Graphical Model. Robustness is defined as how much the classifier's distribution can be perturbed without changing its prediction, considering various perturbation types (epsilon-contamination, total variation distance, chi-squared divergence).
AI.motivation: The motivation is to provide a way to assess the trustworthiness of classifier predictions by quantifying how robust they are to distribution perturbations. This addresses the need for uncertainty quantification in machine learning predictions.
AI.method: The methods involve calculating robustness within different statistical neighborhoods (epsilon-contamination, total variation distance, and chi-squared divergence balls) by varying the local models of the PGM. The approach is tested on benchmark datasets.
AI.result: The robustness value serves as an indicator for prediction trustworthiness, and the methods were demonstrated to be effective on benchmark datasets.
AI.conclusion: The robustness quantification approach provides a useful indicator for assessing the reliability of generative classifier predictions, offering a principled way to evaluate uncertainty in machine learning models.

title: LLMs as Post-hoc Auditors of Physiological Plausibility in Symbolic Regression: A Clinician-Evaluated Case Study
summary: Genetic Programming and its variants, such as grammatical evolution, are widely used in Symbolic Regression to derive mathematical expressions from multivariate data. In addition to predictive accuracy, models are appreciated for their potential to provide interpretability, offering explicit equations that relate input variables to outcomes. However, achieving interpretability and plausibility remains challenging, as evolved models may be complex or scientifically inconsistent. In this study, we explore whether Large Language Models, can assist in improving the explainability of Symbolic Regression models generated by evolutionary computation methods. Building upon our previous work on estimating body fat percentage using grammar-based Genetic Programming , we investigate the use of LLMs as post-processing tools to analyze and rank evolved expressions according to their interpretability and medical plausibility. Four symbolic expressions are analysed by three LLMs over three repeated runs, and the resulting interpretations and rankings are assessed by a panel of three clinicians. Across the three LLMs, comparative model-ranking outputs received more favorable clinician assessments than isolated term-level interpretations. However, the LLMs also produced physiologically and mathematically questionable explanations, indicating that they are better suited to comparative auditing under expert oversight than to autonomous validation.\blfootnote{The present work is an extended version of a paper submitted into a journal.

AI.tldr: This study investigates whether Large Language Models can assist in improving the interpretability and plausibility of Symbolic Regression models generated by Genetic Programming. Using body fat percentage estimation as a case study, four symbolic expressions were analyzed by three LLMs across three repeated runs, with clinician assessments of the interpretations and rankings.
AI.motivation: Symbolic Regression via Genetic Programming can derive mathematical expressions from multivariate data, but evolved models often lack interpretability and may be scientifically inconsistent. This work aims to leverage LLMs as post-processing tools to analyze and rank evolved expressions according to their interpretability and medical plausibility.
AI.method: The study uses grammar-based Genetic Programming for body fat percentage estimation. Four symbolic expressions were analyzed by three LLMs over three repeated runs. The resulting interpretations and rankings were evaluated by a panel of three clinicians.
AI.result: Comparative model-ranking outputs from LLMs received more favorable clinician assessments than isolated term-level interpretations. However, LLMs also produced physiologically and mathematically questionable explanations in some cases.
AI.conclusion: LLMs show promise for comparative auditing of Symbolic Regression models, but are better suited as assistive tools under expert oversight rather than for autonomous validation, due to occasional erroneous explanations.

title: FreeFlow: A Bias-free Hierarchical Transformer for Optical Flow Estimation
summary: Optical flow methods typically rely on task-specific inductive biases, such as correlation volumes, feature warping, and iterative refinement, among others, to reach high accuracy. While effective, such biases constrain the model to predefined heuristics, which can limit its expressivity and lead to more complex pipelines and additional computational cost. We present FreeFlow, a hierarchical transformer built without any flow-specific components, using instead a single feed-forward encoder--decoder. FreeFlow combines three attention variants: window attention for local processing, shifted-window attention for cross-window information exchange, and a global attention operating at a reduced resolution. The resulting architecture scales naturally with model capacity, enabling a consistent accuracy gain from small to large variants. Despite the absence of standard inductive biases, FreeFlow achieves state-of-the-art results on major benchmarks, including Sintel (0.68/1.48 EPE on Clean/Final), KITTI-2015 (3.23 Fl-all), and Spring (3.192 1px), while remaining memory efficient at 1080p inference.

AI.tldr: FreeFlow is a hierarchical transformer for optical flow estimation that uses a single feed-forward encoder-decoder without any flow-specific inductive biases, combining window attention, shifted-window attention, and global attention at reduced resolution.
AI.motivation: Traditional optical flow methods rely on task-specific inductive biases (correlation volumes, feature warping, iterative refinement) which constrain model expressivity and lead to more complex pipelines with additional computational cost.
AI.method: FreeFlow uses a hierarchical transformer architecture with a single feed-forward encoder-decoder, combining three attention variants: window attention for local processing, shifted-window attention for cross-window information exchange, and global attention operating at reduced resolution. The architecture scales naturally with model capacity.
AI.result: FreeFlow achieves state-of-the-art results on major benchmarks: Sintel (0.68/1.48 EPE on Clean/Final), KITTI-2015 (3.23 Fl-all), and Spring (3.192 1px), while remaining memory efficient at 1080p inference.
AI.conclusion: Despite the absence of standard inductive biases, FreeFlow outperforms existing methods, demonstrating that a general transformer architecture can effectively learn optical flow when properly designed, with consistent accuracy gains from small to large model variants.

title: Prevalence Determines Precision:Silent Contamination in Detector-Defined Datasets
summary: Many ML datasets are constructed by running a detector, heuristic, or model over candidate pools; accepted items become labels. Dataset precision is then governed by true-positive prevalence in each pool via Bayes, not solely by detector quality. Using one instrument and period, we hold a detector-defined event dataset plus an independent official index labeling every detected item as real or phantom. One detector, three pools yield phantom rates 81.7%, 9.0%, and 0.0%. Transferring precision from the two high-rate pools to the low-rate pool predicts 0.955 versus measured 0.183, a +422% error; the Bayes expression predicts all three within 3.3%. The detected response curve is an exact convex combination of a true-event and a phantom component (residual 1.1e-16), with phantoms outnumbering true events 473 to 308, so contamination is a second signal with detector-inherited shape, not additive noise. Contamination direction depends on the estimator: on identical windows one statistic is diluted and another inflated because its denominator is also contaminated. A common normalization turns the estimator into a mean of ratios whose expectation need not exist; on the same 335 events it returns 0.40 where the well-defined estimator returns 0.10.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that ML dataset precision depends on true-positive prevalence in candidate pools via Bayes' rule, not just detector quality. Using one detector across three pools with phantom rates of 81.7%, 9.0%, and 0.0%, the authors show that naive precision transfer leads to +422% error, while Bayes prediction is accurate within 3.3%. Contamination (phantoms) is a second signal with detector-inherited shape, not additive noise, and certain normalizations can produce undefined expectations.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to demonstrate that dataset precision in ML is governed by true-positive prevalence in candidate pools via Bayes' rule, not solely by detector quality. The authors identify that contamination (phantom events) is often misinterpreted as random noise when it's actually a structured signal with detector-inherited characteristics.
AI.method: The authors used one detector and one time period, comparing a detector-defined event dataset against an independent official index that labels each detected item as real or phantom. They tested three candidate pools with different phantom rates and compared naive precision transfer against Bayes' rule prediction. They also analyzed the detected response curve as a convex combination of true-event and phantom components.
AI.result: The results show: (1) Naive precision transfer from high-rate pools to low-rate pool predicts 0.955 vs measured 0.183 (+422% error); Bayes prediction is accurate within 3.3% for all three pools. (2) The detected response curve is an exact convex combination of true-event and phantom components (residual 1.1e-16), with phantoms outnumbering true events 473 to 308. (3) Contamination direction depends on the estimator - one statistic is diluted while another is inflated because its denominator is contaminated. (4) A common normalization turns the estimator into a mean of ratios whose expectation may not exist, returning 0.40 where the well-defined estimator returns 0.10 on identical 335 events.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion is that contamination in detector-defined datasets is a second signal with detector-inherited shape, not additive noise. Dataset precision depends on true-positive prevalence via Bayes' rule. Naive precision transfer between pools leads to large errors. Common normalizations can produce undefined expectations, and different estimators can give contradictory results on identical data due to contamination effects.

title: Calibration-Aware Uncertainty Cascades for Efficient Heterogeneous Model Collaboration
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables, including appendix. Under review
summary: Heterogeneous model collaboration seeks to exploit the complementary strengths of different models to balance predictive performance and inference cost. Existing approaches typically rely either on trained routers, which tie routing decisions to a fixed task and model pool, or on raw-confidence cascades, whose thresholds lack consistent reliability semantics across heterogeneous models. Consequently, these approaches adapt poorly to changing model pools and deployment budgets. We propose Calibration-Aware Uncertainty Cascades (CAUC), a simple post-hoc framework that independently calibrates each model's confidence and selects deployment policies using validation data. The resulting calibrated confidence scores establish a common reliability scale for accepting an early prediction, invoking a stronger model, or selectively combining model outputs. This unified decision criterion decouples deployment policies from any particular model pool or operating budget. We further show theoretically that calibration gives confidence thresholds an explicit selective-risk interpretation, whereas uncalibrated scores offer no comparable reliability guarantee. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, across six language benchmarks, CAUC achieves an average relative accuracy improvement of 1.9% over strong-model-only inference while avoiding approximately 47% of strong-model calls. On image classification benchmarks, it maintains or improves predictive performance while reducing measured GFLOPs by up to 57%.

AI.tldr: CAUC (Calibration-Aware Uncertainty Cascades) is a post-hoc framework for heterogeneous model collaboration that independently calibrates each model's confidence scores to establish a common reliability scale. It enables flexible deployment policies for accepting early predictions, invoking stronger models, or combining outputs, decoupling decisions from specific model pools or budgets.
AI.motivation: Existing heterogeneous model collaboration approaches have significant limitations: (1) trained routers are tied to fixed tasks and model pools, making them inflexible; (2) raw-confidence cascades lack consistent reliability semantics across heterogeneous models. These approaches adapt poorly to changing model pools and deployment budgets.
AI.method: CAUC is a simple post-hoc framework with two key components: (1) Independent calibration of each model's confidence using validation data; (2) Deployment policy selection based on calibrated scores. The calibrated confidence scores establish a common reliability scale for three decision options: accepting an early prediction, invoking a stronger model, or selectively combining model outputs.
AI.result: Experiments on six language benchmarks show CAUC achieves an average relative accuracy improvement of 1.9% over strong-model-only inference while avoiding approximately 47% of strong-model calls. On image classification benchmarks, it maintains or improves predictive performance while reducing measured GFLOPs by up to 57%.
AI.conclusion: Theoretically, calibration gives confidence thresholds an explicit selective-risk interpretation, whereas uncalibrated scores offer no comparable reliability guarantee. CAUC provides a unified decision criterion that decouples deployment policies from any particular model pool or operating budget, enabling flexible adaptation to changing model pools and deployment constraints.

title: Recursive Code World Models: Building Complex Worlds through Recursive Scene Programs
summary: Code world models represent worlds as executable programs, but this representation alone does not determine how to construct a complex world. We introduce Recursive Code World Models (RCWM), a framework for reconstructing complex 3D worlds in code from a single reference image. RCWM couples a Recursive Scene Program (RSP) representation with a construction solver that recursively calls itself. An RSP represents the executable world as compositional scene code, while each solver call follows the same complete process: establish the whole, recursively reconstruct unresolved parts, and revisit the whole to refine their composition. This global-local-global recursion gives fine-scale structures their own perception-and-editing loops while preserving scene-wide geometry and relationships. Reference-aligned views propagate a shared camera projection across levels, while parent revisitation addresses boundaries, spatial relations, and shared errors that emerge after local refinement. A vision-language coding agent directly compares reference images with scene renders to guide refinement, recursive descent, and return. Across complex scenes, RCWM outperforms prior code-based image-to-scene reconstruction methods. Ablation studies further support the benefits of recursive construction and suggest that deeper calls can improve finer-scale reconstruction. RCWM provides a recursive construction principle for building complex executable worlds from visual evidence.

AI.tldr: RCWM is a framework for reconstructing complex 3D worlds as executable code programs from a single reference image, using recursive scene programs coupled with a self-recursive construction solver that follows a global-local-global refinement pattern.
AI.motivation: Existing code world models represent worlds as executable programs but lack a method for constructing complex worlds. The challenge is how to build detailed, hierarchical 3D scenes from visual evidence while maintaining both fine-scale structure and scene-wide coherence.
AI.method: RCWM couples a Recursive Scene Program (RSP) representation with a recursive construction solver. The solver follows a global-local-global pattern: (1) establish the whole scene, (2) recursively reconstruct unresolved parts, and (3) revisit the whole to refine composition. Reference-aligned views propagate shared camera projection across recursion levels, while parent revisitation addresses boundaries, spatial relations, and shared errors. A vision-language coding agent compares reference images with scene renders to guide refinement.
AI.result: RCWM outperforms prior code-based image-to-scene reconstruction methods on complex scenes. Ablation studies confirm the benefits of recursive construction, showing that deeper recursion levels improve finer-scale reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: RCWM provides a principled recursive approach for building complex executable worlds from visual evidence, enabling both fine-scale perception-and-editing loops and scene-wide geometry preservation through global-local-global recursion.

title: Combining Synthetic and Real Data for Low-Resource Historical OCR: A Manchu Case Study
summary: Manchu, now critically endangered, was one of the principal languages of the Qing empire (1636-1912), and its extensive archival record is increasingly digitized but remains difficult to search and analyze at scale. Previous work showed that vision-language models (VLMs) trained only on synthetic Manchu word images can reach 87.4% word accuracy on real Qing manuscripts and prints, leaving a substantial synthetic-to-real gap. This study examines how synthetic and real historical training data should be combined for low-resource OCR. Using 60,000 synthetic and 20,306 real historical word images, we evaluate three pretrained VLMs and a compact convolutional recurrent neural network (CRNN) under four regimes: synthetic-only, real-only, joint synthetic-real, and sequential synthetic-to-real training, following a common checkpoint-selection and archival evaluation protocol. Introducing real training images raises the leading configurations to between 95.09% and 96.28% word accuracy, while no synthetic-only configuration exceeds 87.92%. Synthetic supplementation substantially improves all three VLMs, whereas its marginal effect for the CRNN is sensitive to the training objective. Joint and sequential training yield broadly similar archival accuracy under the tested practical pipelines. A compact CRNN also reaches the leading performance range once real images are available, showing that model scale alone does not determine recognition accuracy. Finally, complementary errors among strong recognizers allow voting to raise accuracy to 98.27% without additional training, while an eighteenth-century Manchu dictionary provides a principled rule for adjudicating disagreements.

AI.tldr: This study improves OCR for critically endangered Manchu language historical documents by combining synthetic and real training data. Using 60K synthetic and 20K real word images across 3 VLMs and 1 CRNN, the research achieves up to 98.27% accuracy through model voting and dictionary-based adjudication.
AI.motivation: Manchu is critically endangered but has extensive Qing dynasty archival records that are difficult to search at scale. Previous work showed a substantial synthetic-to-real gap (87.4% accuracy), necessitating research on how to effectively combine synthetic and real training data for low-resource OCR.
AI.method: Evaluated three pretrained VLMs and one compact CRNN under four training regimes: synthetic-only, real-only, joint synthetic-real, and sequential synthetic-to-real. Used 60,000 synthetic and 20,306 real historical word images with checkpoint-selection and archival evaluation protocol. Applied voting ensemble with an 18th-century Manchu dictionary for error adjudication.
AI.result: Introducing real training images raised accuracy to 95.09%-96.28%, versus maximum 87.92% for synthetic-only. Synthetic supplementation substantially improved all VLMs. Joint and sequential training yielded similar accuracy. Compact CRNN reached leading performance with real data. Voting ensemble achieved 98.27% accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Real training data is essential for closing the synthetic-to-real gap in low-resource OCR. Model scale alone does not determine accuracy—compact CRNNs can match large VLMs with appropriate data. Complementary errors among recognizers enable effective voting ensembles, further improved by dictionary-based adjudication.

title: RouteRepair: Instance-Level Failure Diagnosis and Targeted Repair in LLM-Based Automated Heuristic Design for Routing Optimization
summary: Efficient routing optimization is essential to freight transportation, urban logistics, and shared mobility, where high-quality heuristics are often required under limited computational budgets. Recent large language model (LLM)-based automated heuristic design methods can generate effective routing rules, but aggregate evaluation may mask recurrent failures on particular instance structures. To address this limitation, this study develops RouteRepair, which diagnoses parent-specific weaknesses from instance-level performance and applies targeted modifications to the corresponding heuristic components while protecting behavior that already performs well. Routing evidence, solver behavior, and program context are combined to define bounded repair objectives, and each intervention is validated through matched parent-child evaluation of failure recovery and collateral degradation. Experiments on the traveling salesman problem (TSP) and capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) span constructive search, guided local search, and ant colony optimization. RouteRepair-GLS reduces the mean TSP optimality gap from 1.7476% to 0.7587%, while the constructive CVRP heuristic lowers average route cost by 1.91% relative to the savings heuristic; the generated ACO priors also outperform matched hand-designed priors. These results show that failure-aware, evidence-constrained refinement can improve routing heuristics on difficult instances while preserving performance on cases they already solve well.

AI.tldr: RouteRepair is a method that diagnoses weaknesses in LLM-generated routing heuristics at the instance level and applies targeted fixes while preserving well-performing components. It combines routing evidence, solver behavior, and program context to define bounded repair objectives, validated through parent-child evaluation. Experiments on TSP and CVRP show significant improvements: TSP optimality gap reduced from 1.7476% to 0.7587%, CVRP heuristic improved by 1.91%, and ACO priors outperform hand-designed ones.
AI.motivation: LLM-based automated heuristic design for routing problems can generate effective rules, but aggregate evaluation masks recurrent failures on particular instance structures. The authors aim to address this limitation by developing a failure-aware refinement approach that diagnoses parent-specific weaknesses and applies targeted modifications.
AI.method: RouteRepair diagnoses parent-specific weaknesses from instance-level performance data and applies targeted modifications to corresponding heuristic components while protecting behavior that already performs well. It combines routing evidence, solver behavior, and program context to define bounded repair objectives. Each intervention is validated through matched parent-child evaluation of failure recovery and collateral degradation.
AI.result: RouteRepair-GLS reduces mean TSP optimality gap from 1.7476% to 0.7587% (56.6% improvement). The constructive CVRP heuristic lowers average route cost by 1.91% relative to the savings heuristic. Generated ACO priors outperform matched hand-designed priors. The method improves heuristics on difficult instances while preserving performance on cases already solved well.
AI.conclusion: Failure-aware, evidence-constrained refinement can improve routing heuristics on difficult instances while preserving performance on cases they already solve well. This approach addresses the limitation of aggregate evaluation in LLM-based heuristic design by enabling instance-level diagnosis and targeted repair.

title: UBone3D: Physics-Rectified Conditional Flow Matching for Anatomical 3D Shape Completion from Ultrasound
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Camera-ready Author Version
summary: Three-dimensional ultrasound (US) is a safe, radiation-free complementary modality to CT and X-rays for longitudinal monitoring, yet its segmentation-derived partial point clouds are extremely artifact-laden. Consequently, it is challenging to recover a clean and complete anatomical structure from such US point clouds. In this paper, we present UBone3D, a novel framework based on physics-rectified conditional flow matching (CFM) that performs point cloud completion directly from partial US observations. UBone3D models deterministic physics artifacts (e.g., surface thickening, streaking, dropouts) via a simulated physics proxy, and introduces test-time physics rectification to steer the shape completion. At inference, the completion is jointly steered by two decoupled forces: (1) anatomical plausibility enforced by a CT-trained generative shape prior, BoneFM, and (2) physics consistency enforced by USimNet in the ultrasound formation space. Extensive experiments on simulated and in-vivo data demonstrate significant improvements in reconstruction accuracy and anatomical fidelity over existing baselines.

AI.tldr: UBone3D is a novel framework that uses physics-rectified conditional flow matching (CFM) to complete partial, artifact-laden 3D ultrasound point clouds into clean anatomical structures, leveraging a CT-trained shape prior (BoneFM) and ultrasound physics simulation (USimNet).
AI.motivation: Three-dimensional ultrasound is a safe, radiation-free imaging modality useful for longitudinal monitoring, but produces extremely artifact-laden partial point clouds that are challenging to recover into clean, complete anatomical structures.
AI.method: The framework models deterministic physics artifacts (surface thickening, streaking, dropouts) via a simulated physics proxy and introduces test-time physics rectification. At inference, completion is jointly steered by two decoupled forces: (1) anatomical plausibility from a CT-trained generative shape prior called BoneFM, and (2) physics consistency enforced by USimNet in the ultrasound formation space.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on simulated and in-vivo data demonstrate significant improvements in reconstruction accuracy and anatomical fidelity over existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: UBone3D effectively combines physics-based artifact modeling with generative shape priors to achieve superior point cloud completion from challenging ultrasound observations, offering a promising approach for clinical ultrasound imaging applications.

title: Flexible and Interpretable Accent Distance Measurements
summary: Determining the differences between two speakers' accents is a fundamental task in linguistics and speech technology research. The methodology used to measure these differences depends on the specific research area. A phonetics researcher may demonstrate accent variation by comparing vowel formants in paired recordings of individual words. These results will be interpretable, but the recordings will be time-consuming to collect and may not be representative of connected speech. Accented Text-to-Speech (TTS) research has pushed towards using accent embeddings derived from accent classification tasks. These embeddings can be produced from any speech recording, but are not readily interpretable. In this paper, we demonstrate that articulatory representations created through articulatory inversion can be used as an interpretable basis for accent comparison and that optimal transport provides a framework for accent comparison across arbitrary recording types.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using articulatory representations from articulatory inversion as an interpretable basis for comparing accents between speakers, combined with optimal transport as a framework for comparison across arbitrary recording types.
AI.motivation: Current methods for accent comparison have limitations: phonetic approaches using vowel formants are interpretable but time-consuming and not representative of connected speech, while accent embeddings from TTS research are easy to obtain but not interpretable. There is a need for a method that is both interpretable and applicable to various recording types.
AI.method: The paper proposes using articulatory representations created through articulatory inversion, combined with optimal transport for accent comparison across arbitrary recording types.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates that articulatory representations can serve as an interpretable basis for accent comparison, and optimal transport provides a framework for comparing accents across different recording types.
AI.conclusion: Articulatory representations from articulatory inversion offer an interpretable alternative to existing accent comparison methods, and optimal transport enables comparison across arbitrary recording types, bridging the gap between phonetic interpretability and practical applicability.

title: Harnessing Intrinsic Subject-Aware Attention for Controllable Multi-Subject Video Generation
summary: Multi-subject video generation faces two key challenges: uncontrollable fidelity strength and potential semantic drift. We address these by analyzing the internal mechanisms of Diffusion Transformers (DiTs). We found that certain attention blocks naturally form an Intrinsic Spatial Grounding Map (ISGM) that precisely locates reference subjects. Building on this insight, we propose Dual-phase Intrinsic Attention Leveraging (DIAL), a framework that uses these internal signals for both training and inference. In low-noise stages, we use ISGM to guide the attention mechanism, allowing precise control over fidelity strength during inference without retraining. In high-noise stages, we use these same maps to automatically build preference pairs at no additional cost for Reinforcement Learning (RL). This RL procedure effectively anchors the model's attention to reference subjects and mitigates semantic drift.
