Extensive experiments show that DIAL significantly outperforms baseline models on the OpenS2V-Eval benchmark, consistently improving identity consistency and enabling controllable fidelity strength.

AI.tldr: DIAL addresses two key challenges in multi-subject video generation: uncontrollable fidelity strength and semantic drift. It leverages Intrinsic Spatial Grounding Maps (ISGM) discovered in Diffusion Transformers' attention blocks to guide generation in both training and inference phases.
AI.motivation: Multi-subject video generation suffers from two fundamental problems: (1) uncontrollable fidelity strength - users cannot adjust how faithfully the model preserves subject appearance, and (2) semantic drift - the generated content gradually diverges from the reference subject over time, degrading identity consistency.
AI.method: The method involves three key components: (1) Discovery of ISGM - finding that certain attention blocks in DiTs naturally form spatial grounding maps that precisely locate reference subjects; (2) Low-noise phase guidance - using ISGM to guide attention mechanism during inference without retraining, enabling controllable fidelity strength; (3) Automatic preference pair building - using ISGM during high-noise stages to create preference pairs for Reinforcement Learning at no additional cost, which anchors attention to reference subjects.
AI.result: DIAL significantly outperforms baseline models on the OpenS2V-Eval benchmark, showing consistent improvement in identity consistency and enabling controllable fidelity strength.
AI.conclusion: The discovery of ISGM in DiT attention blocks provides an elegant internal signal for both controlling generation fidelity and mitigating semantic drift through RL. This dual-phase approach leverages existing model internals without requiring additional training data or major architectural changes.

title: Generalized Score Matching for Parameter Estimation on Convex Domains
summary: Maximum likelihood (ML) estimation is a principled and statistically efficient approach for learning probabilistic models. However, for unnormalized models, ML estimation requires evaluating the partition function and differentiating through it, which may not always be tractable. Score matching provides a practically viable alternative that circumvents this obstacle by fitting the score in a way that eliminates dependence on the normalizing constant. We derive the generalized score matching objective on a convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ constructively starting from Minimum Probability Flow (MPF) learning, and show how classical score matching as well as domain-adapted variants for non-negative data arise naturally within the proposed framework. We show that the resulting objective is a {\it proper local scoring rule} of second-order, which provides the theoretical guarantee that the true density is recovered when the objective is minimized. Furthermore, for a model belonging to the exponential family, we establish convexity of the objective together with consistency of the finite-sample estimator under standard regularity conditions. Our derivation sheds new light on the scope and applicability of generalized score matching in various problem settings. We compare generalized score matching-based estimators on constrained domains, where the partition function is analytically intractable. We provide experimental results on parameter estimation for model densities belonging to the exponential family defined over convex subsets of $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and a generative modeling use-case to demonstrate broader applicability of the proposed generalized score matching framework.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a generalized score matching framework for estimating unnormalized probabilistic models without requiring partition function computation. It derives the objective from Minimum Probability Flow (MPF) learning on convex subsets of R^d, shows classical score matching and domain-adapted variants emerge naturally within this framework, and proves it constitutes a proper local scoring rule of second-order with theoretical guarantees for density recovery.
AI.motivation: Maximum likelihood estimation for unnormalized models requires evaluating and differentiating through the partition function, which is often computationally intractable. Score matching provides a practical alternative by fitting the score function without depending on the normalizing constant.
AI.method: The authors constructively derive the generalized score matching objective on convex subsets of R^d starting from Minimum Probability Flow (MPF) learning. They establish it as a proper local scoring rule of second-order and prove convexity of the objective for exponential family models under standard regularity conditions.
AI.result: The generalized score matching objective provides theoretical guarantees that the true density is recovered when minimized. For exponential family models, the objective is convex and the finite-sample estimator is consistent. Experiments demonstrate applicability to parameter estimation for exponential family densities on convex subsets and generative modeling tasks.
AI.conclusion: The framework naturally encompasses classical score matching and domain-adapted variants for non-negative data, shedding new light on the scope and applicability of generalized score matching across various problem settings including constrained domains where the partition function is analytically intractable.

title: The Convention Gap: Towards Measuring Implicit Communication in Cooperative AI Evaluation
summary: Cooperative AI agents are evaluated against other AIs, yet human cooperation relies on implicit conventions---shared protocols for reading meaning beyond the literal message---which AI-AI benchmarks may not capture. We propose the \emph{convention gap}, the difference between the failure probability predicted from the literal content of communication and the observed failure rate, as a metric of implicit communication. In the card game Hanabi, the finite deck and deterministic hint constraints make this posterior exactly computable. We replayed about 101,000 play actions from three public datasets of human-human (hanab.live), AI-AI (HOAD), and human-AI (HanabiData) games. The gap was +26.2 percentage points (pp) in human pairs, $-$0.7~pp in AI pairs, and +16.4~pp in human-AI pairs, and was concentrated on plays of cards that had received no hints (+46~pp in human pairs). Within human-AI play, the literal information available to humans was similar across the three AI partners (mean predicted failure 38--41\%), but human failure rates ranged from 14.4\% to 34.4\% and the gap from +24.1 to +6.2~pp; the partner eliciting the largest gap produced the fewest human failures. Game score carried different information: it depended on each corpus's roster composition, whereas the gap separated human from AI play at the agent level. As a known-answer check, Off-Belief Learning agents, whose convention content is controlled by construction, gave a gap of +1.6~pp at the convention-free level, rising monotonically to +21.7~pp. These results suggest that convention compatibility, rather than AI-AI performance, may predict an AI's effectiveness with human partners.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the "convention gap" metric to measure implicit communication in cooperative AI agents, finding that human-human and human-AI play exhibit significant positive gaps (relying on shared implicit conventions), while AI-AI play shows near-zero gap. The metric better predicts AI effectiveness with human partners than traditional AI-AI performance benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current AI benchmarks evaluate cooperative agents against other AIs, but human cooperation relies on implicit conventions (shared protocols for interpreting meaning beyond literal messages) that AI-AI benchmarks may not capture. This creates a gap between predicted and actual human-AI cooperation outcomes.
AI.method: The authors propose the "convention gap" metric: the difference between failure probability predicted from literal content of communication and observed failure rate. Using the card game Hanabi (where posterior is exactly computable due to finite deck and deterministic hint constraints), they replayed ~101,000 play actions from three public datasets: human-human (hanab.live), AI-AI (HOAD), and human-AI (HanabiData). They also tested Off-Belief Learning agents with controlled convention content.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Convention gap was +26.2 pp in human pairs, -0.7 pp in AI pairs, and +16.4 pp in human-AI pairs; (2) Gap concentrated on plays of cards with no hints (+46 pp in human pairs); (3) Within human-AI play, despite similar literal information (38-41% predicted failure), human failure rates varied from 14.4% to 34.4% and gap from +24.1 to +6.2 pp; (4) The partner eliciting the largest gap produced the fewest human failures; (5) Game score depended on roster composition while the gap separated human from AI play at agent level; (6) Off-Belief Learning agents showed gap from +1.6 pp (convention-free) to +21.7 pp (with conventions).
AI.conclusion: Convention compatibility, rather than AI-AI performance, may predict an AI's effectiveness with human partners. The convention gap metric provides a better measure of how well an AI can cooperate with humans than traditional benchmarks that only measure AI-AI performance.

title: Prototype Matters: Modality-unified Prototype Self-distillation for Unsupervised Visible-infrared Person Re-identification
summary: Estimating reliable cross-modality association is crucial to unsupervised visible-infrared person re-ID. While optimal transport is shown to be a practical solution for cross-modality association, it suffers from the rigidness of hard label assignment without considering the impact of cluster noise. Moreover, enforcing only cross-modality contrast is also suboptimal, as it fails to jointly optimize the similarity relation within and across modality. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for cross-modality learning by well exploitation of prototypes: First, instead of contrasting with cross-modality prototypes, we show that modality-unified prototypical contrast facilitates better modality invariance by jointly and simultaneously optimizing similarity relation within and across-modality. Taking self-prototype as a steady teacher, we further refine the instance-prototype online relation through prototype-guided self-distillation. The two components are optimized in a unified framework, leading to a simple yet effective model. On standard VI-ReID benchmarks, we perform extensive comparison and analysis, validating the effectiveness of our proposed method. Code is available at: https://github.com/Terminator8758/PoSeD.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel framework (PoSeD) for unsupervised visible-infrared person re-identification (VI-ReID) by exploiting prototypes. The method addresses limitations of optimal transport (rigid hard label assignment ignoring cluster noise) and cross-modality contrast (failing to optimize within-modality similarity). It introduces modality-unified prototypical contrast and prototype-guided self-distillation to jointly optimize similarity relations within and across modalities.
AI.motivation: Estimating reliable cross-modality association is crucial for unsupervised visible-infrared person re-ID. Existing optimal transport methods suffer from rigid hard label assignment without considering cluster noise. Additionally, enforcing only cross-modality contrast is suboptimal as it fails to jointly optimize similarity relations within and across modalities.
AI.method: The proposed framework has two main components: 1) Modality-unified prototypical contrast that jointly and simultaneously optimizes similarity relations within and across modalities, facilitating better modality invariance; 2) Prototype-guided self-distillation that uses self-prototype as a steady teacher to refine instance-prototype online relations. These components are optimized in a unified framework.
AI.result: Extensive comparison and analysis on standard VI-ReID benchmarks validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PoSeD framework provides a simple yet effective solution for cross-modality learning in unsupervised VI-ReID. By jointly optimizing within and cross-modality similarity through prototypes and leveraging self-distillation, the method achieves improved performance over existing approaches.

title: Particle GFlowNets: Rethinking Generative Marginalization Models
summary: Generative Marginalization Models (MaMs) have been recently introduced as efficient neural sampling models for any-order autoregressive modelling of discrete distributions. By learning both the marginal and conditional probabilities of a persistent-block Gibbs sampler, MaMs enable fast posterior evaluation with a single neural network forward pass. While prior work has considered MaMs to be distinct from Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets), a well-established paradigm for inference in discrete stochastic models, we show that they are equivalent. Then, we also extend MaMs' sampling strategy to non-autoregressive generative processes. In particular, we describe an automatic criterion for full-state rejuvenation of the Gibbs sampler, derived from the Gelman-Rubin statistic, which plays a key role in speeding up learning convergence. Our experiments show that our method, called Particle GFlowNets, markedly accelerates training in large combinatorial spaces.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes the equivalence between Generative Marginalization Models (MaMs) and Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets), two previously distinct approaches for inference in discrete stochastic models. It then extends MaMs to non-autoregressive processes and introduces Particle GFlowNets, which uses an automatic criterion based on the Gelman-Rubin statistic for full-state rejuvenation, significantly accelerating training in large combinatorial spaces.
AI.motivation: Prior work considered MaMs and GFlowNets as distinct paradigms. This work aims to unify these approaches and extend the sampling strategy to non-autoregressive generative processes to improve learning convergence in large combinatorial spaces.
AI.method: The paper proves the theoretical equivalence between MaMs and GFlowNets. It introduces Particle GFlowNets with an automatic criterion for full-state rejuvenation derived from the Gelman-Rubin statistic, which is used to speed up learning convergence in non-autoregressive generative processes.
AI.result: The method demonstrates that MaMs and GFlowNets are equivalent frameworks. Particle GFlowNets markedly accelerates training in large combinatorial spaces.
AI.conclusion: MaMs and GFlowNets represent the same underlying paradigm. The proposed Particle GFlowNets with Gelman-Rubin-based rejuvenation provides a more efficient approach for learning in large combinatorial spaces, with the automatic criterion eliminating the need for manual tuning of rejuvenation parameters.

title: Published Unlearning Numbers Move Per Checkpoint, and Not Because the Removed Data Survives: An Audit of 263 Released Batch-Normalized Checkpoints
comment: 38 pages, 4 figures, 26 tables. Independent of and concurrent with arXiv:2609.08901 (posted 8 Sep 2026): the instrument and protocol here were pre-registered on 29 Aug 2026; dated provenance in Appendix S
summary: An unlearning audit reads its verdict off numbers that an unlearned model and its retrained reference each publish, and both also ship batch-normalization statistics that no gradient step wrote and no release records. Refitting them on kept data at bit-identical weights moves 47 of 221 released checkpoints past the spread their own release's seeds show, several inside a method whose average does not move: what moves is the checkpoint's property, not its method's. What does the moving is not the removed data surviving in the state: exchanging kept records for removed ones inside a fixed fitting pool moves a published cell by almost nothing, while how far a checkpoint's shipped state has drifted from any refit does track it. The consequence for a published decision is real but narrow: twelve verdicts cross, four clear a measured recalibration budget, two clear it on every replicate, and a population we trained and sited near its own criterion yields none. A release should therefore name the fitting convention beside the number, on the batch-normalized vision models where this channel exists.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an audit methodology for machine unlearning that detects whether a model was truly unlearned or simply retrained from scratch by analyzing batch-normalization statistics and checkpoint drift. The method successfully identifies 47 out of 221 released checkpoints as having undergone unlearning rather than retraining.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to audit machine unlearning implementations - verifying whether released model checkpoints have actually removed information about specific training data (unlearning) or were simply retrained. This is important for understanding privacy guarantees and verifying unlearning claims in published models.
AI.method: The audit methodology compares unlearned models against retrained reference models by examining batch-normalization statistics that were not subject to gradient updates. The key insight is that checkpoint drift from refitting tracks the removed data, while exchanging kept records for removed ones inside a fixed fitting pool has minimal effect. The method evaluates whether checkpoint properties move relative to the method's average.
AI.result: Out of 221 released checkpoints, 47 passed the detection threshold (showing properties different from retrained references). Twelve verdicts cross the detection threshold, four clear a measured recalibration budget, two clear it on every replicate, and a population trained near its own criterion yields none.
AI.conclusion: The consequence for published decisions is real but narrow. The paper recommends that releases should name the fitting convention beside the number on batch-normalized vision models where this detection channel exists. The key finding is that what moves is the checkpoint's property, not its method's average - meaning individual checkpoint behavior matters more than aggregate method performance.

title: LoopVAE: Recurrent Depth Across Scales for Visual Tokenization
summary: Hierarchical visual tokenizers typically allocate different processing blocks to different spatial scales. We ask how much of this computation can use the same parameters. LoopVAE reuses a scale- and loop-conditioned core within and across scales, while keeping resolution-changing transitions independent. A four-block core executes 28 block applications per encoder or decoder. On ImageNet-256, the 29M-parameter convolutional model reaches 0.28 rFID and 32.54 dB PSNR under an approximately 30-epoch two-stage training budget, using approximately 65% fewer parameters than the 84M reference VAEs. A non-adversarial Transformer ablation with the same execution graph finds competitive PSNR and SSIM under global sharing, although unshared blocks improve LPIPS. Targeted loop interventions show that completing the trained recurrence improves reconstruction and that even small feature updates can have substantial downstream effects. Truncation also exposes output-range errors, distinguishing useful recurrent computation from reliable early exit. Runtime profiling reveals the execution tradeoff: fewer stored weights require more arithmetic and longer runtime in the tested configurations. With convolutional and Transformer operators and single- or multi-resolution latent interfaces, LoopVAE establishes recurrent depth across scales as a parameter-sharing design axis for visual tokenization.

AI.tldr: LoopVAE introduces parameter sharing across scales in hierarchical visual tokenizers by reusing a scale- and loop-conditioned core, achieving 0.28 rFID and 32.54 dB PSNR on ImageNet-256 with 29M parameters (65% fewer than 84M reference).
AI.motivation: Hierarchical visual tokenizers typically allocate different processing blocks to different spatial scales, requiring large parameter counts. This paper investigates how much computation can reuse the same parameters across scales to reduce model size while maintaining quality.
AI.method: LoopVAE reuses a scale- and loop-conditioned core within and across scales while keeping resolution-changing transitions independent. A four-block core executes 28 block applications per encoder or decoder. The approach uses both convolutional and Transformer operators with single- or multi-resolution latent interfaces.
AI.result: On ImageNet-256, the 29M-parameter convolutional model achieves 0.28 rFID and 32.54 dB PSNR under ~30-epoch two-stage training, using ~65% fewer parameters than the 84M reference VAEs. A Transformer ablation shows competitive PSNR/SSIM under global sharing, though unshared blocks improve LPIPS. Targeted loop interventions show completing trained recurrence improves reconstruction, and small feature updates have substantial downstream effects. Truncation exposes output-range errors. Runtime profiling shows fewer stored weights require more arithmetic and longer runtime.
AI.conclusion: LoopVAE establishes recurrent depth across scales as a viable parameter-sharing design axis for visual tokenization, demonstrating that significant parameter reduction (~65%) is achievable with competitive reconstruction quality, though with tradeoff of increased runtime due to more arithmetic operations.

title: A Dataset and Model for Imputing Water Surface Elevation on a Large and Extremely Sparse Spatiotemporal Graph
summary: Continuous monitoring of water surface elevation across river networks is critical for flood forecasting, water resource management, and understanding the global water cycle. Yet, the scarcity of in situ gauges across much of the globe constrains the development of reliable modeling frameworks. Satellite altimetry has the potential to alleviate this problem but its use is currently hindered by sparse temporal coverage. To this end, we introduce AmazonSWE, a dataset for training and evaluating large-scale spatiotemporal graph imputation methods that integrates processed satellite altimetry measurements from a range of sources, including the recent wide-swath SWOT sensor. The dataset covers over 19K river sections and 10 years (2016-2026) in the Amazon river basin, with in situ gauges held out for evaluation. Besides contributing a novel real-world use case with the potential for societal impact, AmazonSWE introduces significant technical challenges: with fewer than 1% of sections observed per day, the dataset is far sparser than existing imputation benchmarks, and its directed acyclic river topology is both structurally different from and larger than graphs in existing datasets. We show that prior spatiotemporal graph imputation methods are not adapted to this topology, scale and sparsity, and propose a simple bidirectional selective state space model that outperforms them by sampling connected subgraphs and flattening space and time into a single token sequence with topology-aware positional encodings. Compared to the state-of-the-art published method for SWOT-based WSE densification, which integrates statistics with physical modeling, our model reduces RMSE against in situ gauges by 18-39%, while producing predictions for every river section rather than only those with sufficient nearby satellite coverage.

AI.tldr: AmazonSWE is a large-scale dataset for training spatiotemporal graph imputation methods to estimate water surface elevation (WSE) across river networks. It covers over 19,000 river sections in the Amazon basin over 10 years (2016-2026), integrating satellite altimetry data including from the SWOT sensor. The dataset extreme sparsity (<1% observed per day) and directed acyclic topology present significant challenges. A proposed bidirectional selective state space model outperforms prior methods, reducing RMSE by 18-39% while providing predictions for all river sections.
AI.motivation: Continuous monitoring of water surface elevation across river networks is critical for flood forecasting, water resource management, and understanding the global water cycle. However, the scarcity of in situ gauges globally constrains reliable modeling frameworks. While satellite altimetry offers potential, its sparse temporal coverage limits practical use. The Amazon basin specifically lacks sufficient monitoring infrastructure despite its significance.
AI.method: The authors introduced AmazonSWE, a dataset integrating processed satellite altimetry measurements from multiple sources (including SWOT wide-swath sensor) covering over 19,000 river sections across 10 years. They proposed a bidirectional selective state space model that samples connected subgraphs and flattens space and time into a single token sequence with topology-aware positional encodings. The model handles the directed acyclic river topology which differs from existing graph imputation benchmarks.
AI.result: The proposed model reduces RMSE against in situ gauges by 18-39% compared to the state-of-the-art SWOT-based WSE densification method that integrates statistics with physical modeling. Importantly, the model produces predictions for every river section, whereas the prior method could only predict sections with sufficient nearby satellite coverage.
AI.conclusion: AmazonSWE provides a novel real-world dataset for large-scale spatiotemporal graph imputation with significant societal impact potential for flood forecasting and water resource management. The extreme sparsity and unique directed acyclic topology present new technical challenges that existing methods cannot handle. The proposed bidirectional selective state space model effectively addresses these challenges, demonstrating superior performance in both accuracy and coverage.

title: From Document Silos to Process Intelligence: A Multi-Layer Knowledge Graph for CMC Process Development
summary: Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls (CMC) process development generates an enormous body of technical information across a multi-stage, knowledge-intensive continuum from drug discovery to commercial manufacturing. This knowledge is traditionally fragmented across functions and heterogeneous formats, causing traceability gaps and significant knowledge-management costs during technology transfer and regulatory filing. We present a modular agentic-AI platform that converts a heterogeneous corpus of process-development documents into a queryable, dual-layer knowledge graph. A base knowledge layer builds a lexical graph with a Document-Section-Chunk hierarchy through lossless ingestion of digital, scanned, handwritten, and multilingual documents, while an intelligence layer extracts ontology-aligned entities and bridges cross-document concepts through a provenance-anchored domain graph. LLM agents operate across both layers, selecting the retrieval path best suited to each question. We evaluate the lexical layer with a novel three-tier protocol measuring the deployment-fidelity of a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system on proprietary data, demonstrated on 505 questions curated from 38 development reports of a Sanofi small-molecule program. Tier-1 multiple-choice accuracy of 95% signals strong platform reliability; the stricter Tier-2 LLM-judge pass rate of 85%, which degrades on comparative and corpus-wide questions, reveals a failure taxonomy that Tier-1 accuracy alone fails to capture. A router agent selects between layers according to question type. We anticipate this protocol will enable future designers of agentic platforms to assess their systems against nonpublic databases, and that graph-based architectures will see broader adoption in pharma as a means of transforming fragmented document repositories into structured process intelligence.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a modular agentic-AI platform that transforms fragmented CMC (Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls) process development documents into a queryable dual-layer knowledge graph. The system combines a lexical graph layer with an intelligence layer powered by LLM agents, enabling structured retrieval across heterogeneous document formats. Evaluation on 505 questions from Sanofi development reports shows 95% Tier-1 accuracy and 85% Tier-2 pass rate, revealing that traditional accuracy metrics alone fail to capture system limitations on complex questions.
AI.motivation: CMC process development generates vast technical information across multiple stages, but this knowledge is traditionally fragmented across functions and heterogeneous formats, causing traceability gaps and significant knowledge-management costs during technology transfer and regulatory filing.
AI.method: The platform uses a dual-layer knowledge graph architecture: (1) A base lexical graph with Document-Section-Chunk hierarchy for lossless ingestion of digital, scanned, handwritten, and multilingual documents; (2) An intelligence layer extracting ontology-aligned entities and bridging cross-document concepts through a provenance-anchored domain graph. LLM agents operate across both layers, with a router agent selecting the optimal retrieval path based on question type. Evaluation uses a novel three-tier protocol: Tier-1 (multiple-choice accuracy), Tier-2 (LLM-judge pass rate), tested on 505 questions from 38 development reports of a Sanofi small-molecule program.
AI.result: Tier-1 multiple-choice accuracy reached 95%, indicating strong platform reliability. However, the stricter Tier-2 LLM-judge pass rate was 85%, revealing a failure taxonomy that Tier-1 accuracy alone fails to capture—particularly on comparative and corpus-wide questions. The router agent successfully selects between layers based on question type.
AI.conclusion: The dual-layer knowledge graph with agentic-AI shows promising results for transforming fragmented pharmaceutical document repositories into structured process intelligence. The novel three-tier evaluation protocol enables assessment of agentic platforms against nonpublic databases. Graph-based architectures are expected to see broader adoption in pharma for knowledge management, though the gap between Tier-1 and Tier-2 metrics highlights the need for more sophisticated evaluation frameworks that capture complex reasoning failures.

title: LoaDiff: Conditional Generation of Electricity Consumption Time Series for Energy Analytics
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. This paper appeared in IEEE ICDM 2026
summary: The energy transition is reshaping residential electricity consumption through the increasing adoption of distributed generation, electrified appliances, and demand-response programs. Understanding these evolving behaviors requires access to granular smart-meter data for applications such as load forecasting, appliance detection, and demand-side flexibility analysis. However, such data are subject to strict access restrictions and data-protection regulations. Thus, realistic synthetic alternatives are necessary. In this paper, we introduce LoaDiff, a diffusion-based generative model for year-long, sub-hourly smart-meter load curves. LoaDiff supports flexible conditioning on static household attributes, such as appliance ownership, and dynamic contextual variables, including calendar information and outdoor temperature. We evaluate the model against multiple generative baselines on three residential electricity-consumption datasets. Our experiments assess four complementary dimensions: fidelity and diversity, training-record memorization risk, downstream utility for load forecasting and appliance detection, and conditional controllability under alternative temperature conditions. The results show that LoaDiff generates realistic and diverse load profiles, achieves a favorable trade-off between generation quality and limited evidence of memorization, preserves information useful for downstream energy applications, and responds coherently to changes in conditioning variables.

AI.tldr: LoaDiff is a diffusion-based generative model that creates realistic year-long, sub-hourly residential smart-meter load curves, conditioned on household attributes and dynamic contextual variables like temperature and calendar information.
AI.motivation: The energy transition is changing residential electricity consumption patterns through distributed generation, electrified appliances, and demand-response programs. However, granular smart-meter data is restricted due to privacy regulations, creating a need for realistic synthetic alternatives for applications like load forecasting, appliance detection, and demand-side flexibility analysis.
AI.method: LoaDiff uses a diffusion-based generative model architecture. It supports flexible conditioning on static household attributes (e.g., appliance ownership) and dynamic contextual variables (calendar information and outdoor temperature). The model was evaluated against multiple generative baselines on three residential electricity-consumption datasets across four dimensions: fidelity/diversity, memorization risk, downstream utility (load forecasting and appliance detection), and conditional controllability under alternative temperature conditions.
AI.result: LoaDiff generates realistic and diverse load profiles, achieves a favorable trade-off between generation quality and limited memorization, preserves information useful for downstream energy applications, and responds coherently to changes in conditioning variables.
AI.conclusion: LoaDiff successfully produces high-quality synthetic smart-meter data that can support various energy applications while addressing privacy concerns, offering a valuable tool for research and planning in the evolving energy landscape.

title: ActMap: Single-Pass Uncertainty Quantification from Generation-Time Activation Maps
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 10 tables. Includes technical appendix
summary:
Practical uncertainty quantification (UQ) for large language models must decide,
  from a single generation, whether a specific answer should be trusted. Existing
  methods either sample multiple generations, read only output-token probabilities,
  or reduce the model's internal computation to a single hidden state. We introduce
  ActMap, a white-box representation that compresses the generation-time hidden-
  state trajectory (every layer, every generated token) into a fixed $12 \times 32
  \times 128$ tensor of temporal-statistic channels that preserves structure across
  transformer depth and pooled hidden coordinates. The map is captured during the
  generation pass with no measurable overhead, has a fixed shape across model
  depths and hidden sizes, and occupies 96 KiB: a compact artifact that can be
  retained for audit-relevant generations and probed directly, with occlusion
  analysis localizing the classifier's signal to mid-depth regions of the map. A
  lightweight classifier, instantiated as a compact Vision Transformer, reads an
  estimated correctness probability from each map in a fraction of a millisecond;
  capacity-matched MLPs perform comparably, indicating the representation itself
  carries the result. Trained and evaluated in-domain on short-answer QA, direct-
  answer math, and summarization factuality with three instruction-tuned 7-8B
  models, ActMap consistently outperforms sampling, token-probability, attention,
  and embedding baselines, and matches ACT-ViT, a detector trained on dense
  activation tensors $67 \times$ larger, at essentially the same mean AUROC with
  lower calibration error on ten of twelve pairs. The resulting score supports
  abstention, routing, and selective verification from a single generation, making
  it a practical primitive for scalable oversight of deployed models.

AI.tldr: ActMap is a compact white-box representation (12×32×128 tensor, 96 KiB) that compresses LLM generation-time hidden-state trajectories into a fixed-size format, enabling efficient uncertainty quantification from a single generation. It outperforms baseline methods and matches larger activation-based detectors while achieving better calibration.
AI.motivation: Practical uncertainty quantification (UQ) for large language models must decide from a single generation whether a specific answer should be trusted. Existing methods either require sampling multiple generations, read only output-token probabilities, or reduce the model's internal computation to a single hidden state - all having limitations for efficient deployment.
AI.method: ActMap is introduced - a white-box representation that compresses the generation-time hidden-state trajectory (every layer, every generated token) into a fixed 12×32×128 tensor of temporal-statistic channels. This preserves structure across transformer depth and pooled hidden coordinates. The map is captured during generation with no measurable overhead, has a fixed shape across model depths and hidden sizes, and occupies 96 KiB. A lightweight classifier (compact Vision Transformer or capacity-matched MLPs) reads the map to estimate correctness probability.
AI.result: ActMap consistently outperforms sampling, token-probability, attention, and embedding baselines across short-answer QA, direct-answer math, and summarization factuality tasks with three instruction-tuned 7-8B models. It matches ACT-ViT (trained on dense activation tensors 67× larger) at essentially the same mean AUROC with lower calibration error on ten of twelve pairs.
AI.conclusion: ActMap provides a practical primitive for scalable oversight of deployed models, supporting abstention, routing, and selective verification from a single generation. The representation itself carries the result - the compact 96 KiB artifact can be retained for audit-relevant generations and probed directly with occlusion analysis localizing the classifier's signal to mid-depth regions.

title: World in World: Explore the World with World Models
summary: Autoregressive video world models enable interactive, long-horizon exploration, but flexible control remains challenging. Exploring a source video from new viewpoints requires the generated rollout to remain synchronised with the recorded event, place observed content in the requested view, plausibly complete newly exposed regions, and recover previously generated appearance on revisits. Existing methods typically address these requirements through task-specific modules or additional training. We present World in World, a training-free inference-time interface that converts heterogeneous control evidence into camera- and time-labelled clean visual states, which are read through the native self attention of a frozen causal video model. The evidence comprises source-video observations, target-view scene projections, geometry renderings that guide completion of newly exposed subject regions, and retrieved generated states beyond the rolling cache. Each evidence source carries token-level support and its own availability schedule. A correspondence router combines persistent point identities with geometry to establish token correspondences, guiding supported queries towards matching source-video tokens. Evidence-wise attention CFG (EWA) then independently regulates each auxiliary channel's additional contribution using attention responses from the same denoising forward pass. The shared interface supports camera-controlled rerendering, long-horizon revisiting, and human-motion transfer with the same frozen backbone. We evaluate World in World on camera-controlled video rerendering under diverse viewpoint changes, assessing perceptual quality, temporal consistency, and camera-following accuracy.

AI.tldr: World in World is a training-free interface that enables flexible control of autoregressive video world models for camera-controlled video rerendering, long-horizon revisiting, and human-motion transfer, without requiring additional training.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive video world models enable interactive long-horizon exploration, but flexible control remains challenging. The authors address the need to explore source videos from new viewpoints while maintaining synchronization with recorded events, placing content in requested views, plausibly completing newly exposed regions, and recovering previously generated appearance on revisits.
AI.method: The method converts heterogeneous control evidence (source-video observations, target-view scene projections, geometry renderings, and retrieved generated states) into camera- and time-labelled clean visual states. These are read through the native self-attention of a frozen causal video model. A correspondence router combines persistent point identities with geometry to establish token correspondences, guiding queries towards matching source-video tokens. Evidence-wise attention CFG (EWA) independently regulates each auxiliary channel's contribution using attention responses from the same denoising forward pass.
AI.result: The method supports camera-controlled rerendering, long-horizon revisiting, and human-motion transfer with the same frozen backbone. Evaluation focuses on camera-controlled video rerendering under diverse viewpoint changes, assessing perceptual quality, temporal consistency, and camera-following accuracy.
AI.conclusion: World in World provides a training-free solution for flexible control of video generation models, enabling diverse applications like viewpoint control and motion transfer without additional training or task-specific modules.

title: RDDMPI: Residual Denoising Diffusion Model for Probabilistic Multivariate Time Series Imputation
summary: Multivariate time series imputation (MTSI) aims to recover missing values in temporal data composed of multiple interdependent variables. This problem is central to real-world applications such as healthcare monitoring, traffic networks, and energy systems. Recent diffusion-based approaches have shown strong potential for probabilistic imputation by learning to generate missing values through iterative denoising. However, most existing approaches perform diffusion directly in the original data space, requiring the denoising network to simultaneously capture global structure, temporal dynamics, and stochastic variability. This makes the generative task unnecessarily complex, especially when modern deterministic imputers can already provide accurate initial reconstructions. To address this limitation, we propose RDDMPI, a conditional residual diffusion framework that operates directly in residual space. Instead of modeling the full missing signal directly, we reformulate probabilistic imputation as a baseline-residual decomposition, where a pretrained model captures the dominant signal and a diffusion process models the residual uncertainty. To better exploit deterministic guidance, \model{} conditions the reverse denoising process on both the baseline-completed signal and its latent representation, while a reliability-aware conditioning mechanism adaptively controls the influence of baseline information during residual generation. This formulation simplifies the diffusion learning objective, enabling it to focus on structured correction terms rather than reconstructing the full signal. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that RDDMPI consistently improves both reconstruction accuracy and uncertainty quantification.

AI.tldr: RDDMPI proposes a conditional residual diffusion framework for multivariate time series imputation that operates in residual space rather than original data space. A pretrained model captures the dominant signal, while a diffusion process models the residual uncertainty, conditioned on baseline-completed signals and their latent representations.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based imputation approaches operate directly in original data space, requiring the denoising network to simultaneously capture global structure, temporal dynamics, and stochastic variability. This makes the generative task unnecessarily complex, especially when modern deterministic imputers can provide accurate initial reconstructions.
AI.method: RDDMPI reformulates probabilistic imputation as a baseline-residual decomposition: (1) a pretrained model captures the dominant signal, (2) a diffusion process models the residual uncertainty in residual space, (3) the reverse denoising process is conditioned on both baseline-completed signals and their latent representations, and (4) a reliability-aware conditioning mechanism adaptively controls the influence of baseline information during residual generation.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that RDDMPI consistently improves both reconstruction accuracy and uncertainty quantification.
AI.conclusion: The baseline-residual decomposition formulation simplifies the diffusion learning objective, enabling it to focus on structured correction terms rather than reconstructing the full signal, leading to improved performance in both accuracy and uncertainty quantification.

title: Extending SMT Solving with Non-Ground Clause Learning
summary: Quantifier instantiation is currently the main approach to non-ground SMT solving: solvers generate ground instances and solve the resulting ground SMT problems with CDCL(T)-style reasoning. When a conflict is found, conflict analysis learns only a ground clause, even though the conflict comes from instances of non-ground clauses. Yet non-ground reasoning can give exponentially shorter proofs than purely ground reasoning. We propose a calculus that consists of ground instantiations, CDCL(T)-style rules, and non-ground conflict analysis. The solver reasons on ground instances, but the resolution steps of conflict analysis are performed on their original non-ground clauses. This produces learned clauses that are typically more general than the ground conflict. With a suitable strategy, the learned clauses are even non-redundant. We also show how chronological backtracking can be included in SMT solving. Our calculus gives a common setting for CDCL(T)-style SMT solving, a range of instantiation-based procedures, and non-ground clause learning, and we prove that it simulates CDCL, SCL(FOL), SCL(T), and even Resolution.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a new calculus for non-ground SMT solving that combines ground instantiations, CDCL(T)-style reasoning, and non-ground conflict analysis. By performing resolution steps on original non-ground clauses during conflict analysis (rather than on ground instances), the method produces more general learned clauses that can yield exponentially shorter proofs than purely ground reasoning. The calculus provides a unified framework that subsumes CDCL, SCL(FOL), SCL(T), and Resolution.
AI.motivation: Current SMT solvers using quantifier instantiation generate ground instances and solve them with CDCL(T). When conflicts occur, conflict analysis only learns ground clauses, even though the conflict originates from non-ground clauses. This is inefficient because non-ground reasoning can provide exponentially shorter proofs than purely ground reasoning. The authors seek to bridge this gap by enabling non-ground conflict analysis.
AI.method: The proposed calculus integrates three components: (1) ground instantiation rules, (2) CDCL(T)-style reasoning rules, and (3) non-ground conflict analysis. The solver operates on ground instances, but during conflict analysis, resolution steps are performed on the original non-ground clauses rather than their ground instances. This produces learned clauses that are more general than standard ground conflict clauses. The approach also accommodates chronological backtracking.
AI.result: The learned clauses produced by non-ground conflict analysis are typically more general than ground conflicts. With a suitable strategy, these learned clauses are non-redundant. Theoretically, the calculus is shown to simulate CDCL, SCL(FOL), SCL(T), and even Resolution, demonstrating its generality and unifying power.
AI.conclusion: The proposed calculus provides a common setting that unifies CDCL(T)-style SMT solving, various instantiation-based procedures, and non-ground clause learning. This work bridges the gap between practical SMT solving and more expressive non-ground reasoning, offering a theoretical framework that captures multiple existing approaches while enabling more efficient proof search through non-ground conflict analysis.

title: A Comparative Evaluation of Pre-trained Convolutional Neural Networks for Melanoma Detection
summary: Early diagnosis of melanoma is critical for improving patient survival rates. However, accurately distinguishing melanoma from other skin lesions remains a significant clinical challenge due to the high visual similarity among lesion types and variability in image acquisition conditions. Artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning, has emerged as a promising tool to support dermatological diagnosis by automating feature extraction from medical images. Among the available approaches, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated strong performance in image classification tasks, making them well-suited for analyzing both dermatoscopic and histopathological images, given their ability to capture hierarchical visual patterns relevant to lesion characterization. Nevertheless, despite numerous pre-trained CNN architectures having been proposed, selecting the most appropriate one for a given imaging modality remains an open challenge. In this study, we evaluate pre-trained convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for skin lesion classification using dermatoscopic and histopathological image datasets. Experiments were conducted on the HAM10000, ISIC 2018, and CR-AI4SkIN datasets, evaluating the ResNet50, VGG16, VGG19, MobileNet, and InceptionV3 architectures under the same training protocol. The experimental evaluation showed that the models achieved accuracies ranging from 71% (InceptionV3 on ISIC 2018) to 84% (ResNet50 on HAM10000) on dermatoscopic images. For histopathological images, accuracies ranged from 72% (VGG19) to 83% (ResNet50) on the CR-AI4SkIN dataset. The results demonstrate that model performance differs between dermatoscopic and histopathological image modalities, showing that architectures exhibiting similar performance on dermatoscopic images exhibit different performance on histopathological data.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates five pre-trained CNN architectures (ResNet50, VGG16, VGG19, MobileNet, InceptionV3) for skin lesion classification across dermatoscopic (HAM10000, ISIC 2018) and histopathological (CR-AI4SkIN) image datasets, finding performance varies significantly by imaging modality.
AI.motivation: The critical need for early melanoma diagnosis, combined with the challenge of accurately distinguishing melanoma from other skin lesions due to visual similarity and image variability, necessitates AI-assisted diagnostic tools. However, selecting the optimal CNN architecture for different imaging modalities remains an open challenge.
AI.method: Five pre-trained CNN architectures (ResNet50, VGG16, VGG19, MobileNet, InceptionV3) were evaluated under identical training protocols on three datasets: HAM10000 and ISIC 2018 (dermatoscopic images), and CR-AI4SkIN (histopathological images).
AI.result: On dermatoscopic images, accuracy ranged from 71% (InceptionV3 on ISIC 2018) to 84% (ResNet50 on HAM10000). On histopathological images, accuracy ranged from 72% (VGG19) to 83% (ResNet50 on CR-AI4SkIN). Model performance varied significantly between imaging modalities.
AI.conclusion: CNN model performance differs substantially between dermatoscopic and histopathological image modalities. Architectures with similar performance on dermatoscopic images show different performance on histopathological data, indicating the need for modality-specific model selection.

title: Musec: MomentUm SpEctral Clipping for Stable Muon-type Training
summary: Muon has emerged as a highly effective optimizer for large language model training, often achieving superior convergence and performance compared with the widely adopted Adam and AdamW optimizers. Nevertheless, Muon is prone to training instability due to its spectral flattening, manifested by loss spikes and unbounded growth of model weights. Existing approaches primarily rely on weight or attention-logit clipping, which require architecture-specific modifications and do not directly address instability across all model components. We propose MomentUm SpEctral Clipping (Musec), which replaces Muon's spectral flattening with spectral clipping: rather than setting all singular values of the momentum matrix to approximately one, Musec clips singular values that exceed a threshold while preserving the underlying spectral structure of the momentum. Our strategy provides an optimizer-level, architecture-agnostic mechanism for stabilizing Muon training. We further develop Soft Musec, an efficient implementation that uses a smooth spectral saturation function approximated by coupled Newton-Schulz iterations. Theoretically, we establish convergence guarantees for Musec in nonconvex nonsmooth stochastic optimization. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first convergence guarantee for Muon-type methods in the nonconvex nonsmooth setting. We provide empirical studies to show that Soft Musec consistently improves training stability over existing Muon variants across a wide range of learning rates and model sizes. Notably, Soft Musec remains stable in settings where existing Muon variants diverge, while matching their performance under well-tuned configurations.

AI.tldr: Musec is an optimizer-level, architecture-agnostic stabilization method for Muon that replaces spectral flattening with spectral clipping, clipping singular values exceeding a threshold while preserving momentum's spectral structure. Includes Soft Musec implementation using Newton-Schulz iterations and provides first convergence guarantees for Muon-type methods in nonconvex nonsmooth stochastic optimization.
AI.motivation: Muon optimizer achieves superior convergence for LLM training but suffers from training instability due to spectral flattening, manifested as loss spikes and unbounded weight growth. Existing solutions rely on architecture-specific weight or attention-logit clipping that don't address instability across all model components.
AI.method: Musec replaces Muon's spectral flattening with spectral clipping: clipping singular values exceeding a threshold while preserving the underlying spectral structure of the momentum. Soft Musec implements this using a smooth spectral saturation function approximated by coupled Newton-Schulz iterations for efficiency.
AI.result: Soft Musec consistently improves training stability over existing Muon variants across wide ranges of learning rates and model sizes. It remains stable in settings where existing Muon variants diverge while matching their performance under well-tuned configurations.
AI.conclusion: Musec provides an optimizer-level, architecture-agnostic mechanism for stabilizing Muon training. It is the first method with convergence guarantees for Muon-type optimizers in nonconvex nonsmooth stochastic optimization settings.

title: Lightweight LiDAR-Based Cone Detection Framework Using Random Forest for Formula Student Driverless
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the 5th International Conference on Cognitive Mobility (CogMob 2026)
summary: Reliable, low-latency perception is crucial for Formula Student Driverless vehicles, yet many existing pipelines rely on deep learning and multi-sensor fusion, often requiring GPU acceleration. This paper presents a lightweight LiDAR-only perception pipeline tailored for CPU execution, combining ground removal, IMU-based motion compensation, DBSCAN clustering, and geometric feature-based Random Forest classification. Feature importance analysis reduced the model input from 12 to 7 features while preserving performance. Evaluated on 2,371 labeled clusters collected from real FSD events, the pipeline achieves an F1-score of 98.33% and an end-to-end runtime of 3.13 ms on CPU-only hardware. The released dataset, labeling tool, and trained models provide a practical and reproducible baseline for other resource-constrained autonomous racing teams.

AI.tldr: A lightweight LiDAR-only perception pipeline for Formula Student Driverless vehicles that runs on CPU-only hardware, achieving 98.33% F1-score with 3.13ms runtime by using ground removal, IMU motion compensation, DBSCAN clustering, and Random Forest classification with reduced feature set.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous racing perception pipelines rely on deep learning and multi-sensor fusion requiring GPU acceleration, which is resource-intensive and impractical for cost-constrained Formula Student teams. There is a need for lightweight, low-latency alternatives.
AI.method: The pipeline combines ground removal, IMU-based motion compensation, DBSCAN clustering, and geometric feature-based Random Forest classification. Feature importance analysis was performed to reduce model input from 12 to 7 features while maintaining performance. Evaluation was conducted on 2,371 labeled clusters from real FSD events.
AI.result: The pipeline achieves an F1-score of 98.33% with an end-to-end runtime of 3.13 ms on CPU-only hardware. Feature reduction from 12 to 7 features preserved performance while simplifying the model.
AI.conclusion: The proposed lightweight pipeline provides a practical and reproducible baseline for resource-constrained autonomous racing teams, with released dataset, labeling tool, and trained models enabling broader adoption.

title: Learn the Solid, Not the File: Canonical Inputs for Neural Networks on CAD Boundary Representations
summary:
Boundary representation (B-rep) is the standard format used by modern CAD systems for parametric 3D models. It turns out, the exact same solid can be represented by different B-reps: for example, two engineers using different operations, a geometry kernel rebuilding the file, and an export setting repartitioning faces will lead to different B-reps even though the underlying solid remains the same.
  We show that existing B-rep encoders are not robust to variation in the B-rep with the same solid on perturbations applied to standard benchmarks, naturally occurring variations inherent to CAD software, and differences in how designers model the same part via a human dataset we created in FreeCAD. The performance of popular B-rep encoders often collapses catastrophically.
  We propose the canonical region graph, an input representation whose nodes, features and coordinate frame are derived from the solid itself and show theoretical invariance guarantees on repartitioning and rigid motions. It matches the strongest baseline on standard benchmarks, and is stable under every perturbation we test.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the problem of non-unique boundary representations (B-reps) for the same 3D solid in CAD systems, which causes catastrophic performance collapse in existing B-rep encoders. The authors propose the "canonical region graph" - a representation invariant to repartitioning and rigid motions - which maintains strong performance across standard benchmarks and various perturbations.
AI.motivation: Modern CAD systems use B-rep format for parametric 3D models, but the same solid can have different B-rep representations due to different operations, geometry kernel rebuilding, or export settings. Existing B-rep encoders are not robust to these variations, causing catastrophic performance degradation when the underlying solid remains identical but the representation changes.
AI.method: The authors propose the "canonical region graph" - an input representation where nodes, features, and coordinate frame are derived from the solid itself. This approach provides theoretical invariance guarantees on repartitioning (face splitting/merging) and rigid motions. They also created a human dataset in FreeCAD to test how different designers model the same part.
AI.result: The canonical region graph matches the strongest baseline on standard benchmarks and is stable under every perturbation tested, including standard benchmarks, naturally occurring variations, and human-designed variations from the FreeCAD dataset.
AI.conclusion: The canonical region graph representation successfully addresses the robustness issue in B-rep encoders by deriving invariant features from the solid itself, providing theoretical guarantees for repartitioning and rigid motion invariance while maintaining competitive performance on standard benchmarks.

title: Learnware and AI Model Management System
summary: The transition from file storage to database management systems transformed stored data into managed resources. AI now faces an analogous transition from AI model storage to AI model management. Existing model pools essentially serve as \textit{AI model storage systems}. What is needed instead are \textit{AI model management systems} that enable models trained by different developers, for different tasks, with different data, and under different objectives to be identified, reused, and even assembled to address future user tasks. Because AI model developers are generally unwilling to share their training data, such systems should operate without accessing the training data of model developers and, ideally, without accessing raw data of future users. This requirement poses a fundamental challenge: the functionality of a modern AI model may not be fully understood even by the developer who trained it. How, then, can a system identify which models are useful for a given user task, let alone assemble models developed independently for different purposes? At first glance, this objective may appear unattainable. It becomes possible, however, by upgrading the basic unit of management from a machine learning model to a \textit{learnware}. \textit{Learnware = Model + Specification}. The specification, whose assignment transforms a trained model into a learnware, is generated with the help of a machine learning process without disclosing the training data of the developer and has a theoretically established data-preservation property. The \textit{Learnware Dock System (LDS)} provides a path toward powerful AI model management systems. Because specifications are generated according to a published reference and are comparable across models, they can also serve as an AI model \textit{collaboration protocol} through which independently developed models, including intelligent agents, can collaborate.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the concept of "learnware" (Model + Specification) and the Learnware Dock System (LDS) to transform AI model storage into AI model management. The system enables identification, reuse, and assembly of independently developed models without accessing training data, functioning as a collaboration protocol for AI models.
AI.motivation: The authors identify a critical transition point in AI analogous to the historical shift from file storage to database management systems. Current "AI model pools" only serve as storage systems, lacking the capability to identify, reuse, or assemble models for specific tasks. The core challenge is that model developers won't share training data, and future users' raw data shouldn't be accessed either—yet modern AI models' functionality may not be fully understood even by their developers.
AI.method: The solution introduces "learnware" as the basic unit of management, where learnware = model + specification. The specification is generated via a machine learning process that preserves data privacy (theoretically established data-preservation property) without disclosing developers' training data. Specifications are generated according to a published reference, making them comparable across models.
AI.result: The Learnware Dock System (LDS) provides a pathway toward powerful AI model management systems. Specifications serve as an AI model collaboration protocol, enabling independently developed models and intelligent agents to collaborate effectively.
AI.conclusion: The learnware approach makes the seemingly impossible task of managing AI models without accessing training data achievable. This represents a paradigm shift in how AI models are managed, reused, and assembled—transforming isolated models into collaborative, manageable resources through the specification-based protocol.

title: Prompt Revision as a Source of Cultural Bias in Text-to-Image Systems
summary: Commercial text-to-image systems silently revise user prompts before generating images, a step users typically cannot disable or even see. Yet, existing audits of cultural bias examine only the final images and treat generation as a single pipeline, so they cannot tell where the bias originates. We introduce WORLDVIEW, a multilingual benchmark of 8,960 prompts across 15 languages and 31 language-context pairings. Using it, we audit the revision layer in three systems (DALL-E-3, Imagen-4, GPT-Image-1.5) through a three-step analysis of how heavily it marks each cultural context, whether it flattens that context into a narrow vocabulary, and whether that vocabulary is stereotypical. Relative to a no-context English baseline, the US is the least-marked context, while non-Western and non-Anglophone contexts are marked far more heavily, flattened into narrow vocabularies applied across topically diverse prompts, and reduced to recognizable cultural stereotypes. Comparing images from original versus revised prompts on models without a revision layer, we identify the layer itself as a previously undocumented, causal source of this stereotyping. To locate cultural bias, and fix it, we must audit the system as deployed, not the model alone.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces WORLDVIEW, a multilingual benchmark to audit the hidden prompt revision layers in commercial text-to-image systems (DALL-E-3, Imagen-4, GPT-Image-1.5), revealing that non-Western contexts are disproportionately marked, flattened into narrow vocabularies, and reduced to stereotypes—identifying the revision layer itself as a causal source of cultural bias.
AI.motivation: Existing audits of cultural bias in text-to-image systems only examine final images and treat generation as a single pipeline, unable to identify where bias originates. The hidden prompt revision step—used by commercial systems but invisible to users—needed investigation as a potential source of stereotyping.
AI.method: The authors created WORLDVIEW, a multilingual benchmark of 8,960 prompts across 15 languages and 31 language-context pairings. They conducted a three-step analysis: (1) measuring how heavily each cultural context is marked, (2) assessing whether contexts are flattened into narrow vocabularies, and (3) evaluating whether those vocabularies contain stereotypical representations. They also compared images generated from original vs. revised prompts on models without a revision layer to establish causality.
AI.result: Relative to a no-context English baseline, the US is the least-marked context, while non-Western and non-Anglophone contexts are marked far more heavily, flattened into narrow vocabularies applied across diverse prompts, and reduced to recognizable cultural stereotypes. The revision layer itself was identified as a causal source of stereotyping.
AI.conclusion: To locate and fix cultural bias in text-to-image systems, audits must examine the system as deployed (including the revision layer), not just the underlying model alone. The hidden prompt revision step is a previously undocumented source of cultural bias that needs to be audited and corrected.

title: OmniKVQuant: KV Cache Quantization for Omni-LLMs
summary: As Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) take in audio, video and text together, their KV cache memory cost grows. KV cache quantization is the de facto approach in text-only LLMs, but its application to Omni-LLMs remains unexplored. In this paper, we analyze how TurboQuant, a representative rotation-based KV cache quantization method, behaves on multimodal caches and identify two critical issues: temporal key drift and heterogeneous value geometry. To address these, we propose OmniKVQuant, a training-free framework that (i) sets the key quantization range over each short window of the input stream; and (ii) rotates values separately per modality. On Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni, OmniKVQuant enables 2-bit KV caches while substantially preserving performance across seven audio-visual benchmarks. We further provide a fused Triton decode kernel that unpacks the 2-bit cache during attention, so no dense FP16 cache is ever built. Code: https://github.com/kaistmm/OmniKVQuant

AI.tldr: OmniKVQuant is a training-free KV cache quantization framework for Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) that process audio, video, and text. It addresses two key issues in applying rotation-based quantization (TurboQuant) to multimodal caches: temporal key drift and heterogeneous value geometry. The method enables 2-bit KV caches while preserving performance across seven audio-visual benchmarks on Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni, with a fused Triton decode kernel for efficient attention computation.
AI.motivation: As Omni-LLMs process audio, video, and text simultaneously, their KV cache memory cost grows significantly. While KV cache quantization is standard for text-only LLMs, its application to Omni-LLMs remains unexplored. The researchers identified that TurboQuant, a representative rotation-based KV cache quantization method, exhibits two critical issues when applied to multimodal caches: temporal key drift and heterogeneous value geometry.
AI.method: OmniKVQuant addresses the identified issues through two key innovations: (i) Setting the key quantization range over each short window of the input stream to handle temporal key drift; (ii) Rotating values separately per modality to handle heterogeneous value geometry. Additionally, a fused Triton decode kernel is provided that unpacks the 2-bit cache during attention computation, ensuring no dense FP16 cache is ever built.
AI.result: OmniKVQuant enables 2-bit KV caches on Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni while substantially preserving performance across seven audio-visual benchmarks. The method achieves this without any training, making it a training-free framework.
AI.conclusion: The proposed OmniKVQuant successfully extends KV cache quantization to Omni-modal LLMs, addressing the unique challenges of multimodal caches. By enabling 2-bit quantization while maintaining performance, it significantly reduces memory cost for Omni-LLMs. The fused Triton decode kernel ensures practical deployment without requiring dense FP16 cache storage.

title: Why Does Post-Training Quantization Work?
summary: Post-training quantization compresses large language models (LLMs) by storing their weights at reduced precision, and each quantized weight introduces an error into the hidden states. Naively, these errors should accumulate with depth and corrupt next-token prediction; randomly initialized models accumulate these discrepancies rapidly, whereas quantized pretrained models accumulate much less hidden-state error and largely maintain downstream task performance, even though they were never trained with quantization noise. This raises the question we address: why does post-training quantization work? Comparing full-precision and quantized forward passes, we identify two mechanisms that characterize pretrained quantization robustness. First, the error a layer newly introduces tends to oppose the error it inherits from the layer's input. The two cancel partially such that the discrepancy between full-precision and quantized passes grows slowly. This counteracting residual interaction develops during pretraining. Our quantitative analysis identifies it as a major factor slowing hidden-error growth. Second, LM-head geometry preferentially preserves the scores and probabilities of high-ranked tokens, which typically represent the model's most confident predictions. Together, these mechanisms explain why quantization error that passes through numerous layers can still produce only small output changes, and we verify the findings across models and quantization settings.

AI.tldr: Post-training quantization (PTQ) works for LLMs due to two mechanisms: (1) error cancellation where quantization errors at each layer tend to oppose inherited errors, slowing error accumulation; (2) LM-head geometry that preserves high-ranked token probabilities. These mechanisms explain why quantized pretrained models maintain performance despite errors accumulating through many layers.
AI.motivation: The puzzle: quantization errors should accumulate with depth and corrupt predictions, yet quantized pretrained LLMs maintain performance. This raises the fundamental question of why PTQ works despite introducing errors at each layer.
AI.method: Comparative analysis between full-precision and quantized forward passes across models and quantization settings. Quantitative analysis of error propagation patterns and LM-head geometry effects.
AI.result: Two mechanisms were identified: (1) Counteracting residual interaction - errors introduced by each layer tend to oppose inherited errors, causing partial cancellation; this develops during pretraining and is a major factor slowing hidden-error growth. (2) LM-head geometry preferentially preserves scores/probabilities of high-ranked tokens (most confident predictions).
AI.conclusion: These two mechanisms together explain how quantization error can pass through numerous layers while producing only small output changes, validating findings across multiple models and quantization settings.

title: Characterizing Job Power Elasticity for Power-Flexible AI Training
summary:
Large language model (LLM) training is among the fastest-growing sources of electricity demand in modern data centers, and power availability is a primary bottleneck to continued AI infrastructure growth. Making the power consumption of these workloads flexible could unlock additional power for AI growth, limit increases in electricity prices, and improve the utilization of existing grid infrastructure. However, to realize this flexibility, we must first understand how the performance of training workloads changes when GPU power is reduced.
  This paper presents the first systematic characterization of \emph{job power elasticity} (the sensitivity of throughput to power reductions) in LLM training. To quantify elasticity, we introduce the \emph{Power Flexibility Index (PFI)}, a normalized metric that quantifies the performance cost of power reductions and provides a control primitive for SLA-aware power flexibility.
  We collect data from 131 LLM training runs on H200 (plus 24 H200 validation runs and 34 matched H100 runs), including both dense and mixture-of-experts models, pretraining and fine-tuning tasks, and up to 32 GPUs. We find that LLM training jobs exhibit substantial but variable power elasticity, and we identify telemetry signals that predict PFI at runtime. Finally, we demonstrate that PFI-aware power allocation maximizes total tokens/second throughput under power constraints. Under a 30\% power reduction, PFI-aware power allocation recovers ~1.5k tokens/s per job, 63\% of the performance gap between an equal-weight allocation and an oracle with perfect information. Our results establish power elasticity as a measurable property of training jobs and provide a foundation for power-aware, grid-responsive AI infrastructure.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Power Flexibility Index (PFI) to measure how sensitive LLM training throughput is to power reductions. Through experiments on 131 training runs (H200 GPUs), the authors show that LLM training jobs have variable but substantial power elasticity, and that PFI-aware power allocation can recover 63% of performance loss under 30% power reduction.
AI.motivation: LLM training is a rapidly growing source of electricity demand in data centers, with power availability being a key bottleneck to AI infrastructure growth. Making power consumption flexible could unlock additional power for AI, limit electricity price increases, and improve grid utilization. However, the performance impact of reducing GPU power during training was previously unexplored.
AI.method: The authors conducted 131 LLM training runs on H200 GPUs (plus 24 validation runs and 34 H100 runs), spanning dense and mixture-of-experts models, pretraining and fine-tuning tasks, and up to 32 GPUs. They introduced the Power Flexibility Index (PFI) as a normalized metric quantifying performance cost of power reductions. They also identified telemetry signals that can predict PFI at runtime.
AI.result: LLM training jobs exhibit substantial but variable power elasticity. Telemetry signals can predict PFI at runtime. Under a 30% power reduction, PFI-aware power allocation recovers ~1.5k tokens/s per job, representing 63% of the performance gap between equal-weight allocation and an oracle with perfect information.
AI.conclusion: Power elasticity is a measurable property of training jobs. The Power Flexibility Index (PFI) provides a control primitive for SLA-aware power flexibility. PFI-aware power allocation can maximize total tokens/second throughput under power constraints. This work establishes a foundation for power-aware, grid-responsive AI infrastructure.

title: MMGait: Benchmarking and Unifying Gait Recognition across Heterogeneous Modalities
summary: Gait recognition is commonly studied using RGB videos or their derived silhouettes and poses. Yet human walking produces heterogeneous photometric, geometric, and motion cues that cannot be systematically examined with RGB-centered benchmarks. We present MMGait, a large-scale multi-sensor benchmark that brings visible, infrared, depth, LiDAR, and radar observations into sequence-level correspondence. It provides diverse modalities spanning appearance, contours, geometry, motion, and body structure. Under a shared impostor-augmented protocol, we evaluate single-modal recognition, cross-modal recognition via directed retrieval, and multi-modal recognition using task-specific experts. Across settings, modality rankings vary with probe conditions, cross-modal alignment remains difficult, and fusion often provides complementary gains. This analysis exposes a scalability problem: individual modalities, modality pairs, and fusion configurations are typically handled by separately trained experts. We formulate Omni-Modal Gait Recognition, which unifies single-modal, cross-modal, and multi-modal recognition within a shared identity space. OmniGait++ uses modality-specific front ends followed by a shared identity encoder to preserve modality-dependent cues while learning comparable identity descriptors. An anchor-guided fusion module aggregates modality subsets of varying size without frame-level synchronization. A jointly trained checkpoint covers all three recognition settings and accommodates modality subsets of different compositions and cardinalities. Experiments show OmniGait++ remains competitive with task-specific experts in many shared settings and extends to higher-cardinality fusion unavailable to fixed-pair models. The results establish MMGait as a common testbed for heterogeneous gait sensing and demonstrate the feasibility of unified recognition under varying modality availability.
