AI.tldr: MMGait is a large-scale multi-sensor gait recognition benchmark containing visible, infrared, depth, LiDAR, and radar data. The paper proposes OmniGait++, a unified framework that handles single-modal, cross-modal, and multi-modal recognition within a shared identity space, addressing the scalability problem of training separate experts for each modality configuration.
AI.motivation: Current RGB-centered gait recognition benchmarks cannot systematically examine the heterogeneous photometric, geometric, and motion cues produced by human walking. Existing approaches require separately trained experts for individual modalities, modality pairs, and fusion configurations, creating a scalability problem.
AI.method: MMGait provides multi-sensor data under a shared impostor-augmented protocol. OmniGait++ uses modality-specific front ends followed by a shared identity encoder to preserve modality-dependent cues while learning comparable identity descriptors. An anchor-guided fusion module aggregates modality subsets of varying size without frame-level synchronization. A jointly trained checkpoint covers all three recognition settings.
AI.result: Across settings, modality rankings vary with probe conditions, cross-modal alignment remains difficult, and fusion often provides complementary gains. OmniGait++ remains competitive with task-specific experts in many shared settings and extends to higher-cardinality fusion unavailable to fixed-pair models.
AI.conclusion: MMGait establishes a common testbed for heterogeneous gait sensing, and OmniGait++ demonstrates the feasibility of unified recognition under varying modality availability, accommodating modality subsets of different compositions and cardinalities with a single trained model.

title: Predicting Privacy Leakage from Weight Spectral Density
summary: Membership inference attacks (MIAs) are widely used to audit the privacy disclosure risk of machine learning models, however current state-of-the-art attacks require training computationally expensive shadow models, making large-scale privacy evaluation impractical. In this work, we investigate whether inexpensive spectral metrics derived from the heavy-tailed self-regularisation framework can serve as proxies for MIA vulnerability. We evaluate several WeightWatcher spectral metrics on image and tabular classification tasks and compare their relationship with MIA privacy leakage against conventional measures of generalisation. Across datasets, stable rank exhibits a strong positive correlation with overall MIA success, while Log alpha-Norm shows a consistent negative correlation with MIA vulnerability at the low false-positive regime. These associations are observed to be stronger than those obtained using the generalisation gap. The results indicate that neural network spectra may contain information about privacy leakage that is not fully captured by conventional measures of overfitting, motivating spectral analysis as a promising direction for scalable privacy auditing.

AI.tldr: Spectral metrics from the heavy-tailed self-regularisation framework (specifically stable rank and Log alpha-Norm) can serve as inexpensive proxies for computationally expensive membership inference attacks (MIAs) to audit privacy leakage in neural networks, offering a more scalable approach to privacy evaluation than traditional methods.
AI.motivation: Current state-of-the-art membership inference attacks require training computationally expensive shadow models, making large-scale privacy evaluation impractical. The authors investigate whether inexpensive spectral metrics can serve as proxies for MIA vulnerability.
AI.method: The authors evaluate several WeightWatcher spectral metrics on image and tabular classification tasks and compare their relationship with MIA privacy leakage against conventional measures of generalisation.
AI.result: Stable rank exhibits a strong positive correlation with overall MIA success, while Log alpha-Norm shows a consistent negative correlation with MIA vulnerability at the low false-positive regime. These associations are stronger than those obtained using the generalisation gap.
AI.conclusion: Neural network spectra may contain information about privacy leakage that is not fully captured by conventional measures of overfitting, motivating spectral analysis as a promising direction for scalable privacy auditing.

title: Enabling Knowledge Graph Understanding at Scale with the EXplore Your Graphs ENgine (EXYGEN)
summary: We present EXYGEN (EXplore Your Graphs ENgine), a framework for knowledge graph (KG) understanding that enables conversational access to KGs at scale. We address two questions in sequence. First, how effectively can LLMs perform text-to-SPARQL generation given only automatically derived structured metadata and small graph samples, rather than task-specific fine-tuning? We integrate VoID descriptions and ShEx schemas into a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline and ablate KG-derived context on the SciQA benchmark. Our best configuration -- combining ShEx schemas, retrieved triples, and example question-query pairs -- reaches an exact match of 0.419 on execution results without any LLM fine-tuning. We further find that lexical metrics such as F1 poorly predict query correctness, and that larger general-purpose LLMs can outperform smaller code-specialized ones once given sufficient context. Second, we ask how to generate the structured metadata that this method relies on from very large KGs, where KG metadata generation becomes computationally intractable. We introduce a predicate-coverage-aware parallel graph sampling strategy that preserves structural diversity while remaining computationally tractable. On OpenCitations Meta and GESIS, it retains high predicate coverage with minimal triple loss and reduces runtime by over 80x; on ORKG, sampling is not just faster but the only tractable path to obtain complete metadata. Together, these results show that structured schema context and lightweight prompting can substantially reduce reliance on fine-tuning for scalable conversational access to KGs, though closing the remaining gap to fully fine-tuned approaches will likely require reducing dependence on curated question-query exemplars -- whether through synthetic generation or an execution-feedback-driven approach -- and validating these findings beyond a single benchmark.

AI.tldr: EXYGEN is a framework for knowledge graph (KG) understanding that enables conversational access to KGs at scale through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). It addresses text-to-SPARQL generation without LLM fine-tuning by integrating VoID descriptions and ShEx schemas, achieving 0.419 exact match on SciQA benchmark. The paper also introduces a predicate-coverage-aware parallel graph sampling strategy for metadata generation from very large KGs, reducing runtime by over 80x while preserving structural diversity.
AI.motivation: The research addresses two key challenges: (1) enabling LLMs to perform text-to-SPARQL generation without task-specific fine-tuning, which is computationally expensive and not scalable; (2) generating structured metadata from very large KGs where traditional metadata generation becomes computationally intractable.
AI.method: 1. RAG pipeline integrating VoID descriptions and ShEx schemas with retrieved triples and example question-query pairs; 2. Predicate-coverage-aware parallel graph sampling strategy for large KGs; 3. Ablation studies on KG-derived context using SciQA benchmark
AI.result: Best configuration (ShEx schemas + retrieved triples + example pairs) achieves 0.419 exact match on execution results without any LLM fine-tuning. Lexical metrics (F1) poorly predict query correctness. Larger general-purpose LLMs can outperform smaller code-specialized ones with sufficient context. The sampling strategy retains high predicate coverage with minimal triple loss and reduces runtime by over 80x on OpenCitations Meta and GESIS; on ORKG, it becomes the only tractable path for complete metadata.
AI.conclusion: Structured schema context and lightweight prompting can substantially reduce reliance on fine-tuning for scalable conversational access to KGs. However, closing the gap to fully fine-tuned approaches requires reducing dependence on curated question-query exemplars through synthetic generation or execution-feedback-driven approaches, and validating findings beyond a single benchmark.

title: LangStreet: Persistent Language Fields for Anchor-Decoded Street Gaussians
summary: Language Gaussian fields implicitly assume that the primitive carrying semantics remains identifiable across views. This assumption breaks in scalable anchor-decoded representations, where persistent anchors generate view-conditioned child Gaussians whose geometry and appearance vary with the camera. We introduce Ours, a persistent language field for such structured Gaussian scenes. Our key idea is semantic ownership: transient children route observations, while persistent decoder slots and their parent anchors own the language field. We use alpha-compositing responsibilities to accumulate additive directional evidence at slots; these statistics marginalize exactly to anchors. We then complete weakly supported slots with anchor-aligned evidence while preserving the anchor direction, and represent slot detail through low-rank residuals in anchor-relative semantic coordinates. Our primary model, Ours (base), stores anchor features together with compact slot residuals. Ours (light) retains only anchor features, whereas Ours (max) stores the full-dimensional completed slot features explicitly. Without scene-specific semantic optimization, Ours (base) nearly matches Ours (max) across KITTI, Virtual KITTI, and Waymo. On KITTI, it achieves 34.19 2D mIoU with a 2.72 GiB effective feature footprint, compared with 34.20 mIoU and 12.90 GiB for Ours (max). The same accuracy-storage trend holds on Virtual KITTI and Waymo. These results show that language fields on view-conditioned splats require persistent semantic ownership, conserved evidence, and a hierarchy that balances stability, detail, and representation cost. Our code, checkpoints, and benchmark suite will be publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a persistent language field method for structured Gaussian scenes that solves the semantic ownership problem in anchor-decoded representations where view-conditioned child Gaussians have varying geometry and appearance. The method uses semantic ownership where persistent decoder slots own the language field, with alpha-compositing for evidence accumulation and low-rank residuals for slot detail. The base version achieves near-identical accuracy (34.19 vs 34.20 mIoU) with 4.7x less storage (2.72 vs 12.90 GiB) on KITTI.
AI.motivation: Language Gaussian fields assume primitive semantics remain identifiable across views, but this assumption breaks in scalable anchor-decoded representations where persistent anchors generate view-conditioned child Gaussians with varying geometry and appearance across cameras.
AI.method: The method uses semantic ownership where transient children route observations while persistent decoder slots and parent anchors own the language field. Alpha-compositing responsibilities accumulate additive directional evidence at slots, which marginalize to anchors. Weakly supported slots are completed with anchor-aligned evidence while preserving anchor direction, and slot detail is represented through low-rank residuals in anchor-relative semantic coordinates. Three variants: base (anchor features + compact slot residuals), light (anchor features only), and max (full-dimensional completed slot features).
AI.result: On KITTI, Ours (base) achieves 34.19 2D mIoU with 2.72 GiB effective feature footprint, nearly matching Ours (max) at 34.20 mIoU with 12.90 GiB. The same accuracy-storage trend holds on Virtual KITTI and Waymo. Without scene-specific semantic optimization, the base version nearly matches the max version across all datasets.
AI.conclusion: Language fields on view-conditioned splats require persistent semantic ownership, conserved evidence, and a hierarchy balancing stability, detail, and representation cost. The low-rank residual approach achieves near-identical accuracy with significantly reduced storage.

title: Dynamic language model representations for multi-objective reaction optimisation
summary: Optimising chemical reactions across multiple objectives, such as yield, selectivity, and safety, is central to chemical synthesis, and model-driven approaches depend critically on how reaction components are represented. Established featurisations are either chemically uninformative, as with one-hot encodings, or, as with molecular descriptors, do not readily extend across chemically distinct components. For structurally and functionally diverse components, it is therefore unclear what a shared representation should contain. Constructing such a representation is itself a challenging research undertaking that must be revisited for each new reaction system. Here we bypass this step by learning the reaction representation dynamically from text. Textual descriptions of reaction conditions are encoded by a fine-tuned language model trained jointly with Gaussian process surrogates, yielding task-adaptive representations within a multi-objective Bayesian optimisation loop. Across nickel- and palladium-catalysed cross-couplings in both sequential and parallel experimentation regimes, this approach reaches optimisation convergence in fewer experiments than descriptor libraries or one-hot encoding. Applied prospectively to a palladium-catalysed cyanation spanning mixed ligand denticity and heterogeneous additives, and to a three-objective asymmetric hydrogenation across chiral iridium and ruthenium catalyst families, two rounds of high-throughput experimentation (192 reactions, under 3% of each design space) delivered conditions translating directly to gram scale in 94% and 84% isolated yield, the latter at 99.6% enantiomeric excess.

title: Making Alternative Data Work: Context-Augmented LLMs for Financial Forecasting
summary: When forecasting a firm's future financial performance, alternative data - data collected from non-traditional sources such as consumer transactions, web traffic, and prediction markets - can provide timely signals about firms' operating activities and broader market conditions. These signals may reveal information that is not captured by traditional public sources and can therefore provide complementary information for forecasting firms' future financial performance. However, firm-level alternative data often have limited historical coverage, are relevant only to specific prediction targets or subsets of firms, and are distributed across numerous heterogeneous channels, making them difficult to incorporate flexibly into conventional forecasting approaches. Meanwhile, large language models (LLMs) can interpret instructions, learn from in-context examples, and generate predictions by combining heterogeneous information without task-specific parameter updates. Motivated by this potential flexibility, we investigate whether an LLM can forecast firm performance by integrating alternative data with other financial information through in-context learning. We propose a two-agent framework that first identifies the firms for which each alternative data channel is likely to be informative and then predicts revenue using firm- and channel-specific context. We evaluate the framework across four commercial alternative data channels. In our experiments, adding alternative data in context alongside other financial information improves the LLM's forecasting relative to either source alone, and these forecasts are more accurate than those of standard forecasting baselines. These findings suggest that LLMs provide a flexible and practical approach to integrating alternative data with heterogeneous financial information.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a two-agent framework using LLMs to integrate alternative data (consumer transactions, web traffic, prediction markets) with traditional financial information for forecasting firm revenue performance, demonstrating improved accuracy over single-source or baseline forecasting methods.
AI.motivation: Alternative data can provide timely signals about firm performance that traditional sources miss, but it has limitations: limited historical coverage, narrow relevance to specific firms/targets, and heterogeneous distribution. LLMs can flexibly integrate heterogeneous information through in-context learning without task-specific training.
AI.method: The authors propose a two-agent framework: (1) An agent identifies which firms each alternative data channel is informative for, and (2) Another agent predicts revenue using firm- and channel-specific context. They evaluate across four commercial alternative data channels, comparing LLM forecasts with alternative data alone, traditional financial data alone, and standard forecasting baselines.
AI.result: Adding alternative data in context alongside other financial information improves LLM forecasting relative to either source alone, and outperforms standard forecasting baselines. LLMs provide a flexible and practical approach to integrating heterogeneous alternative data with financial information.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can effectively leverage alternative data for firm performance forecasting through in-context learning, offering a flexible solution to combine heterogeneous data sources that traditional methods struggle to integrate.

title: Vidu S2: Real-Time Interactive, Editable, and Spatial Video Generation
summary: We present Vidu S2, which comprises Vidu S2-Avatar, a real-time interactive digital-character model, and Vidu S2-Editing, a real-time video editing model. Moreover, we explore the feasibility of real-time spatial video generation for both Vidu S2-Avatar and Vidu S2-Editing. Compared with Vidu S1, Vidu S2-Avatar supports real-time 720p video generation, generation with dynamic references that can be updated at any moment, and stronger instruction following, such as dancing. Vidu S2-Editing supports editing a video stream in real time, including style rendering, clothing replacement, character replacement, and background replacement. Experiments show that Vidu S2 outperforms all baselines. A playable online demo is available at https://vidu.com/vidu-stream.

AI.tldr: Vidu S2 is a real-time video generation and editing system comprising Vidu S2-Avatar (real-time interactive digital-character model) and Vidu S2-Editing (real-time video editing model). It supports 720p video generation with dynamic references and strong instruction following (e.g., dancing), along with real-time editing capabilities including style rendering, clothing/character/background replacement.
AI.motivation: To improve upon Vidu S1 by adding real-time 720p video generation, dynamic reference updates, stronger instruction following, and real-time video editing capabilities including style rendering, clothing replacement, character replacement, and background replacement.
AI.method: Developed two models: (1) Vidu S2-Avatar for real-time interactive digital character generation with dynamic references and instruction following, and (2) Vidu S2-Editing for real-time video stream editing. Explored feasibility of real-time spatial video generation for both components.
AI.result: Vidu S2 outperforms all baselines in experiments. Successfully supports real-time 720p video generation with dynamic references, stronger instruction following (such as dancing), and real-time editing features.
AI.conclusion: Vidu S2 successfully achieves real-time video generation and editing capabilities, demonstrating superior performance compared to baseline methods. A playable online demo is available.

title: Thinking with Looped Flows
summary: Humans and machines often solve harder problems by spending more time on computation. In deep learning, looped models implement this idea during inference by recurrently updating a hidden state. In practice, however, their training backpropagates through only one or a few updates, making it hard to train early updates to support future ones. We propose looped flows, an approach that sidesteps this issue by training the recurrence with local denoising objectives. By imposing temporal association across denoising objectives through progressively decreasing noise levels and shared noise, the model is incentivized to learn recurrent states that transfer useful computation over time, even when gradients cover only a few updates. We then formulate inference as integrating the velocity of a probability flow parameterized by the learned denoiser, coupled with recurrent states. This allows solving harder problems by spending more computation through a finer temporal grid and enables multiple valid predictions from different initial noise samples. Across six reasoning benchmarks including two multi-solution benchmarks, looped flows outperform prior state-of-the-art looped models overall, achieving 58.8% test accuracy on ARC-AGI-1 and 12.2% on ARC-AGI-2.

AI.tldr: Looped flows is a novel approach that trains recurrent deep learning models using local denoising objectives with temporal association across noise levels, enabling models to solve harder problems by spending more computation time. It achieves state-of-the-art results on six reasoning benchmarks, including 58.8% on ARC-AGI-1 and 12.2% on ARC-AGI-2.
AI.motivation: Humans and machines solve harder problems by spending more computation time. In deep learning, looped models (recurrent models) implement this during inference by recurrently updating hidden states. However, training backpropagates through only one or a few updates, making it hard to train early updates to support future ones. This creates a fundamental training-inference mismatch.
AI.method: The proposed looped flows approach trains the recurrence with local denoising objectives. Key innovations include: (1) imposing temporal association across denoising objectives through progressively decreasing noise levels, (2) using shared noise to couple the objectives, which incentivizes learning recurrent states that transfer useful computation over time even when gradients cover only a few updates. Inference is formulated as integrating the velocity of a probability flow parameterized by the learned denoiser, coupled with recurrent states.
AI.result: Looped flows outperform prior state-of-the-art looped models across six reasoning benchmarks. Specifically, it achieves 58.8% test accuracy on ARC-AGI-1 and 12.2% on ARC-AGI-2. The approach enables solving harder problems by spending more computation through a finer temporal grid and supports multiple valid predictions from different initial noise samples.
AI.conclusion: Looped flows successfully bridges the training-inference gap in recurrent deep learning models by using local denoising objectives with temporal association. This allows models to effectively leverage additional computation time for harder problems, achieving new state-of-the-art results on reasoning benchmarks including multi-solution tasks.

title: Distributed Optimization of Modular Production Systems using Model-based Reinforcement Learning with Inverse Models
summary: This paper presents a novel approach for data-driven self-learning control of highly flexible, modular manufacturing systems. Specifically, we employ a novel framework for model-based reinforcement learning which introduces approximate inverse process models within the training of reinforcement policies. This approach disentangles the learning of actuation dynamics and the dynamics in state space, resulting in RL-based training solely within the task space. We propose a lightweight feedforward architecture for approximate inverse models and integrate them within the policy network of standard RL algorithms. We apply the approach to a laboratory modular production testbed with heterogeneous production modules. The results underline the efficiency improvements for modular manufacturing units in terms of both performance and training speed, particularly for off-policy algorithms.

AI.tldr: A novel data-driven self-learning control approach for modular manufacturing systems using model-based reinforcement learning with approximate inverse process models, enabling efficient training in task space.
AI.motivation: Enable efficient self-learning control for highly flexible, modular manufacturing systems that can adapt to heterogeneous production modules without extensive manual tuning.
AI.method: Introduce approximate inverse process models within RL training framework; use lightweight feedforward architecture for inverse models; integrate with policy network of standard RL algorithms; train solely in task space by disentangling actuation dynamics from state space dynamics.
AI.result: Efficiency improvements in both performance and training speed for modular manufacturing units, particularly with off-policy algorithms.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach effectively combines model-based RL with approximate inverse models, achieving faster training and better performance for modular production systems.

title: Self-Supervised Cardiac Phase Detection via Single-Parameter Latent Orbits
comment: Accepted for oral presentation at the ASMUS workshop at MICCAI 2026
summary: Accurate identification of end-diastole (ED) and end-systole (ES) in echocardiography underpins the quantification of ventricular function, yet manual selection of these key frames is subjective and introduces clinically significant inter-operator variability. Recent self-supervised methods either prescribe strict periodic trajectories or learn an unconstrained low-dimensional motion subspace from reconstruction or registration objectives. The former offers interpretability but imposes restrictive assumptions on temporal progression, whereas the latter leaves cardiac phase implicit and ED/ES must be recovered through post-hoc geometric processing of the learned trajectory. We translate the physiological observation that cardiac phase is a one-dimensional signal into a prior by constraining the latent motion component to a single-parameter latent orbit, i.e., a global linear trajectory in latent space indexed by a bounded scalar phase variable. Mapping this variable through a sinusoidal nonlinearity yields an oscillatory motion signal with consistent temporal ordering, enabling direct identification of ED and ES from the learned phase signal. This inductive bias allows the model to capture an interpretable representation of the cardiac cycle, while maintaining flexibility to capture irregular heartbeats. Trained on EchoNet-Dynamic without annotations, our minimal single-parameter cardiac phase model learns an effective latent orbit, significantly improves upon the previous state of the art in ED localisation and matches it in ES localisation while using a more constrained representation and fewer training epochs. This demonstrates that a principled physiological inductive bias can match or exceed the performance of more complex representations. Code is available at: https://github.com/BonniciJ/OrbitalEcho/

AI.tldr: A self-supervised deep learning method for identifying end-diastole (ED) and end-systole (ES) frames in echocardiography by constraining the latent motion representation to a single-parameter orbital structure with sinusoidal nonlinearity, achieving improved ED localization and comparable ES localization to state-of-the-art while using fewer parameters and training epochs.
AI.motivation: Manual selection of ED and ES frames in echocardiography is subjective and introduces inter-operator variability. Existing self-supervised methods either impose overly restrictive periodic assumptions or learn unconstrained representations where cardiac phase must be recovered through post-hoc processing.
AI.method: The method constrains the latent motion component to a single-parameter latent orbit—a global linear trajectory in latent space indexed by a bounded scalar phase variable. This variable is mapped through a sinusoidal nonlinearity to produce an oscillatory motion signal with consistent temporal ordering, enabling direct identification of ED and ES from the learned phase signal.
AI.result: The model significantly improves upon previous state-of-the-art in ED localization and matches it in ES localization on EchoNet-Dynamic, while using a more constrained representation and fewer training epochs.
AI.conclusion: A principled physiological inductive bias (modeling cardiac phase as a 1D oscillatory signal) can match or exceed the performance of more complex representations, demonstrating the value of incorporating domain knowledge into model architecture design.

title: Model-Aware Schedules Improve Generation via Fiberwise Optimal Transport
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures. Keywords: Diffusion models; flow matching; schedule optimization; fiberwise optimal transport; time reparameterization; empirical universality
summary: Diffusion and flow-matching schedules control the signal and noise coefficients that mix data and noise along affine probability paths. Minimizing a kinetic action defined on coefficient paths, motivated by optimal transport, helps explain strong baselines but remains model-agnostic and ignores prediction error. Here we introduce a model-aware schedule construction based on fiberwise optimal transport. At a fixed time and state on the probability path, compatible signal/noise decompositions form an affine fiber. We define a fiberwise prediction risk by averaging optimal-transport costs between the true and predictor-induced decompositions within these fibers. On a fixed coefficient curve, combining this risk with coefficient-path kinetic action yields a closed-form optimal time allocation. This construction extends to general linear prediction targets, and the risk profile can be estimated from an early baseline checkpoint. We evaluate DDPMs and flow matching across prediction targets, training configurations, risk-estimation checkpoints, datasets, and architectures. Our model-aware schedules consistently outperform strong baselines, including a 38.6% relative FID reduction for flow matching on CIFAR-10 at 16 function evaluations. Each model-agnostic kinetic baseline determines its own kinetic reference coordinate. In these coordinates, fiberwise-risk profiles from independently trained models in different settings align closely after normalization to unit area. The resulting schedule deformations used in training also align, suggesting empirical universality across the evaluated models and settings. Pretrained-checkpoint diagnostics extend this normalized-risk agreement to larger conditional latent diffusion and 2-RF models. A frozen analytic allocation template retains most of the model-aware improvement without further risk estimation or model-specific fitting.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a model-aware schedule construction for diffusion models and flow matching based on fiberwise optimal transport. The approach defines a fiberwise prediction risk by averaging optimal-transport costs between true and predictor-induced decompositions within affine fibers. Combined with coefficient-path kinetic action, this yields a closed-form optimal time allocation. The method achieves a 38.6% relative FID reduction on CIFAR-10 and shows empirical universality across different models and settings.
AI.motivation: Current diffusion and flow-matching schedules are model-agnostic and ignore prediction error. They control signal and noise coefficients along affine probability paths but remain disconnected from the actual prediction quality of the model. This paper aims to create model-aware schedules that optimize time allocation based on prediction risk.
AI.method: The method introduces fiberwise optimal transport at fixed time and state on probability paths. Compatible signal/noise decompositions form an affine fiber. A fiberwise prediction risk is defined by averaging optimal-transport costs between true and predictor-induced decompositions within these fibers. This risk is combined with coefficient-path kinetic action on a fixed coefficient curve to yield a closed-form optimal time allocation. The risk profile can be estimated from an early baseline checkpoint.
AI.result: The model-aware schedules consistently outperform strong baselines across DDPMs and flow matching with various prediction targets, training configurations, risk-estimation checkpoints, datasets, and architectures. A 38.6% relative FID reduction was achieved for flow matching on CIFAR-10 at 16 function evaluations. In kinetic reference coordinates, fiberwise-risk profiles from independently trained models align closely after normalization. A frozen analytic allocation template retains most of the improvement without further risk estimation.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that model-aware schedule construction based on fiberwise optimal transport significantly improves diffusion and flow-matching models. The empirical universality across different models and settings suggests the approach has broad applicability. The method can be implemented using a frozen analytic allocation template without requiring model-specific fitting or additional risk estimation.

title: MAPLE: Memory-Augmented Planning with Language and Evolution
summary: Domain practitioners understand their business constraints but may lack operations-research expertise or dedicated support. LLM-based optimization agents translate natural-language requirements into models or solver programs that established optimization tools can execute. This progress makes optimization more accessible, but real-world operations are dynamic: changing demand, resources, and priorities require updates to data, constraints, and objectives. Methods centered on isolated requests offer limited support for rapid adaptation that preserves earlier decisions and reuses useful search results. We introduce MAPLE (Memory-Augmented Planning with Language and Evolution), an agent for maintaining optimization problems through successive natural-language requests. MAPLE combines language-based problem construction with mathematical programming and evolutionary search. It retains the optimization program, accepted plans, earlier updates, and candidate solutions for subsequent requests. We introduce NLDO, a benchmark of 15 trajectories and 180 updates spanning selection, scheduling, rostering, routing, and cloud-resource placement. In the main evaluation, MAPLE completes all trajectories and achieves online scalar quality of 0.951 and a Pareto hypervolume ratio of 0.875. Controlled comparisons further show that maintaining executable state improves update validity and can preserve useful search information across substantial revisions.

AI.tldr: MAPLE is an AI agent that helps domain practitioners maintain and update optimization problems through natural language requests, combining language models with mathematical programming and evolutionary search. It introduces NLDO benchmark with 15 trajectories and 180 updates, achieving 0.951 online scalar quality and 0.875 Pareto hypervolume ratio.
AI.motivation: Domain practitioners lack operations-research expertise, and real-world operations are dynamic—changing demand, resources, and priorities require frequent updates to optimization problems. Existing methods centered on isolated requests offer limited support for rapid adaptation that preserves earlier decisions and reuses useful search results.
AI.method: MAPLE combines language-based problem construction with mathematical programming and evolutionary search. It maintains executable state by retaining the optimization program, accepted plans, earlier updates, and candidate solutions for subsequent requests.
AI.result: MAPLE completes all 15 trajectories in the NLDO benchmark. It achieves an online scalar quality of 0.951 and a Pareto hypervolume ratio of 0.875. Controlled comparisons show that maintaining executable state improves update validity and can preserve useful search information across substantial revisions.
AI.conclusion: MAPLE successfully enables domain practitioners to maintain optimization problems through natural language requests, making optimization more accessible and adaptable to dynamic real-world conditions.

title: Multimodal Taxonomic Conditioning for Generative Plankton Imagery
comment: European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV) 2nd Workshop on Marine Vision
summary: Automated plankton imaging produces severely long-tailed datasets, where the rare taxa of greatest ecological interest have too few images to train or evaluate classifiers reliably. We generate synthetic plankton imagery conditioned on taxonomy: a CLIP encoder is adapted on a large plankton corpus with a ranked contrastive objective extended to deep, ragged taxonomies, then frozen to condition a parameter-efficient diffusion transformer. We evaluate synthetic sample quality on distributional fidelity and downstream classifier utility.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the long-tailed distribution problem in automated plankton imaging by generating synthetic plankton imagery using a CLIP-conditioned diffusion transformer. The approach adapts a CLIP encoder with a ranked contrastive objective for deep, ragged taxonomies, then uses it to condition a parameter-efficient diffusion model for synthetic data generation.
AI.motivation: Automated plankton imaging produces severely long-tailed datasets where rare taxa of greatest ecological interest have too few images to train or evaluate classifiers reliably. This creates a significant challenge for building accurate and reliable plankton classification systems.
AI.method: The authors propose generating synthetic plankton imagery conditioned on taxonomy by: (1) Adapting a CLIP encoder on a large plankton corpus using a ranked contrastive objective extended to deep, ragged taxonomies, (2) Freezing the adapted encoder to condition a parameter-efficient diffusion transformer for synthetic image generation.
AI.result: The abstract indicates that synthetic sample quality is evaluated on two criteria: distributional fidelity (how well the synthetic images match the real data distribution) and downstream classifier utility (whether synthetic images improve classifier performance on rare taxa).
AI.conclusion: The paper presents a novel approach to address data scarcity in rare plankton taxa using synthetic data generation, combining CLIP-based conditioning with diffusion transformers adapted for taxonomic constraints.

title: AdamX: Cosine similarity meets gradient descent
summary: We introduce AdamX, a first-order optimizer that incorporates cosine similarity as an adaptive mechanism for controlling update magnitudes. The proposed method is scalable, model-agnostic, and straightforward to integrate into existing training pipelines. We further introduce a variance rectification scheme that promotes smoother optimization during the early stages of training. Overall, we provide empirical evidence that AdamX achieves competitive convergence rates across a range of benchmark datasets and architectures. Performance is evaluated in terms of the number of epochs required to reach predefined performance thresholds under a fixed hyperparameter budget. Code and Experiments available at: https://github.com/FranciscoCaldas/adamX.

AI.tldr: AdamX is a first-order optimizer that uses cosine similarity as an adaptive mechanism to control update magnitudes, combined with a variance rectification scheme for smoother early-stage training. It achieves competitive convergence rates across benchmark datasets and architectures.
AI.motivation: The motivation appears to be improving upon existing first-order optimizers (like Adam) by introducing a novel adaptive mechanism based on cosine similarity to better control update magnitudes, and addressing early-stage training instability through variance rectification.
AI.method: AdamX incorporates cosine similarity as an adaptive mechanism for controlling update magnitudes. It also includes a variance rectification scheme that promotes smoother optimization during early training stages. The method is designed to be scalable, model-agnostic, and easily integrable into existing training pipelines.
AI.result: AdamX achieves competitive convergence rates across a range of benchmark datasets and architectures. Performance is evaluated based on the number of epochs required to reach predefined performance thresholds under a fixed hyperparameter budget.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that AdamX is a viable first-order optimizer that can compete with existing methods in terms of convergence speed while being straightforward to implement and integrate.

title: Autonomy, Social Norms, and Alignment: Towards a Developmental Framework for Autonomous Artificial Agents
comment: In publication in the proceedings of SIpEIA 2026 conference
summary: In recent years, artificial intelligence has made extraordinary progress thanks to large-scale models capable of generalization and the generation of complex outputs. However, transferring this potential into embodied agents reveals a significant limitation: the most advanced systems rely on pre-existing datasets and human feedback strategies that are powerful but insufficient in dynamic or unknown contexts. To adapt, an agent must acquire knowledge through direct interaction with its environment. One strategy to address this challenge involves introducing higher-level mechanisms, such as intrinsic motivations, which leverage curiosity and competence, to guide exploration and learning in complex environments. While this flexibility expands autonomy, it complicates the task of ensuring agents remain aligned with human goals. Alignment, already a challenge for artificial systems in general, becomes even more complex in unstructured and dynamic contexts where predefined rules prove insufficient. To be effective and adaptable, norms must be rooted in experience through an epistemological process that starting from simple, situated principles allows for the gradual construction of more complex rules through experience, autonomous learning, and cooperation with other moral agents. Similarly to children learning social norms by exploring their environment and participating in collective practices, artificial agents must also be educated toward alignment. Following Dennett, the status of a moral agent is not innate but is attributed gradually based on the ability to responsibly manage increasing degrees of freedom. From this perspective, the regulatory sandboxes can be viewed as pedagogical environments for AI: dynamic spaces where alignment develops as a formative process, progressively shaping autonomous behaviors through interaction and cooperation in scenarios of increasing complexity.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of aligning embodied AI agents with human goals in dynamic, unknown environments. The authors argue that traditional approaches relying on pre-existing datasets and human feedback are insufficient. They propose that agents should learn through intrinsic motivations (curiosity, competence) and that regulatory sandboxes can serve as pedagogical environments for AI alignment, similar to how children learn social norms through interaction and cooperation.
AI.motivation: The research aims to solve the limitation that advanced AI systems rely on pre-existing datasets and human feedback, which are insufficient in dynamic or unknown contexts. The authors seek a way for agents to acquire knowledge through direct interaction with the environment while remaining aligned with human goals.
AI.method: The paper proposes an epistemological approach where norms are rooted in experience, starting from simple situated principles and gradually building more complex rules through autonomous learning and cooperation. Following Dennett's philosophy, moral agent status is gradually attributed based on the ability to responsibly manage increasing degrees of freedom. Regulatory sandboxes are proposed as pedagogical environments for this formative alignment process.
AI.result: The paper concludes that alignment should be viewed as a formative/pedagogical process rather than a static rule-following mechanism. Agents must be "educated" toward alignment through interaction in progressively complex scenarios, similar to how children learn social norms by exploring their environment and participating in collective practices.
AI.conclusion: To achieve effective alignment in unstructured and dynamic contexts, AI agents need to develop norms through experience, autonomous learning, and cooperation with other moral agents. Regulatory sandboxes can serve as dynamic pedagogical spaces where alignment develops progressively through interaction and increasing complexity.

title: Single-Stream Multi-Feature Fusion with Temporal Robustness for Gait Emotion Recognition
comment: Accepted at the 35th International Conference on Artificial Neural Networks (ICANN 2026)
summary: 3D skeleton-based gait emotion recognition faces high annotation costs, data scarcity, and poor generalization on heterogeneous data. This paper proposes SV-GCN, a single-stream multi-feature fusion framework with temporal invariance. We introduce intra-frame relative motion features to eliminate frame-rate sensitivity and embed heterogeneous cues at shallow layers, enabling early fusion without multi-stream complexity. For variable-length sequences, we design a global mask-guided valid-frame spatio-temporal graph convolution module, introducing frame-rate insensitivity for the first time in this domain. On the E-Gait dataset, our method achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art while demonstrating strong generalization across varying sequence lengths and frame rates, offering a viable pathway for pre-training on large-scale skeleton-based action recognition datasets.

AI.tldr: SV-GCN is a single-stream multi-feature fusion framework for 3D skeleton-based gait emotion recognition that addresses annotation costs, data scarcity, and poor generalization through temporal invariance and early fusion of heterogeneous cues.
AI.motivation: 3D skeleton-based gait emotion recognition faces three major challenges: high annotation costs, data scarcity, and poor generalization on heterogeneous data. Existing methods struggle with varying frame rates and limited training data.
AI.method: The paper proposes SV-GCN with three key innovations: (1) Intra-frame relative motion features to eliminate frame-rate sensitivity; (2) Embedding heterogeneous cues at shallow layers for early fusion without multi-stream complexity; (3) Global mask-guided valid-frame spatio-temporal graph convolution module for handling variable-length sequences.
AI.result: On the E-Gait dataset, SV-GCN achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods while demonstrating strong generalization across varying sequence lengths and frame rates.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method offers a viable pathway for pre-training on large-scale skeleton-based action recognition datasets, potentially addressing data scarcity issues in gait emotion recognition.

title: The Last AI Built by Humans: Toward Genuine Recursive Self-Improvement
summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) enables AI systems to turn experience and feedback into persistent changes that improve both their capabilities and the process of future improvement. We first use the Headroom-Closed Index (HCI) to reveal the problems of existing LLMs, then introduce the RSI concept and its development roadmap: from improvement-execution autonomy, improvement-strategy autonomy, experience-acquisition autonomy, and environment-adaptation autonomy, to recursive meta-improvement. Next we examine RSI across scenarios (e.g., scientific discovery, embodied intelligence, software engineering), highlighting their distinct requirements and development speeds. Drawing on diverse industry practices and preliminary empirical evidence, we connect RSI research with practical systems and identify key challenges to achieving genuine RSI.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) for AI systems, which enables persistent capability enhancement through experience and feedback. The authors propose a development roadmap progressing through five autonomy levels and examine RSI applications across scientific discovery, embodied intelligence, and software engineering domains.
AI.motivation: Existing Large Language Models (LLMs) have limitations revealed by the Headroom-Closed Index (HCI). The research aims to address these limitations by exploring how AI systems can not only improve their capabilities but also enhance the improvement process itself—a concept termed recursive self-improvement.
AI.method: The authors use the Headroom-Closed Index (HCI) to diagnose problems in existing LLMs, introduce the RSI concept with a five-stage development roadmap, and examine RSI across multiple application scenarios including scientific discovery, embodied intelligence, and software engineering, drawing on industry practices and preliminary empirical evidence.
AI.result: The paper presents: (1) HCI analysis revealing LLM limitations, (2) A five-stage RSI development roadmap: improvement-execution autonomy → improvement-strategy autonomy → experience-acquisition autonomy → environment-adaptation autonomy → recursive meta-improvement, (3) Domain-specific RSI requirements across scientific discovery, embodied intelligence, and software engineering, and (4) Identification of key challenges toward achieving genuine RSI.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that while RSI represents a promising direction for AI advancement, significant challenges remain to achieve genuine recursive self-improvement. Different application scenarios (scientific discovery, embodied intelligence, software engineering) have distinct requirements and development speeds, requiring continued research to bridge the gap between the proposed RSI framework and practical implementations.

title: Geospatial AI, Dataverse Metadata, and the Study of Place-Based Government
summary: Harvard Dataverse hosts over 150,000 research datasets, but the geographic information those datasets carry is entered as free text by depositors and has never been assembled into a searchable structure. We construct a knowledge graph from the repository's public data and metadata, organizing 102,650 datasets within a 215,985-node network of 528,003 edges linking datasets to keywords, publications, subjects, journals, and locations. Of those datasets, 43,991 (42.9 percent) carry at least one geospatial field, geographic coverage, geographic unit, or a bounding box and 96.9 percent of all nodes sit in a single connected component, so datasets remain reachable from one another even when their geospatial metadata share nothing in common. A conservative keyword search identifies 7,654 geospatially tagged datasets (17.4 percent) as directly policy-relevant, with elections and legislatures the largest cluster, followed by government administration, health policy, transportation, and education. Five datasets illustrate how this metadata behaves across policy domains and spatial scales, and an extended use case shows how community language models, stance detection with geographic aggregation, and partisan language bridging tools can attach discourse to place. The central obstacle is place resolution: the same location appears as many disconnected nodes. We argue that the graph provides a concrete setting for developing AI-driven metadata enrichment and entity resolution, and we document its coverage skew toward American, city-level data.

AI.tldr: This paper describes the construction of a knowledge graph from Harvard Dataverse's 150,000+ research datasets, organizing 102,650 datasets into a network with 215,985 nodes and 528,003 edges. The analysis focuses on geospatial metadata, finding 42.9% of datasets contain geographic information, with 17.4% being policy-relevant. The study identifies place resolution as the central challenge and demonstrates applications using language models for discourse analysis tied to geographic locations.
AI.motivation: Harvard Dataverse contains over 150,000 research datasets with geographic information entered as free text by depositors, but this geographic metadata has never been assembled into a searchable structure. The researchers aim to organize this data into a knowledge graph to enable better discovery and analysis of geospatial research.
AI.method: The researchers constructed a knowledge graph from Harvard Dataverse's public data and metadata, linking datasets to keywords, publications, subjects, journals, and locations. They used conservative keyword searches to identify policy-relevant datasets and demonstrated use cases with community language models, stance detection, and partisan language bridging tools.
AI.result: The knowledge graph contains 102,650 datasets within a 215,985-node network with 528,003 edges. Of these, 43,991 datasets (42.9%) carry geospatial metadata (fields, coverage, unit, or bounding box). 96.9% of nodes exist in a single connected component. Conservative keyword search identified 7,654 geospatially tagged datasets (17.4%) as policy-relevant, with elections and legislatures being the largest cluster, followed by government administration, health policy, transportation, and education.
AI.conclusion: The knowledge graph provides a concrete setting for developing AI-driven metadata enrichment and entity resolution. The central obstacle is place resolution—same locations appear as disconnected nodes. The researchers document significant coverage skew toward American, city-level data, and demonstrate how community language models can attach discourse to place through geographic aggregation.

title: Spectral Adapters for Segment Anything Model-based Segmentation of Colorectal Liver Metastases in Computed Tomography
summary: Accurate segmentation of colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) in contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) is important for response assessment, surgical planning, and follow-up. We propose two parameter-efficient spectral adapters for the Segment Anything Model (SAM): the Directional Spectral Adapter (DiSECT) and Spectral Instance-Guided Adapter (SiGA). DiSECT uses singular value decomposition of frozen weights to constrain residual updates to leading spectral directions, while SiGA adds global and input-conditioned gating through a multilayer perceptron. We evaluate these methods on 446 contrast-enhanced CT volumes (355 training, 91 testing) and compare them with LoRA, QLoRA, convolutional adapters (CAD), and a 3D nnU-Net baseline. Experiments consider single-point, three-point, bounding-box, and no-prompt regimes. SiGA achieves the best single-point performance with a Dice score of 0.77, IoU of 0.69, and HD95 of 35.39 mm. Under no-prompt inference, SiGA reaches 0.76 Dice, 0.68 IoU, and 46.76 mm HD95, comparable to the nnU-Net baseline (0.758 Dice). DiSECT uses only 0.14 million trainable parameters. These results show that spectral adapters can efficiently adapt SAM for CRLM segmentation while retaining strong accuracy with limited trainable parameters.

AI.tldr: Two parameter-efficient spectral adapters (DiSECT and SiGA) are proposed to adapt SAM for colorectal liver metastases segmentation in contrast-enhanced CT, achieving competitive performance with only 0.14M trainable parameters.
AI.motivation: Accurate segmentation of colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) in contrast-enhanced CT is important for response assessment, surgical planning, and follow-up, requiring efficient adaptation of foundation models like SAM with limited trainable parameters.
AI.method: Two spectral adapters are proposed: DiSECT uses singular value decomposition of frozen weights to constrain residual updates to leading spectral directions; SiGA adds global and input-conditioned gating through a multilayer perceptron. Evaluated on 446 CT volumes under various prompt regimes (single-point, three-point, bounding-box, no-prompt).
AI.result: SiGA achieves best single-point performance with Dice 0.77, IoU 0.69, HD95 35.39mm. Under no-prompt inference, SiGA reaches 0.76 Dice, 0.68 IoU, comparable to nnU-Net baseline (0.758 Dice). DiSECT uses only 0.14M trainable parameters.
AI.conclusion: Spectral adapters can efficiently adapt SAM for CRLM segmentation while retaining strong accuracy with limited trainable parameters, offering a parameter-efficient alternative to existing adapters like LoRA, QLoRA, and CAD.

title: CoRA-NAS: Coarse Ranking and Anchor-Residual Refinement for Neural Architecture Search
summary: Zero-cost proxies rank architectures cheaply, but their reliability varies across search spaces. We introduce CoRA-NAS (COarse Ranking + Anchor-residual), a two-stage framework combining a static ranking prior with low-cost learning-curve refinement. CoRA-Rank aggregates capacity and structure-at-initialization proxies through an equal-weight log-rank consensus and a target-free consensus gate. CoRA-Refine samples anchors across this prior, extrapolates their early validation curves, and propagates a learned residual correction with an ExtraTrees model. The refinement uses approximately 1% of the cost of fully training the candidate set. Fully trained architecture-accuracy labels are not used to fit the ranker. One configuration is used across spaces, with space-specific architecture encodings. Across NAS-Bench-201, NAS-Bench-101, TransNAS-Bench-101, and NATS-SSS, CoRA-Refine achieves mean Spearman correlations of 0.946, 0.715, 0.786, and 0.894, respectively. Its worst-space correlation of 0.715 is the highest among the compared methods. On NAS-Bench-201/CIFAR-100, its selected architecture reaches 73.32% accuracy, near the reported ground-truth best of 73.37%. On the pure size space, refinement recovers the static prior's shortfall relative to parameter count, while remaining tied with the strongest capacity proxies within noise. The resulting framework combines cross-space ranking robustness with low-cost architecture selection.

AI.tldr: CoRA-NAS is a two-stage zero-cost neural architecture search framework that combines static ranking priors (CoRA-Rank) with low-cost learning-curve refinement (CoRA-Refine). It uses ExtraTrees to extrapolate early validation curves and learns residual corrections, achieving high Spearman correlations (0.715-0.946) across multiple NAS benchmarks while using only ~1% of full training cost.
AI.motivation: Zero-cost proxies for ranking neural architectures are unreliable across different search spaces. The authors aim to develop a more robust ranking method that maintains low computational cost while improving correlation with true performance across diverse search spaces.
AI.method: The framework has two stages: (1) CoRA-Rank aggregates capacity and structure-at-initialization proxies through equal-weight log-rank consensus and target-free consensus gate; (2) CoRA-Refine samples anchors across the prior, extrapolates early validation curves, and propagates learned residual correction using an ExtraTrees model. Uses approximately 1% of full training cost. One configuration works across spaces with space-specific architecture encodings.
AI.result: CoRA-Refine achieves mean Spearman correlations of 0.946 (NAS-Bench-201), 0.715 (NAS-Bench-101), 0.786 (TransNAS-Bench-101), and 0.894 (NATS-SSS). Worst-space correlation of 0.715 is highest among compared methods. On NAS-Bench-201/CIFAR-100, selected architecture reaches 73.32% accuracy, nearly matching ground-truth best (73.37%).
AI.conclusion: CoRA-NAS successfully combines cross-space ranking robustness with low-cost architecture selection. The two-stage approach using static ranking prior plus learning-curve refinement significantly improves zero-cost proxy reliability across diverse search spaces while maintaining low computational overhead.

title: COBRA-Skills: Contextual Bandit-Guided Evolution for Agent Skill Optimization
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can benefit from reusable skills distilled from prior task experience, yet existing skill optimization methods often rely on costly execution-based evaluation and substantial task data. We introduce \textbf{COBRA-Skills}, an efficient framework that formulates skill optimization as budgeted sequential optimization over a dynamically evolving candidate space. COBRA-Skills couples contextual-bandit-guided prioritization with evidence-grounded skill evolution, selectively allocating evaluations to promising or informative candidates while continually refining the skill population from execution feedback. Across six heterogeneous agent benchmarks and three target models, COBRA-Skills consistently achieves the strongest average performance among compared methods, while reducing optimization cost by 55--58\% relative to SkillOpt and using only 50 unique optimization examples per benchmark. Further analyses show that COBRA-Skills remains robust to changes in the agent harness and performs effectively when the target model itself is used for skill generation and refinement.

AI.tldr: COBRA-Skills is an efficient framework for optimizing reusable skills for LLM agents, using budgeted sequential optimization with contextual-bandit-guided prioritization and evidence-grounded skill evolution to reduce evaluation costs while maintaining strong performance.
AI.motivation: Existing skill optimization methods for LLM agents rely on costly execution-based evaluation and require substantial task data, making them expensive and inefficient to apply.
AI.method: COBRA-Skills formulates skill optimization as budgeted sequential optimization over a dynamically evolving candidate space. It couples contextual-bandit-guided prioritization with evidence-grounded skill evolution, selectively allocating evaluations to promising or informative candidates while continually refining the skill population from execution feedback.
AI.result: Across six heterogeneous agent benchmarks and three target models, COBRA-Skills consistently achieves the strongest average performance among compared methods, while reducing optimization cost by 55-58% relative to SkillOpt and using only 50 unique optimization examples per benchmark. It remains robust to changes in the agent harness and performs effectively when the target model itself is used for skill generation and refinement.
AI.conclusion: COBRA-Skills demonstrates that efficient skill optimization for LLM agents is achievable through intelligent evaluation prioritization and continuous skill refinement, achieving superior performance with significantly reduced computational cost and minimal training data requirements.

title: Language-Augmented Semantic Priors for B-Spline Surface Fitting
summary: The use of B-splines and Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines surfaces constitutes the mathematical foundation of contemporary computer-aided design (CAD) systems. Despite long-term progress, geometric kernels in traditional CAD still rely heavily on predetermined heuristic initialization for surface fitting and parameterization. Meanwhile, the procedural semantics and design intent encoded in modeling histories are largely ignored during geometry generation. This disconnect creates a gap between high-level design intent and solver-executable geometric configuration, often leading to suboptimal and semantically inconsistent fitting results. To bridge this gap, we introduce LASP, a Language-Augmented Semantic Priors framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to infer structured, solver-usable B-spline priors from procedural modeling histories. Rather than modifying the geometric kernel itself, LASP operates as a semantic reasoning layer above existing solvers. It first translates modeling histories into rich textual descriptions that capture design intent, geometric context, and functional relationships, and then uses a fine-tuned LLM to predict structured B-spline prior parameters. LASP is trained through a two-stage scheme that combines local geometric regularities with long-range contextual dependencies, producing priors that are both interpretable and semantically coherent. This approach furnishes inductive signals that direct the conventional B-spline fitting process toward solutions that more accurately encapsulate the intended design objectives and demonstrate heightened semantic coherence. Compared to traditional machine learning schemes, the experiments demonstrate that language-driven reasoning can serve as a powerful inductive bias for geometric solving, establishing a new paradigm of language-guided geometric optimization in modern CAD systems.

AI.tldr: LASP (Language-Augmented Semantic Priors) is a framework that uses large language models to infer structured B-spline priors from procedural modeling histories in CAD systems, bridging the gap between high-level design intent and solver-executable geometric configuration.
AI.motivation: Traditional CAD geometric kernels rely on predetermined heuristic initialization for surface fitting, ignoring the procedural semantics and design intent encoded in modeling histories. This disconnect leads to suboptimal and semantically inconsistent fitting results.
AI.method: LASP operates as a semantic reasoning layer above existing solvers. It translates modeling histories into rich textual descriptions capturing design intent, geometric context, and functional relationships, then uses a fine-tuned LLM to predict structured B-spline prior parameters through a two-stage training scheme combining local geometric regularities with long-range contextual dependencies.
AI.result: The approach produces priors that are both interpretable and semantically coherent, providing inductive signals that direct conventional B-spline fitting toward solutions that more accurately encapsulate intended design objectives. Experiments demonstrate that language-driven reasoning serves as a powerful inductive bias for geometric solving.
AI.conclusion: Language-guided geometric optimization represents a new paradigm for modern CAD systems, where LLM-based semantic reasoning can effectively bridge design intent and geometric configuration.

title: CausalArena: Benchmarking Causal Discovery in the Foundation Model Era
summary: Causal discovery aims to uncover causal structures from data and is fundamental to scientific reasoning and intervention-based decision making. Its evaluation relies heavily on structural causal models (SCMs), which specify a causal graph together with the mechanisms that generate data, yet existing studies differ substantially in graph families, mechanisms, and evaluation protocols. The emergence of causal discovery foundation models (CDFMs) further complicates evaluation: performance may reflect not only causal discovery ability, but also overlap between pretraining environments and test SCMs, making results on fixed synthetic benchmarks difficult to interpret. We introduce CausalArena, a unified and evolvable benchmark for causal discovery under a common protocol. Synthetic SCMs supply controlled breadth over structures and mechanisms; semantic operational SCMs provide human-auditable, semantically grounded environments beyond standard synthetic generators; and formula-grounded SCMs test discovery under explicit scientific mechanisms. Public real-world datasets provide an additional external-validity check. Experiments across classical, neural, and pretrained methods reveal substantial ranking shifts across SCM families and protocols, showing that strong performance in one benchmark regime does not reliably transfer to others. These results highlight benchmark diversity and pretraining--evaluation overlap as central challenges for evaluating causal discovery in the foundation model era.

AI.tldr: CausalArena is a unified benchmark for evaluating causal discovery methods, addressing inconsistencies in existing evaluation protocols. It combines synthetic, semantic operational, formula-grounded SCMs, and real-world datasets to comprehensively assess causal discovery algorithms, including foundation models.
AI.motivation: Existing causal discovery evaluation varies widely in graph families, mechanisms, and protocols. The rise of causal discovery foundation models (CDFMs) further complicates evaluation because performance may reflect pretraining-test overlap rather than true causal discovery ability. This makes results on fixed synthetic benchmarks difficult to interpret.
AI.method: The paper introduces CausalArena, a unified and evolvable benchmark with three types of SCMs: (1) Synthetic SCMs for controlled breadth over structures and mechanisms; (2) Semantic operational SCMs for human-auditable, semantically grounded environments; (3) Formula-grounded SCMs for testing discovery under explicit scientific mechanisms. Public real-world datasets provide external-validity checks. Experiments test classical, neural, and pretrained methods across these SCM families.
AI.result: Experiments reveal substantial ranking shifts across SCM families and protocols. Strong performance in one benchmark regime does not reliably transfer to others, demonstrating that current evaluation practices may not capture true causal discovery ability.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark diversity and pretraining-evaluation overlap are central challenges for evaluating causal discovery in the foundation model era. The proposed CausalArena provides a more comprehensive and interpretable evaluation framework.

title: When Agents Disagree: Bayesian Backward Reasoning as a Label-Free Anchor for Multi-Agent Collective Decision-Making
summary: When multiple LLM agents yield conflicting answers, the decision-making process dictates whether agent diversity improves performance or merely compounds shared errors. Existing collective decision-making methods, including voting, electoral rules, and LLM judges, rely on forward reasoning: they map evidence to labels in one direction. Although these methods can combine diverse forward traces, they still aggregate estimates that share this evidence-to-label factorization and can inherit correlated errors within the forward pool. We therefore construct a reverse posterior for each instance through Bayesian backward reasoning from an explicit likelihood. The forward and reverse posteriors provide differently factorized approximations of the underlying posterior. Because estimates from different factorizations may tend to share the same error less often, we use Jensen-Shannon divergence to rank agents by cross-path consistency. This cross-path consistency signal underlies three strategies: hard selection (MinJS), soft reweighting (FwdJS), and log-linear fusion (LogLin). Evaluated on DDXPlus across five LLM backbones, our proposed strategies show consistent improvements: MinJS outperforms random selection across all backbones, FwdJS generally improves over the strongest baseline, and LogLin achieves the best performance among the evaluated methods, with its largest gains on the subset where the agents disagree. Despite its weaker standalone accuracy, the reverse posterior serves as a more useful anchor than forward-only alternatives, providing complementary information for collective decision-making. When labeled data are available, a lightweight two-stage calibration can further refine the reverse anchor and improve aggregation performance.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem of conflicting answers from multiple LLM agents in decision-making. The authors propose combining forward reasoning (standard evidence-to-label) with reverse posterior (Bayesian backward reasoning) to reduce correlated errors. They use Jensen-Shannon divergence to measure cross-path consistency and develop three aggregation strategies: MinJS (hard selection), FwdJS (soft reweighting), and LogLin (log-linear fusion). Evaluated on DDXPlus with five LLM backbones, these methods show consistent improvements, with LogLin achieving the best overall performance.
AI.motivation: Existing collective decision-making methods (voting, electoral rules, LLM judges) rely on forward reasoning, which maps evidence to labels in one direction. These methods share the same evidence-to-label factorization and can inherit correlated errors within the forward pool, limiting the benefit of agent diversity.
AI.method: The authors construct reverse posteriors for each instance through Bayesian backward reasoning from an explicit likelihood. They use Jensen-Shannon divergence to rank agents by cross-path consistency (comparing forward and reverse posteriors). Based on this, they develop three strategies: (1) MinJS - hard selection choosing the agent with minimum JS divergence, (2) FwdJS - soft reweighting based on forward JS, and (3) LogLin - log-linear fusion combining both paths. When labeled data is available, a two-stage calibration refines the reverse anchor.
AI.result: On DDXPlus across five LLM backbones: MinJS outperforms random selection across all backbones; FwdJS generally improves over the strongest baseline; LogLin achieves the best performance, with largest gains on subsets where agents disagree. The reverse posterior, despite weaker standalone accuracy, serves as a more useful anchor than forward-only alternatives, providing complementary information for collective decision-making.
AI.conclusion: Combining forward and reverse posteriors with different factorizations reduces shared errors compared to forward-only aggregation. The reverse posterior provides complementary information that improves collective decision-making. Log-linear fusion (LogLin) is the most effective strategy, and a lightweight two-stage calibration can further improve performance when labeled data is available.

title: MC-DeTra: Motion-Consistent Joint Object Detection and Socially-Aware Trajectory Forecasting in Bird's-Eye-View Images
summary: Unified models for object detection and trajectory forecasting aim to merge perception and prediction for autonomous driving, refining actor trajectories directly over shared bird's-eye-view (BEV) images rasterized from LiDAR and high-definition maps. Their accuracy on dynamic, moving actors, however, remains the hardest part of the task, and the strongest such model, DeTra, has no public implementation. We contribute an openly released DeTra reimplementation with documented approximations, and on top of it MC-DeTra: a family of motion-consistency mechanisms that add supervision through two annotation-derived auxiliary signals -- each actor's observed past motion and the occupancy of the surrounding traffic that forms its social context -- and one inter-output consistency constraint that aligns an actor's predicted heading with its predicted direction of motion. Every proposed loss is train-only and inference-safe: it shapes the shared BEV representation during training and is removed at test time, adding no inference latency. On the Waymo Open Dataset, evaluated under a strict, detection-conditioned forecasting protocol, MC-DeTra improves dynamic, socially-situated trajectory forecasting while preserving or improving detection accuracy; a gradient-based loss-calibration analysis exposes how the auxiliary objectives compete at the shared backbone, and our ablation identifies which signals contribute most. We release code, configurations, and evaluation tooling at https://github.com/diuzhevVlad/MC-DeTra.

AI.tldr: This paper presents MC-DeTra, a motion-consistency enhanced reimplementation of the DeTra model for unified object detection and trajectory forecasting in autonomous driving. The method introduces three auxiliary signals (past motion, social context occupancy, heading-motion consistency) that only add training supervision without inference latency. On Waymo Open Dataset, it improves forecasting accuracy while preserving detection performance.
AI.motivation: Unified detection and forecasting models aim to merge perception and prediction for autonomous driving using shared BEV representations. However, accuracy on dynamic, moving actors remains challenging, and the state-of-the-art DeTra model has no public implementation. This work addresses these gaps by providing an open-source reimplementation and enhancing it with motion-consistency mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors: (1) Released an open DeTra reimplementation with documented approximations; (2) Proposed MC-DeTra with three motion-consistency mechanisms: two annotation-derived auxiliary signals (actor's observed past motion and surrounding traffic occupancy for social context) and one inter-output consistency constraint (aligning predicted heading with predicted motion direction). All proposed losses are train-only and inference-safe, shaping the shared BEV representation during training but removed at test time.
AI.result: On Waymo Open Dataset under strict detection-conditioned forecasting protocol, MC-DeTra improves dynamic, socially-situated trajectory forecasting while preserving or improving detection accuracy. Gradient-based loss-calibration analysis reveals how auxiliary objectives compete at the shared backbone, and ablation identifies which signals contribute most.
AI.conclusion: The motion-consistency mechanisms effectively improve trajectory forecasting for dynamic actors without adding inference latency. The open-source release of code, configurations, and evaluation tooling enables reproducible research in unified detection-forecasting models.

title: TART: A Modular Tool for Technique-Aware Audio-to-Tablature Guitar Transcription
summary: Automatic Music Transcription (AMT) for guitar remains limited by three challenges: existing systems often fail to capture expressive techniques such as slides, bends, and percussive hits; they often assign notes to incorrect string-fret combinations; and they are typically trained on clean recordings, limiting their generalization to noisy real-world audio. To address these challenges, we propose TART, a modular four-stage audio-to-tablature pipeline consisting of (1) an audio-to-MIDI transcription model, (2) an expressive technique classifier, (3) an audio-conditioned T5 encoder-decoder for string-fret assignment, and (4) an automated tablature generator. We evaluate TART in a zero-shot setting on GuitarSet, EGDB, and two augmented benchmarks, Noisy GuitarSet and Noisy EGDB. Averaged across these four benchmarks, TART achieves 81.35% audio-to-MIDI F50 (+6.67 points over the best prior baseline), 71.8% string-fret Tab F1 (+8.5 points over the best prior baseline), and 54.08% end-to-end Tab F1. To our knowledge, TART is the first framework to generate guitar tablature with both fingering and expressive technique annotations directly from guitar audio.

AI.tldr: TART is a novel four-stage audio-to-tablature pipeline for guitar that addresses limitations in capturing expressive techniques, string-fret assignment, and noise robustness. It achieves state-of-the-art results, being the first system to generate guitar tablature with both fingering and expressive technique annotations from audio.
AI.motivation: Automatic Music Transcription (AMT) for guitar faces three key limitations: (1) failure to capture expressive techniques (slides, bends, percussive hits), (2) incorrect string-fret combination assignments, and (3) limited generalization from clean training recordings to noisy real-world audio.
