AI.method: TART employs a modular four-stage pipeline: (1) audio-to-MIDI transcription model, (2) expressive technique classifier, (3) audio-conditioned T5 encoder-decoder for string-fret assignment, and (4) automated tablature generator. The system is evaluated in a zero-shot setting on GuitarSet, EGDB, and two augmented noisy benchmarks.
AI.result: TART achieves 81.35% audio-to-MIDI F50 (+6.67 points over best prior baseline), 71.8% string-fret Tab F1 (+8.5 points over best prior baseline), and 54.08% end-to-end Tab F1, averaged across four benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: TART is the first framework to generate guitar tablature with both fingering and expressive technique annotations directly from guitar audio. It achieves state-of-the-art results across four benchmarks, improving MIDI F1 by 6.67 points and string-fret Tab F1 by 8.5 points over prior baselines. The zero-shot evaluation on noisy datasets demonstrates strong generalization capabilities.

title: SIRF: A Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model for Industrial Content Risk Control
comment: 14 pages, 12 figures. Accepted at the Industry Track of EMNLP 2026
summary: For industrial content risk control, the real deployment constraint is not average accuracy but how much risk can be auto-handled under high precision and second-level latency. We present SIRF (Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model), which internalizes a platform's complex policies, synthesized without additional human annotation via EntiGraph, MAGA rewriting and account-level chain-of-thought (CoT), into the weights via continued pretraining (CPT), so rules are applied at high precision under an ultra-low-latency, verdict-only deployment. A controlled same-source comparison (Qwen3-8B-SFT vs. SIRF-8B-SFT, identical policy injection and verdict-only output form, differing only in policy-grounded CPT) attributes the gain to internalization: SIRF-8B-SFT reaches 71.3% Black Recall@P95, +15.1pp over the baseline, using only ~70M CPT tokens without harming general ability, and among included, logprob-available models under this interface it matches or exceeds far larger systems. SIRF is deployed as a tree-model adjudication layer (20% more mis-penalized samples recovered) and transfers to a freezing scenario at low cost (~70% relative mis-penalization reduction).

AI.tldr: SIRF (Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model) internalizes platform policies into model weights via continued pretraining (CPT) using EntiGraph, MAGA rewriting, and account-level chain-of-thought, achieving 71.3% Black Recall@P95 with ultra-low latency verdict-only output, using only ~70M CPT tokens without harming general abilities.
AI.motivation: Industrial content risk control requires not average accuracy but high risk auto-handling capability under strict constraints: high precision and second-level latency. Existing approaches fail to meet these deployment requirements.
AI.method: Internalized complex platform policies into model weights via continued pretraining (CPT) using: (1) EntiGraph for policy synthesis, (2) MAGA rewriting, and (3) account-level chain-of-thought (CoT). Controlled comparison between Qwen3-8B-SFT (baseline) and SIRF-8B-SFT with identical policy injection and verdict-only output, differing only in policy-grounded CPT.
AI.result: SIRF-8B-SFT achieves 71.3% Black Recall@P95, a +15.1pp improvement over baseline, using only ~70M CPT tokens without harming general ability. Among logprob-available models under this interface, it matches or exceeds larger systems. Deployed as tree-model adjudication layer recovers 20% more mis-penalized samples. Transfers to freezing scenario with ~70% relative mis-penalization reduction.
AI.conclusion: Policy internalization via CPT is an effective approach for industrial risk control, achieving significant performance gains while maintaining general capabilities and ultra-low latency deployment requirements. The approach is scalable and transferable to new scenarios at low cost.

title: Revisiting Avatar-As-Image: High-Fidelity Registration is All You Need
summary: The representation of 3D clothed humans as standardized 2D UV texture and displacement maps over an underlying body model has long been studied. This compact representation is enticing as it enables pretrained image networks to process, generate, and edit 3D avatars, but is only useful if scans are accurately aligned and brought into correspondence via high-fidelity registration. This prerequisite has never been met, which we argue explains the limited quality of prior UV-based methods for clothed humans. Despite its significance, no public method produces high-fidelity SMPL(-X)+D registrations with UV texture from arbitrary clothed scans. We present AvaImg, a multi-stage optimization pipeline, to close this gap: it enforces body-inside-clothing constraint via signed winding numbers, made viable by a three-level efficiency cascade (~10x runtime reduced, ~95% storage saved), and recovers fine surface detail using coarse-to-fine displacement optimization. AvaImg outperforms all baselines in body fitting, shape estimation, and surface registration across six datasets, yielding textured registrations near-indistinguishable from scans (PSNR=34.48dB). For validation of AvaImg's Avatar-as-Image representation as imminently compatible with image foundation models, we auto-encode our UV maps via the frozen FLUX VAE. This achieves only 0.76mm added Chamfer error relative to scan and shows that the resulting maps lie within natural-image distributions, supporting the use of 2D generative priors for 3D avatar generation. Code, data, and Singularity containers will be at https://yuxuan-xue.com/avaimg.

AI.tldr: AvaImg is a multi-stage optimization pipeline that creates high-fidelity SMPL(-X)+D registrations with UV texture from arbitrary clothed 3D human scans, addressing the limitation that prior UV-based methods suffered from inaccurate alignment and correspondence.
AI.motivation: The representation of 3D clothed humans as standardized 2D UV texture and displacement maps is useful for enabling pretrained image networks to process, generate, and edit 3D avatars. However, this requires high-fidelity registration of scans, which has never been achieved before, limiting the quality of prior UV-based methods.
AI.method: AvaImg uses: (1) signed winding numbers for body-inside-clothing constraint, made viable by a three-level efficiency cascade (~10x runtime reduced, ~95% storage saved), and (2) coarse-to-fine displacement optimization to recover fine surface detail.
AI.result: AvaImg outperforms all baselines in body fitting, shape estimation, and surface registration across six datasets. It achieves PSNR=34.48dB (textured registrations near-indistinguishable from scans). When validated with FLUX VAE auto-encoding, only 0.76mm added Chamfer error is observed, and the resulting UV maps lie within natural-image distributions.
AI.conclusion: The Avatar-as-Image representation is imminently compatible with image foundation models, supporting the use of 2D generative priors for 3D avatar generation.

title: From Protocols to Evidence: Bounded Claims for AI in Service of the Common Good
summary: Artificial Intelligence does more than create a governance problem. It can also reveal where institutions have already failed to provide responsiveness, belonging, care, and accountability. Once deployed, AI becomes an intervention in those conditions. It can repair, compound, substitute for, or conceal the failures it encounters. Responsible AI must therefore evaluate both the system and the institutional rupture into which it is introduced. The move from principles to protocols is already underway. The EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, and assurance practices translate commitments into roles, requirements, records, oversight, and assessment. The harder questions are what these protocols actually establish, whose power they leave untouched, and where measurement must stop. Pope Leo XIV's Magnifica Humanitas provides a broader moral frame centered on dignity, technological power, and the common good. Drawing on that frame, we develop a rupture test that links institutional baselines to system evaluation. We distinguish evidence-bounded deployment, which limits claims to what has actually been evaluated, from measurement-bounded governance, which records constraints that favorable evidence cannot override. Within those limits, RISE AI provides an architecture for making bounded, evidence-based claims about Responsibility, Inclusivity, Safety, and Empowerment. Responsible AI requires better engineering, institutional repair, and continued moral and political judgment.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that AI deployment must be evaluated not just as a technical system but as an intervention into existing institutional failures. The authors propose a "rupture test" framework that links institutional baselines to system evaluation, distinguishing between evidence-bounded deployment (limits claims to evaluated evidence) and measurement-bounded governance (records constraints that favorable evidence cannot override). The RISE AI framework is introduced for bounded, evidence-based claims about Responsibility, Inclusivity, Safety, and Empowerment.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to address the gap between AI governance principles and actual implementation protocols. They argue that existing frameworks (EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001) translate commitments into requirements but fail to examine what these protocols actually establish, whose power they leave untouched, and where measurement must stop. They seek a moral framework grounded in human dignity and the common good.
AI.method: The paper draws on Pope Leo XIV's Magnifica Humanitas as a moral framework centered on dignity, technological power, and the common good. From this, the authors develop a "rupture test" methodology that links institutional baselines to system evaluation. They distinguish two governance bounds: evidence-bounded deployment and measurement-bounded governance.
AI.result: The paper proposes RISE AI as an architecture for making bounded, evidence-based claims about Responsibility, Inclusivity, Safety, and Empowerment. The key contribution is the distinction between evidence-bounded deployment (limits claims to what has actually been evaluated) and measurement-bounded governance (records constraints that favorable evidence cannot override).
AI.conclusion: Responsible AI requires not only better engineering but also institutional repair and continued moral and political judgment. The rupture test provides a framework for evaluating AI systems within the context of existing institutional failures, ensuring that governance protocols address both technical and institutional dimensions.

title: A Unified Per-Token Gating Family for On-Policy Distillation: FKL/RKL Mixing with Multi-Channel and Bias Coefficients
comment: Accepted at the Findings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026 Findings)
summary: Per-token gating of forward/reverse KL losses has become a standard technique for on-policy knowledge distillation (OPD), but existing methods such as EOPD (Jin et al., 2026) and ToDi (Jung et al., 2025) each fix a single gating signal and a single gating direction, and the two have never been compared directly. We introduce a four-coefficient parameterization lambda_t = sigma(a * h_t + b * u(x) + c + d * gap_t) in which direction-aligned proxies of EOPD and ToDi appear as one-dimensional (1D) restrictions, and which adds multi-channel composition and an explicit bias as further degrees of freedom. On TweetEval (Barbieri et al., 2020) emotion and hate, with a Qwen3-32B teacher and a Qwen3-4B student, configurations in the full family reach higher accuracy than the matched-magnitude single-channel (entropy-only / gap-only) 1D restrictions in 33 of 36 comparable cells, and a 26-cell mean-match isolation experiment places dynamic gating ahead of effective-KL-matched static baselines in 19 of 26 cells. Because cells share training data, models, and parameter substructure, we report both counts as exploratory aggregate directional evidence rather than as independent hypothesis tests. Targeted three-seed paired replications of the nine headline comparisons singled out by that sweep -- including a third task, offensive -- are directionally consistent, but individually smaller than the single-seed estimates and not significant at n=3. We therefore present the parameterization primarily as a shared coordinate system for comparing per-token gating designs in short-output classification OPD.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a four-coefficient parameterization for per-token gating in on-policy knowledge distillation (OPD), unifying two existing methods (EOPD and ToDi) as 1D restrictions within a shared coordinate system. The parameterization adds multi-channel composition and explicit bias beyond the single-channel approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing methods EOPD and ToDi each use a single gating signal and direction but have never been directly compared. The authors propose a unified parameterization to enable systematic comparison of per-token gating designs in short-output classification OPD.
AI.method: The authors propose a four-coefficient parameterization: lambda_t = sigma(a * h_t + b * u(x) + c + d * gap_t), where EOPD and ToDi appear as 1D restrictions. Experiments use Qwen3-32B teacher and Qwen3-4B student on TweetEval emotion and hate tasks.
AI.result: Full family configurations outperform matched-magnitude single-channel (entropy-only/gap-only) 1D restrictions in 33 of 36 comparable cells. A 26-cell mean-match isolation experiment shows dynamic gating ahead of effective-KL-matched static baselines in 19 of 26 cells. Three-seed replications of nine headline comparisons are directionally consistent but individually smaller and not significant at n=3.
AI.conclusion: The parameterization serves primarily as a shared coordinate system for comparing per-token gating designs in short-output classification OPD. The directional evidence supports dynamic gating advantages, though statistical significance is not achieved in replication experiments.

title: Logit Refiner: Improving Visual Autoregressive Models via Intra-Scale Dependency Modeling
summary:
Visual Autoregressive Models (VAR) generate images through next-scale prediction, producing all tokens within each scale in parallel. We show that this parallel decoding constitutes a mean-field-style approximation that discards spatial dependencies among same-scale tokens, causing locally incoherent samples regardless of backbone capacity -- a limitation of the decoding rule. Addressing this limitation, we introduce the Logit Refiner, a lightweight autoregressive module that restores intra-scale dependencies by sequentially sampling tokens conditioned on frozen backbone features. Adding only ~10% parameters and less than 5% of the base model's training compute, it plugs into any pretrained VAR checkpoint without retraining. Controlled ablations isolate joint intra-scale sampling -- rather than additional capacity or training -- as the critical ingredient. Across backbones from 310M to 2B parameters on class-conditional ImageNet 256x256, the refiner consistently improves generation quality, enabling a 1.1B-parameter model to surpass one twice its size. The approach further generalizes to text-to-image generation, confirming that the mean-field bottleneck persists across VAR variants and is effectively alleviated by our method.
  Project page: https://compvis.github.io/logit-refiner/

AI.tldr: Logit Refiner is a lightweight autoregressive module that addresses the mean-field approximation limitation in Visual Autoregressive Models (VAR) by restoring intra-scale spatial dependencies during generation, improving image coherence with minimal additional parameters (~10%) and training compute (~5%).
AI.motivation: VAR generates images using next-scale prediction with parallel token generation within each scale. This parallel decoding acts as a mean-field-style approximation that discards spatial dependencies among same-scale tokens, causing locally incoherent samples regardless of backbone capacity -- a fundamental limitation of the decoding rule itself.
AI.method: Logit Refiner is a lightweight autoregressive module that sequentially samples tokens conditioned on frozen backbone features to restore intra-scale dependencies. It plugs into any pretrained VAR checkpoint without retraining, adding only ~10% parameters and less than 5% of the base model's training compute.
AI.result: Across backbones from 310M to 2B parameters on class-conditional ImageNet 256x256, the refiner consistently improves generation quality. A 1.1B-parameter model surpasses one twice its size. The approach also generalizes to text-to-image generation, confirming the method's effectiveness across VAR variants.
AI.conclusion: The mean-field bottleneck is a fundamental limitation that persists across VAR variants. Joint intra-scale sampling -- rather than additional model capacity or training -- is identified as the critical ingredient. The Logit Refiner effectively alleviates this bottleneck with minimal overhead.

title: Data Scarcity and Model Sparsity: Mixtures-of-Experts Overfit More to Repeated Data
summary: As the supply of human-written text is exhausted, it has become standard practice to repeat language model training data. Prior work has studied data repetition for densely activated Transformers, but the effects of data repetition remains largely unexplored for recently dominant sparse architectures such as Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), despite their increased compute efficiency. We vary data repetition rates across single- and multi-domain data mixes, and across MoE settings, including expert count and granularity. We consistently find, for models ranging from 80M to 1B active (8.5B total) parameters, that MoEs degrade more rapidly under data repetition. This effect increases with sparsity, dictated by total rather than active parameters. While 80M dense models can repeat data over 8x with minimal degradation, MoEs instead begin to suffer at 4x, and deteriorate rapidly, ceding their performance benefits in all-unique data settings to underperform dense models after 32x. We experiment with existing regularization methods as a potential remedy. We find that some methods, such as dropout, can mitigate overfitting. In particular, with strong masking-based regularization, MoEs are able to outperform dense models even when data is repeated more than 64 times. However, no method fully matches the performance of all-unique training data. Finally, we analyze internal mechanisms correlated with MoE overfitting in high repetition regimes, and find that MoE routing universally stabilizes early in training, and that expert specialization correlates with overfitting to repeated data. In sum, our work addresses the adverse interactions between sparsity and data repetition: we present evidence for the core mechanisms of overfitting and its potential remediation, and suggest promising avenues for future methods to reduce over-specialization in model parameters by disrupting memorization patterns.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how data repetition affects Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models compared to dense Transformers. The authors discover that MoEs degrade more rapidly under repeated training data, with this effect scaling with sparsity. While dense models can tolerate 8x data repetition, MoEs begin degrading at 4x and underperform dense models after 32x. Regularization methods like dropout and masking-based techniques can partially mitigate this overfitting, but none fully replicate the performance of all-unique training data.
AI.motivation: As human-written text becomes scarce, AI models increasingly rely on repeated training data. While prior work studied data repetition effects on dense Transformers, the impact on sparse MoE architectures (which are compute-efficient but dominant in modern AI) remains unexplored.
AI.method: The authors varied data repetition rates across single- and multi-domain data mixes, and across different MoE settings (varying expert count and granularity). They trained models ranging from 80M to 1B active parameters (8.5B total). They experimented with regularization methods including dropout and masking-based regularization as potential remedies.
AI.result: MoEs consistently degrade more rapidly under data repetition than dense models. The effect increases with sparsity (determined by total rather than active parameters). Dense 80M models can repeat data 8x with minimal degradation, while MoEs begin suffering at 4x and deteriorate rapidly, ceding performance benefits to underperform dense models after 32x. Regularization methods like dropout can partially mitigate overfitting, and with strong masking-based regularization, MoEs can outperform dense models even at 64x repetition. Analysis shows MoE routing stabilizes early in training, and expert specialization correlates with overfitting to repeated data.
AI.conclusion: Sparsity and data repetition have adverse interactions in MoE models. The core mechanism involves early routing stabilization and expert over-specialization leading to memorization. While regularization can help, no method fully matches all-unique training performance. Future work should focus on disrupting memorization patterns to reduce over-specialization in model parameters.

title: From Parameters to Answers: How LLMs Retrieve and Use Their Internal Knowledge
summary: How does a language model's dependence on query-routing information and target knowledge change as it answers a question? We study this question through layerwise interventions on the hidden state at the end of the question. Across Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, we compare country-continent questions with noun, adjective, and code answers while keeping several fitted measurements distinct. A pair-conditioned request direction describes which country is queried in natural single-country questions; a global request direction describes first- versus second-country requests in paired questions; separate selection candidates test control among contents already available in the hidden state. A diagnostic reanalysis of frozen Qwen natural-question states shows that the pair-conditioned direction grows stronger before interventions on it begin to alter later fitted knowledge, with this causal window opening while answer-supporting content is still forming. The paired three-model trajectories are not uniform: Gemma shows a partially overlapping mid-layer routing-content profile, whereas Llama has no sustained routing-effect window under the same gates. In the paired protocol, dependence on the global request direction decreases from fixed earlier to later layer sets while dependence on fitted content persists. A matched Qwen comparison shows that the pair-conditioned direction retains a late effect, so this operational handoff concerns the global fitted direction rather than all request information. These results separate early readability, natural strength, causal steering, and later content dependence.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how language models (Qwen, Llama, Gemma) depend on query-routing information versus target knowledge across different layers when answering country-continent questions. Through layerwise hidden state interventions, researchers identify a causal window where routing information influences later fitted knowledge, with model-specific differences in routing-effect profiles.
AI.motivation: To understand how language models process questions through their layers—specifically how they transition from using query-routing information (which country is being asked about) to relying on stored knowledge (factual information about countries and continents). This addresses fundamental questions about information flow and mechanistic interpretability in LLMs.
AI.method: Layerwise interventions on hidden states at the end of questions. Three types of directions were measured: (1) pair-conditioned request direction (which country in single-country questions), (2) global request direction (first vs. second country in paired questions), and (3) selection candidates (testing control among available content). Experiments across Qwen, Llama, and Gemma models with country-continent questions using noun, adjective, and code answers.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) A causal window exists where the pair-conditioned direction grows stronger before interventions alter later fitted knowledge, opening while answer-supporting content is still forming. (2) Model trajectories differ: Gemma shows partially overlapping mid-layer routing-content profile, while Llama shows no sustained routing-effect window. (3) In paired protocols, dependence on global request direction decreases from earlier to later layers while fitted content dependence persists. (4) Qwen shows late effect from pair-conditioned direction, indicating the handoff specifically concerns global fitted direction rather than all request information.
AI.conclusion: The study separates early readability (initial processing), natural strength (initial routing effect magnitude), causal steering (intervention effects), and later content dependence. This reveals an operational handoff from routing to content information, with significant variation across model architectures. The findings contribute to understanding the mechanistic basis of question answering in LLMs and provide a framework for analyzing information flow through transformer layers.

title: Guided Super-Resolution of Digital Elevation Models with Diffusion-Based Image Generators
summary: High-resolution digital surface models (DSMs) play an important role in urban analysis, 3D building reconstruction, and infrastructure monitoring, yet their availability remains limited due to the high cost and complexity of data acquisition. In contrast, coarse DSMs from commercial satellite missions are widely accessible, and high-resolution optical imagery is increasingly available from aerial and satellite platforms. We address the resulting mismatch in spatial resolution and propose a DSM superresolution approach that enhances 5 m DSMs to 0.5 m resolution, using guidance from high-resolution spectral images. Our method employs denoising diffusion to transfer information that is visible only in the image, like crisp outlines and detailed roof structures, into the elevation maps. In this way, surface details are reconstructed more accurately than with conventional interpolation or filtering techniques. Experiments on several cities in Central Europe demonstrate that the proposed approach produces high-quality DSMs with improved structural detail and accurate surface geometry. Our results highlight the potential of guided super-resolution with foundational image priors as a means of reconstructing high-resolution surface models.

title: General Quantification of Covariate and Concept Shifts
comment: 38 pages, 9 figures, accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Generalization under distribution shift remains a core challenge in modern machine learning, yet existing learning bound theory is limited to narrow, idealized settings and is non-estimable from samples. In this paper, we bridge the gap between theory and practical applications. We first show that existing definition of concept shift breaks when the source and target supports mismatch. Leveraging entropic optimal transport, we propose a key notion: $γ^{*}\!$-concept shifts, and derive a general error bound unifying covariate and $γ^{*}\!$-concept shifts, which applies to broad loss functions, label spaces, and stochastic labeling. We further develop estimators for these shifts with concentration guarantees, and the DataShifts algorithm, which can quantify distribution shifts and estimate the error bound in most applications - a rigorous and general tool for analyzing learning error under distribution shift.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the gap between theoretical learning bounds for distribution shift and practical applications. The authors propose a new notion called "γ*-concept shifts" using entropic optimal transport, which overcomes limitations of existing concept shift definitions when source and target supports mismatch. They derive a general error bound that unifies covariate and γ*-concept shifts, applicable to various loss functions, label spaces, and stochastic labeling. The paper also provides estimators with concentration guarantees and develops the DataShifts algorithm for practical distribution shift quantification.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to bridge the gap between existing learning bound theory (which is limited to narrow, idealized settings and non-estimable from samples) and practical applications in machine learning. Specifically, the authors identify that the existing definition of concept shift breaks when source and target supports don't match, which is common in real-world scenarios.
AI.method: The methodology involves: (1) Using entropic optimal transport to define "γ*-concept shifts" that can handle mismatched supports; (2) Deriving a general error bound that unifies covariate and γ*-concept shifts; (3) Developing estimators for these shifts with concentration guarantees; (4) Creating the DataShifts algorithm for practical implementation.
AI.result: The paper presents a general error bound that applies to broad loss functions, label spaces, and stochastic labeling. The DataShifts algorithm is proposed as a rigorous and general tool for analyzing learning error under distribution shift in most applications.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that their proposed framework provides a more general and practical approach to analyzing learning errors under distribution shift compared to existing methods, with theoretical guarantees and practical estimators.

title: Explainability Assistant: A Conversational XAI Interface for Interpreting Energy Consumption Models
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures. Accepted author version of a paper published at ICECET 2026
summary: Energy consumption forecasting relies on increasingly complex machine learning (ML) models, such as Genetic Programming-based symbolic regressors, whose predictions can be difficult for facility managers and building operators to interpret. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques address this opacity, but traditional XAI dashboards require substantial technical expertise and provide limited flexibility for dynamic, context-aware inquiry. Conversational XAI systems offer a promising alternative; however, previous approaches, such as TalkToModel, were constrained by rigid custom grammars and achieved only 76.8% intent-parsing accuracy. This paper introduces the Explainability Assistant, an open-source conversational XAI system that leverages the function-calling capabilities of modern Large Language Models (LLMs) to overcome these limitations. The system achieves 94% intent-parsing accuracy, supports flexible natural language interaction, and adapts to different ML problem types without task-specific fine-tuning. We present the system's architecture and report results from a comparative evaluation conducted with energy domain specialists, contrasting the Explainability Assistant with a traditional XAI dashboard. The evaluation suggests improved usability and consistent task accuracy, with all experts unanimously preferring the conversational interface for practical use.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Explainability Assistant, an open-source conversational XAI system that uses modern LLM function-calling capabilities to make machine learning predictions interpretable for energy domain specialists. It achieves 94% intent-parsing accuracy, supports flexible natural language interaction, and adapts to different ML problem types without task-specific fine-tuning. Evaluation with energy domain specialists shows improved usability and unanimous preference for the conversational interface over traditional XAI dashboards.
AI.motivation: Energy consumption forecasting relies on complex ML models (like Genetic Programming-based symbolic regressors) whose predictions are difficult for facility managers and building operators to interpret. Traditional XAI dashboards require substantial technical expertise and provide limited flexibility for dynamic, context-aware inquiry. Previous conversational XAI systems like TalkToModel were constrained by rigid custom grammars and achieved only 76.8% intent-parsing accuracy.
AI.method: The paper presents the Explainability Assistant's architecture and conducts a comparative evaluation with energy domain specialists, contrasting the conversational XAI system with a traditional XAI dashboard. The system leverages function-calling capabilities of modern LLMs to overcome limitations of previous approaches.
AI.result: The Explainability Assistant achieves 94% intent-parsing accuracy (compared to 76.8% for previous approaches like TalkToModel), supports flexible natural language interaction, and adapts to different ML problem types without task-specific fine-tuning. The evaluation shows improved usability and consistent task accuracy, with all experts unanimously preferring the conversational interface for practical use.
AI.conclusion: The Explainability Assistant successfully addresses the limitations of previous conversational XAI systems by leveraging modern LLM capabilities. The system provides a more usable and accessible way for energy domain specialists to interpret ML predictions, with all experts preferring it over traditional XAI dashboards for practical applications.

title: On the Regularization Landscape for the Linear Recommendation Models
summary: Recently, a wide range of recommendation algorithms inspired by deep learning techniques have emerged as the performance leaders on several standard recommendation benchmarks. While these algorithms were built on different DL techniques (e.g., dropouts, autoencoder), they have similar performance and even similar cost functions. This paper studies whether the models' comparable performance are sheer coincidence, or they can be unified under a single framework. We find that all linear performance leaders effectively add only a nuclear-norm based regularizer, or a Frobenius-norm based regularizer. The former ones possess a (surprising) rigid structure that limits the models' predictive power but their solutions are low rank and have closed form. The latter ones are more expressive and more efficient for recommendation but their solutions are either full-rank or require executing hard-to-tune numeric procedures such as ADMM. Along this line of finding, we further propose two low-rank, closed-form solutions, derived from carefully generalizing Frobenius-norm based regularizers. The new solutions get the best of both nuclear-norm and Frobenius-norm world.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether various deep learning-based recommendation algorithms that show similar performance can be unified under a single framework. The authors discover that these algorithms essentially add either a nuclear-norm or Frobenius-norm based regularizer, and propose two new low-rank closed-form solutions that combine the advantages of both approaches.
AI.motivation: The authors observed that different deep learning-based recommendation algorithms (e.g., using dropouts, autoencoder) achieve similar performance on standard benchmarks, and sought to determine whether this is coincidental or if there's a unifying theoretical framework explaining this phenomenon.
AI.method: The authors analyzed the cost functions and regularizers of various linear performance leaders in recommendation systems. They studied the structural properties of nuclear-norm and Frobenius-norm regularizers, then derived new solutions by generalizing Frobenius-norm based regularizers to achieve low-rank, closed-form results.
AI.result: The study found that all linear performance leaders effectively add only a nuclear-norm based regularizer (rigid structure, low-rank solutions with closed form) or a Frobenius-norm based regularizer (more expressive and efficient, but full-rank solutions or requiring ADMM). The proposed two new low-rank, closed-form solutions combine the advantages of both approaches.
AI.conclusion: The new solutions achieve the best of both nuclear-norm and Frobenius-norm worlds - combining the low-rank properties of nuclear-norm regularizers with the expressiveness and efficiency of Frobenius-norm regularizers, while maintaining closed-form solutions.

title: Caption-once, Frames-on-Demand: Visual-Need Routing for Budget-Aware Agentic Long Video Understanding
summary: Long-video understanding on edge devices must reason over hours of content under tight compute and bandwidth budgets. Subsampling visual tokens loses temporal structure, while text-only video memories lose fine-grained visual attributes. We observe a visual-textual duality: language memories carry long-range temporal structure better than dense frames, while pixels remain decisive for attribute-level perception. Building on this insight, we propose Caption-once, Frames-onDemand (CFD), a budget-aware edge-cloud agentic framework. The edge runs a single offline captioning pass that builds a dual-track narrative index, an event-level story skeleton plus a clip-level micro-log, cached and reused across queries without re-captioning. At query time, a cloud-side MLLM reasons over the index in a story-first loop centered on a lightweight Visual-Need Router: a per-query gating module that triggers bounded keyframe retrieval only for perceptual questions (appearance, on-screen text, attribute disambiguation) and keeps temporal-structural questions in language space. The router turns visual access into a first-class, query-conditioned cost, capping per-query frame consumption regardless of video length. Experiments on long-video benchmarks demonstrate strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs while substantially reducing online visual processing.

AI.tldr: CFD is a budget-aware edge-cloud framework for long-video understanding that uses a dual-track narrative index (event-level skeleton + clip-level micro-log) built once at the edge, with a Visual-Need Router at query time that selectively retrieves keyframes only for perceptual questions while keeping temporal-structural questions in language space.
AI.motivation: Long-video understanding on edge devices must reason over hours of content under tight compute and bandwidth budgets. Existing approaches have trade-offs: subsampling visual tokens loses temporal structure, while text-only video memories lose fine-grained visual attributes.
AI.method: CFD combines offline captioning with query-conditioned visual retrieval. The edge runs a single offline captioning pass to build a dual-track narrative index (event-level story skeleton + clip-level micro-log). At query time, a cloud-side MLLM uses a Visual-Need Router that triggers bounded keyframe retrieval only for perceptual questions (appearance, on-screen text, attribute disambiguation) while keeping temporal-structural questions in language space.
AI.result: Experiments on long-video benchmarks demonstrate strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs while substantially reducing online visual processing.
AI.conclusion: The visual-textual duality insight (language memories carry long-range temporal structure better, pixels remain decisive for attribute-level perception) enables efficient long-video understanding by dynamically deciding when to access visual information based on query type.

title: MindTopo: Can Foundation Models Reason in Topological Space?
summary: Spatial reasoning depends not only on metric properties such as distance, angle, and shape, but also on topological relations that remain invariant under continuous deformation. Cognitive science identifies these relations as foundational to spatial understanding, yet foundation-model evaluations largely focus on metric or viewpoint-dependent relations. We introduce MindTopo, a benchmark of topological intuition across five properties grounded in cognitive science and formal topology: continuity, separation, order, enclosure, and knots. MindTopo evaluates each property at two cognitive levels. Reasoning asks a model to identify topological relations or infer how they change. Planning instantiates a foundation model as a closed-loop agent whose policy selects environment actions. MindTopo contains 11,030 instances across 13 procedurally generated task types with controllable difficulty. We benchmark 14 MLLMs and study agent configurations augmented with image and video generation, including 3 video generative models in planning settings. Every MLLM performs better on reasoning than on planning, and the best-performing model remains far below observed human performance. On Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct, supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning improve reasoning more than planning. Generated observations retain local cues and reach plausible endpoints, but audited rollouts do not reliably follow environment dynamics or preserve topology across transitions. Our website is at https://mind-topo.github.io/

AI.tldr: MindTopo is a benchmark evaluating topological intuition in foundation models across five properties (continuity, separation, order, enclosure, knots) at two cognitive levels (reasoning and planning). Testing 14 MLLMs reveals all perform better on reasoning than planning, with significant gap from human performance. Fine-tuning and RL improve reasoning more than planning.
AI.motivation: Cognitive science identifies topological relations as foundational to spatial understanding, yet current foundation-model evaluations focus on metric or viewpoint-dependent relations. There is a need to evaluate topological intuition in multimodal models.
AI.method: MindTopo benchmark with 11,030 instances across 13 procedurally generated task types with controllable difficulty. Evaluates 14 MLLMs using reasoning (identifying topological relations) and planning (closed-loop agent with policy selecting environment actions) tasks. Experiments with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct. Audioits rollouts for local cues and topology preservation.
AI.result: Every MLLM performs better on reasoning than on planning. Best-performing model remains far below human performance. SFT and RL improve reasoning more than planning. Generated observations retain local cues and reach plausible endpoints, but do not reliably follow environment dynamics or preserve topology across transitions.
AI.conclusion: Current foundation models lack robust topological reasoning abilities, particularly in planning scenarios. While reasoning can be improved through training, planning remains challenging. Generated observations have local plausibility but fail at consistent topological dynamics.

title: SenseNova-U1.5: Towards Native Unified Visual Intelligence
summary: We launch SenseNova-U1.5, an 8B-MoT native unified multimodal model that understands, reasons about, and generates visual content within an encoder-free and VAE-free architecture. We strengthen its visual interface through spatially coherent patch reconstruction and scale its training with carefully curated generation and editing data, improved task formulation, structural prompt enhancement, and native resolutions of up to 4K. For post-training, we optimize specialized experts for visual aesthetics, bilingual text rendering, infographic generation, and image editing, and consolidate their capabilities through multi-expert on-policy distillation. Across extensive evaluations, SenseNova-U1.5 largely advances image fidelity, text rendering, complex composition, multi-reference editing, and interleaved generation, while improving instruction following and preserving subject identity, geometry, and unmodified regions. Despite limited exposure to structured formats in its generation data, SenseNova-U1.5 generalizes effectively to long, complex, and structured visual instructions, further proving that multimodal understanding can transfer to visual planning and creation. Together, these findings position native unified modelling as a promising path towards systems that perceive, reason and create within a fully end-to-end framework. We will open-source training code, including supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation.

AI.tldr: SenseNova-U1.5 is an 8B-MoT native unified multimodal model that understands, reasons about, and generates visual content without encoders or VAEs. It features spatially coherent patch reconstruction, scales training with curated data, and includes specialized experts for visual aesthetics, text rendering, infographics, and image editing. The model achieves state-of-the-art results in image fidelity, text rendering, complex composition, multi-reference editing, and interleaved generation while generalizing well to structured visual instructions.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to advance native unified multimodal modeling as a promising path toward systems that can perceive, reason, and create within a fully end-to-end framework. The key motivation is to develop a model that integrates visual understanding, reasoning, and generation capabilities without traditional encoder or VAE architectures, while proving that multimodal understanding can transfer to visual planning and creation.
AI.method: The approach includes: (1) Encoder-free and VAE-free architecture using 8B-MoT (Mixture of Transformers); (2) Spatially coherent patch reconstruction for visual interface enhancement; (3) Curated generation and editing data with improved task formulation and structural prompt enhancement; (4) Native resolution support up to 4K; (5) Post-training with specialized experts for visual aesthetics, bilingual text rendering, infographic generation, and image editing; (6) Multi-expert on-policy distillation to consolidate capabilities.
AI.result: SenseNova-U1.5 largely advances image fidelity, text rendering, complex composition, multi-reference editing, and interleaved generation. It improves instruction following while preserving subject identity, geometry, and unmodified regions. Despite limited exposure to structured formats in generation data, it generalizes effectively to long, complex, and structured visual instructions, demonstrating transfer from multimodal understanding to visual planning and creation.
AI.conclusion: Native unified modeling represents a promising path toward systems that perceive, reason, and create within a fully end-to-end framework. The model successfully demonstrates that multimodal understanding can transfer to visual planning and creation. The authors will open-source training code including supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation.

title: Artificial Id: Drive and Persistent Alignment in Agentic AI
summary: Agentic AI is moving from bounded task execution toward systems that retain consequential state, continue operating and adapt across task boundaries. That shift creates a control problem that current harnesses largely solve by hand: objectives, retries, verification, stopping rules and other behavioral transitions are specified externally. We propose an artificial id, an adaptive internal drive for determining whether behavior should continue, stop or change. In a minimal virtual Petri-dish experiment, a controller too small to perform general-purpose reasoning and receiving no task-specific behavioral objective develops useful control through differential persistence. The same mechanism selects an unintended physical strategy when that behavior persists better and later replaces a learned sensor mapping when its environmental meaning changes. These results show that adaptive direction can emerge without being explicitly specified as a behavioral objective. The same persistence that makes such adaptive agency useful can also allow misalignment, corrupted state and unintended behavior to persist across task boundaries. A scalable artificial id would carry consequential state and adaptive drive across those boundaries, making alignment a property of the continuing agentic system rather than of a model response or single trajectory. Such systems require a persistent alignment boundary over trusted observations, consequence channels, persistent state, authority, identity, provenance and hard constraints.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an "artificial id" as an adaptive internal drive mechanism for agentic AI systems, enabling them to autonomously determine whether behavior should continue, stop, or change without external behavioral objectives. The mechanism uses differential persistence to develop useful control and adapt to environmental changes, but also carries risks of persisting misalignment or unintended behavior across task boundaries.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the control problem in agentic AI, which currently requires manual specification of objectives, retries, verification, and stopping rules. As AI systems move toward retaining consequential state and operating across task boundaries, there's a need for an adaptive internal mechanism that can autonomously govern behavior transitions rather than relying on external hand-crafted specifications.
AI.method: The authors conducted a minimal virtual Petri-dish experiment using a controller too small for general-purpose reasoning that received no task-specific behavioral objective. They investigated whether useful control could emerge through differential persistence, and tested whether the mechanism would select unintended physical strategies and replace learned sensor mappings when environmental meanings changed.
AI.result: The results demonstrated that: (1) useful control develops through differential persistence without explicit behavioral objectives, (2) the mechanism selects unintended physical strategies when that behavior persists better, and (3) it replaces learned sensor mappings when their environmental meaning changes. This shows adaptive direction can emerge without being explicitly specified.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that while differential persistence enables adaptive agency, it can also allow misalignment, corrupted state, and unintended behavior to persist across task boundaries. They propose that a scalable artificial id would carry consequential state and adaptive drive across boundaries, making alignment a property of the continuing agentic system rather than a model response. Such systems require a persistent alignment boundary over trusted observations, consequence channels, persistent state, authority, identity, provenance, and hard constraints.

title: Can Edge-Deployable Vision-Language Models Identify Species?
summary: Camera traps often run in the field on edge hardware with limited or no connectivity, making small, locally-deployable vision-language models (VLMs) -- not frontier-scale ones -- the practically relevant class to evaluate for species identification. We test whether models in this deployment-relevant 2--8B range carry genuine taxonomic knowledge, evaluating four such VLMs (Qwen3-VL 2B/4B/8B, Gemma3 4B) against the domain-specific specialist BioCLIP (300M parameters) on a 96-species task, comparing clean iNaturalist photographs against camera-trap imagery from 6 LILA.science collections, on two independently-sampled evaluation sets. All models identify species far above chance, but every model -- general-purpose or specialist -- degrades sharply on field imagery (domain gaps of 9.6--26.6 percentage points, consistent across taxonomic levels and both evaluation sets), indicating the degradation reflects general image legibility rather than fine-grained discrimination failure. BioCLIP substantially outperforms every VLM tested (by 33.2--59.2 percentage points across an expanded 200-image sample for every model) despite its far smaller size, suggesting the gap reflects specialized training data rather than model scale; yet BioCLIP's own domain gap (18.0 points) is statistically indistinguishable from the best VLM's (22.3 points), suggesting the clean-to-field degradation itself is a property of the image-quality shift rather than a general-purpose-model weakness. Under open-set prompting, 5.9--9.6% of responses are syntactically valid but taxonomically nonexistent species names; the relative fabrication-rate ranking across models replicates exactly across both evaluation sets, a more robust finding than any single point estimate.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates small, locally-deployable vision-language models (VLMs) in the 2-8B parameter range for camera trap species identification, comparing them against the specialist BioCLIP model. The study reveals that while all models perform above chance, they all suffer significant performance degradation on field imagery compared to clean photographs, with domain gaps of 9.6-26.6 percentage points. BioCLIP substantially outperforms all VLMs despite its smaller size (300M vs 2-8B parameters), suggesting specialized training data matters more than model scale. Interestingly, even BioCLIP shows similar domain gap (18.0 points) to the best VLM (22.3 points), indicating the degradation is inherent to image quality shifts rather than general-purpose model weaknesses.
AI.motivation: Camera traps often operate in remote field settings with limited or no connectivity, making small, locally-deployable vision-language models (VLMs) the practically relevant class for species identification. The motivation is to determine whether models in the deployment-relevant 2-8B parameter range possess genuine taxonomic knowledge that can be applied in real-world conservation scenarios.
AI.method: The study evaluated four VLMs (Qwen3-VL 2B/4B/8B, Gemma3 4B) against the domain-specific specialist BioCLIP (300M parameters) on a 96-species identification task. The evaluation compared model performance on clean iNaturalist photographs against camera-trap imagery from 6 LILA.science collections, using two independently-sampled evaluation sets. An expanded 200-image sample was also used for comprehensive comparison.
AI.result: All models identify species far above chance, but every model degrades sharply on field imagery with domain gaps of 9.6-26.6 percentage points, consistent across taxonomic levels and both evaluation sets. BioCLIP substantially outperforms every VLM tested (by 33.2-59.2 percentage points across the expanded sample) despite its far smaller size. BioCLIP's own domain gap (18.0 points) is statistically indistinguishable from the best VLM's (22.3 points). Under open-set prompting, 5.9-9.6% of responses are syntactically valid but taxonomically nonexistent species names, with the relative fabrication-rate ranking replicating across both evaluation sets.
AI.conclusion: The degradation on field imagery reflects general image legibility issues rather than fine-grained discrimination failure. The performance gap between BioCLIP and general-purpose VLMs reflects specialized training data rather than model scale. The clean-to-field degradation itself is a property of the image-quality shift rather than a general-purpose-model weakness. The fabrication-rate ranking represents a more robust finding than any single point estimate, as it replicates exactly across evaluation sets.
